At this point, I cannot really recommend this game.
It started out as a Mars Rover/Probe game which is currently all you do in the campaign part of the game. It's mostly complete with some missing features such as science results, I think the rovers still never actually run out of power and last I played it, it was still confusing as to what type of science a POI actually wants you to do. The biggest problem is the amount of time it takes for a rover to get anywhere. Obviously the rovers are slow, but there's no auto navigation and while you can trick the rover into driving forward without having to press a button constantly, you have to keep correcting as the rover will constantly veer off course.
The second part of the game, where the focus seems to have shifted entirely is the manned section, which is very interesting in theory, but falls short in terms of actual gameplay. Everything you do as a Mars colonist is very buggy and clunky with physics going haywire at the slightest provocation. For example, I managed to take out a bulkhead out of the large vehicle when trying to open a door, decompressing myself in the process. This is in part due to the UI being tied to game objects, which require precise clicking and even though you can change from interaction with the center of screen dot and cursor you can move independantly of the view, the UI is inconsistent about which input it will accept.
Another issue I have with object interaction is handling basically anything - you pick up an object and when it's in your hands, you can control how far from your body you hold it by scrolling the mouse wheel, the rotate it with one key and rotate it in a different way by pressing a modifier button in addition to the rotation button. Most objects won't connect with another object unless they're position in a particular way and when you add the weird handling of objects, pile it on top of the physics you will probably watch the resource container you've been fiddling with fly off into the distant martian landscape.
Content is being added but I'm not even interested in trying it out any more because the underlying issues persist and it seems backwards to add interesting things without having a stable framework that would allow you to have fun with all the elements present. The game is supposed to be nearing the end of its development cycle and I don't see it changing much in ways that would make it fun to actually play.
In short the game has many interesting elements that are combined with clunky, buggy gameplay, making a potentially fun and interesting experience dull and annoying.

Early Access Review - October 2015
I can't recommend this game at the moment. It's not what it says on the tin.
I bought it having looked at the screenshots, watched the videos, and read the reviews thinking it was a base building/ mars colonisation game. It's not at all.
The main campaign of the game is just sending probes to mars, which involves pick a location, then watch the probe land, then depending on the mission you click "Capture" to either take a photo or take a sample of some gas. After a couple of hours you can make a more complicated probe that requires you to press one or two other buttons.
Eventually you'll get a rover, which is just a tedious experience. In my experience it always ends up hundreds of meters from my target, which then means I have to remote drive it to the location. It travels so slowly that it can take 15 minutes just pressing the forward key to reach your destination. Sometimes your rover runs out of power so you have to wait for it to recharge from it's solar cells. This takes around 15-20 minutes, and you can't skip time, so this is a good time to make coffee and maybe have a sandwich, perhaps have a tidy up of the house.
There are some single mission "screnarios" that have astronauts in them, but having played them that component of the game seems pre-alpha. It is very clumsy and unpolished. Arms and legs clip through walls, nothing has tooltips so you don't know what is interactable and what isn't, an issue compounded by the fact there are no tutorials. The UI on the 3D printer made me laugh out loud, there is no UI, just a list of things you can make in no particular order.

Metro 2033 is a post apocalyptic FPS horror based in the nuclear ruins of Moscow, Russia. You play as Artyom, a citizen of metro station Exhibition. You awaken to your father speaking to you, concerned of the well being of Exhibition after recent attacks from an unknown horror, leaving the station in a state or terror and despair. You walk with your father, through the crowded corridors of the station, listening to conversations between wives and war torn soldiers. You look at children playing and drawing along the walls, hearing the faint song playing from a guitar in the distance. You feel a sense of peace, just to be shaken back to reality by the alert of another attack.
This is, the reality deep within the Metro of post apocalyptic Moscow. Families trying to survive desperate times and soldiers trying to survive mutants. Around every corner are unknown dangers waiting to strike.
It is the morning when your friend enters your small room to get you ready for the caravan delivery you will be embarking on. It is the first time you've left the safety of your home station, but are assured it will be a safe and a short trip between here and a neighboring station, you have other plans to journey to Polis station however. You ride the caravan with your friends feeling calm when you're told by workers the main tunnel is closed off, and that you will have to use an alternative access tunnel. This is where things take a turn for the worse.
You will have to fight, sneak and survive your way through the metro on your odyssey to Polis station. Every table is turned against you willing for your failure, whether that be bandits, hostile soldiers or horrifying creatures, mutated from living and breathing the nuclear radiation on the surface above, in the dead city of Moscow. Few allies are made but you rely on them with your live and vice versa. In the metro a man is his word so be careful who you trust.
The gameplay graphics are in a word, great. Shadows are strong as is the darkness and the overall atmosphere is intense. As I travel outside in the ruins of the city I appreciate the lighting and the reflections.
Snow and ice have a more traditional life like look about them over being overly bright. The many buildings are fairly detailed and as we go down into the metro tunnels I can see light sources and lighting reflections are top notch. The game uses a wonderful stealth system, though it can be buggy at times.
Hostile soldiers will be alerted to excessive sound and from seeing you crawl around the metro in dimly lit areas. In the game you wear a watch that acts as both a gasmask timer alarming you to replace your gasmask filters, as well as a light indicator telling you how visible you are in lit areas. The less light shining on you the more stealthy you are.
The game controls are relatively easy to use. Among standard shooter game controls we see a few extra controls required for game specific items like your universal charger, that keeps your flash light and night vision goggles charged if you have them, and along with controls for fitting your gasmask and replacing filters. We have controls for swapping out ammunition in assault rifles from regular low quality metro made bullets to premium prewar military ammunition. Be careful using prewar ammo as it also serves as currency within the metro.
The game is honestly poorly optimized, as at highest settings and anything above 1080p you'll need some serious central processing and graphics processing power. Using a 3570k paired with a r9 280x and 8gb of system memory, I can run high settings at 1080p in direct X 10 and achieve more than acceptable frame rates however. Setting to direct X 11 is where things get tough, along with other settings like anti aliasing and PhysX for those of you with Nvidia graphics.
Overall Metro 2033 is an amazingly fresh horror first person shooter. It offers a wonderful atmosphere to experience with some tough challenges, especially at higher difficulty settings.
If you like games similar to whats been described I'd give Metro 2033 a look for sure.

I saw this gem of a game a while back on the smartphone of my sister and now gave it a go. I puzzled my way through The Room as well as The Room 2 and am really sad, since its over now.
I love doing riddles and puzzles for years now, so it only took me roughly 2 hours on any of the two games but hell, it was worth any second of it and if I could, I would erase my memory to play it again slower, to ge more of the vibe.
But now to the review itself:
keeping in mind that it came from mobile devices I really like the ingame graphics and also the cinematics in between. Also, on a technical level I like how seamless interactive objects fit into the scene; a thing older puzzle games have hugh problems with. Lighting might be a little gloomy at times but that is part of the flair of the game and didn't hinder my puzzlesolving.
Only little melody but a nice amount of background noises(good for the gloom). And distinct sounds for clicking mechanics so you know if something happens.
is as you would expect, fluid and such. They transisioned from a game that used touch controls but controling the game with a mouse works just as well and after a few moments without much thinking. The only downside are turning motions, there sometimes the game doesn't recogniss the directions. I am not quite sure, but I think it doesn't even matter in most cases in which direction you turn the key. And I only once had a moment where mouse movement and object interaction didn't fit(some sort of scaling issue I asume).
If I should give some advice, turn off the hint system. Not because it is bad, just so you feel more of the rush, when your thoughts connect and something you thought would move, does so. It makes the game harder, sure, but since it is not that long, that is a nice thing. Also it can be turned on and off while playing so so harm.
The system itself works quite well in giving of hints(maximum 3 per riddle) without directly showing you the solution. It helps if you feel like you missed something or if you get lost between different puzzle objects in a room.
I really hope they get to port The Room 3 soon, since my phone is not able to run it...

As a long-time sub player I was really looking forward to this. Although my experience with Cold Waters has generally been positive, I do have a few reservations. Bear in mind I'm writing this in mid-July 2017, by the time you read this most of the problems listed might be done away with. The devs do appear to be listening to player feedback intently, which makes me hopeful for the future.
Tl;dr - it's a good game with some serious flaws, get it when it's on sale and after it's been patched with an improved campaign.
The Pros:
- Setting. The 1984 campaign is perfectly placed time-wise, as it offers a great diversity of subs, lots of opponents that range from easy peasy to terrifying and it gives a good glimpse of modern submarine tactics. It's also a very interesting historical period in terms of East-West relations. Haven't tried the '68 campaign yet so can't comment on that.
- Immersion. It's been a while since I've had a thrill like this in a sub game. Dodging homing torpedoes that are mere feet away from your ship can give you goosebumps on more than one occasion. Also... Those blasted ASW helicopters!
- Balance. You can enjoy all the game's features while playing at a relatively low difficulty setting. I found the Realistic setting to be exactly to my liking, as it gives equally as many hair-rasing moments as it does easy kills. I've jumped entire wolfpacks of enemy subs and was jumped myself by a lone SSN on more than one occasion, with a desperate torpedo dodge saving the day.
The Cons:
- Repetitive campaign. After a while you discover the campaign has 5 basic mission types - intercept a submarine (or a wolfpack), intercept a resupply convoy, destroy an amphibious landing force, make a ballistic missile strike on a port, insert a special forces team into enemy territory. With the exception of a few random encounters along the way the campaign gets boring quite quickly, even if you rack up a lot of kills and get plenty of silverware pinned to your chest.
- You never meet any allied ships. Every single vessel you find is a Soviet one. Forget about allies or neutral ships, all you have is targets. While that's a positive thing for some I find it to be a negative, as it gives a feel of a Soviet zombie infestation and not a massive campaign with hundreds of units on both sides.
- Mission design and orders from HQ, which can be infuriating at times. There seems to be little correlation between your conduct in the war and missions received, not to mention the advances made by each side. Inserting a SEAL team into Murmansk doesn't make much sense when the war is practically won. As of mid-July 2017 this, along with the repetitive campaign, are by far the biggest cons of this game.
To give you an example of all the game's problems in one paragraph, here's a description of a mission I had today.
I'm at the helm of USS Narwhal, SSN-671. I've just returned from a successful TLAM strike on Arkhangelsk. I'm low on torps and have a damaged torpedo tube from a hairy encounter with two Soviet SSNs in shallow waters, leaving me with a total of 3 working tubes. I get orders to intercept some LSTs heading to Narvik. Once I get my initial contacts the whole enemy escort comes my way and forces me to retaliate. I sink them all (2x DDG, 2x FFG iirc) but I'm left with no torps so I can't sink the LSTs. 'They're probably going to get sunk anyway, they don't have any armed escort', I thought to myself. Well, I was wrong. Apparently four unarmed and unarmoured LSTs can just waltz into Narvik unopposed and take it by storm... And NATO HQ has known about this operation for days! Don't they have aircraft with anti-ship missiles and other subs in the area? Anyway, I'm ordered back to port to resupply (so they must've known about my torpedo situation beforehand) and I'm told to... Attack an amphibious landing group heading to Narvik. Yup, the very same. REALLY? I need to stay in port to repair my broken no. 4 tube, it takes 32 hours to do so. In the meantime I'm informed my mission has failed because I failed to intercept the convoy in time. GUYS, SERIOUSLY? IS NARWHAL THE ONLY SSN IN THE WHOLE BLOODY REGION? Shouldn't you give me orders AFTER the necessary repairs have been made? I then get orders to make my third SEAL team insertion into Arkhangelsk. You'd think thought the Russians would be better prepared for my arrival this time, but I won't bother checking. At that point I quit the game and took a break.
What can be done to turn Cold Waters from a case of flawed genius into a brilliant little independent game:
- Bring the price down. For the current features it offers the 37€ price tag is just too high. I only bought this because I was excited for it. I wouldn't recommend it to a friend who's new to the genre, not without a sale on anyway.
- More mission types. It's not a good sign when you find after a mere 20 hours that the campaign can get very repetitive.
- Add allied and neutral ships, both in mission and in off-screen events. If it wasn't for the HQ messaging you from time to time you'd think you were the only NATO sailor in the North Sea area. There's no news of successes of your brothers in arms and you feel like you're the guy who carries the entire NATO naval operation on your back.
- More campaigns and ships. Having no British ships to choose from feels odd in a game that primarily takes place in and around the North Sea. The Churchill, Swiftsure and Trafalgar-class subs are all there for the taking, with plenty of data readily available. A Soviet campaign would be great too, driving a Victor III or a Sierra-class armed to the teeth with USET-80 torpedoes would be a lot of fun. Modders have done that within a month of the game being released, within limits of course. Why can't the base game have that too?
- Interface changes. Having a hotkey for periscope depth and a slider for automatically guiding your sub to a set depth would make for simple yet great quality of gameplay improvements.
- A better tutorial. If it wasn't for me watching countless YouTube videos before buying the game I would've died many more times than I did.
All in all it's a fun little game, but for now I'll put it on the back burner to see what the devs and modders can come up with in the coming months.

Atmospheric and well-crafted story-driven exploration game that's like a mad fusion of Amnesia, Heavy Rain and Alan Wake. The environments are undoubtedly the star of the show here: Red Valley Creek is just begging to be explored and the soundtrack is a wonderful accompaniment as you soak up the scenery. Some light - yet engaging - puzzles drive you forward as you uncover a plot full of neat little surprises. Recommended for fans of games like Amnesia and Dear Esther and fans of weird fiction like Bradbury and Lovecraft.

A slow-paced, thoughtful game. Visually stunning, and with audio to match, very few games match this for sheer atmosphere. If you're looking for action, go elsewhere. If you're interested in seeing what games are capable of as opposed to the likes of Call of Duty, dive right in. You will find it a rewarding experience.

First, let me confirm: this game is simply beautiful. The richness of the environment draws you in and makes you
to explore Red Creek Valley. From the lighting, to the variety of flora and its movement in wind, to the sounds of the country side, you feel completely immersed. This gorgeous area is directly (and deliciously) juxtaposed to the tension that you feel while moving through it.
And tension abounds. Imperceptible changes in volume of music, coupled with nothing really guiding your way through this mystery, leaves you with a threatening anxiety that hovers all around you, but not so much that you lose your desire to push on.  This invisible tension could be so great at times that when Propspero, the character you play, would rarely muse something aloud, it would cause me to jump!
The game isn't stacked with monster filled closets that are on the ready to jump out at you, though. The atmosphere is baked from anticipation and the emptiness of this picturesque lakeside town. Nothing in the game feels disingenuous; all element are borne from the story first, no puzzle is a pixel hunt. Indeed, one of the best aspects of the game is sometimes you have to figure out what the puzzle is before you can actually begin to solve it!
There are some missteps, of course. For one, the chronological mystery puzzles were so enjoyable that you find yourself disappointed as they become easier instead of harder as the game goes on. For another, its silent save system provides another kind of tension--the unwanted kind--as you are not exactly sure when the last save point was.  This game cries out for “save anywhere,” and it is a shame that it doesn't have it. Fortunately, this shortcoming is partly mitigated by the fact that this a video game “short story,” which means it is best played, in my opinion, in one sitting:  it can be played in a single afternoon or evening.
All in all
was a thoroughly enjoyable departure from tropes of the adventure genre, and one that I certainly recommend. It's not for everyone, of course, as this is an exploration/adventure game and one that takes a much more relaxed (albeit tense) pace to many  other game offerings.

The following is the story of playing as Austria, on a Huge Earth map, beginning in the Ancient Era, Standard pace, with 11 other civilizations and 36 city states, on King difficulty...
We begin this tale on the Northern coastline of the continent of Africa. As the foundations of the Capital city are laid, our earliest scouting efforts show, that yes, there is in fact water to our immediate North and uninhabitable desert to our immediate South. Great.
The Austrian people struggle to found new cities along the mountainous coastline. With little arable land, the cities are slow-growing. A settlement founded South-Easternly from the Capital, intent on harvesting the abundant Incense resources in that area, are set upon by a small contingent of specialized Aztec Warriors. It seems the Aztecs had their eye on the Incense as well. They outnumber the Austrian forces 3 to 1. However, utilizing Ranged advantage, and their indigenous terrain, the Austrians were able to rally a sufficient response to put down the invaders. The Aztecs accept Peace flatly, and one can consider their formal introduction as Austria's neighbor across the Sahara, now complete.
Not a fortnight after the Peace with Montezuma, the Greeks ride in from the East across the Sinai. They too, set their sights on the abundant Incense resources, knowing they would provide both a needed luxury benefit domestically as well as fetch a worthy trade with other civilizations. The Greek Hoplites and specialized Horsemen come rushing in, but make one fatal error... they mobilized over half their forces across the Mediterranean Sea, where Austrian Composite Bowmen are able to sink their ships before they even make it ashore.
After an embarassing defeat, Alexander of the Greeks flatly accepts Peace. The scrappy little Austrian empire repelled two superior forces of aggressors, establishing itself in the process, but as a result, missing its opportunity to create a religion like many other civilizations already had. No matter, the Austrian empire will now continue to focus on its internal growth.
Many years pass, and it is becoming apparent that the Aztecs are aggressively colonizing across the continent with an army that is vastly superior to the Austrian empire's. The Austrian leadership sits back and allows the Aztec Catholic missionaries to spread their preposterous religion in their lands, all in hopes of averting direct confrontation with Montezuma's forces. The Aztecs later announce they will follow the ideology of Autocracy, and the Austrians follow suit, augmenting the fascade of comraderie.
The Austrians completely forgo any ambitions of scouting the world, or making relationships with its inhabitants. The Aztecs become the sole motivating factor for growth and survival of the empire. The Aztecs see the Austrians as their vassal, so offer a declaration of friendship, only to shortly after demand they declare war on the Greeks. Well, the Austrians agree, and the Aztec forces head to the East to engage their enemy. Austria does not send a single unit. Their entire contribution to the war is on paper. Yet, a crafty peace deal struck with Alexander as the Aztec forces closed in on Athens, granted the Austrians control of Argos, a Greek city that was founded at the entrance to the Red Sea, a fine strategic location. Soon Athens falls, and with that defeat, the Greeks are no more.
While the Aztecs fought ceaselessly in the East, the Austrians made a break across the Mediterranean into the area of Europe. Much to the explorers' surprise, it was only inhabited by two city states along the Eastern portion. Austrian forces set about colonizing as much of the European continent as possible. Through Diplomatic Marriage, the Austrian empire is able to acquire both of the city-states, and integrate them. Austria now controls all of Europe, all of the Mediterranean, and all of the North coast of Africa.
Austria spends the next several centuries building educational and transportation infrastructure. A network of trade and industry, focusing on implementing social policies such as Fortified Borders, Elite Forces, and Total War. While the Austrian standing army may be low in its membership, each unit that will be trained henceforth will be an unparalleled fighting machine. By this time, through the Aztecs, Austria meets the world, at the aptly named, World Congress.
Austria becomes the second civilization to complete their Manhattan Project. The Austrians begin to feverishly convert Uranium into Nuclear Bombs, then Nuclear Missiles. Upon utilizing all 16 deposits available domestically, the Austrians begin to trade for the Uranium of lesser civilizations. Pacal of the Maya gives up his Uranium for some Furs and Iron. (lol)
All civilizations are suddenly Afraid of the Austrians. The reserved, even-tempered folks with no opinions on anything, the world had known for a few centuries, were no more. Now a high tech, nuclear superpower, with a modern navy, the Austrians began to plot their world domination, and more importantly... their revenge on the Aztecs.
The year was 2011, and the world's top 3 civilizations are the Iroqois, the Aztecs, and the Austrians. Montezuma comes to the Austrian leadership with a proposal to wage war against Hiawatha and the Iroqois. The Austrians wisely request 10 turns to prepare. The next 10 turns are used to position nuclear-armed Missile Cruisers and Battleships. The war begins, and countless city-states pledging their allegiance to the Austrian empire become the frontline against the Iroqois who come from the area of Indo-China. The Aztecs journey great distances and engage the Iroqois, advancing on Onondaga. Heavy fighting ensues, and the world sees its first use of nuclear arms. Austria shows up as well, launching a tactical Nuclear Missile directly at the Iroqois capital. Direct hit. Population goes from 28 to 8.
The war waged for many more years, and through Gunboat Diplomacy, a monsterous economy, and social policies in the Patronage specialty, Austria is able to garner 40 of the 48 delegates it requires to win a Diplomatic Victory through the United Nations. By bribing long time ally Russia, to support their proposal in exchange for 2500 gold, the Diplomatic Victory is assured... but not before raining nuclear inferno upon the Aztec civilization. The missiles smite the war mongering heathens who threatened the Austrians' very existence millenia ago. And so the Aztec people and their cities, were reduced, ashes to ashes, and dust to dust, left to dance in the breeze amongst the dunes of the Sahara.

I only just purchased this game, and haven't had a lot of time to play. I'll address what I have experienced so far, and give an update after I've hit 40+ hours of gameplay (and I will get there, this game has definitely impressed me):
First, the scary..
The first start-up took about 5 minutes of sitting through a black screen. I was patient, made some coffee, returned to my desk, twiddled my fingers, and finally it booted. Not sure what was happening there but it worked for me (contrary to some of the negative reviews).
I played through a tutorial mission, where I couldn't press any of the buttons on the right side of the screen. After determining that my computer did not, in fact, have a stroke, I looked up online and found a quick fix: Alt+tab out, alt+tab back in. Problem solved.
With all the kinks ironed out (so far)...
Since then, it has been nothing but a smooth, enjoyable experience. I have made the unfortunate mistake of trying to ram a much larger, nastier ork ship with my much smaller, squishier ship. I've fired torpedo missiles from a range of over 26000 and held my breath for what felt like an hour hoping with the will of the emperor that I'd hit my target and win an otherwise failure of a mission. I've spent an entire 20 minutes studying the user interface to understand the grand scheme behind a deceptively simple-looking strategy game, and, while in agreeance with other reviews claiming the overall difficulty and pain associated with the game, I have to say that there is a way, its just hidden in strategy and this game does a very good job of making you think carefully about your ship upgrades, customization choices, and overall fleet composition for every battle.
Also, shout out to Selina727's negative review about the second mission (escort). Have you ever tried running head-on at a bull while its charging at you? Probably not, because you'd be dead.

BattleFleet Gothic: Armada; my favorite space match-based RTS since Empire at War.
I did have some gripes when I initially purchased the game shortly after it came out of early access as it still featured a high amount of bugs back then, but I am happy to say that many of these now seem to be fixed. Constant crashing issues that plagued me at first dont seem to exist anymore, I played probably five campaign turns straight with four deployments each turn wiht no crashes in between.
As far as universe accuracy it seems on point to me, that said my only exposure to the 40k universe is the squad based Dawn of War titles. The musical score is compelling and really helps set the tone, and the level of detail on the ships is incredible. As others have said the comic based story-telling is a bit old-age but then again I would much prefer the develpers use their budget to develop the core gameplay and I dont mind it at all its almost like playing through a warhammer 40k comic book. The campagins main character admiral Spire does seem like a bit of a naive doofus at times but I enjoy watching him grow in courage and tact to confront the seemingly insurmontable threat of the black crusade.
I havent bought Tau or tried multiplayer yet but would highly recommend this game based on the single player campagin and skirmish system alone. The persistent customization of ships is a unique feature and especially shines in the campagin when tough decisions have to be made between upgrading newer ships or repairing older workhorse units. Gameplay itself is hectic and learning what works and what doesn't when it comes to commanding your fleet takes quite awhile.
This game has a massive learning curve, many of the negative reviews claim the game is too hard specifically some campaign missions but I can say I beat them after persistentce and practice but often failed my first several attempts. I actually lost the entire first campagin I attempted, having underestimated the effects of losing differents planets/missions but am doing much better on my second go around. Gameplay in battles itself is some of the most immersive space-based strategy I have ever tried, it is not suitable to simply point your horde of ships at the enemies pile of ships and wait for one pile to win. You often arent given a horde of ships to work with and have to push those you do have to their limits and often accept that some may take heavy damage or be destroyed in order to achieve victory. Some abilities can be set to auto-use but winning requires learning to efficiently micromanage key abilities based on your craft's role.
All that said, the developers have discussed plans for further expansion content in the future and I strongly hope that it includes a new single player campagin, I would be willing to fork over a fair-bit more than $5 if I was getting a race along with a new campagin to take them for a test drive. Or maybe at least a randomly generated non-story driven replayable campaign that might add some additional variety to the single player experiences. I also had hoped for a bit more interactivity with the planets in campaign mode, they are currently essentially just a checkmark for a bonus/penalty which either is or is not applied based on if you win a battle there. Some ability to customize or foritfy certain key planets might be interesting.
Overall I highly recommend this excellent space strategy title and will be sinking many more hours into it in the future.

A strategic, tactical FPS, this is not really the kind of game you want to play solo. While it can be done (and several do so rather fondly and have a blast), this games true potential shines with the Multi-player and character creation system.
Offering 7 chapters of campaign mayhem with anywhere from three to six checkpoints, there's easily 72+ hours of gameplay if you simply try to rush through it without fully trying to enjoy the game.
The Terrorist Hunt mode offers a chance to futher hone your skills and tactics for both Campaign and Online Versus modes. AI can vary from downright predictable, to completely unforgiving and brutal. Even on the lowest difficulty, the AI can stiff offer a variety of commentary and skill to throw down against the player. Again, trust not the AI paired up with you, BRING A FRIEND. Playing on Hunt? BRING THREE FRIENDS. The higher you set the scale, the harder this game can mess with you.
The ability to semi-realistically alter your loadouts armor-wise is amazing. The better the armor, the heavier it is, and the slower your character can move, while taking more hits (aside from the ever annoying headshot or grenade). With multiple options for gear and weaponry, you'll be hard pressed to find someone that looks exactly alike. Word to the wise, try to pick a bright color, the enemy tends to stick to darker camo options, and you don't want to be confused for an enemy at long distances.
Like any game, it does have it's quirks and glitches. Getting hit from long range with a shotgun (and it being a headshot) is downright evil. The bots also seem to have a better grasp on bullet penetration and just how to throw grenades. They also tend to spawn in random places during the Terrorist Hunts, so any areas you might have cleared, are not 100% clear. Always check your six.
Definitely more than one way to complete the game, and with the option to replay quite literally from any checkpoint in the campaign, there is always something to do. I adore this game; every single aspect of it is fun and exciting in almost every way. I won't go into a huge amount of detail because I'm sure that there are other reviews that achieve that for me. Instead, I'm looking at this from a very casual viewpoint.
For starters, lets talk about the positives:
-Game runs amazing. I do have a beefy computer (Intel I7 I think over 3 GHz, 16 GB of ram, and a Nvidia 1060) so it runs great on it. No frame rate drops at all and the graphics look great. I honestly do not know how well this game will run on lower end PCs but I believe it to be well optimized so you shouldn't have a problem with it.
-Extremely fun. Right from the start I was having a blast playing this, from free-running around the city and slums, to bashing zombies' heads in, to running from them at night, everything I did was a blast, even the fetch quests were fun
-Story is awesome. It's nothing award winning, but it is still a good story nonetheless. Will try to get you emotionally attached to certain characters, but because of the nature of the game, it's rather hard to.
-Actually is terrifying in some points. Techland does a great job on making the zombies look and act scary. There were multiple moments where I was yelling because something jumped out at me, or I was being chased by a pack of zombies.
-Nice weapon varity. Yes, you'll be using the weapons in roughly the same way, bashing zombies. But each class of weapons behaves differently. A giant fireaxe hits harder and slower than a crowbar, while the crowbar has more knockback power than the knife, while the knife hits faster than all of them. Regardless, each weapon class feels unique and forces me to adjust my tactics depending on what I am using. Even the guns, bows, and crossbows feel different, mostly to their one hit kill power. Be careful though, because guns tend to attract even more zombies!
-Freerunning is great. Most games that have freerunning tend to be either hit or miss, with most falling into the miss category. Dying Light however is a sure hit; the free running is fun and exciting. The controls are okay, but I'll get to that in a second. Overall however, the freerunning is a solid addition to the game.
This is great and all, but nothing is perfect. I have my fair share of issues with this game.
-The controls. Yes, the controls are tight, but they tend to not behave how I want them to, leading to a lot of deaths. Sometimes I don't grab a ledge when I should, or other times I get stuck and can't move out of a group of zombies, as in I'm mashing buttons and nothing happens. NOW, I could very well just suck at this game, I admit, so take that one with a grain of salt. However, I do believe that you'll encounter some issues.
-The missions and side quests are very generic. "Hey man, go run over there and do that/grab this/kill him/turn on that" Every mission, be it story or side, feels the same. Very rarely do they change in some way, and when they do it's so much fun. But 80% of what you're doing is the same thing, over and over and over and over and over and over again.
-The game can get very frustrating. I play on hard, so yes, it's HARD. But there are a lot of times where I throw my hands up and yell ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Some instances include:
-Being spawned in a location filled with hard enemies that spawn killed me
-Trying to kill gun users when I haven't even found a gun. (surprise surprsie, they kill me in 3 shots)
-Certain challenges feel impossible, both in what you're supposed to use and where it places you
-Driving the jeep in The Following is extremely frustrating, as it seems as though if you drive out at night and the fast zombies see you, you're screwed as there isn't a good way to knock them off.
-Multiple times during missions I can't find what I'm looking for because I'm searching in a huge area for a cell phone the size of my fist.
-In addition, the game isn't hard on higher levels, it's frustrating, which is a big difference. Hard would be more zombies added and fewer weapons and supplies, but as it stands, on higher difficulties zombies just have more health. Which means it takes FOREVER to kill a single zombie sometimes. In fact, I've had instances where they just don't die, even though I'm using extremely powerful weapons. The zombies also hit harder, which is fine if they wouldn't 3 shot you from the start. I remember playing on console with the difficulty being on normal, I would get really hurt if I ran into a group of zombies but it was at a point where I could escape, but at a heavy cost. This encouraged me to play smart because I would waste supplies. On hard...not so much. Zombies down you very fast, so even if you get hut twice, you're buring through your supplies to get yourself back. In fact, it's better to keep dying on Hard if you're trying to do something, as that way you're not wasting a bunch of supplies. That's not fun.
-The game kind of looses its charm after awhile. Sure, what game doesn't at 40 hours, but a good game will keep you going with an awesome story, awesome gameplay, or both. Dying Light doesn't have this. Yeah, the story is decent, but it doesn't pull you in; I stopped caring after awhile and used story missions solely when I needed better loot and expereince. Yeah, the gameplay is fun, but when you have a series of frustrating events happen to you, you loose the desire to keep playing; why even attempt that challenge when you get two shotted and loose, for the 17th time?
Overall, I do believe Dying Light is a solid game; it's incredibly fun and rewarding when you play well, but can be extremely frustrating when even the slightest thing goes wrong. I do believe that the postives overshadow the negative parts but only up to a certain point. That point could very well have been 40 hours to me; to you, it might hit at 10 hours or it could never be hit at all, it just depends on how you approach the game. Regardless, this game is a solid 8/10, and is something that I would recommend to everyone.

The decisions you make as a developer will be how the consumer remembers you.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was an experience, I came into it immediatly struck in awe at the simple beauty of the enviroment, without anything meant to draw the eye, everything came at you at one, giving you so much to observe. The way the player travels gives time to enjoy the scenery, obviously lovingly crafted by a team who knew their intention and how to reach it.
But, Ethan Carter has a major flaw.
Without spoiling, I will say there are three distinct points that ruined the game for me. Two of them completely deimmerse you from the game, shaking you awake from a dream by simply slamming confusion into your face, where you wake up and immediatly realize, "This doesn't fit" forcing you to shake your head, only to try to get yourself back into the story. As well, the ending of the game (Again, without spoiling) completely erradicates the immersion and interest in the story by simply telling you "Nothing you experienced mattered" making any analysis of lines of dialogue, narrative, and story telling null and void.
The game itself was a nice, narrative experience, but it leaves a bitter taste in ones mouth simply with a drop of the plate, taking what could have been a finely crafted piece of art into a shabble as the explanation to the events clears all of the paint from the canvas.
The game left me unsatisfied, and not that I was wanting more, it was that I felt that the thought and time I invested into the story was simply thrown away when the developers took the easy route out plot wise.
I sadly cannot recommend this game, watch a Let's Play if you're curious, but the dissatisfaction with how the story holds together in the end isn't enough to warrant even 20 dollars.

The type of horror found in this game is entirely unique. The rusty, autumn visuals exhibit a spooky beauty to the dead town of Red Creek Valley. Honestly, this is the only game in my knowledge where I can feel anxiety by simply staring at a waterfall. Where most horror games instill a fear of what is to come, this game focuses on the gruesome mystery of what has already happened, heavily relying on the player’s own imagination. Feelings of fear and wonder will combine to create an aura of anxiety, present throughout.
The plot is all over the place. It’s fairly experimental and nonlinear, but poetically satisfying. It’s not the type of game that needs to be played in one sitting.
The music sounds like someone threw a million dollars at it. The different tracks are fairly catchy too, and they support their visual environments.
There are a few cons to this game. Maneuvering around can be a bit choppy. The voice acting is adequate but not amazing. The save system is automatic and too infrequent.  There are a few typos, and the transposition of the audible dialogue to the text on screen is not always perfect.
All in all though, this was quite an ambitious idea for a game, and it actually turned out amazing.

I remember when I saw my nephew play this game on his Wii U... I nearly bought a Wii U just for it (and Xeno 2). Then I learned the game was coming out on Steam. I made an exception to my 'wait for bundling!' policy and bought it on sale.
And of course, I had to get a game-breaking bug at the start of chapter 3, not being able to build the first ferry despite having enough bricks for it. After mourning the loss of my advancement, I resolved to restart from scratch, and this time I managed to get past through the bug, and even went past the Bluebell Mine bug that a lot more users were having (I backed up my save and posted it to the Steam forums, it's been confirmed to work for them. Yay.)
After that misadventure, I'm happy to say I never again got stuck with a bug. I did have a crash while the game was loading a cut scene when unlocking free ride at the top of the Honey hotel, but that's all.
So... Is it worth risking crashes & bugs? Yes it is. I never stuck with GTA games because I thought they were too serious. Lego City has the freedom of a GTA with good-hearted humor at every turn. There are no consequences to anything you do, you're just in for a fun ride. The story mode takes about 15 hours to complete (the fastest speedrun for it is under 5 hours though), and after you complete it, you have full access to everything in the open world. The game offers many 'activities' (I'd rather say that than 'missions', because it's really optional stuff, mostly on the silly side), and every district in the city has one of each. I didn't like that you have to complete the game before you get any rewards for most of the activities, since the final district (Lady Liberty Island) can only be unlocked after getting a missable character token that gets dropped in the final chapter. Fine with me, I don't intend to complete the game 100%, but my heartfelt congratulations to anyone who did.
Because, seriously, there is so much to do! You make new discoveries at every turn. And some of the activities are a bit more hardcore -- most notably half of the missions that involved driving (and for some reason, even if you enable the cheat bricks that make your car faster, other cars ALSO get faster so it's pointless), or doing huge jumps. I'd recommend watching walkthrough videos for those, because sometimes you need to be very precise.
I should add that I've never been a skilled player (I'm more of a match 3 or point & click guy!), so precision platforming is not for me, but I guess Lego games are easier to handle because they're designed to be finishable by kids.
So I swallowed my pride and played like a kid then.
And had fun like a kid.

As Crab said in his recommendation: "Nothing happens in this game... I mean really you can skip it." Of course there is a grain of truth in that statement, when held in the light of Episode 2 or even Half-Life 2, Episode One leaves much to be admired. This can be attributed to the games eco-centric location throughout the ruins of City 17 and the Citadel and the lack of varying companions throughout the game. While doing an excellent job making Alyx seem like a more believable character with well scripted combat sequences and animations you can't help but feel that she's holding your hand through it all. Personally I loved EP1 because the raw urban combat of the final levels of Half-Life 2 were my favorite levels, and Episode One extended on that making for an entire game focused on the best part of HL2. All that being said it's not imperative that you play it, and you can go from HL2 straight to EP2 without worry about missing on vital story points.

This is the next part, of the award-winning Half-Life 2. The gamemplay is very similar, and this is basically, like a new part. However the story is not the same. This takes place much more indoors, and some in the post-apocalyptic warzone of City 17 (The city where HL2 takes place).

This is a solid little game in the action shooter franchise but don't go expecting too much from it. While it definitely looks pretty and is fairly satisfying to play it suffers a serious case of "xbox port-itis". Many of the seperate action buttons have been combined into press and hold menus which, while perfect for a controller, really is a pain for anyone used to PC gaming. In addition, the multiplayer and co-op connections are a mild pain, though both do usually work. Finally, be aware you must create an ubisoft account, even when playing through Steam.
Like other later Tom Clancy franchise games, this one too only dabbles in realism while being a console game at heart. Being able to take a shotgun blast and live. Shot teammates can be magically resurected with one quick jab of a needle. Super human accuracy on full automatic. Just don't go expecting something like the original Rainbow Six or Ghost Recon titles.
The ability to customize your operative with a variety of unlockable load outs, armor, and gear is a nice touch but there is very little point to use too many guns past the initial offering you start with and all other choices seem to be almost purely cosmetic. However, pulling off trick shots and specific kill types in the game to unlock things is a satisfying reward as you grind through the play.
All in all, I considered it well worth the money after buying it on sale. You'll likely play through it once, enjoy your time, and then have no further use for it.

-- This comment includes instructions on how to play with Steam friends --
This game is an HD remake of Quake III with online and Steam support. Playing with your friends over LAN can be a bit tricky, but not impossible. Much easier than with Quake III actually.*
Upsides: the game has native support for HD resolutions, has better quality models than Quake III, with the addition of a few extra characters, allows you to choose between 3 narrators (Vadrigar -Q3-, Default and Daemia -new-), has all of Q3A, Q3TA and QLive game modes as well as a few new ones, has many classic maps plus a few new ones made by the community, has native support for bots and everything else that was great with Q3A and Q3TA.
The only negative aspect I'd like to point out is the lack of a community to play online with at some times of the day (depending on your region, of course) and the AI for some game modes is completely flawed (e.g. 1-Flag CTF or Attack and Defend, where bots will just circle around their base and do absolutely nothing).
All the negative reviews I read are of people who had free access to the game for 5 years and now are required to pay some money for it (I think $10). There are no negative reviews about the game itself because, like Quake III Arena and Team Arena, QLive is pretty much perfect. Just a one-off 10 USD payment for full privileges. You pay for Counter Strike, Overwatch, Call of Duty or Battlefield. So why would you not pay for Quake?
The problem with the game being free was that you could not set up your own match or play over LAN or with bots. You would regularly encounter tons of empty servers, others that you could not play in because they'd put a minimum of reputation to get in, but to get reputation you needed to win matches. Sometimes you'd encounter cheaters dominating the arena unfairly and increasing ping to other players on purpose. And worst of all, if you didn't live in the US or UK, it would be hard to find a low ping server with people on it.
On the contrary, if you wanted to pay for extra privileges, you'd have to pay 50 USD annually to create servers that you still wouldn't be able to enjoy, because nobody would join.
If you played it during the 5 years it was free, you get it for free on your Steam account. Enjoy it. Else, pay the 10 dollars, or wishlist and let Steam warn you when it's on sale. If you want free there's Team Fortress 2.
*All you have to do is select "Create Match" and THEN invite your friends to a lobby. Once the game rules and map have been selected, make sure you choose to NOT put a password AND make it a LAN game (as opposed to Offline or Internet), and start the match. All other players will automatically join your game. Console commands work perfectly fine once inside and you can even add bots as well as change map or vote after the match is over.

Despite only playing on the low side of 30 hours of this game, I regard Civilization 5 as one of the best strategy games in which I have played.
This game allows for the player to have complete freedom of how they choose to tackle the game. It offers a diverse range of civilizations in which to choose from, as well as, a variety of ways to win. This game also allows the player to customise how the game will be. Whether it is faster paced, has many or no city states (AI controlled cities in which the player can aline themselves with or even conquer), enables the player to choose if there will be barbarians, choice of weather, and much, much more.
If you choose to play against AI rather than human players you will come to realise how well the game actually works. The AI will each have a different strategy of winning and will all play differently (providing a challenge for the player). As in many games the player can manipulate the difficulty of the AI as to suit their skill level. This game requires player to have patience as the games can last several hours to complete.
This game also allows players to use the steam workshop as a means of further extending their experience. I would highly reccomend this game to players despite how much experience they have with strategy games.
Solid 9/10 (I don't believe games can be a perfect 10 as there is always room for improvement, however it is amazing regardless)
Hope this review helped players determine the worth of this game for themselves.

An easily approachable game depicting nuclear powered attack submarine operations in two hypothetical World War 3 campaigns. If you remember playing Microprose's "Red Storm Rising" then you will be right at home with this game. Three thumbs up!

If you're coming from hours and hours of playing Dangerous Waters, Cold Waters will give you a refreshing twist on sub combat.
Instead of switching between radar screens, sonar waterfall displays, and maintaining your own TMA plotting, Cold Waters focuses more on combat tactics and positioning then gathering and maintaining information.
The game does some things automatically for you, as a real crew would, like maintaining sonar tracks, weapon transients, radar and ESM plots if your masts are up, active sonar ping returns, and TMA plots on all tracked contacts.
The things that you must control yourself still keeps the game extremely interesting for a sub captain, such as rudder, bow planes, ballast, and speed.
Once your sonar crew pickup a contact, it's your job to position the sub to get the solution percentage as close to 100% as possible, and the way you maneuver the sub matters which brings tactics into play.
Weapon settings can be changed, including active/passive torp homing, straight or circle tracking, and depth. Weapons can be wire guided, as long as you're within a 60 degree arc or so from your torps that you fired.
Wires can be broken based on your speed, depth changes, and angle to target.
Like Dangerous Waters this game also models thermal layers, but takes it a step beyond and introduces surface duct....how noisy it is near the surface based on the ocean conditions. Layers can be strong or weak, as well as surface duct conditions, which influences how you control your own depth to track contacts or hide from them.
A towed array is modeled, and it does have a blindspot just as your ship sonar has a blindspot directly behind it in the baffles.
Tactics involving sneaking up on targets in their baffles are completely doable, and at times you can sink a target without them even knowing you were behind them.
Sub launched cruise missiles and harpoon anti-ship missiles have firing restrictions that must be observed, which again forces the player to make choices on what depth to run at during contact against surface vessels.
New players to naval combat can turn the difficulty down to an arcade like experience, and experienced players who want a challenge can bump it up beyond "Realistic" to "Elite", which provides a very lethal enemy.
For difficulty settings this high, mechanics like "silent running" are of more importance as even reloading a torpedo tube can increase your sub's noise output.
The game is already able to be modded, and as of this review a handful of mods already exist such as a 2004 campaign (the game ships with a 1960's and 1980's campaign with era-appropriate ships and tech).
As this is a fairly new title, the platform they have is a solid one that can only improve as new features and content is added to it.
The only downside to this title right now is a lack of multiplayer and a dedicated mission editor, but those two things detract very little from playing this game.
Workshop support could only improve the quality of the mods, so hopefully that's something they will add in the future.

This is perhaps what you wouldn't expect from a open world GTA type of game, it is funny, had loads of references from movies, video games, memes and so on + takes a big departure from previous installations by getting very wacky. I have owned this game for a while on Windows 7, but recently gave the Linux port a try.
Game review: The game is a open-world GTA style game, where you have a large city you can have fun in. The missions can be repetitive sometimes, but other than that the level of humor and super-hero level gameplay makes it very entertaining, if not very amusing. What makes it different from GTA is not only the wacky gameplay, but also the whole setting seems isolated from the typical gang world environment. The length of gameplay is very satisfying and the replay value is high, as you can always play again and do things differently. The missions are quite linear, you have some non-linear choices in the main missions but not like you did in Saint's Row 3 or before.
Windows review:
Runs at 49 FPS average on maximum settings with 3 monitors. Nvidia surround resolution 4940x900. The game runs acceptable and I have rarely experienced a crash or stuttering. The field of view is not acceptable to me, so I used a third party tool to edit the FOV to acceptable playstyle. Audio is good, alt-tab friendly and multiplayer runs just fine.
Linux/SteamOS review:
Runs at 37 FPS average on maximum settings with 1 monitor. The game initially has lots of stuttering problems due to the fact that eON is loading all the shaders in the game. This makes it somewhat obnoxious for the first 10 minutes of playtime, as you run around or drive around and your game stutters; possibly screwing up your direction. To improve performance, I took off Post-Processing and turned Ambient Occlusion to medium, which boosted my FPS up to 48 FPS average. The stuttering remained, but was infrequent for the remainder of gameplay after I reached 9 - 10 minutes of ingame time. I advise that the developers responsible for this comes out with a patch to fix this problem. Audio is good, but sometimes when there is too much going on, some sounds will not work until it calms down; multiplayer is flawless. (I even played with a friend who was running the game on Windows.) This indicates good cross-platform interactivity. Unfortunately, because Nvidia has not really implemented surround technology for Linux as much, I am unable to play on 3 monitors. Some games do not need Surround to run 3 screens, Serious Sam 3: BFE is one such example.
Conclusion:
The game is fun, the humor is nice, the gameplay itself is unconventional and the replay value is high. Windows version is my preferred one because of triple monitor support + the ability to use a tool to change the FOV as well as no stuttering. The Linux version however, is running decent considering the fact it is using eON and is not a native port. For those who play only on Linux, it is playable and enjoyable if you have the patience to let the stuttering die down; some linux gamers have reported better performance/less stuttering than me, which indicates it will be different per user. All in all, I recommend this game for both Windows and Linux gamers. Unfortunately, the modding support for this game is not really great; so if you want more content be prepared to pay for DLC (if the DLC actually contains content you want.) In terms of multiplayer: I really wish Volition would have added 4-player coop in Saint's Row 4; since a lot of players from 3 were asking for it.
Windows Rating: 8/10
+Gameplay is unconventional and fun.
+Runs very solid, no issues with performance.
+Replay value is high.

The one and only thing FTL: Faster Than Light reminds me of is Star Trek. Being a big fan of the original series, this game made me feel as if I were part of a crew from a similar canon. Managing your own starship and making tough calls as the starship captain is probably the closest I've ever gotten to playing the role of James T. Kirk, but without all the romance.
I will begin by stating the two issues I have with the game. The first being that there is barely any storyline to speak of. Sure, as the captain of the ship, you will make decisions based of very brief scenario prompts, but the flavor text is there only as a placeholder of sorts. With the exception of some in-game achievements that are sought only for the purpose of ship unlocks, the small amount of plot that does exist only fulfills opportunities for the random number generator to provide the player with either a positive outcome, a negative outcome, or a neutral outcome. One could happily play the entire game, unlocking most achievements, while not reading one word of story text, and the entertainment value would not be diminished. The second problem with the game is its difficulty. FTL: Faster Than Light is one of the most difficult modern era games I have played. It's not that its tricks are unfair, but simply way too aggressive and unforgiving. There are three difficulty levels to choose from (easy, normal, hard). Easy mode is about the equivalent of an average game's normal mode, while hard mode is probably about the same as the average game's nightmare mode. I never even wasted my time with hard mode, as easy mode is quite challenging enough as it is. "Normal" mode takes away all the fun and natural challenge of "easy" mode and turns playing the game into an unpleasant annoyance. Normal and hard modes are not fun at all, unfortunately.
Despite those two major concerns, if one plays on the adequate difficulty setting, there is much fun to be had commanding a starship. Everything in the game is randomly generated with the exception of the ship you choose to start with, and the final boss. After a few dozen hours, you will realize which systems work best against the game, as well as which weapons are the best, but because there is so much variety between your starting ships and the randomness of what can be bought from stores and loot collected from battles or random events, every playthrough feels fresh and completely different from each other. I beat the game once with every ship class, and I must say that each game played seemed unique. Of course, there is a very specific strategy against the final boss that could be repeated each time to defeat it, but because each playthrough affords the player to equip a wide variety of weapon combinations and systems, even the final boss fight could potentially have a varying feel to it, as your attacks and approach against this enemy will depend on how well you were able to maximize your ship on the road to your final destination, given the game's random circumstances. Even though many people will have interesting ship tier lists, I think that most ships really are well balanced, and that any player could make a winning ship/weapons combination with enough experience. FTL: Faster Than Light is exciting, fun, and a strong opponent for anyone who wants a harsh challenge. I'm glad the developers were able to make seasoned starship captains out of anyone willing to give this difficult game a chance.

I adore this game; every single aspect of it is fun and exciting in almost every way. I won't go into a huge amount of detail because I'm sure that there are other reviews that achieve that for me. Instead, I'm looking at this from a very casual viewpoint.
For starters, lets talk about the positives:
-Game runs amazing. I do have a beefy computer (Intel I7 I think over 3 GHz, 16 GB of ram, and a Nvidia 1060) so it runs great on it. No frame rate drops at all and the graphics look great. I honestly do not know how well this game will run on lower end PCs but I believe it to be well optimized so you shouldn't have a problem with it.
-Extremely fun. Right from the start I was having a blast playing this, from free-running around the city and slums, to bashing zombies' heads in, to running from them at night, everything I did was a blast, even the fetch quests were fun
-Story is awesome. It's nothing award winning, but it is still a good story nonetheless. Will try to get you emotionally attached to certain characters, but because of the nature of the game, it's rather hard to.
-Actually is terrifying in some points. Techland does a great job on making the zombies look and act scary. There were multiple moments where I was yelling because something jumped out at me, or I was being chased by a pack of zombies.
-Nice weapon varity. Yes, you'll be using the weapons in roughly the same way, bashing zombies. But each class of weapons behaves differently. A giant fireaxe hits harder and slower than a crowbar, while the crowbar has more knockback power than the knife, while the knife hits faster than all of them. Regardless, each weapon class feels unique and forces me to adjust my tactics depending on what I am using. Even the guns, bows, and crossbows feel different, mostly to their one hit kill power. Be careful though, because guns tend to attract even more zombies!
-Freerunning is great. Most games that have freerunning tend to be either hit or miss, with most falling into the miss category. Dying Light however is a sure hit; the free running is fun and exciting. The controls are okay, but I'll get to that in a second. Overall however, the freerunning is a solid addition to the game.
This is great and all, but nothing is perfect. I have my fair share of issues with this game.
-The controls. Yes, the controls are tight, but they tend to not behave how I want them to, leading to a lot of deaths. Sometimes I don't grab a ledge when I should, or other times I get stuck and can't move out of a group of zombies, as in I'm mashing buttons and nothing happens. NOW, I could very well just suck at this game, I admit, so take that one with a grain of salt. However, I do believe that you'll encounter some issues.
-The missions and side quests are very generic. "Hey man, go run over there and do that/grab this/kill him/turn on that" Every mission, be it story or side, feels the same. Very rarely do they change in some way, and when they do it's so much fun. But 80% of what you're doing is the same thing, over and over and over and over and over and over again.
-The game can get very frustrating. I play on hard, so yes, it's HARD. But there are a lot of times where I throw my hands up and yell ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Some instances include:
-Being spawned in a location filled with hard enemies that spawn killed me
-Trying to kill gun users when I haven't even found a gun. (surprise surprsie, they kill me in 3 shots)
-Certain challenges feel impossible, both in what you're supposed to use and where it places you
-Driving the jeep in The Following is extremely frustrating, as it seems as though if you drive out at night and the fast zombies see you, you're screwed as there isn't a good way to knock them off.
-Multiple times during missions I can't find what I'm looking for because I'm searching in a huge area for a cell phone the size of my fist.
-In addition, the game isn't hard on higher levels, it's frustrating, which is a big difference. Hard would be more zombies added and fewer weapons and supplies, but as it stands, on higher difficulties zombies just have more health. Which means it takes FOREVER to kill a single zombie sometimes. In fact, I've had instances where they just don't die, even though I'm using extremely powerful weapons. The zombies also hit harder, which is fine if they wouldn't 3 shot you from the start. I remember playing on console with the difficulty being on normal, I would get really hurt if I ran into a group of zombies but it was at a point where I could escape, but at a heavy cost. This encouraged me to play smart because I would waste supplies. On hard...not so much. Zombies down you very fast, so even if you get hut twice, you're buring through your supplies to get yourself back. In fact, it's better to keep dying on Hard if you're trying to do something, as that way you're not wasting a bunch of supplies. That's not fun.
-The game kind of looses its charm after awhile. Sure, what game doesn't at 40 hours, but a good game will keep you going with an awesome story, awesome gameplay, or both. Dying Light doesn't have this. Yeah, the story is decent, but it doesn't pull you in; I stopped caring after awhile and used story missions solely when I needed better loot and expereince. Yeah, the gameplay is fun, but when you have a series of frustrating events happen to you, you loose the desire to keep playing; why even attempt that challenge when you get two shotted and loose, for the 17th time?
Overall, I do believe Dying Light is a solid game; it's incredibly fun and rewarding when you play well, but can be extremely frustrating when even the slightest thing goes wrong. I did not play on the PvP official servers, or PvE official servers until the Master Builder server came out, and I am thoroughly enjoying that (Despite a few bugs). The servers are good though, and everything seems to be going well gameplay-wise.

Now lets start of by saying do you believe in werewolves and the supernatural,YES ? or NO ? it makes no difference as if you like hidden object games you'll love this one.
The game starts with Ashley (who you play throughout the entire game) looking over some old photos and then talking about something that happened a while ago and then of you go into the game through a story that is being told in the present but you are living through in the past (so whatever you do you know that at least Ashley survives the adventure-and no spoiler as this happens right at the start).
Then you travel to your Grandma's to find out why you havent heard from her in a while and to find out exactally what is going on and why ??
Now to say more than this will spoil the story no end but lets just say some things you will see just are'nt for the faint hearted,but its one game you will enjoy playing through if your heart will let you,as you wonder just when something will jump out at you or you will see something horrible.
The graphics in game on the most part are of the static variety (are'nt they allways in these games) but they are presented and drawn in such a way as to draw you in and when the game does throw some moving images at you they are all the more attention grabbing for it.
The music in game really suits the nature of the game and the spoken dialogue is all delivered well by the cast (most of the time though you will just be listening to Ashleys voice and we could have done with a few more characters to flesh things out).
The gameplay consists of the static find the object variety to the solve the water by moving the pipes ones,but all in all these are entertaining and never get old or outstay their welcome (there is no button to bypass the puzzles which does make it more challenging than most HOG's as some puzzles can be quite abstract).
The games story is really well written and i for one did see what was coming but it was still a very satisfactory ending to what is a well developed and well put together game.
Now let me say this i think this hidden object game is aimed more at the mature audience than most as some scenes can be quite (for use of a better word) horrific and therefore some may find them unnerving,but for this reviewer i just wish there were more games of this type out there in the hidden object genre that focused more on telling an adult story.
Will you like this hidden object game,well if you like this type of game and are thirsting for more then yes you will as its one of the best out there,if its not your sort of game then i dont think any of this genre will ever change your mind.
Just remember whilst playing some parts are really quite challenging so dont let it get to you or make you "HOWLING" mad.

TL;DR: Gameplay isn't very fun, graphics are good, atmospheric as hell. Also very expensive for the amount of game you get. I paid $20 for it and that was probably still too much.
Pros:
-Good art direction, writing, and voice acting make this a really good "Warhammer game," which is something of its own genre now. As somebody who's played almost every "Warhammer video game" including the crappier ones, I can speak to the quality of the work that's been put into making it seem Warhammer-y.
-Graphics are fine. The ships are rendered beautifully and the battlefield hazards are all very interesting to look at.
-Space Marines are suitably OP.
-Cheaper, less time-intensive, and more fun than the board game. Of course, there's no real interaction with another human either, which cheapens the experience. But it beats the hell out of putting a second mortgage on your house and spending uncounted aeons painting each individual cathedral spire on your fidly Imperial ships just to watch some guy with a XXXL Metallica t-shirt and bad breath smash your pretty fleet to bits with a thousand unpainted Ork Kroozers.
Cons:
-Not a fun game. The basic gameplay mechanic essentially amounts to waiting for your slow-moving ships to float close enough to the enemy's slow-moving ships so they can exchange some courtesy laser-fire and then go on their merry way. The game's "skill" system doesn't do much to switch this up, either, and the genuinely execrable AI complicates matters further. Ships are slow and unresponsive. This is true of both the Imperial ships, which are apparently supposed to be slow, and the Eldar ships, which are supposed to be swift but fragile. (I think their recipe for the Eldar ships contained too much fragile and not enough swift.) The other races deal with the same issues of bloated irresponsiveness, but slightly overcome them in different ways; Chaos ships all have LAZORS which hit from a really long range so it doesn't matter that their ships are slow as molasses. Space Marines and Orks, by contrast, actually move pretty quick, and have heavy armor and a fun ramming mechanic, respectively. Not sure what the Tau play like; I'm not a filthy fish-communist.
-Unfortunately, as far as I'm aware, you can only play the campaign as the dull-as-dishwater Imperial Navy, which has probably the least intersting gameplay of any of the factions. This is sad, as I like story-driven games, and I liked the characters in the campaign (though I'll admit I haven't gotten far into it), but I was chased off by the boring and frustrating gameplay.
-It's too pricey. There's not $40 worth of game here. There's hardly $20 worth of game here. If it goes on sale at ~75% off, then it's worth it. Otherwise, they're charging you too much. (Still cheaper than the actual miniatures though. Thanks, GW.)

Should you buy this game? Yes.
Is this game worth it's price tag? Probably.
A tight, well made, detailed, elaborate submarine sim without all the drawbacks a tight, well made, detailed, elaborate sim provides. Six(ish) beautifully crafted playable US SSNs, as well as about twenty more unplayable Soviet naval vehicles, from cruisers, to destroyers, to recommisioned civilian ships, to AIRCRAFT CARRIERS, I could spend hours rambling on about the effort put into the models alone. The variety, and classing system, makes it so that the more you play, the more you truly feel like a sub commander, identifying vehicles by their sonar waves, and knowing what that vehicle is capable of puts you in hotseat, where your desicions impact the outcome of not just the battle, but the entire war.
The game has two playable modes, campaign, and single missions. Single missions is pretty much just campaign missions but you can choose the encounters, but campaign is probably the best, most fleshed out single-unit command game I've seen in ages. It's real-time movement, where, deployed from your port in Holy Loch, you are assigned tasks ranging from inserting a marine task force into a soviet naval base, to raiding a valuable convoy escorted by destroyers. Each time you return to Holy Loch for R&R there are messages about the mood of the men, as well as your own thoughts and messages from your XO, really putting you in the game. News clippings inform you of the land war's progress as well, and when you manage to sink an enemy landing task force, heading for a friendly port, the next day you may see a clipping concerning the sucessful defense of said port, and you think; "I had a hand in that"
It's just great, trust me.
As for the sub combat itself, the gameplay can range from sneeki breeki silent sub, skirting enemies into their baffles, and then nailing them from behind while they never even detected you, to sending three torpedoes at the flagship of a fleet, then diving while the rest of the fleet pummels the sea around you, to sneaking into the center of a convoy, undetected, incinerating the high value merchant ships, and then running while the escorting destroyers rush back to protect their now-flaming charges. It all comes down to your desicions, and abilites as sub commander.
The one thing I dislike about this game is the price tag. I think it's fair for a game dev to charge the price they want, but in this day and age I'm pretty sure most "Non-AAA" titles charge between 10-30 dollars for their games. Killerfish is arguably more significant than indie devs, but I wouldn't go comparing them to Ubisoft or EA. The other thing is, this title was one of the few that opted out of the summer sale, which was disappointing, considering nearly every current game on the store tends to do that.
In the end, I just think you should buy the game dude.

Great fun game - but a leeetle buggy
I reckon I'm just coming to the end of the story mode (roughly 20% complete).  It's been great fun - the voice acting is superb, and the jokes are great.
. The gameplay is classic lego - Missions off a hub world consisting of simple little puzzles and minigames piled on top of one another in one great lovable heap.  The driving element is very well executed, and you can do some quite spectacular short cuts once you've found your way around the city - don't always rely on your Satnav.
However - the game *is* bugged -  I've had a couple of crash-to-desktops, unfortunately normally on a transition - which also normally means it's at the *end* of a trip across the map.  Thankfully the saves have been preserved, and you only have to do the last bit of the journey again - but it's still an annoyance.  There is a user-supplied mod available (See the 'guides' page) that allows you to tweak the graphics settings (which appears to be the source of the issue), and it also removes the FPS cap, if such things bother you.  It does seem to have also made some stability improvements.
If you're used to the later Lego games, you'll find this one doesn't hand-hold you quite as much.  There's a few elements that you have to definitely figure out for yourself, but it's no worse for that
I got it in the Steam summer sale 2017 for about £15, and I consider it well worth the money.  The crashes were infrequent, and appear to have stopped with the installation of the mod.
In summary - tad buggy, but full of juicy lego goodness for both adults and kids.
