I am a huge fan of the original X-Com, I used to play it for days at a friend's house.  I've had this in my inventory for a couple years now and finally sat down to play it.  There are hints of that game here... then it falls apart.
First off, the game is linear.  It feels like it's walking you through a tutorial for a looooong time because of this.  You get this awkward hand holding mission to mission.  Meanwhile my whole team is ranking up and getting real powerful.
Then I realize why.  The mechanics in the game are awful.  I'll have an enemy surrounded, make a kill with my sniper, then miss the last guy with the remaining 5.  Then I get to watch as the enemy kills my sniper who is way at the back of my crowd and behind the smoke screen (doesn't count though because he isn't actually in it).  Makes literally 0 sense.
The movement aspect SUCKS.  I'm sorry but you get two moves, only one is allowed to be a shot (with few exceptions). You can't adequately crawl out.  I've had times where a unit see an enemy mid run and I would have taken the shot there, but they keep going and end up in a position that is somehow out of sight.  I don't get another move to correct this because if I move, I won't get to shoot.  Not at all like the original X-Com.
Team sizes are too small.  Really, 6 people, AFTER you train up?
Missions are very linear, as in it's usually a straight line with little lateral size to the maps.  You just crawl across the map.
Sometimes mission triggers (did I mention the whole game is linear?) occur behind you based on the mission mindlessly.  You just cleared an area and the enemy literally gets to drop in behind you.
The spawn mechanics are bad.  You find one enemy, usually it's 2-3 instead. Hope your team is ready to kill them this turn or you are going to take damage, possibly die to a random crit.
Outside of the missions, the strategic global aspect, once again with linear missions, pushes you along.  SO much terror happens you will continuously lose members and you will lose them right away in the first month.
The base map resembles Fallout shelter or a tiny tower rip-off.  It's not interesting.  Mostly because you only work on one base, so there's no strategy to building bases globally.  It's replaced with uninteresting satelite programs, which you have to focus on to get more scientists, engineers, and to prevent countries from dropping funding.  It's such a linear goal in the map screen and by the time you realize you should ONLY be making satelites and more satelite uplinks you lose a country at the end of your first month because it takes too long to build a satelite to keep them around (or if you built one, hopefully you didn't place it blindly).
I miss full teams, I miss building up stats, I miss having to get my team off of the skyranger(or whatever craft you had built up to to carry your team), I miss buying robotic tanks.  I miss having large maps to cover.  I miss being able to do more than one thing a turn, I miss a base system that requires proper coverage on the map, I miss being able to build what I want and sell it to make large piles of money.
There's so much this could have been and it really just has the tech tree and name of the original, but it's a shell of that game.

I thoroughly enjoyed the Steam release of The Room, so I picked this up upon release.
Many reviewers have commented that they found The Room Two to be less challenging, and that's how it seems to me as well.  There were very few instances where I really had to sit and think about (or hunt around for) what to do next.  In some cases, that's because the solutions are often very "literal" (or perhaps "intuitive"), in the sense that objects do exactly what they appear to do, and in many cases you're explicitly told or shown what to do and you just have to find where to do it.  Perhaps my experience in The Room prepared me for The Room Two's puzzles, but I believe developers (especially those of puzzle games) should design sequels that presume the player has experienced the games that came before and ratchet up the challenge accordingly.
That said, I still enjoyed the 3 hours it took me to complete The Room Two.  Even if it wasn't a complete brain-twister, there's the same extreme level of polish found in the Steam release of The Room.   There's defintely more "rooms" in contrast to the previous game's "boxes" and it's all gorgeous to look at.   It's obvious that the game was originally designed for a touch interface, with an abundance of handles to pull, objects to spin, knobs to twist, and secret panels to slide, but those interactions still give a sense of weight and presence even when using the mouse.
If you enjoyed The Room and don't go in expecting the sequel to tie your brain in knots, then you'll probably enjoy coasting through The Room Two.
I'm eagerly anticipating the Steam version of The Room Three, whenever it's ready.

A very unique and different RTS game compared to other RTS titles and 40K games. Battlefleet Gothic is based on the table-top game of the same name, set in the 40K universe during an event known as the Gothic War. Unlike the Dawn of War series or Starcraft, Battlefleet focuses on space-combat, similar to Homeworld, instead of ground-combat.
Gameplay involve building and controlling (in real-time) a fleet of massive, hulking piece of armoured space ships from the many diverse races of the 40K universe. The big and massive hulking, heavily armoured cathedral battleships of the Imperial Navy to the mechanical ramshackles that are the Greenskins ships or the light and highly manuverable Elder ships. Battlefleet Gothic: Armada brings the ships to life. A from time to time, you will enter tactical mode were you'll slow time and move your ships to new positions to either attack or retreat from incoming attacks.
Buy if:
Looking for a new and fresh take on RTS games and you are fan of the 40K or  RTS space battles. Also like micromanaging multiple ships at once and at a fast pace.
Pass if:
Not a fan of RTS Space Combat, Micromanagement, 40K universe or looking for a simpler game.

This is one of the more unique space RTS's I've played, and I've played quite a few. While there are technically three different game modes to choose from, (Story based single player campaign, Skirmish versus AI and Multiplayer versus human), the style of gameplay remains the same across all modes.
Instead of gathering resources with worker drones, building and researching a fleet to go shoot the enemy, and maybe blow up their base (or have yours shot out from under you) in 15-30 minutes, Battlefleet Gothic is all about finite fleet engagements in a very short time. The longest mission I've been on took about 10 minutes, and that was because I was playing squishy speedy Eldar trying not to get shot.
In all missions, you start with a fleet. At the beginning of the campaign, and every time you make a new admiral in Skirmish mode and Persistent Multiplayer, these fleets are really tiny. But, as you complete missions (either by getting ventilated by Tau railcannons or by introducing said Tau to Ork boarding parties), you and your ships recieve experience and renown. Experience gives your ships better crew and better gear, and gives you, as the admiral, more (and bigger!) ships to choose from. Renown is used to buy said ships and gear.
The most unique thing about this game, compared to others in the same genre (Space Combat RTS) is the persistent-ness of the fleets. I've never seen a game that lets you keep ships across Skirmish battles before, and I find that concept really cool and neatly implemented here. Dawn of War II is a helpful comparison here. Your troops and commander leveled up in skirmishes, sure, but every skirmish started at level 1. Now imagine if you could take your level 10 hero from the end of one skirmish, complete with full upgrades, and drop him/her/it right in the start of the next match.
I would certainly enjoy seeing more games using this mechanic, but do note that it has the potential to really screw over the new kid on the block when they bring their level 1 light cruisers into a slug-fest of grand cruisers and battleships. But that's what rankings and balancing are for.

Here are a few things I've noticed while playing Take On Mars:
-Airlocks and other doors are broken.  Airlocks are intended to permit passage between exterior and interior spaces without depressurizing the interior, as opposed to depressurizing everything BUT the space between the two airlock doors.  And regular interior doors have a chance of depressurizng everything as well, even if the pressure on either side is safe.
-Damage to space suits is global, rather than on a per-instance basis.  In other words, if you damage the legs on your medium suit, then take it off and put on a completely unused heavy suit, the legs of the heavy suit are also damaged.
-It's insanely easy to get stuck in geometry.  Attempting to get unstuck is also risky, as the physics engine loves throwing players around at high velocities.
-Things that look like they should fit together don't.  For example, the corners of airlock corridors have the same radius as regular curved walls, but refuse to be attached to anything but airlock passageways.
-The editor is both difficult to use and completely undocumented.  There's no indication that snapping is even a thing in the editor, making it impossible to construct a base outside of the scenario itself.
-Mouse acceleration is ridiculous and impossible to disable, meaning that a movement of the mouse as small as a few centimeters can sometimes rotate the camera completely around three or four times.  (Keep in mind I'm not talking about mouse lag, which is thankfully nonexistent, mouse speed, which can be changed using the incorrectly-named "mouse resolution" setting, or the "fluid camera" setting, which can be disabled.)
I do understand that this is a beta, and thus a number of the things I mentioned will probably be addressed before the game is officially released, but for now I have to give it a thumbs-down.

I found NEOTOKYO to be a wonderful game, if you like Counter-Strike: Source, you'll love this.Basically a more futuristic version of it. A must have F2P game. So basically, download it now. You won't have any regrets if ya don't like it, because it's free!

Worth downloading for the soundtrack alone.
It's also an amazing round based FPS with an emphasis on tactical play over gunplay and reflexes. There's 3 distinct classes (Recon, Assault, Support) each with their own strengths and purposes. Recon is fast and agile with access to thermo-optic camouflage and night vision, while support is a slow juggernaut that sacrifices sprinting for a smoke grenade, thermal cam and stronger armor. Assault is a balance between the two and uses both thermo-optic camouflage and a motion detector.
There's an XP system that allows you to unlock more weapons as the round goes on, but it resets every game. You get XP through kills, assists, surviving the round and completing objectives.
There's two different gamemodes: Team Deathmatch and Capture The Ghost, a sort of Capture The Flag variant where you pursue the upper half of your very own android waifu.
Most maps are centered around CTG and the maps themselves are pretty damn good. Expect lots of sneaky flanking and prolonged, exciting firefights at chokepoints.
While the gameplay is great, Neotokyo's best aspect is the atmosphere. It nails the cyberpunk vibe with its tight urban environments filled with flashy neon lights, various electronic clutter, thoughtful graffiti and references to Japanese pop culture. When you're not fighting in♥♥♥♥♥♥riddled streets, you'll be shooting it out on top of skyscrapers, in military facilities or even in and out a traditional shrine. The two factions, the NSF and Jinrai are as badass as you'd expect. While the NSF is a civilian special-ops group fighting for the government and Japan's constitution, the Jinrai are a nationalistic, militarist terrorist organisation with a clear Samourai vibe in their attitude and looks. There's heavy influences from Ghost in the Shell and it definitely feels like a 2035 Japan. So if you dig the whole cyberpunk subgenre like I do, or if you're just a big weeb, you'll absolutely love it.
Since it runs on the 2006 version of the Source Engine, the game is very outdated graphics and technology wise. Though, that doesn't stop it from looking good aesthetically and that fantastic vibe is still there (in the same way that Half-Life 2 and Deus Ex manage to have that special cyberpunk vibe to them despite looking old). Unfortunately, it does mean that crashes are kinda frequent.
The community is pretty small but there's usually 2-3 servers with lots of activity on them. It's also super friendly and helpful, but due to its nature as a tight, niche game you can expect a vocal minority of elitists.
Did I mention the soundtrack is superb? 'Cos it is. Ed Harrison is a musical genius. You can listen to it in game by typing !radio in the chat. The Ghost in the Shell soundtrack, Industrial, Noise, Drone, Hip-Hop and Jazz all fit the game nicely if you're looking to listen to something else while playing.
It's free to play so be sure to try the game out. You might just find yourself hooked and even if it's not to your appeal, you don't lose much!

I was quite pleasantly surprised when I learned of Battlefleet Gothic: Armada weeks before it entered open beta. Already a big fan of the 40k universe and wishing I could play the original Battlefleet Gothic tabletop, the thought of at least doing so on screen positively excited me. And I was not disappointed.
The game is not an AAA-title, that is true. Nonetheless it is beautifully made. The developers put a lot of effort into getting the visuals, style and atmosphere of space naval combat in the grim dark future right. And while it might not be as perfectly balanced as StarCraft, the gameplay has no reason to be ashamed of itself either. There have been curb-stomps, but there have also been exciting and drawn out clashes with torpedoes screaming through the void and desperate boarding actions.
What this game truly needs, however, is more players. It deserves to have a bigger community than it has.
So I call upon you, naval cadet, to enlist in one of the glorious fleets of 40k!

This game is a lot of fun, I think when you play this game you definitely get the Tom Clancy cold war kind of feel.
Pros: Models, textures, effects, gameplay and sounds are all well done and pretty true to sub warfare. It doesn't fall into the whole hyperactive adhd trend that a lot of games these days focus on to keep the player "entertained" at all times. If you like subsims, you'll love this game. You don't have to micromanage everything, but you still get a good dose of action that requires thoughful strategy.
Cons: Needs some more polish before it really shines. Some of the textures and effects are clearly 2D renders and could be better, like when a sub or ship breaks up or sustains damage. I would have liked to have seen better wrecks, asset collisons, and realistic behavior/effects after being hit with a weapon all around. I also would have liked to have seen a wider range of player subs, animated sections of the sub (like torpedo doors opening and torps going out the tubes)  as well as easier access to mod tools for modders.
I would recommend this game.

Cold Waters is a fun mix between game and sim, a lot of good research went into it and many details are very well reprisented, but the gameplay itself remains fun most of the time. It is not a realistic game in many ways although some argue that the 1964 campaign is more realistic than the 1984 one, however the 64 one is a pain unless you mod it and get some proper subs with proper torpedoes to use :)
It is a game however that is not forgiving, even on easy things can turn from all is fine to o ♥♥♥♥ing hell full dive, flank speed as you get torpedoes airdropped on you in close range. To me there are two main ways to play the game, USN way or Soviet way provided you use a mod to unlock the Soviet subs for player use (can be found on subsim and is really easy to instal). USN is all about beeing as sneaky as you can using your superior sonar and arguably torpedoes. Soviet way is a lot more agressive using speed and active sonar more often to get in close, unleash hell and then run like hell. Both are fun in their own ways.
The Campaigns can be drawn out quite long, or can be completed in a few hours. I completed the 84 campaign in 10 in days in game with just 1 resupply for example. That said I was lucky not to have to deal with the land strike missions or seal team insertions which can be a pain to pull off successfully, but the devs are working on it and that is a key things the devs are very much involved and listening and coming up with changes which is a great boon these days.
So is the game worth getting? Well if you enjoy the setting and a sub sim light I suppose you can call then I would say yess. If you are not sure check out some streams from people like Jive Turkey and see what you think. At 40 Bucks it is a lot for what can be precieved as limited content, but I think how each mission works it is never the same and I rarely feel bored.

Generally I don't like linear first person shooters, but this one stands out. It has an expertly crafted storyline, most likely because it is based directly off of a novel. Playing through on the hardest difficulty, you learn what fear is as you huddle in a dark corner hoping the nosalies don't see you, because you don't have enough ammo to fight them off. Needless to say, I get very attached to characters and like to put myself in their shoes whenever I play a game with a really good storyline. The variety of unique characters and the supernatural elements you encounter in the game add a lot to the connection with the game as well.

This is a really fun game. The good old core mechanics of CoH 1 are there and some minor improvements that really add to the experience. There are also some minor steps back as well, so really this game doesn't amount to better than CoH 1. In fact if you own that game already and enjoy it, keep enjoying it, this game might not be for you.
If you are new to the game alltogether, know it has a steep learning curve. Not as bad as starcraft 2 as far as microing and stuff goes, but it has really deep strategy, and there is a lot to know about the different units and ablities. That being said, it's way easier for a new person to get into than a lot of RTS games. Some of it can been pretty intitutive, as you all know tanks are really powerful and hard to kill with a rifle in real life, well guess what, same holds true in this game.
Pros:
1. While this isn't about gameplay, I think it's important. Graphics are improved. This does look better, but only if you had the hardware to show it off. If your graphics card is just meh or okay, you might think CoH 1 will look better on your PC.
2. Various minor aspects of the game have been changed. I think, whle minor, they are helpful changes.  Examples: Veteran status is displayed as stars above your unit. This makes it easier to see your vets, and to keep them safe. You know longer have to walk straight up to a point to capture it, you just have to be in a circle around the point. This is nice because you can protect your guys a little better, put them in cover.
Cons:
1) game could have been more. I'm not sure what it is, but something is missing. I suppose I expected more out of the sequel to company of heroes 2. Really I just got company of heroes 1 with nicer graphics and minor improvements. Which is fine, since it's still a really fun game, but a little disappointing. If you don't already own the first one, you might as well get this one with the better graphics and minor improvements.
2. U.S. forces is what I play, and it doesn't seem to play the way I expected. Expect the gameplay for the americans to be very different from CoH 1.
3. Game is burdened with earned bonuses and such, that I think imbalance the game. It would take a lot of work to get this game ready for esports. I really just like fair balanced, and consistant gameplay, and while I recongize when you have a game with different factions with their own unique units and ablities, balanced gameplay is really hard to achieve, the little bonuses and things you earn from playing are not necessary.

There  could have been . . .
More interesting factions, the original U.S. Forces for example, were better. They had better units and ways to use them.
Could have created this game better for esports.  Standardized fair and balanced gameplay.
Could have been more focused. They are working on too many factions, campagins and the like. They should be more focused on improving and refining a basic set of factions and the core gameplay. Instead of adding a new faction, add new units to existing factions, balance them, and through help UI improvements.
So while it's fun. I can't recommend it like the original.

This is one of just a few games I've taken the time to review, and I do so because it's just that good. I'm not even going to talk about the graphics (which are breathtaking), but the story itself is gripping. I was very pleased by the ending, and the way it makes sense of the whole ride. It actually reminded me of one of my own stories.
As for gameplay, if you like detective stories, mysteries, spooky settings and the like, then this game is for you. It's an incredible ride through a run-down town looking for a missing kid while all the evidence points to homicidal maniacs killing everyone around. There are traps, puzzles, and some freaky stuff that would be right at home in an HP Lovecraft story. But in the end, it's a mind-bending twist that would put M. Night Shyamalan to shame.
For $20 it's the perfect level of entertainment. There are a few annoying things about it, such as an auto-save design that doesn't let you choose where to save it, so you have to be careful about when you plan on logging off. But for the most part it's a smooth run and so much fun. If your computer can handle the graphics requirements, treat yourself and get this.

I do not like running games, with Deadlight being a bit of a rare exception.
Dying Light is NOT a running game. Yes there is parkour, but still...not really a running game. You could play this game without pressing shift(run) once.
Also, don't expect a lot of "Prince Of Persia"-style hopping and jumping about. Yes, at times it leans towards that, but not quite the same. Not quite the frustration.
Now plenty of people love infinite running games and PoP/Tomb Raider-style jumping about, but I do not like them. I hate them with a passion. Having said that, I do like this game. Yeah, I get mad sometimes, but it isn't a deal breaker.
So what is my one con with this game? NO PROPER SAVE SYSTEM. Look, game developers, (oh no, here goes another Jack Attack) you have to put proper save systems on these games to encourage exploration and FUN. I buy games for 2 reasons: 1) FUN; 2) challenge. But see, if I have 1200 survivor points racked up, it isn't likely I will jump off that tall ledge just to see what happens; I probably won't stay way under water just to see what is down there; and I won't crawl way back into that pipe just to see if it goes anywhere; and that sucks, because like in Witcher 3, you can save before every encounter and reload if you don't like what happened or want to save a part for later.
In this game, it saves when it darn well pleases. NOT GOOD! I believe this is a console developer trick to make the game SEEM longer by having you have to replay stupid or tedious parts longer and repeatedly. This is a dirty ploy. Eh well, what to do but put up with it? Otherwise a good game.

Really nice cafe management game.
Interesting game mechanics:
1. A lot of different items for sale:
a. normal items that you can buy from several shops, some shops are rare and available only temporarily
b. items that you have to farm for in different locations
c. items that you can grow on your own farm (like Ish-World egg that you can get if you buy some chickens for your farm)
d. items that you can make after you sell enough of other items (like selling 200 of Steamed rice allows you to make Ish-World riceballs and Rice porridge from it)
e. items that you can make after you sell a certain combinations of other items (like selling 50 Chileroo tofu and 50 Ish-World clams allows you to auto-buy Chileroo miso soup)
2. Progress in each item
a. at 100 items sold you become able to auto-buy this item in the morning
b. at 200 items sold some items allow you to use them to produce other items
c. at 500 items sold you become able to auto-buy this item at any time when amount reaches 0
d. at 999 items sold you can use some items on altar to gain extra boosts.
3. Different workers accumulate merits by doing their job and become able to do other better jobs (not sure if it is possible to upgrade workers, they seem to be stuck with the same skills forever)
4. No rush. You have to pay about 2k each month, but it is not hard to get that amount and it seems it does not increase later, on the opposite you repay the debt and payment decrease, so you can just focus on developing
There are some problems with the game though.
1. Translation may look confusing so it's better to experiment with different options and ask on forum if you are confused to see if someone else managed to understand the game better and can explain some problem. Personally I did not find this too big a problem, enjoyed exploring and experimenting
2. Crashes happen often and there is no autosave system, so you tend to lose your progress ocassionally if you don't save often. On the other hand all crashes that I've seen are reproducable so if you report them with exact steps on how to reproduce them there is a chance that devs will fix them. Also because they need certain steps to be reproduced you can just avoid those steps and walk around the crash (for example, I had a crash when one guy was requesting a Healthy herb, I just removed the herb from the storage and the crash disappeared. did not complete a quest though). I got another crash that blocked my progress - it happens at the beginning of a day when certain person comes to request an umbrella, so there is no way to avoid it.
Overall I think the game deserves positive review due to interesting mechanics although it still requires some patches.

Whether or not you like the 40k universe I would say that this title is worth your time, if you like grand space battles with lots of explosions and... who doesn't
The game features a campaign which is interesting even if you (like me) are new to the 40k Universe and haven't read/played etc. anything from there before. I would argue that the storytelling rather gets you interested in the 40k Universe, if you weren't before and will want to check more.
Most of your time in the game will be spent maneuvering battles with a varying number of ships that depend on the mission that you choose to accept and pursue. As a result I would think that the space combat will be top notch and work well, thankfully it does. I haven't had any problem with the space combat during play, I find it enjoyable and sufficiently "deep" to require you to take actions and manage your ships properly so as not to lose them all and have to repair the ships with valuable resources.
It is in other words, not an right-click to win type game, that approach miiiiight work, however you are much more likely to lose all your ships long before your opponent does, get outmaneuvered and explode in awesome space fireworks.
The battle maps are all gorgeous looking with fantastic backdrops of black hole, asteroid belts, planets etc. the whole game if beautiful and almost worth the price for the aesthetics alone. ;)
The multiplayer aspect aslo works very well, there are enough people playing that you never have to wait for too long before you find a game and the games are also short enough (time limit 20 min (I have never reached that)) that you won't feel tied to it for too long periods at one time. Also, haven't we all at some point wanted to become admirals of a space armada in a galaxy far far away, build out dream fleet and then use it to explode someone else's in fantastic fireworks? This game lets you do just that.
Overall I would recommend this game to you regardless if you like 40k or not, as long as you are interested in becomming a space admiral, customise your own battlefleet and blow up space Okrz and so on, this game should be right up your alley. I thoroughly recommend it.

This is a really fun game. The good old core mechanics of CoH 1 are there and some minor improvements that really add to the experience. There are also some minor steps back as well, so really this game doesn't amount to better than CoH 1. In fact if you own that game already and enjoy it, keep enjoying it, this game might not be for you.
If you are new to the game alltogether, know it has a steep learning curve. Not as bad as starcraft 2 as far as microing and stuff goes, but it has really deep strategy, and there is a lot to know about the different units and ablities. That being said, it's way easier for a new person to get into than a lot of RTS games. Some of it can been pretty intitutive, as you all know tanks are really powerful and hard to kill with a rifle in real life, well guess what, same holds true in this game.
Pros:
1. While this isn't about gameplay, I think it's important. Graphics are improved. This does look better, but only if you had the hardware to show it off. If your graphics card is just meh or okay, you might think CoH 1 will look better on your PC.
2. Various minor aspects of the game have been changed. I think, whle minor, they are helpful changes.  Examples: Veteran status is displayed as stars above your unit. This makes it easier to see your vets, and to keep them safe. You know longer have to walk straight up to a point to capture it, you just have to be in a circle around the point. This is nice because you can protect your guys a little better, put them in cover.
Cons:
1) game could have been more. I'm not sure what it is, but something is missing. I suppose I expected more out of the sequel to company of heroes 2. Really I just got company of heroes 1 with nicer graphics and minor improvements. Which is fine, since it's still a really fun game, but a little disappointing. If you don't already own the first one, you might as well get this one with the better graphics and minor improvements.
2. U.S. forces is what I play, and it doesn't seem to play the way I expected. Expect the gameplay for the americans to be very different from CoH 1.
3. Game is burdened with earned bonuses and such, that I think imbalance the game. It would take a lot of work to get this game ready for esports. I really just like fair balanced, and consistant gameplay, and while I recongize when you have a game with different factions with their own unique units and ablities, balanced gameplay is really hard to achieve, the little bonuses and things you earn from playing are not necessary.
Unfortunately, while this game may be great for a lot of people, and I'll probably play it from time to time since I already own it, I have to ask myself, would I buy again? The answer is probably not. While this is one of the best RTS out there, it could have been a LOT better.
There  could have been . . .
More interesting factions, the original U.S. Forces for example, were better. They had better units and ways to use them.
Could have created this game better for esports.  Standardized fair and balanced gameplay.
Could have been more focused. They are working on too many factions, campagins and the like. They should be more focused on improving and refining a basic set of factions and the core gameplay. Instead of adding a new faction, add new units to existing factions, balance them, and through help UI improvements.
So while it's fun. I can't recommend it like the original.
Still good, but COH much better.

I would recommend FTL because it is a delightful game with many different features.
Pros:
- Vast rogue-like universe with various races and encounters with abhorrant aliens that will mind control your engineer into destroying the warp core
- Charming Retro graphics; to lull you into a sense of comfort before you watch your ship detonate because you didn't save enough salvage to repair your armor

- Fully customizable space ship and crew so that you become attached to your space friends and your crushing defeats feel worse as you are forced to watch them suffocate because the life support is on fire and the hull breach has disabled the medbay.

Cons:

If you don't have this game, then reading this review would be a waste of valuable time in which you could be acquiring and then playing the game. Go and do it now, I'll wait.
Now you've played it for a bit, I'm sure you'll agree that this is a fantastic game!
At first glance, it's hard to see why FTL is so good. Fairly basic retro graphics? Been done! Text-based story, lots of micro management? Yawn! But dive in, and FTL is a slick, tightly-designed, and massively compelling experience. It all just works.
At its heart, FTL is quite simple, but its core gameplay is polished to a shine. You command a ship, burdened with a heavy duty to save the galaxy, etc, etc. This is explained in a few lines of text and then you're thrown in to managing your plucky little ship. You balance the power, choose from a brilliant range of upgrades, give orders to your crew and operate the weapons and other systems directly. The path you take and the decisions you make determine your success on what will inevitably be one of many, many, runs through. Because you'll lose. A lot. Maybe you'll catch on fire, and maybe accidentally asphyxiate your crew in your attempts to get it under control. Perhaps you'll get out-gunned then have your engines shot into flames as you try to escape. It could be that invaders will run through your crew and smash all of your systems. And the less said about giant alient spiders, the better. (They're no joke.)
What really compels about FTL is that each play through might show you something completely new. There are situations which can branch in different ways depending on how your ship is configured, or what crew complement you have. There are also random events that happen, some requiring very rare sequences of events spanning large portions of the game. Not to mention that each system is a randomly-generated mesh of enemies, traders, shops, and eclectic encounters. The story may be presented in simple bite-size text chunks, but the variety, not to mention the humour, draws you in. It does sometimes feel like all you're doing is rolling the dice, but at other times your quick-thinking and good management can get you a very satisfying win.
The bottom line: FTL may be simple on the surface, but it has a depth and a polish that make it truly excellent.

I see many reviews here bashing EAs version of Battlefront, but I feel it necessary to highlight many problems with this game:
Poor AI. (Forgivable, as the game came out over a decade ago)
Terrbile flight controls.
Inconsistencies with the movies.
Bad hero design.
Bad graphics, if you haven't played this game in a while you might remember it looking better (I did) but the graphics have not held up very well. (Again, forgivable given the game's age)
Can be very problematic on certain hardware setups.
Lack of multiplayer servers without installing a third party program.
And now for the good points:
Nostalgia. Probably the reason most people buy this game. If you had fun playing this game as a child you will probably find some enjoyment in it today.
Multiple Eras. This game spans both The Clone Wars and The Galactic Civil war and features many vehicles and characters from both.
Decent campaign. Overall the campaign is alright, but nothing to write home about. It gives insight into the thoughts of the clone troopers you see in episodes 2 and 3 and shows the Republic's transformation into the Empire from their point of view. The gameplay during campaign missions is fairly simple. It's either: Fight to and objective, capture it, become hero, finish, or fight to objective, destroy it, become hero, finish. It's alright but can become repetitive and boring at times.
Many Maps. Practically every iconic location from the Star Wars movies is represented in Battlefront 2.  The maps aren't particularly well designed, but the do a decent job of portraying the areas and usualy feature an easter egg or two.
I would recommend this game if you are a massive Star Wars fan or someone looking for a nostalgia kick, but compared to many modern shooters, and even some shooters from the time, it doesn't hold up. I may hold an unpopular opinion, but I prefer the newer Battlefront to this one in nearly all aspects besides content. Overall I would give Battlefront 2 a 6/10.

This recommendation comes with a caveat. Although I enjoyed all the hours I spent on this game, there were just too many factors that prevented me from finishing it, much less giving it a definite thumbs up.
First off, let me enumerate what this game gets right:
- Punishing gameplay that rewards smart and patient planning. The best defense is almost always the best offense. Rushing in blindly will most likely get your squad wiped out.
- The base-building, time-management, juggling of funds, and taking risks on missions all make this game a very oppressive experience. In a good way. You're constantly poor and struggling to get by, you make a choice to sell things you might need just to get a bit ahead. You take gambles with every decision you make, each action requiring intense deliberation.
- The difficulty is comparable to having a job. There is absolutely no way you're ready for this♥♥♥♥♥♥but you HAVE to do it, you HAVE to be ready. The game grinds you into the dirt, giving you little time to pull yourself together, so you either give up and get a new job (new game) or soldier through it, licking your wounds and dragging your reputation through the mud because daddy didn't raise no quitter.
- The skill progression of characters provides more and more combat possibilities and new strategies, and each new rank gained could give you a massive tactical boost in battle. Furthermore, you can't help but be attached to your characters, especially if you've given them names, and customized their appearances. Which makes seeing them die all the more devastating.
And now, the bad stuff:
- Allowing the player to save at any point in the battle isn't a very good design choice, since the goal is to force players to deal with their decisions.
- So I can't help but save-scum. It's so easy to do. If it's in the game, then I don't see a problem with using it. But it gets bad because I tend to overuse it. It really sucks having to place your all your trust on an RNG. Mistakenly put your faith in a 90% hit chance only to have everything backfire and go horribly, horibly wrong. In a single move. It punishes you for things completely out of your control. Which is why I feel like it's fair to "cheat" with save-scumming, as I feel like the game "cheats" me with its ridiculous percentages.
- I was doing pretty well until I came to a mission that had 2 of those massive robots that have a million health points, 2 cyber discs, an ethereal, several mutons, and like a hundred armored floaters. And not even my save-scumming could help me get through the level. I pretty much gave up at that point. Turns out daddy raised a quitter after all.
Yes, I understand that these things are what people love about the game. Perhaps it's not about completion but getting as far as you can with what you have. And reaching the endgame for the first time could be the ultimate accomplishment, something akin to earning a Platinum on a PS game.
Nevertheless, I found it exasperating to persist under a system that screws you over with absurd RNG and ridiculously imbalanced enemies. The odds are always stacked against you. But unlike games like Dark Souls, XCOM doesn't give you any hope to recover, and whether or not this is permissible is up to you, as a player.
All in all, I give this game a cautious Thumbs Up, albeit slanted at around 35°.

Primarily a tactical turn-based combat game with a "strategic layer" of base building and UFO interception on a global map.  Your soldiers begin the game with modern day weapons and armor, the aliens come at you with plasma guns and psychic powers.  The weakest enemy in the game can one-shot your rookies at the start of the game, if you aren't careful. You need to capture alien tech (and bodies) for analysis and reverse-engineering so you can learn about your enemy and build the things you need to defeat them.
I love the gameplay.  From hairy tactical battles with aliens, to building up my base and launching satellites to monitor UFO activity, to managing the panic levels in funding council nations around the world.  Everything about the gameplay draws me into the mindset of a military commander trying desperately to learn about and defeat a technologically superior foe.
The game is buggy sometimes.  Mostly visual issues like arms clipping through walls and such, although there are occasionally cases where aliens see you through a wall (mostly happens with rounded surfaces, such as the roofs of landed UFOs, in my experience.)  It's not game-breaking, but it can be frustrating.
Some people also complain that it's hard, which is true in the sense that your soldiers can die suddenly, and a squad wipe mid-game can cripple you.  But these things can be managed by taking the time to learn the game's ways.  And if you feel like cranking it up to 11, check out a third-party mod called "The Long War." ;)

I remember seeing this game when it came out for the Wii U and thougt it looked like fun, however I had no intentions of getting a Wii U.  I was surprised and excited that it came out for PC after all this time.  I'll try to break this review into two segments, 1) Technical and 2) Gameplay.
1)  I understand that the game had some issues at launch and I also had an issue originally but they seem to be fixed.  For me the game would run in a small window (literally smaller than my thumbnail) and I could not get it to get any bigger even after trying to force a different resolution by editing the settings file.  Numerous tweaks and reboots did not have any effect.  I contacted the developers and after a few emails back and forth the game was working as it should after about 2 days.  Turns out, all I had to do was change my desktop resolution from 1080p to something else, apply it, and then set it back to 1080p and presto - it worked.  Apparently it had something to do with the Windows 10 Creators update.  The game has worked perfectly fine after that.  My daughter and I play it on her computer (i3 6100, 8 GB RAM and GeForce 750ti = about 60 fps @ 1080p) and it runs nearly flawlessly.  Everyone once in a while the game lags, although I can't prove it, I believe it's probably the computers fault.  The game has only crashed on us once and we had about 40 hours into the game so far.
2) Gameplay - Many have likened it to a family friendly version of GTA and thats a fair assessment.  There is no foul language and no blood.  There is minor violence since you have to fight other Lego characters.  "Stealing" cars is mostly done by commandeering their vehicle for police use.  I love the open world aspect compared to previous Lego games.  Although there is a story driving you forward in the game, you can still go off and do you own thing and explore.  Although my daughter is only 4 years old, she enjoys playing it and can easily run around and interact with most objects, however she also enjoys just running into the water to be eaten by a shark.  My only real "complaint' I have is about the driving experience, the vehicles seem to be really touchy causing you to wreck all the time, it should be more fluid like the driving experience in GTA V.  As an adult, I enjoy playing this game on my own, however the puzzles, chases and the like are not difficult by any means.  For me I keep playing because I find the story is entertaining and there is a ton to see and do.  So if you are young at heart, get it.  If you have young children that enjoy video games, get it.

LEGO City Undercover is basically a free roaming, platformer and puzzle game where the protagonist, Chase Mccain, goes undercover in order to arrest a notorious criminal and save Lego City. The storyline was very enjoyable and easy to follow mostly due to its superb comedy style. It also includes a 2 player spiltscreen function where both players can enjoy co-op gameplay through the same device.
Positive sides:
-Humourous and easy to follow storyline.
-Very easy gameplay and gentle learning curve.
-What you see in the trailer is what you get.
-Good soundtrack.
-Performace wise is pretty good. (Constant 59-60 FPS even though my computer is only average. Only experienced 2 crashes so far. Got a white screen of death when first launched the game, but fixed that in a few minutes with some Googling and help from Steam forums)
-Graphics is well... Legotastic. Good for a Lego game at least. (There isn't many graphics settings that you can change, which won't make much of a difference)
-Non-violent gameplay to a certain extend. Great game for younger ones or family. (No real weapons, no blood, no vulgarities, can't kill pedestrians etc...)   [It is a Lego game, so it is to be expected]
Negative sides:
-Story length could be improved. (Spent around 16 hours to complete main story which is kind of short compared to other free roaming story based games)
-Free roaming is only truly unlocked after you completed all main story missions.
-Can't skip cutscenes, which is good for the most part since most of the comedy part is from the cutscenes. (The cutscenes were one the most enjoyable part of them game for me)
-Missions sometimes get repetitive over time. (Solving mini puzzles and navigate through obstacles)
-After story mode, although there are a lot of exploration and unlockables left, they are mostly obstacle courses around the map, which can get boring after a while. (Story mode is only about 25% game completion, the remaining 75% are all exploration, obstacle courses and a few side missions)
-Camera angle is bad. In most missions and obstacle courses you do not have full control over camera panning.
-Terrible porting of controls to PC. A controller would make this game much more enjoyable. (Mouse is completely useless. Keyboard bindings are basically placed in a controller layout. Although this can be changed, the amount of control configuration is extremely limited)
-Saving system could be improved. (There is no manual saving. It is all automatic. However, auto save can be triggered quite easily by doing certain things)
In conclusion, the game is pretty good. Majority of the cons isn't the gameplay, but the porting from console to PC itself. Is it recommended? Yes, if you aren't too concern about the terrible port and just want it for the gameplay aspect (By gameplay I mean the main story, since after the main story, things start to get pretty boring in my opinion). Is it worth the full price? No. At least not with the current state that the game is in. I would suggest waiting for a 25-50% sale if you want to get it. If you want the game but is afraid of not being able to play the game due to technical issues like crashes or launching issues, you can always refund the game. (Check out steam refund policy for this)
Overall, I rate this game 6.5/10.

I actually didn't enjoy this second game as much as I had enjoyed the first.
I like puzzling with boxes that have a finite set of surfaces, and not hunting through environments to find some forsaken area to click on.

I was able to solve the first game without a single hint, but this game required me to use the hint system maybe 8-10 times, just because you get lost in a jungle of weird things that you don't know what to do.
...but it's a cheap game, even if I didn't buy it on sale. 5€ isn't much.
The game ends with the developers specifically asking the player to write good Steam reviews and promote the game in order to "help them out", and that REALLY rubs me the wrong way.

Let me just say this...
There are probably a lot of games that do what this has set out to do, better than this has. Maybe more polish, maybe more characters. Story, etc.
But Dark and Light does something for me that I haven't experienced since Dissidia Duodecim... They make the game, but... They give you the reigns, you dictate what happens, how often, if ever, and how much time it takes to do it. That alone is worth the 20 dollars.
As far as the crafting goes, it's pretty good, there are nice modifiers to what you get depending on how you get it. As someone who hasn't really ever played a crafting game, I found myself upset with the game because some enemies have no loot. Well, you're supposed to harvest them with your staff or skin them with weapons. If you use something blunt or use a power attack, you'll get more bones than usual, something slashy, you'll get pelts and fur, and meat. Same with trees, you cut a big tree with a sword, you'll get more twine, use an axe, you'll get logs of wood. Basically, RNG done proper.
Levelling is done in a skyrim esque way, with normal levelling in mind. Killing powerful enemies will let you level up fast, but harvesting properly will give you the skill growth necessary to build weapons and armor. Granted repairing your gear is going to get you to do the same, albiet slower. The game will easily level you to 10 by mistake if you like gathering. And there are probably boosts to it for building houses. (something I haven't done at all yet)
The game is rogue like... If you die, you drop everything. You can omit some drops with heavy coin, but the point is the same. The game is also freaking enormous. And has no map! So if you're about to die, do yourself a favor and take a good look around before you die. The game will leave an obvious marker over your body, and if you die tons of times, there will be a bag there instead of your body... the bag doesn't display a timer for when it vanishes, but my stuff was in there so I never waited around to get to it. Again, this game is huge, the areas in the game aren't really the same, but the mountain peaks and designs sort of do, so do yourself a favor and try to measure where you're at instead of seeing the entire map save for the big island trying to find your home base's castle with the back hanging off the mountain. I wanted to get back to the human camp, and ended up finding the elves and dwarves before looking up a map. When your life, and more importantly, your stuff, is on the line, that is a real bummer.
There are items to craft that take you back to your faction. And there are probably house tools like teleporting. Point is, be careful, because it'll probably take a great mount, or some serious know how to get to some places in time.
The graphics are pretty darn good.
In my opinion the character faces seem like they are the weakest link to the design, but I didn't spend very long on it. The last thing I wanted was to be stuck with a game that I didn't want because I spenf two hours messing with the face. The sky and nights are beautiful, and the days are vibrant and colorful... Not god ray beautiful, but pretty close, there was a light option I didn't check, especially after I haf to update the display driver. If you have an old nvidia driver, this game will crash and reliably freeze until you task manager out of it, and it will say your display driver has crashed. If you don't want to update your driver... Don't even try playing this, it will freeze.
In terms of combat... I doubt that's why you are playing this unless you want pvp. But my only gripe outside of that is that some spells need precise aim. The first fireball spell you get makes a large explosion, but only really does the splash damage if you hit an enemy. Maybe I'm wrong but that's what I saw.
And now, for the bad news. Money/Gold has to be the worst implemented thing next to the poor number of npcs you actually interact with. There are only shopkeepers from what I've seen... Even when seeing in every town, they all have their scattered shops, and that's kind of it. So basically the game is a gathering sandbox that has rougue like death in it because...?
There is enough map and mass in this game to hold off someone who's actually playing it for probably 30 or 40 hours, more if they were playing it right and knew how to survive properly without turning the harvest multiplier up. There seems like there are quite a few things going on on the map that need explaining... And there are very interesting places to go, and places I haven't even dared go to yet due to extreme heat or cold.
All in all, this is a 20 dollar sandbox that has enough options to keep you there without buying anything extra or praying the servers stay up. As someone who loves MMO quality and quantity, but not with forced online interactivity, it is a wonderful stroll in a large mass environment with lots to do and lots of loot to run home with. Things I can't get enough of. I haven't even used a mount either. Something I probably need to do to see everything.

This is a good thing because the game could really use an injection of more players and a welcoming environment is key for that.
The one thing that was extremely frustrating is the lack of balance to some of the monsters. Specifically the Vicious Barghesh. They are hard for even really geared players to kill and pretty much invincible to new players and they spawn all over the place. To add salt to the wound these and similar enemies also camp your corpse so you have no chance of retrieving what little you had. Recent patches introduced bonus character stats through the various skill trees and now the player character in general survives much better after progressing through the levels a bit which feels very nice.
My only gripe now is poor support. A game in early access should have an active support team. After having been raided by hackers/cheaters and making a report all i got was an automated response asking for information all of which i had already provided in my original report.
I still very much recommend the game as it is evident development is moving along nicely. There is a new dungeon coming in the near future updates as well as airships which is very exciting. I'm just hoping for new creatures to roam the lands too and some improvements to building system to allow more interesting structures.

As both an avid gamer and a longtime fan of 40k, I would rate this game as slightly better than average.
PROS:
-Superb 10/10 immersion, from graphics, to music, to voice acting this is one of the best portrayals of the 40k universe.
-Awesome battles - from booming broadsides to whooping when you land a full torpedo strike. Cruiser clashes can be a decisive decapitation or drawn-out slugfest
CONS:
-Steep, STEEP learning curve. There's a great deal of nuance and subtlety to this game. Aside from the barebones intro, you're essentially left to learn for yourself faction and ship strengths and weaknesses. I would recommend playing skirmish mode A LOT to learn the basic strengths and weaknesses of each ship and faction.
-Repetitive: There are only about 5 different mission types, and after a while, gameplay becomes very repetitive.
-Absolutely brutal single player campaign: unless you've gone through the campaign a few times as a test run, or rung up enough hours in skirmish to know the ropes you are going to be punished by the single-player campaign. Don't expect help, or scaled victory conditions, you will seriously be coming up against some pulling-your-hair-out-punching-your-fist-through-the-monitor difficulty levels.
That said, it's still a fun game more often not, especially if you're a fan of 40k or the BFG tabletop game.

Pros:
+ unique atmosphere
+ attention to detail
+ faithful to source material (one of the best sci-fi books ever written)
+ many interesting NPCs
+ amazing music and sound effects
+ some epic moments
+ many different modes and gameplay possibilities (from stealth to gun-blazing)
Cons:
+ I would love to have more interaction and spend more time in the settlements in the metro stations
+ shooting part is perhaps not the best feature. I love the game experience as a total much more than the action part (I got the same impression from first Bioshock)
+ sometimes AI is strange
+ rail parts are perhaps too generic.
As a final note I wish that a MMO or RPG game (in the spirit of Witcher) comes out based on the super rich universe of the Metro.

I picked this game up about a year ago when it was f2p, with a pro subscription. I will start off by saying I think ten bucks flat is better since you get all the added features and the features that were previously reserved only for premium subscribers. The game itself is a modernization of q3a and it brings the game into the modern age with some gameplay features. No added classes and other♥♥♥♥♥♥ but modern features like workshop integration, custom maps, a modern looking server browser, etc. I have put over 1000 hours into this game over the course of this past year and see myself playing it till it is 100% dead. It is so easy to get started, mess around with friends in free for all, ctf, etc. Though, if you are more of the competitive type, you will find game modes to suit your play. Though be warned, getting exceptionally good at this game requires you to go down the figurative rabbit hole and practice self-control, coordination, self-reliance, and humility. In duel (the mose common competitive mode) particularly. In duel, it is 1v1 and the goal is to just be a better player than your opponent. I have put  a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of time into practice, reviewing demos, watching and studying pro-matches, etc. This game is such a basic fps on the surface but makes you practice creating quick strategies, forward thinking, and the ability to read an opponent to predict how they will play. If you play this game and get very good, the skills you learn will carry over into other games i.e. counter strike, COD, UT4, Overwatch, and quite possibly, Quake Champions. Only time will tell what the future holds for these cut throat, unforgiving FPS games, but as of now, Quake live is an incredible game and I can not recommend it enough for casual and competitive play alike.

The next run fared little better with the ship catching fire and the crew burning to death while I watched helplessly when I should have been venting the air to quell the fire.
So with a heavy heart I began again on Easy difficulty. Shame! The battes were easier and the upgrades came thick and fast. I finally reached sector 5 and my first achievement. Happy days. Then Sector 6. In a dark nebula I was visciously attacked without provocation by a ship that could shut down the door control to my ship. I was on fire from two seperate sources with no way to vent oxygen to stop it and still under attack from a ship that I could barely scratch the shields of. Two crew died failing to put out the fires despite running back and forth to the med bay to be healed. The enemy finally vanquished I regained control of the doors and hid in the cockpit while the fire was starved and died.
After this epic encounter I became more cautious and managed to limp to the Boss level only to be mercilessly stomped. ON EASY LEVEL. I haven't beaten it yet but i think if I just............
To sum up:
Pros:-
Fantastic feeling of control :- From the power management to the ordering of crew and aiming of weapons the control of the game is easy to pick up. You feel like you are the captain of a starship. "More power to the shields! Fire in Med Bay! Open the airlock and suck the buggers out!"
Fantastic feeling of being out of control :- Despite the above and the ability to pause time you are rarely in total command of an encounter, grinding through opponent after opponent. You have to adapt and play on the fly as well as using well practised strategies.
Pitch perfect graphisc and sound :- The art style is basic but stylish and often amusing. Yes, that is a worm creature running the shield console and yes, that pirate in the engine room was just eaten by your praying mantis chief engineer. To be honest 3d graphics and sparkly effects would add nothing to the experience as you really don't have time to wow at the lens flare. The game music is in an 8bit retro style but is acomplished and catchy. I was humming the tunes in a bathroom break earlier.
Awesome, Outstanding, Original Gameplay :- I won't go on and on and spoil the surprises but just imagine a kind of RTS, TBS, RPG, with a hint of TD with a load of other cool acronyms thrown in for good measure and you still will be way short of how complex the game is.
Cons:-
I should have bought this game 6 months ago when I first spotted it. Oh the wasted time...

What I wanted from this was a vague representation of the realities of a Cold War gone Hot. A chance to see what it would be like if the technically superior US / UK boats had to go up against their generally inferior USSR counterparts. Sneaking up on your Russian enemies using your quieter boat, tagging them with your suprerior Sonar systems and then being able to decide if shooting and giving your position away is worthwhile or holding fire for a better chance.
This is not this game. To put it in simple terms every encounter comes down to shoot them before they shoot you. The concept of running silent, running deep, deciding to keep at all quiet and hope the bad guy gets in to a good position to shoot at or risk it all and run the course before dropping to all quiet and sitting like a 'hole in the water' does not exist at all in this game.
It's clear that the game is meant to be a game version of Hunt For Red October because the in game engine, display and controls give plenty of opportunity for launch counter measures and tanks blow let's put her on the roof gameplay but once the novelty has worn off you see what a shallow gameplay mechanic it is.
The encounters all revolve around assign a fire solution and kill them before they detect you, if they detect you then go full last half hour of Hunt For Red October and hope the five torpedos the enemies have launched at you miss. The only issue is the game has mission in it that actually force you to use stealth, that force you in to waters where you simply cannot recreate those action packed scenes from Hunt For The Red October and when you're crawling along at 1/3 with 'all quiet' and then enemy is showing no signs of seeing you and then all of a sudden they open up with their rocket propelled depth charges and hit your EXACT location to within an 8th of an inch, the illusion that this game is anything more than an arcade sub driving action game is lost.
Oh don't get me wrong it can be tense and it can be fun but it only works when you are in the correct parts of the map doing the correct missions. Those are fleet hunts in deep waters. Any mission that requires work that involves real stealth or takes part in shallow water and you are going to have a bad day and worse still the game does not allow you to pick the location. Once an engagement starts you are forced to engage, now if the situation didn't work in my favour I could at least sit on the bottom and use time accelerate, then quit out once the enemy has moved on, but the enemy doesn't move on, they seem to know you are there and they will hunt and in most cases find you (yup even sitting on the bottom, all quiet with no engines running) and kill you. You are forced to engage. You can if you're lucky go deep, turn away from the enemy and then run at full steam and hope you can get clear, only problem you then leave the engagement drop back to the world map only to then get immediatly put back in to the engagement map with the same enemies you just ran from.
The game looks great, the gameplay is simple but can be fun and tense, but only in the right mission types but it isquiet a long way from being a simulation.
I personally thought this would be like Silent Hunter 3, but more updated and with more content, all i found was complete boredom followed by dissapointment.

If you're looking for a review you're at the wrong place, but heres a receipe for spaghetti!
Step 1: Get Your Supplies
Before you can start making your spaghetti you will need to first get the proper supplies and materials. To make this spaghetti you will need:
a box of spaghetti
a jar of marinara sauce
1-2 pounds of ground beef or Italian sausage
two large pots, one for boiling the pasta and the other for making the sauce
serving untensils
salt
water
You can use as much meat as you want, really - but anywhere from 1-2 pounds per large jar of sauce should work out best. I tend to use 1 pound of meat nearly every time.
Step 2: Cooking the Meat + Get the Water Boiling
Before you start, fill up a large pot with water and add a handful of salt. Put it on the stove and turn it to high so it'll start boiling!
Next you will need to cook the of meat. Take all of the meat out of its container and set it all in a large pan, then put the pan on the stove and set the stove to medium.
After that you will need to break the meat into smaller pieces. When the meat is in small pieces you will then need to start flipping the meat and make sure it gets brown all-around and cooked thoroughly. The cooking should take approximately 10-15 minutes. When all of the meat is brown and cooked you can add in the sauce.
Step 3: Mixing in the Sauce
Next you will need to mix your marinara sauce with your cooked meat. Take your jar of marinara sauce and pour all of it on the cooked meat and then stir it all around until it is all blended together. Then turn the heat down to low and let it simmer while you cook the pasta.
Step 4: Cooking the Spaghetti
Once the water has come up to a boil, you can throw the spaghetti in. Typically it should cook within 7-11 minutes - just follow the time on the box!
Make sure to stir every couple minutes to keep it from sticking.
Depending on your timing, you can either strain the spaghetti and set it aside, or you can put it right into the sauce.
Step 5: Serving Your Spaghetti
You can do this in a lot of ways but I prefer mixing the noodles in the pan with the sauce. I use tongs to drain the noodles and place them in the sauce, and then put in a couple spoons of pasta water. Stir it all together really well - the pasta water coats all the noodles and lets the sauce stick more.
You can also put plain spaghetti on individual plates and spoon the sauce over top. Whatever works for you.
Top with cheese and enjoy!

A good puzzle game, short and sweet (4~5 hours) in a visually stunning setting, probably some of the best graphics of a video game. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a beautifully eerie mystery game with its roots firmly planted in the surreal and abstract. Everything from the gorgeous visuals, to the evocative yet subdued soundtrack, even the slow paced Adventure-esque gameplay and non-linear narrative, all aid in creating in atmosphere that I've never quite experienced in any other game before. It's a puzzler that allows you to take your time with everything, and absorb completely into its world. Although clocking in at a short 4-5 hours, I'd say any longer and it would've grown stale. This title knows it needed to be short and very, very sweet. With an interesting story, an ambigious ending, and simple but engrossing gameplay I can't say I'd do anything but recommend this game. I do not like running games, with Deadlight being a bit of a rare exception.
Dying Light is NOT a running game. Yes there is parkour, but still...not really a running game. You could play this game without pressing shift(run) once.
Also, don't expect a lot of "Prince Of Persia"-style hopping and jumping about. Yes, at times it leans towards that, but not quite the same. Not quite the frustration.
Now plenty of people love infinite running games and PoP/Tomb Raider-style jumping about, but I do not like them. I hate them with a passion. Having said that, I do like this game. Yeah, I get mad sometimes, but it isn't a deal breaker.
So what is my one con with this game? NO PROPER SAVE SYSTEM. Look, game developers, (oh no, here goes another Jack Attack) you have to put proper save systems on these games to encourage exploration and FUN. I buy games for 2 reasons: 1) FUN; 2) challenge. But see, if I have 1200 survivor points racked up, it isn't likely I will jump off that tall ledge just to see what happens; I probably won't stay way under water just to see what is down there; and I won't crawl way back into that pipe just to see if it goes anywhere; and that sucks, because like in Witcher 3, you can save before every encounter and reload if you don't like what happened or want to save a part for later.
In this game, it saves when it darn well pleases. NOT GOOD! I believe this is a console developer trick to make the game SEEM longer by having you have to replay stupid or tedious parts longer and repeatedly. This is a dirty ploy. Eh well, what to do but put up with it? Otherwise a good game.

TL;DR
Still rough around the edges and it's clearly a mod of ARK: Survival Evolved. The animations aren't polished, combat isn't good and progression can be tricky because many skills don't have a proper description of what you have to do to increase them. This game has potential, it will be ARK with magic but as it is right now it's quite punishing for new players, especially when it comes to combat.
Full review:
The following is based on my experience playing on a private single player server with xp and resource yields increased to 5x to compensate for being a lone wolf.
Progression:
Works well overall, you raise skills by doing whatever is related to them. Like gathering wood gets you to level 1 wood structure crafting. Some descriptions are still just placeholders like to raise survival skill you need to do survival 1, survival 2, survival 3. Not very helpful but you can get around that because whenever an activity increases your skill by 1% the games displays the progress on the corner of the screen. Also I get the impression it would be quite grindy at 1x xp gain.
Combat:
Probably my biggest beef with this game right now, you'll get killed by just about anything that fights back if you don't use the terrain to stay out of reach and have already reached a level where you can craft some sort of ranged weapon/combat spell. Armor and extra HP from levelling up don't help much, shields are pretty useless because creatures just atttack you non-stop with a very short interval between attacks, have no stamina limit and you can't attack with your shield raised. So you either trade blows (and most likely die) or sit there with your shield raised trying to block the next attack. Running away only works if the weakest animals are chasing you, the others run faster than you and will catch up just as easily as they will kill you.
Exploration:
Can be quite hard because you're such an easy prey.
Building:
Pretty good but that's mostly because it's the same system as ARKs. Building parts have huge amounts of HP, so even a straw house can hold back a pack of wolves for a very very long time, I wish they weren't so strong because upgrading to the other materials becomes pointless since straw houses are nearly indestructible already.
Magic:
Works ok but could be better. You have to craft spells and they have durability, so they break if you cast them too much and need to be repaired which is odd. Also you can only equip one combat spell at a time, having to open your inventory and drag another to the slot if you want to switch, very cumbersome during combat. You can also craft runes which are used like any other comsumable, equip on the hotbar and hit the appropiate key to cast, much better than the combat spells.
Overall the game is fun if you're into survival/open world, it still needs a lot of polishing before I'd say it's a good game but the potential is there.

Disclaimer: Have you ever wandered trough Steam, checking out several games, their screenshots, checking them out to add to the wishlist (or buying them right there on the spot)? Well, I did. It was a cold winter sales, Steam made a huge sale on this game, the screenshots didn't promise much but since I'm generally hyped for Sci-Fi ships games I went away and got it. Well, it was cheap, it was indie (I like to support indie developers) so it wouldn't be a total loss. I downloaded the game (pretty small download) and the next few hours of my life were lost in this brilliant masterpiece.
This game is an RTS/RPG mixture in wich you have your own ship and crew with minimalistic graphics, you travel trough space and sometimes you encounter some enemy ships (or you decide to turn hostile on them). You have to controll your crew and the game ends when they die. Pretty easy until here right? Now add up the fact that you have several modules on your ship, upgrades, money, fuel and ammunition. Getting more complex isn't it? Now add up the fact that you are prompted with most of the choices you have to do like, for example, you detect a ship who's requesting help, you go near it and they approach you with a question like: "We got out of fuel, could you give us some?" and then they prompt you with 2 choices: a) Give them the fuel (and wander if they'll give you something when you reach a safe spot or maybe you're just a good soul); b) Kill them and steal their money and ammunition. All of this and much more, make one of the most fun, innovative and immersive games I've played recently.
Overall: 9/10
Words can't describe this game at all. It's a immersive experience without using pretty graphics. Using it's own originality it conquered a space among most of the AAA games I've played and I don't regret a single penny from what I paid.
PS: They upgrade everyone to Advanced Edition without asking for a single extra buck, +1 for that!

I played the original rainbow six for the playstation in my younger days. It was a game that at the time, I couldn't necessarily comprehend fully, but I still loved it. I kept meaning to look into a game that offered me the methodical tactical based "choose where your team enters and what they do" gameplay that the original offered. I considered getting swat 4, but I felt that rainbow six was probably going to be the better choice. This however, was merely nostalgia.
In this game, you cannot select where you enter a conflict. There are set spawn points for you and your team and you cannot select any other spawn points or set your own at your descretion. You also seem to have less equipment or at least less equipment that isn't context sensitive, nor does your team really function like an actual counter-terrorism team. Or anything close to that. Your team are essentially two mediocre robots that you send out to either get shot or open doors. Not only do they lack personality but they're totally unnecessary. You could probably complete this entire game on the hardest difficulty with heavy armor, a heavy machine gun and nothing else. The maps aren't very creative in the way they're layed out. They're essentially layed out like counter-strike levels with enemy bots. If you want this type of experience, I recommend looking up a half-life 2 modification called "smod tactical" as it looks and feels better. It offers much more difficulty and you actually feel like you're doing something to your enemies.
This brings me to the other negative of this game. The weapons simply don't feel powerful. Even the strongest weapons in the game feel like sub-machine-guns firing nine milimetre rounds. There's no intensity, barely any difficulty, little creativity and fairly little fun.
If you're one of the people who might think this game might have a good story or good writing to carry the experience, then I regret to report that this game isn't what you're looking for either. From what I remember of the campaign, it felt like a typical call of duty game. Bad guys, shoot them. Help your personality lacking goons do something. Wait at the door until the scripted event triggers to open it. It isn't that fun, as a matter of fact I'd say that a call of duty might actually be better to buy than this. The gameplay in this is less fun and the level layouts are about as linear, if not more so. This game also has the distinct feeling of being a bit of a budget title. I've not researched the game's development, so I can't tell if it is one or not, but it certainly feels that way, and for a series that I would have called one of the greatest tactical shooters of all time at one point in my life, the fact that it has reached such a low note is tragic.
This game is worth just about as much as it costs. Do not expect it to really satisfy you in any real way. I wouldn't tell you to outright avoid it, but it's not that great and I abandoned playing it a quarter of the way through. Opting for instant action instead of campaign.

I played The Room and saw that this was now on sale, so I decided to pick it up.
I'm not one for beating around the bush, so I'll just start off by saying that even though I recommend it, it is definitely not as great as the first game. The puzzles seem way more simple, as if you can easily intuitively know where to go and what to look at next, and how to solve it. The largest example I can give for this is a part where you must navigate a map, and instead of cunningly making it some kind of riddle, they just laid out how to do it. It felt like I was just following instructions laid out for me, and this was not the only part that contained "clues" like this.
Difficulty aside, one other thing that really tugged at me was the buggy controls when interacting with some objects. There are specific parts where you must precicely control levers or dials, but cannot due to the fact that when you grab hold of it, it decides to flail around in every direction possible at mach speed. I'm not entirely sure if it was just my game personally messing up, or if it's everyone. If it is the later, I hope they release a patch for it because messing with certain objects took such a long time that it added about 45 minutes onto my playtime, and the extra time was certainly not enjoyable.
In the end, if you really enjoyed The Room and want more of it, go ahead and grab The Room Two. It's only five dollars, so there's not much harm even if it's not as good as the first game. If you didn't care for the first game either way, then maybe you should save that five bucks and use it on something more useful.
