The Room Two is an excellent blend of the puzzle and horror genres.
Each chapter of the game throws you in a room containing a highly sought-after treasure.
Your task is to solve different puzzles in order to get the treasure. Along the way, you learn about the story behind the
treasure, which typically sheds some light of both the importance and dangers of what you're after. The unraveling of each room's story with its eerie environment provides a great sprinkle of horror into the game, to the point where any door opening or strange sound is enough to send chills down your spine.
In terms of mechanics, it's a point-and-click game with mostly physical and mechanical puzzles. The point-and-click mechanism works very well as it allows the player to focus on the important areas, diving into the central element of the game: the puzzles.
The puzzles are challenging but well designed: you'll be forced to keenly observe the environment, come up with insightful ways to use items, and figure out how different objects fit with each other. In return, you'll be faced with balanced puzzles with no cheap solutions, that will provide inmense satisfaction once you figure them out. The game also provides optional hints if you get stuck, so the game never becomes frustating.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys puzzles, and to horror fans who prefer a creepy atmosphere over jump scares.
Here's my playthrough of the first chapter:

Short and easy, but has an exelent atmosphere, and quite impressive visuals.
Altho it wasn't a big challenge, it was quite entertaining.
Would buy a third installment.

Before saying anything else, I'll highly recommend that you also purchase and play through the first game, The Room. I bought it at a measly $1.32 during the summer sale, but I would pay full price for both games.
The Room Two offers slightly more challenge than its predecessor. I personally didn't find the puzzles in either game extremely difficult, although there were maybe one or two occasions in The Room Two where I had to use a hint to move forward (I might have found the solution eventually after lots of clicking, but still). The puzzles are challenging enough to hold your interest and, when combined with the fantastic controls and feel of operating the puzzles, feel rewarding to solve. The chapters also feel longer than in the first game. I reckon it only took around an hour for me to beat the first game, and The Room Two took around two hours to beat. Each chapter in The Room Two, including the tutorial, is centered around an entire room containing multiple objects and pieces of furniture that you have to switch between to eventually find the glyph that opens the door to the next chapter. In this sense, The Room Two does nothing but improve on the last game. If you weren't a huge fan of using the eyepiece so much in the first game, you'll be happy to find that they've reduced the amount you need to use it in The Room Two.
The storyline delivery is unchanged from the first game; appearing in notes scattered around each chapter, the story is "there" enough to feel like the game has a story that you're following, but is never shoved in your face and never holds you back from progressing through the game at a steady pace. While I wouldn't say the storyline or delivery is necessarily improved significantly from the first game, it is definitely done as well, and is done in a way that I love for this type of game.
The atmosphere changes slightly from what I felt to be more of an alchemic mystery from the first game into more of an eldritch horror atmosphere in The Room Two. It definitely captures some level of horrific/creepy/unsettling atmosphere above what the previous game did. This isn't to say that one has a better atmosphere than the other at all; they're simply slightly different. Both games achieve the same quality on establishing their atmosphere.
The Room games are cheap, quick puzzle games that cram an Eldritch story of Alchemy's darkest pursuits into a short burst while still pulling off the story and atmosphere better than most video games I've played. The Room Two improves on the puzzle aspect of the games in every way from the first game. I can't recommend these games highly enough.

I had undoubtedly high expecations of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. In the week or so leading up to my purchase of the game, I hyped myself up by reading all sorts of articles about the unique way it presents itself, and also many articles about photogrammetry, a texturing technique used heavily in the game. Given how high I set the bar, it's not entirely surprising that my expectations weren't quite met.
Story: 7 - The story and it's presentation was touted as being the high point of Ethan Carter. I was told in advance that none of the puzzles would be too tricky, and that was fine with me. The main thing I was looking for was an interesting story that you could really dive into. Ethan Carter, described by one of the articles I read about it as being "unabashedly bookish" was really nothing of the sort. The "story" aspect of it, which involves a series of murders that the player has to solve, was relatively mundane and far too short to be truly interesting. Each of the murders took a few minutes to solve, and since none of the murders were truly motivated by anything, the only question you end up solving is "how" and not "why". Once you've solved them all you're left with a feeling that you've uncovered the nature of a very short-term event that just sort of happened.
Character: 6 - Perhaps the most important thing to me in any storytelling experience, be it a video game, movie or television program is the characters. Even a story that doesn't move much can be very enjoyable if it features characters that the audience can come to like or relate to. With regard to that, Ethan Carter has a small cast of characters, most of which have no more than a few lines and none of which are particularly accessible. As such, you never really come to like or dislike any of the characters, so it's hard to care about what happens to them.
Animation: 9 - The aesthetic aspect of the game is, in my opinion, one of the places where The Vanishing of Ethan Carter really shines. The whole game is absolutely beautiful, both on the large and small scales. As you walk across the bridge at the beginning of the game, you see the entirety of Red Creek Valley unfold in front of you and you know this is going to be an exceptionally good looking game.
Sound: 10 - The music is another very high point of the game, as it perfectly sets the mood and always leaves you feeling a bit tense and uncertain. You always feel like there's something out there, watching your actions and waiting for you. More than one time I found myself checking my surroundings to make sure that the accellerating tempo of the music wasn't suggesting that something was coming for me.
Enjoyment: 8 - This category has to do with how I felt while playing this game. Simply put, I enjoyed playing this game because I never felt completely sure I knew what was going on. I knew that something was going on, but I was never sure what the implications of that thing were for me. There was good variety in the things you experienced as you played the game, which always left you feeling like you might encounter something new once you got to your next destination. This made you eager, and somewhat anxious, to find and solve the next puzzle.
Overall: 8 - While the characters and the story were somewhat uninteresting, the mood produced by the stunning visuals and music made this game quite enjoyable to play. Is it worth the price that the developers and Steam are asking for it? Maybe, maybe not. The game is very short, and is certainly not the perfect game. Oddly enough, I'd say it's worth playing to find out the very answer to that question.

This game deserves a bigger community. It's amazing and free.. I mean, really.. what reason would you have for NOT trying it?
I suggest checking the key binding before you hop in and either note or rebind what the optic camo and vision toggle keys are, you are going to want to use those.
Basically, you are playing capture the flag, but the flag is called a "ghost." The player who picks up the ghost can choose to actively hold it and it will give them the ability to see how far away and in what direction the enemies are.. but while holding the ghost, the player is left defensless. This adds a strategy to the game, and promotes team play and use of the mic. Simple data can be said quickly over the mic (Bogie 20 meters north).
It is also worth mentioning there are 3 different class types. Recon has thermo optic camo and can jump about 15 meters while running. Assault class has better armor than recon, but can't long jump while running. Support is slow, can't run, but has tons of armor and has heat vision instead of the movement based vision toggle like the other 2 classes. Also, more guns are unlocked as you gain points during a map. More kills means more weapons to choose from.
Don't forget to join a squad so that you can see where your team is!

Disclaimer: Have you ever wandered trough Steam, checking out several games, their screenshots, checking them out to add to the wishlist (or buying them right there on the spot)? Well, I did. It was a cold winter sales, Steam made a huge sale on this game, the screenshots didn't promise much but since I'm generally hyped for Sci-Fi ships games I went away and got it. Well, it was cheap, it was indie (I like to support indie developers) so it wouldn't be a total loss. I downloaded the game (pretty small download) and the next few hours of my life were lost in this brilliant masterpiece.
This game is an RTS/RPG mixture in wich you have your own ship and crew with minimalistic graphics, you travel trough space and sometimes you encounter some enemy ships (or you decide to turn hostile on them). You have to controll your crew and the game ends when they die. Pretty easy until here right? Now add up the fact that you have several modules on your ship, upgrades, money, fuel and ammunition. Getting more complex isn't it? Now add up the fact that you are prompted with most of the choices you have to do like, for example, you detect a ship who's requesting help, you go near it and they approach you with a question like: "We got out of fuel, could you give us some?" and then they prompt you with 2 choices: a) Give them the fuel (and wander if they'll give you something when you reach a safe spot or maybe you're just a good soul); b) Kill them and steal their money and ammunition. All of this and much more, make one of the most fun, innovative and immersive games I've played recently.
Overall: 9/10
Words can't describe this game at all. It's a immersive experience without using pretty graphics. Using it's own originality it conquered a space among most of the AAA games I've played and I don't regret a single penny from what I paid.
PS: They upgrade everyone to Advanced Edition without asking for a single extra buck, +1 for that!

This one's tricky to review, as it suffers from some serious issues but has many redeeming qualities. Overall, I recommend it.
To start with the bad, some NPCs you'll collide with, some you won't; monsters pop around and clip with everything; sometimes sound will be synced, sometimes not; flashlights shine through walls; guns don't feel very "punchy", kills are unsatisfying; child voices sound like adults obviously putting them on; night vision sometimes randomly turns on and off,  and will be stuck on through cinematic sequences.
My biggest complaint: no explanation whatsoever of what the mysterious (SPOILER ALERT) dark figures are, and yet they pretty much haunt you the entire duration of the game.
THE GOOD: you can clearly tell this game was based off a book because the writing is awesome, the story is immersive, it's what kept me going. The tunnels and stations are ambient, I loved listening to NPCs interact, the voice acting was good for the most part. The majority of the game you spend with at least one other companion, and it makes for less of a horror-like experience, which, to me, is a good thing. I appreciated a little company when having to traverse Moscow's mutant-ridden metro system.
Anyway, decent game despite it's few issues, I recommend it!

What a game....
This is one of ,if not the greatest story based FPS i have ever played!!!
Set in the post apocalyptic metro of Moscow in the year 2033 ,this game brings you closer then any other ,from station to station you can feel the struggle in which the metro's people have to endure ,whether it be mutant ,bandit ,or just the harsh conditions left from the atomizing of the world. One thing that stood out to me was the immersion ,from the realistic sounds ,to wiping my gas mask ,and topping it up with filters i have scavenged ,the transition from the metro to the surface is one of the greatest gaming experiences ,due to the sheer detail in which both areas have been constructed.... the contrast of these areas is enough to take ones breath.
The gun play is actually really satisfying ,and after playing many FPS ,simulator or not ,this excels at creating a feeling of power ,and realism to each and every gun (which are all unique). The customization is a great add on to the game ,it allows you to kit out your shooter to how you like it ,mostly between stealth ,long range or a more close and personal PDW.
The enemies in this game vary greatly ,from bandits to mutants to even the Nazis ,each and every one behaves differently leading to a somewhat challenging combat system ,if new to the gerne ,and even some veteran players could be caught off guard. The characters in this game haven't got too much back story ,but the development throughout the game keeps you questioning their beliefs ,and keeps you intrigued.
I would recommend to anyone who likes the post apocalyptic  gerne ,with a little horror added to it along with good shooter aspects. wish i played the first metro 2033 before redux ,but if like me you haven't had the chance ,please get this game!

I think this game strikes a nice balance between sim and arcade, for me anyway.  Obviously your milage may vary there, but suffice to say that the game isn't too complex (you can finish the tutorials in like an hour, leaving you with a mostly full understanding of the games controls), but it's also slower paced than an action game, and your actions have to be well thought out if you want to survive.  On top of that, the game's mechanics are surprisingly deep; your sub's blind spots, water temperature differences, water density effects on your sound levels, and many other physical aspects you have to understand and account for if you want to be successful.
And of course, some of the situations you get into here are tense as hell.  When you have a partial signature on an enemy sub, and you know he's just a few thousand yards ahead of you, and HE knows YOU are just a few thousand yards away from him...it makes every decision you make in that situation, every turn of the rudder, very important.
That said, the campaign mode could use some depth and tweaking.  As it is you just kind of move your sub's icon around the world map until you bump into an enemy and enter combat.  It's servicable but it seems almost like a placeholder for a deeper campaign.
Also, 40 bucks may be a bit steep.  I don't regret buying it but, considering that many of the much-wanted features that the game is missing (notably, a Russian campaign) will likely be released in future DLC, it might be a bit much.

Review with No Spoilers
I'd like to begin by saying that I highly recommend The Room Two to anybody who enjoys puzzle games. I believe that this game is one of the few games that does puzzling excellently. Never have I played a game quite like this, and I'm somewhat sad that I've already finished it. That being said, there are some things that I absolutely adored about this game, some qualms that I had with it that I feel the first game did better, and a few things that I believe the creators could improve upon. As such, I've decided to divide this rather lengthy review into three parts with a nice TL;DR at the bottom.
What I Loved
Ambiance: The Room Two is a work of art. The atmosphere in The Room Two is inquisitive. You're surrounded by all sorts of trinkets, most of which you can directly interact with. The mood is somber, just the right amount of eerie, and simply perfect for the story found scattered throughout the various notes you encounter. There is no background music, and I find that to be perfect. The quiet permits you to concentrate as you tinker around looking for the next secret compartment. That being said, the game is not entirely silent. Sounds will play upon discovery of new game elements, or simply to alert you during some key moment.
Story: The story is only just present enough, and just detailed enough, to keep you completely hooked without distracting you from the main focus of the game: the puzzles. I am a big fan of the scattered nature of the story, keeping it confined to the notes you find here and there left behind by the mysterious AS. There are some other tidbits of story left behind by other unknown characters in letters and notes that provide you with only enough information to keep you guessing. Honestly, the story in The Room and The Room Two is an excellent implementation of the policy Less is More.
Puzzles: Unlike in The Room, the puzzles in The Room Two are not confined to a single box. Instead, you can explore the entire area and mess around with various puzzle units that must work in unison. I loved how the puzzles had to work together to get you from one room to the next. Just like in The Room, the puzzles are very satisfying to solve, and every little secret uncovered is a reward. The difficulty of the puzzles is perfect. I am not a big fan of hints, so I deactivated them, and I was able to solve the puzzles just fine. An important aspect of a puzzle is that help be available when wanted, but help should never be needed. I could go on forever on how excellent the puzzles themselves were, but you'll have to experience them for yourself to understand what I mean.
Interface: One of the simplest I've ever seen. There's not much to do. Literally everything can be achieved with the mouse, and all of the controls are very intuitive. Furthermore, a lovely tutorial is provided that explains the mechanics clearly and succinctly.
What The Room Did Better
I actually preferred how The Room confined the puzzles to single units rather than to several units spread throughout a room. I feel that spreading out the puzzle to several units watered down the units themselves. One of the things that I loved most about The Room is how intricate the puzzles were. They felt as though there were infinite compartments and keyholes. The level of detail was simply mesmerizing, and the sheer impossibility of the spatial dimensions felt like part of the magic of the game. By spreading the puzzle to various units, I feel that the magic was lost. There are few spatial violations in The Room Two, and the detail dedicated to the units was lost.
That said, I understand that this is mostly personal preference, and I don't feel that the game should lose any points because of it.
I further felt that the shift in focus from a single puzzle box to various made some of the puzzle elements required to advance a bit difficult to find. Some parts didn't feel puzzling so much as they felt a tad frustrating, and upon finding them I would find myself thinking "ugh, I just didn't see this thing in that dark corner" or "I had no idea I could interact with that."
Qualms
My biggest qualm was how some messages couldn't be repeated. This game requires a lot of rapid clicking, and sometimes when you click on something you'll get a message, but you'll accidentally skip it because you're clicking so much. You then cannot replay the message. I think the easiest solution would just be to not allow the player to skip messages. Considering that they only play once, this shouldn't be annoying to the player. That said, this was only an issue with some messages, not all.
Another issue was that sometimes when trying to move the camera, you'd just accidentally press on a knob or something and instead activate some small cutscene or transition rather than getting the camera to move. Simply put: I wish the camera behaved a bit better.
Overall, I feel that this game was amazing, and I honestly believe that more could be done with this concept. I really wouldn't mind seeing something bigger come out of this. Perhaps a game in which the story is fully fleshed out. I'd definitely pay for that.
TL;DR: Excellent game. Excellent story. Some things I feel were done better in The Room, but The Room Two is a game that I wholeheartedly recommend.

It all started in 1994 with a title called UFO: Enemy unknown, launched by Microprose - which you can buy here in Steam btw - but to be really fair it comes from the title Laser Squad launcehed in 1988 which started this whole turn based tactics in real time strategy thing.
This game is kind of a reboot of that classic, and even thought the old title has its natural charms - after all Microprose is the company of Sid Meier (Civilization anyone?) - this new title from 2K studios is definitely a must have in any gamers collection.
The story revolves an alien invasion of the planet earth and mankind's efforts to face this threat. The plot thickens with the DLC called Enemy Within and the storyline is well laid out throughout the game. Research new weapons and armor, upgrade your personnel and kill aliens seem to be a nice combo for a winning title.
GRAPHICS
Even though some angles might seem awkward, and the implementation of the floor levels in the missions might sometimes be quirky i beleive that the graphic engine is used almost to perfection considering what is required. You get some FMV during the action but they seem kind of repetitive after a while.
GAMEPLAY
Simple on to the point instructions, but i would love to know exactly the statistics behind cover and hunkering down during the missions. Some things could have been more intuitive and some better explanations regarding the base buildings could improve the overall experience.
SOUND / MUSIC
Not much to say in this chapter, it is adequate and maybe with a little more orchestration could achieve a more epic result. Funny enough some characters have saying in their original country language! Great job on that one!
RESULT - 9.5/10
Awesome game, definitely worth a buy! Especially if you find it on sale or in a bundle! It totally deserves full price if that should be the case. A must buy, a must play! THUMBS UP!

THIS IS A REVISED REVIEW - Where I have changed my rating from a Must Avoid to now ABSOLUTELY RECOMMEND - Must Buy & Try.  Bohemia has made great progress with all the updates, and I'm playing it again after almost a year away.
I liked the concept of this game from the moment that I came across it in Early Access and bought it.  It's the kind of game that I wanted to like so much, and have played for enough hours to give it an honest chance.  As others have said, It is NOT intuitive.  So, you have to find your own way through it most of the time - but I don't fault it for that, and in fact kinda like figuring stuff out.  I'm a 'don't help me - let me figure it out on my own' guy anyway.  So now, the rest of the story...
I break TKOM down into two categories:
1) Multi-Player - Let's be fair: Pass!  I didn't buy it for the multiplayer, and haven't ever launched that part once, so I'd refer you to other reviews for pros and cons on this part. Moving on...
2) Solo Play is divided into two sections:
- First, the "Space Program", where I was immediately bored silly by launching an endless string of probes around the various craters on Mars, and completing photo recon, atmosphere & soil testing, etc.  I'm not knocking it!  It just didn't do it for me, y'know?!  That said, I never had any issues with it, and it was stable - so, the "Space Program" just wasn't my kind of game, but you may like it fine.  Snore.....zzzzzzzzzzzz XD
- Second, the "Scenarios" option.  This is the place where I spend my time.  In this mode you are on the surface and can harvest resources, build a base, and have free rein, and I now find this part absolutely fantastic.  The modding community is active with all sorts of new add-ons and new scenarios to try.  When it comes to base building, you have the original Outpost style that is fairly user friendly to build and looks really good.  But now, you also have a different style base option called Modular, and it opens up the ability to have more complex, multi-level bases.  With the original Outpost style, when you build a wall, floor, window, ceiling, whatever, it just requires lining up the one, single block and your DONE.  But, with the Modular base, OMG, for a single section of wall, you have three layers to build, exterior, interior, and a final finished skin for the interior.  Two things - a) personally I like the simplicity of the Outpost style, and much prefer the looks; b) The Modular can take hours to build a single room, even with the 3D printer right next to you and running non-stop.  It might be worth it to me if it looked better, but I thought it looked like a building from some Gulag prison colony on Mars xD.  That said, I'm sure it would go together in a snap in multi-player with a team working on it.  It's really just a matter of taste.
(BTW - My earlier review detailed the frequency of crashes every 30 minutes during gameplay, and happily, that is a thing of the past - I now find the game quite stable.  Another annoying quirk of earlier version was that when your character exited a bunk, chair, anything, after resting, he would seem to bounce around the cabin as if Zero G, until he died of his injuries LOL - This issue has resolved in newer versions).
Also, in my initial (negative) review I DID SAY  that TKOM had phenomenal potential... and it has completely lived up to that, with all the great updates.  Good work Bohemia.  I would still like to see an auto-save feature built into the game, but manual saves work fine for now.
I hope some of you found this helpful. Cheers.

REASONS TO BUY

+ The DLC weapons (Such as Volatile Hunter) gives a HUGE boost to the game. Yes, people do say that is a P2W DLC but its not broken nor is it weak.
+ Great graphics - Also doesnt require an amazing PC to run.
+ Plenty of sidequests in main game and DLC - There is a huge variety even if some of them are rather boring.
+ Interesting and pointful open world setting
REASON/s TO NOT BUY
- Bozak's Horde does not seem very interesting - The story is practically non-existent as well as the challenges being rather repetitive for the rewards. I got bored of them very quickly.

This game was in my wishlist for a while and I finally took the plunge to purchase it. In one sense i'm glad I did and in another I wish I didn't.
The game does have a lot of bugs at the moment, which is understandable but the developers (from what I have seen and read) are working to correct them which is great. The bugs that irritate me are the four and half minute loading screen to get into a game, menu options that crashes the game and the various text missing from knowledge areas.
Now I really wanted to like this game and I spent a little bit of time yesterday on a server where I had gained a fairly good amount of material to go and build a base and get started. Everything went fine, I setup camp and logged off. This morning I came on to find two death stalkers attacking my base and I couldn't get out. My weapons are weak compared to a level 60+ monster so I could either sit and wait to die or make a run for it to which I chose the latter. I ran and was instantly killed.
I have spent a further six times to return to my body and my base to find multiple death stalkers along the path that instantly kill me. I can barely make it out of the safe town zone before I die. On my last attempt I decided to start again and started gathering materials but then, out of nowhere a death stalker spawns behind me and well, i'm done.
The game is incredibly hard to get started. The knowledge boxes that pop up to help you start are that quick that you can barely read them before they dissapear and then you need to go into your task manager to see them. Some tasks seem to be broken such as gathering apples from barrels. When I break a barrel it is a flower with an apple picture - it doesn't count.
Multiple text missing from knowledge source so you don't really know what you need to do to increase certain knowledge.
This game could be a fantasic game to play if the developers took note of a few of the suggestions put forward by the users. Even making the start points slightly easier - maybe only allow low level monsters and animals to spawn around the towns to make it easier for people to leave the town and begin base building.
As stressful as it has been to play this game and even though I have just rage quit I do think it's on the right path and that is why I have recommended it.

Hugely NOT recommended.
Not because of the bugs, although this game has more bugs than a $20 hotel in Manhattan.
Not because it crashes Windows Explorer when you exit, and locks up your computer for 5-10 minutes at a time.
Not because the servers are so laggy that you can't move and even hitting things with a sword is a chore.
I'm willing to see past those things, because it's "Early Access".  I knew what I was getting into.
I bought this game to "get in early" because I saw the promise that other positive reviews sold me on.  This game has massive potential, but the mind-numbingly stupid user experience and design decisions they have made leave you with VERY little confidence that this will develop into anything more than a pipe dream.
There is so just much WTF involved.  I've played a lot of games on Steam; I've played bad games, pointless games, games that have poor instruction, and games that are so hard they force you on a steep learning curve.  This is all of those rolled into one massive 5-month-long Alpha project.
Why did you take the time to build massive starter cities and then have only 2 NPCs in them?  They're massive, beautiful ghost towns.  No dialogue, no items for sale, nothing but hundreds of guards who all have the same name (Novalie, Galadriel, or Guard).
Why do vendors sell nothing useful?
Why is the option to sell items to vendors so buggy?
Why is there no minimap, or map at all?
Why is casting spells so painful?
Why does the game tell me I'm tired and need to sleep, but doesn't tell me how to sleep, and there's no option to sleep or camp in the key binds?  (Luckily there is a "defecate" keybind option though, I'll be needing that for this review)
Why are animals just outside the town too hard for beginners to kill?
Why do guards kill ME if a crazed animal chases me back to town?  (But hooray, they kill the animal too)
Why do the hunger/thirst meters tick down crazy quickly, and it takes a stack of 10 cooked meat to refill?
Why is the encumbrance meter broken and constantly telling you you're overburdened when you have nothing but a handful of herbs and the clothes on your back?  (and then you drown, because you go in the water, which is the only way to recover your Thirst, and you can't swim back up to the surface because you're overburdened)
Why do items decay so quickly?
Why is the English grammar so poor as to be incomprehensible?
Why don't you tell me how to capture animals so I can do at least one fun thing?
Why do I need to punch herbs to harvest them? (Because we didn't want to make a harvest animation)
Why do I need to spend the first two in-game hours punching plants to get enough experience to craft a box to store my stuff in?
Why don't I think this will ever come to anything?  Because I've worked in IT long enough to see the amount of time and complexity they have added in building this game in a broken way.  I think I can guess how much work it will take to fix it, and I strongly doubt they will have the budget (or ability) to do so.  They're already releasing an unfinished game because they're running out of runway, and there are just so many massive holes to plug.  Given how bizarre their prioritization has been so far, I can't see them getting some sense now and making this fun or intuitive or even reasonable to play.
For example, the amount of time they have invested developing hunger/thirst/item decay systems instead of useful tutorials, cohesive crafting trees, NPCs, dialogue.....


Take a pass on this one.  Has potential but, so many bugs and the development crew seems to be clueless.
I have 248 hours into this game and have always keep the mindset that this game teaches you to not become attached to things you make and tame and to be prepared to lose it all from one bug or another while playing.  Our group has two private servers and we have modified settings back and forth to see what works best.  We have lost dozens of tamed mounts by falling through the ground or a mountain or a rock and any number of other losses that have been related to game stability and bugs.  That being said, we could and have lived with those issues but, the latest 72 hour structure decay rules on the servers (PVP and PVE) that can not be overridden has become the proverbial straw to drive us away.
I really don't mind a game that is a time sink and can live with spending 5 or more hours straight, taming a mount and spending another dozen hours leveling it up only to have it lost or killed because of a bug or game glitch - because there are redeeming game qualities and our group enjoys our social time online together.  The show stopper though is having structures and resources disappear after as little as 72 hours of not logging into a server.  Some of our structures took 20 - 80 hours to build, over a month's time or more, only to come back from a three-day weekend and have it deleted from the server and most or all of the tamed mounts and resources in it gone.
Save yourself some time and look for a better game.
I hope this helps some of you who are wondering if you should buy this game.
Cheers
-D

Decent combat shooter game for it's time. Decent weapon balistics and realism with some fun practical mechanics like fast rope, night and thermal vision, weapon customization and soldier customization. Soldiers have available a myriad of body armors and various combat wear available after ranking up, as well as various camoflauges to further customize and cultivate the look you want your elite squad to portray on the battlefield.
Weapon customization has a number of attachments that you can utilize to improve your aim as well as get the edge you need in close quarters or long range combat.
The ability to mark targets in singleplayer and multiplayer modes is the key squad mechanic laid at your disposal. If you enjoyed full reign over your squad mates like in previous Rainbow Six titles, such as Ravenshield, you'll be a bit disappointed. If you are just coming into the franchise however, I highly recommend this game for it's enjoyable, albeit slightly cliche singleplayer experience.  Once that is finished there is an independant terrorist hunt mode, like in previous titles, and you can use that mode to further rank and hone your skiils.
I did not get to spend a great deal of time in competitive multiplayer as finding matches when I played this game the most, the community had already moved on to other new titles like Call of Duty and Battlefield Bad company.  Either way, it's worth its current price tag and a few play throughs with a friend both in cooperative campaign and some terrorist hunt modes.

Excellent tactical shooter. The AI is a bit less intelligent than I would have liked, but it was still very good. I've played this for countless hours on my Xbox 360, and now several hours on the PC.
One of the biggest things I like about Rainbow Six: Vegas 2 is that there are different ways to approach almost every situation. In the campaign and in single-player Terrorist Hunt, you command two other men, which allows you to plan different entrance strategies, tag enemies for your teammates to engage, and engage the enemy from different angles.
The campaign is pretty well-paced and gives a good mix of opportunities to use different tactics. There are a few intense firefights spread throughout the campaign, some of which take place on a massive area where you have to utilize cover and positioning to make it through. None of the firefights can easily be done in a "run and gun" style that you would typically see in games like Call of Duty. In fact, on Realistic difficulty, you will not survive with such an attitude.
Ranking is fairly intuitive. There is the classic rank (private, corporal, etc, all the way up to general), which unlocks different armor and gear (the gear is mostly cosmetic while the armor actually has stats). There are three different combat ranks as well: Assault, CQB, and Marksman. Getting certain types of kills grants points to one of the three. As you rank up in each of the three areas, you unlock new weapons and gain XP toward your main rank.
Now, for some PC-specific details. The controls can be customized and re-mapped to suit you; if I recall, I actually did re-map some of the keys and am glad that this feature actually exists (I wish I could say the same for certain other games). The graphics settings are a little lacking, especially for a PC game.
I don't know how populated the multiplayer on the PC is, and I might not find out for some time (ranking up takes a while, and I want my guns, dang it!). Having played Multiplayer Co-op and Versus on the Xbox360, I can attest that it's a fun break from the norm. It's more challenging than the rest of the game, and there is even different gear that you can access that can't be accessed in Terrorist Hunt or Campaign mode.
I'll probably update this as I continue to play the PC version.

Ethan Carter is something unusual and memorable.  Equal parts beauty, desolation, and atmosphere pregnant with uncanny menace, it is one of the few games that has made a lasting impression on me.
The core of the game is its story, which could have made a fine short story in its own right.  It's tight and surprisingly emotionally charged for a work of weird fiction.  The storytelling is tight and clever, rewarding attention to detail and encouraging contempation of what you have just seen and what you are not seeing.  The story was genuinely engaging, and had me actively trying to work out what was going on rather than just letting it unfold.
The gameplay supports the story.  Unlike other games of the exploring/ puzzle-solving variety, these puzzles are not mere obstacles to the unfolding of the narrative.  They aren't fiddly locks that bar your progress, tempting you to find a solution online just so you can get on with it.  These puzzles would not make sense without the story, and the story unfolds through the puzzles; they're an integral part of the narrative and do not take you out of the world.  They were not difficult or arbitrary, and I was satisfied to tinker with them when necessary, which it rarely was because everything made sense.  One of the game's few weaknesses was the ease of most of the puzzles.
The only other was its shortness -- I just wasn't ready to leave Red Creek Valley yet. However, these weaknesses are trivialities.  I cannot recommend it enough and I look forward to playing it again some day.

Great game until you get stuck. Then you have 2 choices, wander aimlessly around the game as there are no clues whatsoever or google a walkthrough which right now is almost impossible without reading huge spoilers. Looks great, plays like a game of hide and seek where the one hiding has died.

Vanishing of Ethan Carter, much like recently released story-driven experiences (eg. Gone Home, Dear Esther, Minervas Den) succeeds in creating a discovery-based story. Robert Frost's "The Road Not Taken" may best describe how the puzzles in this game are presented.
The world is beautiful and if you can run it at full resolution with ultra high details: do so. There were moments where I found myself just wandering and gazing at the landscape. It may still only be polygons and shaders, but the amount of detail found in just the juxtaposition of bare faced bedrock along against a subtle man-made pathways made me appreciate the craft of good CG modelling and level design. Things just felt right.
The Sound design is fantastic. I recommend playing with the music on, as it creates a great moody cinematic experience. Some may prefer only the ambience of the forest, but with a little tweaking, I found pushing the music back a couple notches and bringing the ambience up helped immensely with the immersion. Also, I recommend headphones with this experience.
There's so many moments in this game where I doubted the intentions of the storyteller, however, once I realized what I was witnessing, it only empowered my experience.
No doubt this is a game that for those who enjoyed Gone Home or Dear Esther should play. Definitely worth your time and money :)

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an expertly crafted experience that remained in my thoughts well after the credits finished rolling. The game doesn't do anything revolutionary, nor does it require complex problem solving, but it doesn't constrain you from experiencing the story in your own way, at your own pace.
The beautiful vistas of Red Creek Valley - as can be seen from the myriad screenshots in the game's Community Hub, each of which could pass as a desktop wallpaper - are just one aspect where the immense amount of polish put into the game can be seen. This attention to detail extends into the way puzzles and clues are presented to you as well as how tidbits of information suddenly become relevant and enrich the story. Almost every spoken line or scrap of paper carries some significance that might not dawn on the player until the very end (or a second playthrough).
By far the most impressive thing in the game for me, however, was the interplay of natural and supernatural elements and the way these are tied into the narrative. The story can seem cliché and simple at first glance, but once you revisit earlier events and reconsider their significance or the way the protagonist and the other characters react to them, multiple interpretations of Ethan Carter's story suddenly open up. What's in the past and what's in the present, whether what you see is fantasy or reality is up to the observer to decide, and based on the number of contrasting opinions in the game forums, most people have their own version of how the story supposedly goes.
Some locations in the game can evoke a sense of dread, but those annoyed by scripted jump scares can rest easy: if you're attentive, your nerves won't be unfairly tested.
The experience is a short but sweet one and the game resonated with me enough to warrant subsequent visits to the valley. I would have liked the puzzles to be more demanding and the locations to contain more objects providing further backgrund information on the characters, but even so, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter shows that interactive storytelling doesn't have to guide you down a straight path to be memorable and thought-provoking.

Original review, 21th of April
-----------------------
While I recommend the game, there's a lot that needs to be said about what actually is in the game.
All of the the top reviews are about how it's GTA/Saints Row like, free-roam "no crashes for me" etc.
No one actually talks about the game, and their experiences with it.
So here goes.
From launching the game to actually being able to play it can take anything from 1min 15sec to however long it takes if you quit the game after unlocking the train stations.
DO NOT QUIT THE GAME AFTER UNLOCKING THOSE STATIONS! ungh.
Those cutscenes are unskippable, and will take up a HUGE chunk of time on your next reboot.
After a crash (wich is becoming more and more frequent) you will have to, you guessed right, wait 1min and 15seconds before being able to play again, after pressing the play button on steam.
The intro is so bad, and it makes no sense it takes that long to load.
Furthermore, if you want to change your settings (which I bet you will) you will have to reboot the game in order to save/use your new settings.
There are a lot of graphical glitches, and I even found a spot where you would get teleported to a specific spot, just by running along a building on an island (I forgot which one, but I got pictures of it ^^).
While riding the quad bike and getting your wheels on a curb at angle the wheels will do some weird clipping.
Uh, look mountains I can fly ove..
guess not.. Oh look! A gap between two buildings I can fly throu...
guess not >.<
The police siren is bad, and I wish you could turn it off in the menu (for all vehicles) since there's no purpose to it, other than introducing a high pitched annoying sound.
Vehicles don't pull over, nor do people move away from it.. While there's no need for the people to move, since they cause no movement reduction when hit - But still.. it's gameplay related, and bad design.
The camera is... well.. the camera is.. Let's just say I think there was some design issues during developing the game which caused them to lock up the camera in certain situations.
They're trying to give us a 3rd-person-freelook option but it always introduces some kind of issues (especially when the designers don't want us to clipthrough buildings).
When the camera is actually free to move, it's pretty good - But you'll rarely have use to move it (at least so I found).
On wards with the camera/scanner.
The scanner it self is utterly horrible and freakin' broken.
Sometimes it won't show objects so you can add them as a waypoint, but you'll still be able to scan them if you're able to fiddle enough around with the camera angle and placement of your figure.
Taking out the scanner takes to long, and moving it around is very sluggish.
Some people have mentioned they like how each level consist of less things to be done - I dislike how each level consist of so little things to collect and everything is scattered around a town where you're unable to locate the things you need to get.
This is my first Lego game since one of the LOTR games I think - I'm missing "my helper"/"secondary player" mostly because I liked how I was able to manage disguises that way.
Switching from disguises from the shoulder buttons is great and seemless, and the wheel pops up fast - But I do dislike that civilians have no abilities whatsoever :/
Do note I haven't fiddled THAT much with the civilians, so I'm unsure if you can put Rex there (I'll check on my next gameplay) which would make it somewhat viable.
Update: Civilians can have special abilities, so you're able to have one of you're favorite types closer to the police/fireman disguise :)
I simply hate the "colorshops" or what they're called. It's hard to see what colors are in the tank to begin with, and stuck behind a tinted glass only makes it harder.
Uh, let's use the scanner to see what colors they are! For gods sake, let's hope you didn't try some out before using the scanner, because the scanner doesn't update to which colors are in the tanks but rather the original one.
Ah, and you can't use the scanner inside the building, so you'll have to teleport outside to check, and in again, to swap.
*Brain hurts*
The cutscenes, as mentioned previous (The train station part) are horrible.
Some of the scenes aren't skipable even after completing the game, and navigation through each level is half-bad.
There have been occassions (mostly during first playthrough), that I've gone to pass to the next stage, without wanting to, because I wasn't aware/forgot (After 5-10mins of bashing, collecting and completing task) that the door which I'm breaking/the jump I'm about to make/whatever triggers the next event.
Most of the time played will be from sitting and waiting during your first go at the missions.
Then the next huge chunk of time will be used on actually playing the game and collecting everything to 100% the game.
Some of the task are really great, but I really could've been without most of them.
Some of the areas are small and cramped with things to do which could easily have been implemented into either the existing levels, new levels or been used to create bonus/side missions instead.
I don't consider having to color things, fetch a pig/cat as a side missions - That's point A->B walking, and there's simply to much of it I feel.
I'm also thinking some of the bugs/glitches could've been eliminated if so much wasn't stuck into the open world (i.e scanner issues, which I'm thinking might be causing the crashing.. I have no idea).
For everything bad said, it actually is a good game - Once you're able to play it :)
There's a decent amount of things to do, "the world" has a great size and you'll be able to fast travel between spots once unlocked.
And you can't help but love officer Honey :D

The Room 2 (and 1 for that matter) is......an experience.
Technically I suppose it's a series of logical puzzles, none of which are particularly hard.
Make no mistake, you're not getting a fully-fledged mystery game here, it is after all a mobile port.
(besides, what did you expect for a fiver?)
If you want to, you can probably breeze through it in a couple of hours depending on your previous puzzle-game experience.
But that would be the wrong way to do The Room 2.
As I said, the puzzles themselves are fairly easy once you figure out the underlying logic.
But the artwork.....
OMG the artwork!
Fireproof games have created a series of boxes, safes, desks and what have you, with hidden levers, cranks, buttons, thingamajigs and a few other devices I don't know what to call.
And every time you get one thing solved, the whole thing rotates, unfolds, compresses and changes into something else entirely. And it does so in the most wonderfully magical way.
I have played through The Room 1 more times than one would think strictly necessary just to admire the artwork and design, and I suspect I'm in for a similar fate with The Room 2.
Granted, I still like the original better than the sequel (not quite as gloomy, and more emphasis on the physical safes) but I'm still enjoying the hell out of The Room 2.
So do yourself a favor. Buy the game.
Then sit down and savour the experience.

The first Saints Row game was nothing more than a cheap knock off, I liked the 80's metal soundtrack in the game but that was all it had going for it. The second game is when things got entertaining, they just started to parodize the whole gang thing a lot more and poke fun at some relevant societal topics. But the third game is when Volition really started to have fun poking fun at how weird the real world was. Saints Row: The Third wasn't only fun to play but the way it poked fun at the reality tv craze, and Stag was obviously a jab at how Bush handled the war on terror, and it was all done in a very National Lampoon way which was amusing. Well Saints Row IV, it merely picks up where they left off in three and takes even mroe jabs at a lot of the absurd things in the US, and it pays homage to so many things from the 80's you'll lose count. There's the level that totally pays homage to They Live and a Christmas Story (briefly), and then there's tons of weapons from 80's classics like Robocop, Aliens, and GI Joe. And the christmas expansion, the first level is basically a re-creation of the old studio lot where they shot Jaws, Gremlins, and numerous other classics. But towards the end when it pays homage to the animated Transformers film, and even uses the Stan Bush song from the film, that was just a golden moment in the game.
But I'm praising the satire and how they paid homage to so many great films and cartoons and not talking about the gameplay. Gameplay wise the game is pretty fun and the super powers the player can use in the viritual world add a whole new level of gameplay to the franchise since in earlier games, the player had to rely on vehicles to get anywhere fast and always rely on guns or grenades, but in the 4th game the player could still go the gun and grenade route or freeze people or turn them into gold or use telekenisis and throw them into the sky. In short, the game allows players to just go crazy when it comes to taking out pedestrians and the aliens. The controls are as smooth as the third game, which I'm thankful for since Saints Row 2 for the PC, the driving controls were just horrible. If one enjoys open world games where they can just go crazy, this game should please them. But I highly recommend getting the Game of the Century version, or at the very least the base game and the christmas expansion pack. While I adore Volition's sense of humor when it comes ot the SR franchise, Enter the Dominatrix gets a little too corny, while the Christmas expansion is hands down a far better expansion pack. I don't recommend playing any of the expansions until after finishing the main game though since the expansions will spoil a few things otherwise.
However, while I think the game is highly entertaining and totally worth dropping 10-20 on, it does have its flaws and they're the same exact flaws the third game had.
1. All the glowing reviews are right: this game is great. The balance is impeccable. After you spend some time learning the ins and outs, and you have a victory or two under your belt, you realize just how important it is to have a balanced playing field. You lose much more often than not, but there's something about losing 90% of the time that makes the victories so much more satisfying.
Good news, everyone! Many of the losses are fairly quick, so you aren't actually wasting 90% of your time losing at this challenging game. This is the first game in my 26 years of gaming that I don't feel ashamed to play on Easy Mode. I
played a game on easy mode because I
to before this one, and maybe I didn't need to here either. However, the game is hard enough that you are better served learning the ropes on Easy than torturing yourself by losing repeatedly because you don't know what's possible in this universe.
The game was literally designed with a 10% success rate in mind. The in-game "tips" tell you that losing is part of the fun. You will scoff, cringe, and curse at the game (or yourself) when you lose by a sliver of probability. As you learn how to manipulate the events, you will find that you take more chances. You will find that you have a greater understanding of the risks you are taking. You will find that you can just barely squeeze by at the most critical of moments. You will do these things, and it will lead to both your most satisfying victories as well as your most crushing defeats.
Very few times during this game will you know with unquestionable certainty that you will win in the end. Very few times, conversely, will you know that you have no chance at all. After twenty or thirty runs, you will have the experience to know what choices are reasonable or practical, and what choices betray that ideal. In the end, you will win, then you will try again and lose. After that, you will come back for more.
TL;DR: This game is hard. It features perma-death, masterfully crafted balance, and choice. You will like this game if you are good at games, or you will hate it. You could spend your money on so much worse, at least, so give it a shot.

This game is awesome. I love the idea and the feel of the game.
Unfortunately, half a decade after release, this game is still plagued with bugs. This is the main reason I feel compelled to write a review; hopefully others will now know what they're signing on to when they buy this game. If someone can get over the bugs, they might want to give this a try--otherwise it is a very mixed experience.
Bugs:
-All enemy types teleport all over the map until player has initiated their cutscenes.
-Characters occasionally point weapons in directions that differ from projectile path.
-Game freezes semi-frequently (2-4 times freezes over the 2 days I played). Sometimes, if in the middle of a mission on ironman, the game will save over the mission as being "aborted."
I honestly can't believe they haven't fixed these by now. Complete lack of polish on an otherwise 10/10 experience. These bugs--especially the teleporting issue--completely broke the immersion for me. I have no idea why the game would choose to teleport enemies (all types of enemies--even the ones that have no practical way of "teleporting")  all over the map in random directions on a game that is supposed to value strategic and tactical decisions. Scouting is pointless with this bug, and actually punishes people for scouting; if you scout ahead and the enemies teleport they will occasionally land in the middle of the rest of your squad. Real oversight on the developers part, and frankly the fact that this is not finished yet is sheer laziness.
TLDR: Don't buy this game if immersion-breaking bugs bother you. The teleporting bug has not been fixed.
Edit: Enemy within seems like it may fix a lot of these issues. If you're going ot buy xcom: enemy unknown, make sure you buy the expansion with it. Lots of added content.

PROS:
- Good potential
- Physics worked much better than expected
- It is fun, for a limited time.
CONS:
- Structure building is a pain. Even after getting used to the awkward rotation, constantly running back and forth from the "3D Printer" to the place where the part had to be was annoying. The parts are also very VERY specific in how they have to be placed together.
- Carrer mode is a horrible grind, so many of the missions are recyled, and many of them simply involve watching a static drone. And by that, I mean literally watching the drone's camera feed as it crashes to Mars. Mission complete. Now do that 15 times.
- Many of the Scenarios are fun, and have interesting objectives. The issue is that there is no reward of any kind for completion, nothing at all. It just feels pointless.
- For trying to be serious about Mars exploration, some of the features are ridiculous (weird vehicles). The game goes from trying to be really serious about realism, to being more fantasy.
- There's just no point yet. I understand that it's early access, but there is no goal of the game.

As others have said, yes, this is basically ARK with magic and different animals to tame but it's more than that. There are new mechanics in place, some that were added to ARK with mods and some that weren't.
Take the vendors. You can save gold, currently by smashing barrels but eventually by selling various resources to those vendors, and then use that gold to purchase items that you can't make on your own yet.
There are three different races that currently don't have much difference but I imagine that'll change. The races do have their own, distinct, starting locations that each feel like their own area with its own unique challenges.
You can approach combat from a variety of starting points, blending magic and melee as fits your play style. This becomes even better when you play in a group with magic users supporting the melee fighters in an almost mmo type setup without all the complex special abilities.
Building works much the same as with ARK, though there are a few more options and the possibility of placing "Frameworks" to plan out your building ahead of time. The buildings themselves are built from mostly the same type of pieces you're used to from ARK though, ranging from "Straw" to Stone and featuring the usual parts like foundations, walls, ceilings, etc.
The gameplay itself is similar to ARK but just feels more fluid somehow. The textures seem more detailed to me, but that might just be perception. All in all, there is a great potential to Dark & Light and I can't recommend it enough.

The year is 1985 and here I am between svalbard and north norway in our Los Angeles class nuclear attack sub the Hyman G. Rickover. Commands given me the orders prior to this to intercept and if possible destroy an enemy surface taskforce consisting of a moskva heli-carrier. So the satellites peg this taskforce on my map and I move in prepping all hand for battlestations.
I enter the operation area and I'm cruising at 20 knots 300 feet down below a strong layer and sonar is still picking up contacts for a total of about 4 surface contacts. I slow to 5 knots and rise above the layer to a depth of about 40-50 feet hoping to raise up the ESM mast and periscope. Sonar before I could even do this assigns them as the moskva, a cargo ship, and two escorts. The taskforce is running fast and loud pinging hard with active sonar. Command up periscope because I'm ballsy and so I can get a faster firing solution on the moskva. Fire control gives me a solution almost instantly and I let loose with a Mk.48 torpedo whose active sonar setting I've turned on and she runs to the end of her leash and immediately starts pinging picking up on the cargo ship not the moskva. The moskva according to sonar and her two escorts are breaking hard left but pinging all the way. Within all this time I've taken on ballast, ordered all stop, and ordered ultra quiet hoping to hide from all the choppers the moskva and two escorts have gotten in the air.
The Mk.48 slams home on the side of this cargo ship in the meantime and again I let loose a Mk.48 with the hope of the moskva sinking due to it. The fish locks in on her and speeds in, the moskva trying it's best to throw off the torpedo breaks hard right and instead only turns into the torpedo and takes it in the gut starts flooding, catches fire, and sinks. The objective is dead but her escorts are not out of the fight. They ping hard searching for me and now directing the helis of thier dead flagship. One of the two doesnt get far as a Mk.48 slams beneath the keel and cracks and starts sinking. The last escort hearing my torpedo launch somehow steams for me directing the helis to me and fires it's RBU-6000 at what it suspects is me. I let loose with another Mk.48 and she swims to the end of her short firecontrol leash and starts pinging the enemy ship. The escort breaks hard right and the torpedo slams her in the middle and she too sinks.
In this whole engagement I have not moved and only listened to the soviet fleet try and fail to find me. I dive deeper to 700ft and and make for the end of the zone at cruising speed despite still being hunted by the helicopters the whole way. I leave the zone ending our succesfull combat mission against the Soviet taskforce. As we pick up comms again we are informed our actions have had a massive effect on the fight in the norwegian sea and NATO forces are moving into fill the power vacuum we've created for them. We are also informed West Germany has fallen to the Soviet hordes.
Last of all though command has awarded me a bronze star for my actions against the Soviet devils. Captain "Big D*** Rick" and his crew aided the Allied war effort.
Edit: Big D*** got interred into soviet gulag. Captured after insersting navy seals into Archenglsk and proceedingly intercepted by russian attack subs off the coast of finland.

Just when it seemed Saints Row The Third had reached the limits of ridiculousness, IV takes things to a new level.
More hilarious (and occasionally strikingly poignant) writing, a great new villain, some inventive new mechanics and the introduction of super powers make this a highly enjoyable experience. The core super powers in particular - super running and jumping - completely transform how you get around the map, rendering vehicles and aircraft essentially irrelevant. The level of freedom is wonderful, and it's striking how much they are missed when they are taken away.
It's not flawless. There are a few bugs - such as those which instantly completed an activity for me (not that I can really complain about getting Gold level for little work, but it was jarring) and a misson-breaking bug in the Christmas DLC - the quests are unashamedly grindy at times and the game world gets unbalanced quickly once Maurauders get introduced, making it particularly hard to complete some achievements.
However, this is a game which is all about fun, and it well and truly delivers.

Equally long (short?) as the first game. However, this episode has got much less exposition and is far more mysterious - the "what the hell is going on?" kind. Although the level variety in this sequel  is much more diverse (many different settings), the progression did feel a bit disconnected to me as a result of jumping though space and time after each room.
Regarding the puzzles: The possibilities are multiplicated in the sequel since you switch between locations (e.g. from a table in the center of the room, to a chest in the corner). It might lead to a bit of confusion at times, but it does make for some interesting circumstances. The difficulty felt slightly lesser than in the first game, paired with slightly more direct (in pointing the player in the right direction) compared to the first game.
One other thing of note is this game comes with a fair amount of creepy/disturbing vibes. The more faint hearted may feel a shiver or two at some points - but horror is obviously not a main point of this game and the player needn't worry much.

The driving's good, the story is a lot of fun, being a satire on the stereotypes of police movies and books that's good for more than just kids (in fact, I'm willing to bet an adult would find this more fun than a kid), and the combat system is decent enough(very fun throwing mooks around, although fighting's still♥♥♥♥♥♥easy like in every lego game, and this time around you can't just hit anyone on the streets, a mediocre decision in my opinion).
The reason of the huge ammount of bad reviews (and, mind you, it is a valid reason) is the horrible state of this game when it was first released. You couldn't even change the resolution, or use the steam overlay (the game would crash if you tried). The developers released a day-one patch fixing these two issues, and then another one fixing a bunch of other problems, and they're bound to release more. I appreciate it, but honestly, all of these fixes should have been done before releasing the game. That would certainly have improved the overall score here in steam.
I'd say right now, the game's very worthwhile. I haven't experienced the issues everyone is apparently still complaining about, I can boot up the game just fine, the stuttering happens rarely (certainly not twice per minute) and I've experienced only three or four crashes since I bought the game (and I never lost much progress, thanks to the autosave feature). Definitely worth your money, no matter your age.

The story is is good, loaded with cliches (but done in only a way Lego could pull off), annd filled with puns and references to popular culture and famous movies. The voice acting isn't bad (yeah, apparently legos talk now) and the characters while overall not the best written, are at least entertaining enough to keep it going.
Gameplay consists of old school style collection, as well as some (too easy) puzzles, and some decent driving scenes as well. Basically, if you've ever played a lego game, you'll feel right at home. You unlock new abilities by finding new outfits (like the robber costume lets you pick safes and pry open some doors, while the cop one lets you find hidden items), as well as some abilities that you just earn by playing the right mission, like the ability to use special colored blocks to free run. One of my biggest issues is the puzzles are way too easy, and the game feels the need to hold your hand through some of these, even if the solution is obvious. Combat (at least where I am)  feels kind of satisfying but also a tad lackluster. Basically press a button, watch as you tackle the guy, then pres another button to slap the cuffs on them. This isn't the most exciting combat system, but to the dev's credit, the animations were really good for this. Driving is very basic, but handles well. the physics are loose enough that sliding thrrough turns is doable, and while there is no real sense of speed, the driving feels good in the context of the game. A major gripe of mine is you can't look back while driving, which makes me feel just a bit trapped. Overall solid gameplay.
In short:
+Good Story/Fun Characters
+Solid Gameplay
+Nice map
+Good animation
-Puzzles/combat are too easy
-Can't control camera in cars
-Crashes on occasion

Even though it is a sensational squad-based tactical shooter, it is not as good as the older games in the series (e.g. the Original Rainbow Six, Rogue Spear & Raven Shield). Still, it is a pretty fun game to play with your friends, and even by yourself.

Though certainly not the first game series to become worse with each new iteration, it seems that has been the trend with Rainbow Six for some time. However, even the mediocre Vegas 1 was pretty fun with it's four player co-op mode, and while a lot of the tactical elements were stripped away, we were still left with a competent, and occassionally intelligent shooter.
Vegas 2 seems to take those few things that I really enjoyed about the first, removes them, and focuses more on the things that made the first Vegas not very good to begin with. Gone is four player co-op campaign (inexplicably reduced to two player), the ability to customize your soldier right out of the box (for the PC version), and decent map design. Instead, what we get was a tedious and unneccessary progression system of unlocks, AI that seems to wildly alternate between being braindead and clairvoyant, and weaker PC optimization. And not that anyone plays a Tom Clancy game for the story, but for this one, they didn't even write a new script; instead it's the same moronic terrorist attack on Las Vegas, but following a different group of Rainbows, this one even less interesting that the last.
I can't think of one thing that was improved in this sequel, and a large amount of content was made worse. A lazy sequel to a mediocre game, and a lazy port for an almost entirely consolized series. My advice: if you want a good Rainbow Six game, try the original three, or if you want a less tactical game, play the original Vegas. There's nothing here that isn't offered in any of those games, and generally it is done in a way that is far less frustrating.

You've probably noticed a bunch of Warhammer and Warhammer 40k games hitting the market lately, right?
Some of them have been good, others not so good.
This is hands-down the best one by far.
"What? Better than Total Warhammer?!?!" you ask?
Yes. Better than TW. Which isn't to say TW is bad. It's great. But at then end of the day it's still just another Total War game and the odds are that whether or not you enjoy it will depend greatly on how much you enjoy that game series.
BFG is something rather different and quite unique. A very clever re-imagining of a defunct tabletop game from the W40k universe that manages to be faithful to its source while transcending its roots. Rather than making a turn-based game as close to the original as possible the developers of BFG have managed to produced a real-time game of small-scale tactical fleet combat that is true to the spirit of BFG. In doing so they succeeded wildly, producing a game that even an ardent disliker of micro-management couldn't help but love.
I haven't even touched on the campaign. I'll be brief. It's brilliant. It gradually builds and develops, inttroducing more and more complexity as you play. At the same time, it manages to maintain a persistent feeling of encroaching doom. You're in control but you never feel like winning is a fore-gone conclusion.
This is, without a doubt, the finest Warhammer game to have been released in a long time.

It's admittedly got a few issues. The small playerbase means leveling a multiplayer fleet in persistent mode can be a hassle as you are matched up more than not against players with much higher leveled fleets. The majority of the campaign mode consists of a lot of regular skirmish matches you also play in both multiplayer and against AI skirmish modes. Balance can at times feel a bit iffy due to the various factions being significantly differing to one another which can leave you grinding your teeth as you struggle to level.
That being said I would thoroughly recommend the game to any fan of the genre for it's good points outweigh the bad. The unique campaign missions are often interesting and many of them can play out in more than in way depending on whether or not you win or lose with some AI captains being able to survive all the way to the end to help out in some missions. The campaign also manages to steer the fine line between allowing for sufficient player agency through your actions and sticking to the established storyline of yet another of Abbadon's tantrums. You might lose a battle that results in the Chaos fleet making off with a shiny bauble as happened or should you be too loyal for that kind of nonsense you might rewrite history slightly and through effort and more than one victory and stick it to Abby.
Another point in it's favour are the visuals. Any match tends to start zoomed out to offer you a grid based view of what is actually happening allowing you to make with the ordering and the whatnot. But once you zoom in all the way on a ship you'll find it's all remarkably detailed with damage currently done to a ship clearly visible. The campaign likewise tellls the story through use of static scenes that are beautifully drawn in a way that makes Games Worshop's own current use of technically capable but rather uninspired digitally drawn artwork look less than interesting. Perhaps less of a suprise to anyone is the fact that BFG:A manages to continue the trend of excellent voicework that has somehow been a standard in Warhammer 40k video games.
Overall it's a solid game that while not is going to be remembered as one of the greatest ever made, it is one that I have come back to on a regular basis since release to play a few games against people online or play a couple games against the AI in the ever increasingly difficult Elite Mode that matches you up against more and tougher enemy ships. There is simply something cathartic about jamming the prow of the 'His Imperial Girth' into heretics and xenos.

Skirmish mode is the second game type, which has you create your own fleet as a part of your favorite 40k faction/race.  You fight battles against the AI, or with a friend in 2 vs AI.  You can even choose an Elite Mode which has the player face off against ever more powerful AI fleets.  There are also 2 different multiplayer modes.  The first is a classic player vs. player match where you slowly gain ranks after beating other players.  The second starts the players at the maximum rank for both ships and admiral, while also giving you a lot of money for ship upgrades.  The players would then fight multiple battles to determine their rank.
Maybe I'm biased, but I have fun with all of the different types of game modes.

The main negative point would be a lack of players for multiplayer battles, but it could be worse.  Sometimes it is hard to find a game, but normally during "primetime" there is no issue with player population.  It sucks there aren't more people with this title, as it truely is an amazingly fun time.

DoA 5 completely abandoned what made 4 such an awkward game and returned to the core of great gameplay like in DoA 2U and DoA 3. The story isn't particularly phenominal but the fact that they've added it on top of the arcade is a big plus. Online play is decent but the amount of players is very low nowadays. That's not anything to hold against this game however. The triangle system of combat is one of the most balanced systems in place for fighting games today. Stages are incredibly fun with lots of interactive environments, all which help give an edge in fighting but not enough to throw the fights off. Character selection is great, and most of them are balanced with their stats and styles to offer a good variety of whom to play versus whom. If you can get past the stigma of what the series has become, you'll enjoy this game. The only con I can see is how the DLC is so outrageously over-priced. Having to pay for the story and pay for the characters is not acceptable and a major con, but if you are willing to spend $50 you'll pick up most of what you need there.
All in all this is a fighting game and series second only to Street Fighter for the PC. I only chose this over Street Fighter because I don't like SF's style, graphics, and most of their characters on top of the fact that it is a 2D fighting game. Definitely worth a buy if you like balanced 3D fighting games as this is the best one you can buy.

One of the most immersive first person shooters I have ever played. The visuals are absolutely stunning and the engine is a powerhouse. The soundtrack fits the atmosphere of apocalyptic Moscow perfectly. The small communities in the metro are a pleasure to visit and to hear the atmospheric conversations told by the people of the metro. The gunplay is executed well and every weapon is a joy to use. Even the reload animations are amusing. The animations and character models of this game are a sight to behold. The lighting effects are a technical marvel as well. The other aspects of gameplay are refreshing. The game is linear but gives multiple ways to approach goals and players are able to decide between being sneaky or running and gunning. Supplies are only just abundant enough, forcing players to carefully strategize around the use of their ammo. For the game being set in such a unique atmosphere, the environments of the game never become stale or boring. The story of the game is a focused one that does not stray too far from its main ideas. Journals found during gameplay give the player the lore of the metro from Artyom's own eyes. The entire game really is about his interpretation of the metro. The game has a psychological element in it that really allows the player to become entangled in Artyom's outlandish experiences. There is also a dash of paranormal in this game to add more character to the metro. This game sets out to completely immerse the player in the setting, environment, and character of the metro; and it does a pretty damn good job at doing just that. I have only ever played redux but from what I've seen and heard, many improvements have been made over the original. The graphical visuals as well as the ui have been majorly improved, the ai has been fixed and the controls have been nicely revamped. This game goes on sale with its sequel "Metro: Last Light" during every major steam sale for very low prices. Do yourself a favour and pick it up if you enjoy extremely immersive experiences.
