A reboot of the classic 90s series Xcom. If you loved the old UK series UFO then you will love this.
Is it as good as the last one?
It has smaller maps for a start. Now this isn't such a issue. People who played the first one, will remember the hated "hunt the sectoid" craziness. The old maps on the first game were so huge, that you always had one lone sectoid left, hiding somewhere, refusing to come out. You don't have this issue on these maps. The newer maps while being compact have way more opportunities for those who love turn based tactical skirmish games. When you fiendish plan of attack clicks into place with no setbacks, it really is a very satisfying game.
As you progress through the story you reserach alien tech, which will greatly enhance your prospects. Your soldiers also develop as gain experience. New abilites will be made available for your troops, greatly enchancing their odds against an increasingly agressive alien invader.
The only real issues are ones that plagued the original. The RNG or random number generator....well lets be honest here...it does have a tendancy of defying the laws of probability. You will find yourself pulling your hair out as your men miss and spoil that perfect ambush you set up. Happily it is not consistently rolling snake eyes but there is no denying that it can suck the fun out of a mission, particulary the more challenging missions that have key objectives and/or a time limit to achieve it in.
The alien AI while on the whole pretty good - do have the tendancy of being able to see through walls or other obstructions. And at times they feel like their RNG uses loaded dice.  This does tend to lead to more a more cautious and tactical approach by players. You really don't want to lose your men, who you have invested time and resources in, so when it does happen it really stings. (Something the sequel does not cater for with its timed missions and doom clock and imho suffers for it.
Your own teams AI again on the whole is pretty good. But they suffer from poor pathing and while gladly run through fire, hazardous chemicals and other dangerous obstacles to get to where you want them. So you do have to keep a careful eye on this as the game doesn't allow you to modify their path.
On the whole this is a good game with a few issues. The issues are annoying more than game breaking but they don't happen with the sort of frequency that make you storm off in disgust.

Let me start out by stating that adventure games such as these are not my forte.  However, this adventure game seemed to do it right, with amazing visuals, an interesting story, and interesting mechanics. In this game you play as Paul Prospero, a detective, who has been blessed with a gift to see the extraordinary. The game is firmly based around these special powers which help solve the crime(s) and other puzzles that you find. If you however are expecting a game along the likes of L.A Noire, where there is human interaction you will be dissapointed here. The puzzles in this game are fairly easy but they still feel somewhat fresh, they do however lack in quantity. Exploring is a large part of this game giving you a fair amount of freedom to find puzzles and areas as long as you are willing to look for them. Searching for these areas is not to monotonous thanks to the amazing visuals the game waves in your face. The environments in this game are simply gorgeous, visually the only thing I feel the game couldve done better on is the human animations. The music in this game is another high point that you will continuelly take notice of and listen to while being sucked into the beautiful scenery. While the music is great you will notice that the game doesnt always do a great job with sounds, but this doesnt really rob you of much. My main issue with the sound quality of this game is with the voice acting, many characters feel like they are attempting to show emotion but lack specific tones to really complete it. The story does what it sets out to do, which is build suspense and mystery, since the game is so short however it feels like there couldve been more to tell/show.
I feel that if you are on the fence about this game you might want to wait for a sale, but if you are  interested go ahead and buy, you shouldnt be dissapointed.

Cold Waters is a reasonably easy to get into subsim with an emphasis on the tactics of submarine warfare rather than having the player do most of their sensor work and target motion analysis themselves. Acquiring and tracking contacts is simplified from games like Dangerous Waters, but I don't know that I'd necessarily say that's unrealistic- you wouldn't be doing all that as a sub skipper, anyway.
Don't expect this to be easy. Sure, you have a boat that can do 32kts submerged with virtually unlimited endurance and fast homing torpedos. Your submarine is capable, but so are the threats you'll be facing. When you encounter ASW aircraft, buckle in for a few hours of trying to throw them off your trail.
More content would be nice, especially a campaign playing as the Russians vs. NATO (you can play as Russian subs with mods, but you'll still be facing off against the reds), but as it stands Cold Waters is a solid game if you have any interest in modern(ish) submarine warfare.

Just when it seemed Saints Row The Third had reached the limits of ridiculousness, IV takes things to a new level.
More hilarious (and occasionally strikingly poignant) writing, a great new villain, some inventive new mechanics and the introduction of super powers make this a highly enjoyable experience. The core super powers in particular - super running and jumping - completely transform how you get around the map, rendering vehicles and aircraft essentially irrelevant. The level of freedom is wonderful, and it's striking how much they are missed when they are taken away.
It's not flawless. There are a few bugs - such as those which instantly completed an activity for me (not that I can really complain about getting Gold level for little work, but it was jarring) and a misson-breaking bug in the Christmas DLC - the quests are unashamedly grindy at times and the game world gets unbalanced quickly once Maurauders get introduced, making it particularly hard to complete some achievements.
However, this is a game which is all about fun, and it well and truly delivers.

But seriously this game is cool, on the higher difficulties many tears shall be shed as the 7 new contacts on your tactical display all in unison unleash what seems to be the entire arsenal of a small island nation upon you, those torpedoes aren't the WW2 ones either, they will find you, you will have to become an acrobat to survive.
The sub to sub combat is also tense, I remember one specific time where a contact that was initially thought to be quite far away turned out to be, in a naval sense, directly next to me. I had a miniature heart attack and the few seconds before I realised he had no idea I was there were not fun. I spent the next 5 minutes creeping my way past him and his buddy before pulling a u-turn and sinking them. Moments like that shorten your life span, but, they make life worth living.
In terms of control and interaction wth the sub, this game is good, but it's not dangerous waters tier. This is like a more easily accessable dangerous waters with updated graphics. That does not mean the game is bad, it just means that this isn't a hardcore simulator, dont go in expecting that. There is no switching between stations to work the different equipment manually if you choose, all of that is managed by your crew. The ease of access and the smaller learning curve however give this game an edge over dangerous waters in the fact that within an hour you're a pretty capable submariner.
TL;DR-- This game is the best modern / cold war submarine game out there currently, it's a pretty niche genre I guess but I'm still thankful that other people actually took the time to develop this, given time this game can really only get better.

Keeping all the action confined to a single table makes you less likely to miss small details.  Also I don't care for parts where the devs want you to find things in the backgrounds like a column or whatever, it might be easier to spot the cues that something's amiss in the background on mobile where the textures are less detailed but on PC there were a few spots I never would have found if not for the hints system.  Controls are still a bit wonky but I'm not really sure how they could be improved as long as the devs want to keep the odd camera system that's in the game.  As for the positives, atmosphere's even better than the first game, some really fun puzzles, great visuals, and a very nice ambient soundtrack.  Overall, a very fun adventure game and I hope that The Room Three gets ported a bit quicker than this one did.

I picked up this game not too long ago (at the time of this review) to see what it was about. Myself, I never was big on ambient games, or survival horror at all. I launched this game and I was hooked. I was taken off guard by the sense of immersion almost instantly. I truly felt helpless in the first half of the game, being a lone man on a mission to protect his home station, while running into many strangers that would prove to be friends. The horror was very well done. Most horror games that are released today rely on jumpscares too much to invoke fear in the player, Metro did not do this. A dim flashlight is all you have to navigate the almost pitch black tunnels of the metro. Every footstep I heard had me on edge, looking around the room in panic. This game also has a hidden moral system that is used to influence one of two endings. Very subtle things contribute to these points, such as listening to dialogue, or thoroughly searching an area, while also obvious things can influence, such as giving the bullet to the child.
This game is truly a masterpiece, and I'd recommend it to both lovers of survival horror and people new to the genre.

Impressed, appreciative and disappointed are the three words I'd use for my experience with this game.
The whole game has an air of "we had a lot of power but didn't quite know what to do with it." It feels a bit directionless, story and gameplay wise. Clever, but lazy. Perhaps the developers ran out of ideas near the end of the game; at the very beginning of the game, the crime solving had me excited for the rest of the game. An hour later, the puzzles get easier and easier to solve, instead of harder, until they feel less like a puzzles and more like (fetch?) motions to go through to get more cutscenes.
The story is a clever and imaginative play with between-the-lines deduction. If only it could stop trying so hard to be dream-like and ambiguous - the story can be a little confusing, not because of how complex it is, but rather because parts seem to be left entirely up to the player's imagination/choice. There seem to be several concrete solutions operating at the same time, that clash with each other one way or another.
Graphic wise, it's beautiful, even if it feels impersonal, not very lived in. Beautiful views all around, and it all runs with a delicious smoothness that never ceased to amaze me throughout the whole game. Something impressive awaits around every corner, music, graphics or sounds.
Bottom line, I liked and disliked this game in almost equal portions. Don't expect a good game - expect a good novel, and you'll probably, hopefully, enjoy it more than I did.

Its a very strategic assymetrical RTS.  RNG can dictate battles at times, which as a whole isn't a bad thing in my opinion. It is less about base building and more on tactical managment of troops and troop choices.  Once you get a sense of the game mechanics you can begin to pull of complicated manoevers and is very rewarding when this succeeds.
I think Relic have struggled with balance since launch though, they always realeasing mass patches changing a lot of things and dont seem to be fine tuning things.  They had the game good for a few months and then they released the Western Armies for multiplayer and it was like starting from scratch again.
I would buy CoH2 at full price.  They recently released Ardenne Assault single player campaign DLC which they charged £35 for.  I refused to pay this price as it heavily re-used assests from another DLC that we already payed £18 for at realease.  I got Allied Assault for £17 though which seems more on the mark for what you are getting.
Sounds are mostly great.  Some of the sounds on the guns are strange for example the BAR and Thompsons sound nothing like thier real life counter parts and sound very much like pea shooters.  The BAR was well known for the terrifying sound it made when firing but sounds like a pea shooter ingame.
Pretty good, though could be better.  The game engine is very old (same engine as CoH1) and is not optimised very well for todays hardware, for example, the game does not utilize SLI or crossfire at all. It runs satisfactorily though frame rate drops heavily when the game gets busy and particle effects are set to max. It could be better.

Core game is typical CoH which is to say it's pretty good. But the business approach in nickel and diming its fans is just deplorable. You need to pay for everything if you want to get beyond the bare offering of the campaign, one theater of war, two sides. I would still recommend this game if the prices are at least reasonable but they are ridiculous. $12 just so you can play as US? Why isn't US included since I already brought Ardenne Assault?

Notice: A lot of reviews are poor about this game because it is early access and people don't bother to read that they're buying an unfinished game. Actually READ what people have to say and don't be taken in by metascores.
Notice: This is going to be detailed, so if your not into that skip to the next review, you have been warned!
Take on Mars - a game designed with a single purpose in mind - explore, and eventually colonize Mars.
Let's talk about the campaign mode later for now I want to talk about the Scenerios:
Manned Missions to locations including Earth's "Backyard Mars", The Moon, and Mars itself are playable as of the current revision, more over they are playable multiplayer. The Multiplayer system is highly reliable from what i can tell minus the fact that the entire game is prealpha. The best part about manned missions thus far is they are strictly co-op, although there's talk of a future competitive mode.
Your astronauts will attempt to build and maintain a base in manned mode - the ways to do this vary but in general you need three major resources - Food, Fuel, and Water. Food is self-evident so let's talk about Fuel - The fuel is a methane/oxygen electric hybird, that is to say they can run off methane or electricity. Newly built vehicles come with a full charge of electricity but you'll need to preform some basic chemistry to get the Methane and Oxygen depending on where you choose to play (Earth,  Moon, and Mars have vastly differing resources).
The best part about the game in my personal opinion is the resource management - it's all very realistic and highly accruate. Of course if your on Mars, you not only need Food and Water, there's also no air to breathe outside your craft - that's where suits and helmets come into play - they recharge when you put them in holders, and the oxygen drains away as you use them, the helmets and suits can be stored in inventory in order to preserve oxygen in sealed areas but in general this does not restore your tanks.
Now there's three primary resource gathering machines in this game, one for rock, soil, and Atmospheres (gases) - Of these three methods there are about 10 - 12 (edit: closer to 20 "chemical compounds" now supported) different base elements that can be divided among the various conditions, and these can be refined into molecules that use the same elements into a new chemical. It's all very highly thought out.
Also with updates they have added the ability to "Scout" the maps for resource deposits which eventually become depleted (not for a *very* long time though - unless that sector was low to begin with). This is preformed with Hand Drills, and Gas/Soil Collectors and Lab Tables and Equipment.
Chemistry aside you may be wondering "if there's no air where's the Food Get the Oxygen?" - good question, Hydroponic Farms are available for construction which (as of yet) only produce potatos, which fulfill both your vitamen and calorie needs (collectively "Food" Needs) Other supplies can restore only one or the other but in general these are limited. Radition is a very real factor - take shelter during solar storms or roast outside - your choice*. Water is just a simple matter of a water fountain and/or a space fluid pouch.
Also at some point in the cycle they added powering your equipment to the mix - which by release should apply to all "constructable" machines in manned multiplayer minus the water fountain and the Hydroponic Farms (For obvious reasons)
So all told Manned Missions can already be very cool.
So...chemistry aside you also will want to provide a base to operate out of during the manned missions: There is a simple building block process that creates virtually any shelter you want (but be warned though simple it's easy to make mistakes at first and end up with a junkyard of shelter parts) My advice is find a mission on Mars say a multiplayer designed scenerio, and deconstruct their base to see how they are put together, this will save you alot of headaches in the long run. Nearly all of my 15+ Hours in this game have been spent in manned missions, however there is also a more primitive pre-manned phased called "Space Program" in which you don't send men, but machines to Mars, and it is reflective of budget and/or time constraints that the real space program faces. Space Program is like "Campaign Mode" for your everyday RTS - it's got somewhat of a goal, and there's specific objectives to meet, not always revealed all at once.
When you first land you have a large cache of supplies (in cooperitive settings) in multiplayer; but that will quickly prove to deplete (faster on higher time compressions and/or with more active players) quicker than you want; the MDV (Manned Descent Vehicle) is home away from home at first but eventually as described above you wil want to branch out to a real "outpost" or even "modular" design.
For the Campaign Mode there are some things that have changed recently - including the completion of a "manned Story Mode" - this is optional but part of the planned "Overall Experience" - you need not play through the Campaign to play multiplayer/scenerios. The Campaign allows you to choose from two modes: A Robotics Phase, and the Manned Story Missions, Manned Story is largely uneventful to be honest and is largely at the current time a largely incomplete feature - it lacks serious challenge and the implementation of critical limits - Unlike Multiplayer and Scenerios which can range from "Very Easy" to "Extremely Realistic and Hard". This said the story mode is a great way to learn the game (assuming you've atleast done the tutorial first!) in a non-challenging enviroment. The Real Gem of this game is in Multiplayer which is also kind of left as an open development; Bohemia Interactive has said they will continue to update the game post-release so even once Feburary 9th Rolls around we may still be receiving what I would consider "new content" - even if very minor.
Allow me to explain what people have been worried about with regards to Feb 9th as well:
Most people who've played the Early Access version know the games bugs and traits initimately -- and they are worried that BI will stick a "Passing Grade" Mark to this game and abandon it - this doesn't seem to be the actual case of what is transpiring here to my knowledge; Because of Time Limits from Publishers or other entities unknown, they are trying to release before a deadline; even thought they have every intention of completing the game afterwards - it -may not- be in an acceptable state immediately after release. I would expect the game to continue to develop new traits and abilities - especially during manned play even after release, with the number of bugs largely controlled to a soon-to-be non-public test and dev branches. This game still shows great promise - even if it is releasing a bit "half-baked".
All in all Great game lot's of details - Worth a try for sure.
8.5/10 - It's got some room for improvement but it's largely a great game.

Planetary exploration sim for egg heads. For as long as I can remember I have had a fascination with earths red neighbour. Since a child I have watched and read all about the various probes and landers sent to Mars.  Heard all the stories, myths and theories surrounding that place. It won't be long now when we will see a real possibility of a human stepping onto mars for the first time even if it will be a one way trip.  Take on Mars has really surprised me. I was expecting some kind of open world Mars exploration game but oh it is so much, much more than that. So far I haven't even set foot on the place. I am playing the campaign which means I start my journey right at the beginning with simple probes and black / white pictures.
In this mode you literally live through the history of exploration on Mars. Each successful mission earns you money which you can then plough into research to create more advanced exploration vehicles. As you advance it opens up ever more complex missions for your landers to complete. The lander camera view and the rugged Martian landscape really make you feel like you are in mission control.  There are a ton of other things you can do in Take on Mars including scenarios and multiplayer. For less than £10 this early release is a real diamond in the rough. Its fairly stable and very playable. The sounds and visuals that accompany you on your adventure add to the atmosphere.
Take on Mars is not going to be for everybody. Its certainly not fast paced and the only action will come in the form of technical disasters or your astronaut suit running out of oxygen. For me though it gives me a chance to do something I will never experience. Its a wonderful journey about what has been, what is now and what is coming in the near future.
I hope the developers keep putting their love into this title because if they do it will be a superb finished product.

An adaptation of the Battlefleet Gothic specalist minitures game, Armada was created by, like many recent Warhammer 40,000-derived titles in the post-THQ age, what appeared to me to be a largely unproven developer. Also like many recent 40k games, it is an ok game that falls short of being a great one.
Thankfully for me, a strong point is in its campaign: a tale of the famous Gothic War, where Failba-er, Abaddon the Despoiler led his 12th Black Crusade against the Imperium's Gothic Sector in an attempt to gain control of the six Blackstone Fortresses, immense and ancient space stations with the firepower to destroy entire star systems. Through the eyes of original character Admiral Spire, you command the Imperial Navy in battle against Chaos, Ork and Eldar fleets, with branching paths and persistent game flow regardless of the outcome of individual battles, allowing things to go better or worse then they canonically did. The 40k mainstays of Gregorian chanting over thundering orchestras and overacting faux-Englishmen help to set the feel.
However, certain parts of the actual gameplay fall short in portraying the scale and intensity of this war and, I feel, of the setting in general. Gameplay is strictly fleet tactics- there is no base-building or resource gathering, or any other aspects of an RTS. Battles are inconsistently paced thanks to a lot of percent-chance mechanics, and restricted to a two-dimensional plane and limited by an arbitrary "point value" as in the tabletop game, severely limiting the size of the fleet in each engagement, and for whatever reason, you are almost always outnumbered by enemy vessels. Towards the campaign's endgame I was able to field only my four most experienced ships against Abaddon's infamous Planet Killer, not to mention his infinitely respawning escorts.
Combat is extremely micromanagement-heavy, sometimes necessitating the use of the game's bullet-time function. Only your ships basic weapons are automated, requiring you to manage active abilities, heavy weapons such as torpedoes, strike craft, emergency maneuvers and virtually everything else directly. The AI is not smart enough to avoid stage hazards such as minefields and asteroids, or to dodge a speeding Ork Kroozer, though this goes for the enemies as well. The more upgrades and skills you install on your ships to give them greater survivability and lethality, the more difficult it becomes to get the most out of them- so perhaps it is better that you have fewer ships. Still, I preferred Sins of a Solar Empire's fleet combat. Armada's tutorial did not adequately explain all the game features, so much so that I was not aware that automating your abilities made them as efficient as those used by your AI opponents until after I had finished the campaign. Still, I was very proud of myself whenever I manually broadsided a Chaos ship with a full spread of my Retribution-class battleship's torpedoes.
There are a number of other modes, including online multiplayer, custom games, and skirmish vs. AI, allowing for a second player for coop, as well as post-release DLCs that add Space Marine and, if you're into them, Tau fleets

I finally got around to beating this, and the last few hours of the game greatly improved my perception of it. Much akin to Thief: Gold or Styx: Master of Shadows, this game's plot relies on a big twist, and prior to this twist being revealed, the game's plot and tone can be supremely meandering. I suggest new players don't drop the game until "The D6" becomes involved in the plot, as this marks a large uptick in the game's pacing. Some things worth noting:
*The original Metro 2033 has problems with an unwieldy upgrade system, upgrades are locked to weapons. In Redux, any gunsmith can swap out parts.
*Many of the good weapons in the game are restricted to the sequel or DLC in Metro 2033. In Redux, these are in the main campaign.
*Many MANY loading screens have been removed
While I had quite a few issues with the original Metro 2033, porting the game to the Last Light engine fixes a lot of this. When you're less frustrated with the core gun/gameplay, you'll find you can pay a lot more attention to the excellent writing and level design.
The levels Cursed, Front, Black Station, Caves, and D6 are absolutely fantastic, and display the Deus Ex-style of game design wherein players are led on a linear path through completely non-linear levels. Black Station wraps around itself in astounding ways. I snuck past a group of Nazis, only later to approach them from a different entrance to the same room and have to fight them anyway. I never realized it was the same room until I realized I was sneaking through the same crawlspace again! Brillaint!
Metro 2033 Redux looks and runs great on Windows, SteamOS and Linux, and is most certainly the best way to experience the first entry in the Metro series. While GSC's S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games and 4As first crack at Metro 2033 were diamonds in the rough, Redux is a highly polished, brillaintly crafted game with shooting that is as good as its writing. That doesn't happen very often anymore, and it's hard to ignore.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a first person mystery game with some puzzles with an emphasis on narrative. I'd say, if you are in to atmospheric stuff, puzzle games, or just really like good looking environments, this game is absolutely for you.
I'll say it right away; this game is quite short. Like most indie games that seem to surpass that level of quality that we "expect" when something is made on such a small scale (Journey, Dear Esther). As an Indie developer you can only make a game truly good if it's short (we're talking about linear traditional type of games, where it takes a long time to set up environments and set pieces). Either you make it linear and short, or you can make it open (which is a hit or miss design choice) and very long.
Not only is it short, but it also has very little replayability. There aren't many things to "discover" that aren't already integral to your progression in the game. So once you've finished, you've done everything there is to do, as far as I know.
So it's safe to say that TVOEC is one of those games that might not be worth the full price, if you don't appreciate short, but good games. I'm sure it will go on sale soon, anyways.
(I'll try not to spoil anything or even mention the narrative)
You kind of go in to this game not knowing much about it. It's called "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter", but who is Ethan Carter, and why are we here? How do we find Ethan? Do we find him at all? Is he real? Is anything real? What do I do? That's probably my favorite aspect of this game: It doesn't hold your hand, it gives you MINIMAL information and you get to put the peices together at your own pace. That's very much missing in most games these days.
The game starts out putting you right in the beautiful forest of Red Creek Valley. You''ll be impressed by the visual fidelity. Screenshots don't have anything on the actual beauty of seeing this game in motion. It has a very moody, melancholic aesthetic. You could say that it's "photo realistic" but no, I cannot agree with that. It has realistic assets, but the actual treatment of movement, sound, and color are not realistic, they're romantic and depressing (in true Swede nature).
Once you get to the first few puzzles, which are surreal, HP lovecraftian mini-adventures, you'll notice that some of them are thematically unrelated, that's because their only connection are narrative. There's sci-fi, fantasy, modern fiction, ect. all to be found in this game's stories. Which is actually incredibly creepy. It's hard to pinpoint why. I guess the surprise of seeing something so disconnected from what you expect the game to throw at you can be really off-putting (hopefully in a good way though).
The consistent mechanics that go in to the strictly narrative parts of this game are fairly straight forward, you inspect things, find a dead body, and find out what happened by placing everything in the place where they were before the murder, and "contact the dead". It is actually a really cool idea, and the execution is perfect.
Well, that's kind of all there is in this game, not including the story. It's short, but very very sweet. I'd say it's worth a swing if you're not insecure about non traditional gameplay *cough* people calling Dear Esther a walking simulator *cough*.

Its a mystery adventure in first person where you investigate, explore and try and sequence together what happened to make the world end up as it did before you arrived. As such it is very slow, there is no action in it whatsoever, you are there as an observer, investigator and solver. As such you cannot die or fail, however you might end up having an area reset or force you to the beginning of the puzzle.
Graphics: Environments are amazing, it looks extremely good and everything just feels correct, which is good since its 95% of the things that you will look at. This is exactly how I expect Half Life 3 forests to look at, it feels like being back in the forests from Episode 2, but just amazing looking. Characters are probably the weakest point, they look lackluster next to the environment.
Sound: Great great music, reminds me of skyrim, beautiful and calm. Voice acting was ok, the player character is clearly the best, would like to have heard more from him. Only iffy about the sound is that the 3d positioning were at times really bad. In one area I had to stand in the middle of the room to hear the ghostly voices at a correct level, and in another place I couldn't position the enormous water source because the sound didn't come from a specific direction. Minor things but kind of odd when playing with headphones.
Technical things: Worked great on my computer, no crashes or anything. Had some annoying stuttering when I moved around and new assets loaded, otherwise the performance was fine on my 780ti. Might just be my SSD that is kind of bad, not a new thing for me.
Only encountered one bug that forced me to reload to the latest autosave, kind of annoying but didn't happen anywhere else.
If you feel that 20€ for 4 hours is a bit short you will be missing out on a beautiful game. I really enjoyed it and hope you will too, and that there will come more short games like these.

A sub sim that manages to be thrilling and action-packed. A 3rd-person perspective is used, which  may seem unusual but it immediately gives a situational awareness and a feeling of control which normally takes a lot of practice to achieve, and it also raises the tension off the scale when you're jinking around the enemy torpedoes!
A couple of criticisms:
1: I don't like the map screen on Campaign mode. We need to be able to slow it down and pause it because everything moves too fast. You barely have a chance to think. We also need a better way to move the sub than holding the mouse where you want it to go. Creating waypoints with mouse-clicks would be far easier and more intuitive.
2: At the moment, it just feels a bit empty. There's no friendly or neutral units. It all just feels like it needs to be fleshed out a bit more.
3: You need to manually identify sonar targets to speed up the targetting process. This is par for sub sims in general but it feels out-of-place in this game, as it seems to be more focussed on the commanding aspect. I also suspect it'd become a chore after playing for a while as well. Maybe I'm wrong and it wouldn't be as fun without it, but it'd be nice to have the option to turn it off.
Overall, the potential is there for an amazing simulator, and hoping the developers add more content soon!

We thought, we would die, but then we saw Ships on the horizon, coming for our position.
We cheered in joy and waved with our hands... how foolish we were, to believe, we would be rescued by friends...

It's freezing cold on the back of the military truck they've put us on.

Charles Arzon, Commander of the Sturgeon-Class SSN Tautog, 5th of December 1968.

Well it's been a while, so I suppose I'll revisit Cold Waters. Back in June I said the game wasn't worth $40 and as of now I feel that review is still mostly true. HOWEVER, a good modding community and a handful of quality of life updates(still no major content updates) have improved the game. I feel now that Cold Waters is one major content patch and steam workshop support away from being a great game worthy of a beaming review. According to the news, we will be getting a patch with a new campaign soon, so I am eagerly looking forward to that.
To those that are thinking of purchasing Cold Waters: honestly I have to say, don't get this game yet. As of now (June 23rd, post-1.04b patch) there's not much in the game to warrant $40. The game contains a 1984 campaign mode; a 1968 campaign that is identical to the '84 one, but with fewer vessel classes available to choose from, shorter engagement ranges, and dumbfire torpedoes; and about 10 single missions with varying degrees of difficulty.
Some of the single missions are also clones of the campaign missions so that further reduces the games replayability. I've only logged a mere 14 hours into the game and completed the '84 campaign twice, a handful of the single missions that I found interesting, and started on the '68 campaign. I personally do not find the '68 campaign to be enjoyable due to the regular failure of Mk. 17 guided torpedoes, and the need for constant resupply trips back to your home port. There are a couple of annoying bugs that I'm sure we'll see in the game for a breif period of time, but I am also sure they will be patched out since the devs of Cold Waters are actually pretty decent. Overall a nice game, but definitely not worth $40 until more/new content is added. Will update as more content is released.

Great game, but The Room and its sequel are just too short in my opinion. Under 2 hours to complete each one? I know it's a mobile port but really, less than 2 hours?
I love puzzle games and I was loving both of these games up until I finished them and realised that it just didn't feel like a full game to me.
Furthermore, it feels like the puzzles got wider in the sequel, but also more shallow. Completing a puzzle didn't feel anywhere near as rewarding as the original, it just felt like you went to each item and brute forced all the clicks until something, well... clicked. The original had much deeper challenges, locked up in just one box sometimes getting deeper and deeper, but this time the puzzles were spread out over 3 or even 4 tables and mechanisms.
In summary, it really is a great game. It's well-made, the story's great, the graphics are superb for it being a mobile port but it just doesn't feel complete and it's too short. Sure, it's cheap, but I expected at least another hour from both the original and this addition and that's the only reason I wouldn't recommend it - if you just want a couple hours of pleasant, but fairly complex, puzzles I would recommend it however if you want a complete game I would not recommend The Room or The Room Two.
I still can't decide whether to vote this game up or down, yet.

Let me start off with stating: I really, really wanted to love this game. And at what it does - strategic ship combat, be it traditional sea-ships or spaceships - it really is the best thing after Sid Meyer's Pirates!, and the best and only thing if you want to put that into space. I love Warhammer 40K and been waiting for a long time to get a 40K game after Dawn of War II  and Space Marine (the TPS slasher) where everything feels just as... heavy and impactful. And Battlefleet Gothic Armada delivers that, even though the Warhammer 40.000 is missing from it's title which kinda hurts my little 40K thirsty soul.
But what the game lacks in, is everything, beyond that good foundation it has.
The lore, the atmosphere, the overall feeling of being polished. All the ships are to the last square meter are highly detailed (okay, Chaos textures are messy here and there but that's the minor of most minor things), the music is excellent, engaging and immediately pulls you to the 40K feeling of you know, grandiose gothic feeling as if you are watching some medieval armies clash but in space.
Everything that is excellent in atmosphere, fails to live up to that highly set bar regarding gameplay. There an absolute lack of scale, these massive warships unless you zoom in as deep as you can, doesn't really feel big at all. There are barely any other objects in space such as space stations or satellites or any kind of floating building (with the exception of seeing 1 or maybe 2 extremely rarely at specific missions). The first time you start playing and toying around with the camera and watching ships move up close that feeling is there, but after a few hours of real gameplay it feels like a board game. I know, BGA is originally a boardgame and this game is an adaptation of that, but I don't want that feeling when the whole audiovisual concept is so marvelously made to host a real, punching RTS.
It fails to motivate me to launch the game again. All the maps are the same, empty space with randomly generated electric clouds and mines and some very specific missions where you can't go to certain parts of the map because "it hurts, red is bad, red hurts". Take a look at Ancient Space and it's map design, they could make interesting, engaging maps in 2D space that feel like we are on the ground, with chokepoints, routes, spots of strategic importance... but it lacked the great atmosphere BGA game has. If only we could combine the two...
I make no secret of not being a fan of the Imperium - for me, they are the "generic human baseline faction". Be it GDI, Space Marines, Imperial army, Terrans, any kind of human faction really - they bore me. I knew, before buying this game that it only has the Imperium as a playable race in the story mode, but what I did not knew was how homogene all the missions, all the maps are. If you have 95% the same map every time, with no base building, no nothing just an upgrade menu, WHY CAN'T WE HAVE OTHER CAMPAIGNS?
There are the detailed, fantasticly done Chaos, Ork, Eldar ships, but even the Space Marines and the Tau joined in form of DLC, why can't we have campaign for them? The ships are there, the interface is there (for skirmish / multiplayer), everything is there and made. Except a camapign.
Every camapign mission feels like a Skirmish against the AI, and the only additional feature that separates the camapign from Skirmish and Multiplayer is a static map you click on to get to the next mission, and a huge load of text read by campaign characters and their concept art face. Even the cutscenes are barely moving concept arts. All they needed to do, was to make ~20 more concept arts, write some gibberish "for the blood god!" "for the dakka dakka" story, make a voiceover actor read them, and put it on the moving concept arts. This is EXACTLY what the Imperial campaign is.
Why can't we have this for the rest of the factions? Add that the multiplayer is near dead empty, and the additional DLC factions are overpriced (without campaign of course).
A really, excellent game, with great visuals, great audio, true to the W40K universe that many cheap adaptions merely use as a "generic sci-fi skin", but not this one, it's really, that good. The combat is excellent. But the devs absolutely failed to create an enging, meaningful campaign for it that can pull me back to launch it more than twice, with the opportunity there to make a campaign for every race with a little more effort, but they didn't do that either.
Faithful adaptation of the tabletop game! Needs.. more though. Multiplayer can onlybring so much to the table. Hopefully they have more fleets and campaigns soon, similar to Dawn of War.

This is a hard one to review, but I will say straight out that if you're seduced by the synopsis on Steam, as I was, tread carefully. 'First-person story driven mystery game' is not completely inaccurate, but it is slightly misleading. This is much less a game and more an 'arthouse experience with walking simulator'.
The plot is certainly intruiging; you arrive in Red Creek Valley, as a paranormal detective named Paul Prospero. Having received letters from a young boy called Ethan Carter, his vanishing prompts your arrival and intent to discover what happened here. Slowly, piece-by-piece you start to dissect the confusion and put together the truth...
Ok, so the plot doesn't sound THAT exciting when I look back at it, and I'd have to say that's my first big problem with Ethan Carter - this game does not grip you. I felt a real sense of disconnection from the game, and never really felt immersed in it from the word go. There is a real absence of tension, excitement and thrills from a game that implies it's full of the stuff.
Visually, on the other hand, it's stunning. It's easily the best-looking indie game ever made, with graphics akin to Alan Wake on a commercial level. It has that 'coastal small American town' feel to it and it certainly looks the part - the lush vegetation and general scenery are epic.
Back to the more negative aspect though is the length - this game took me 5 hours - and a lot of that was via walking around rather aimlessly thanks to a couple of bugs which cost me at least two hours of gameplay. For £15 you really expect more than just 3-5 hours gameplay, no matter how some people try to justify the 'experience' and it being 'high-brow arthouse that's to be savoured'. My wallet is to be savoured too, and 5 hours doesn't cut it.
Then we have the abominable save system. There ARE some locations which have hard saves written in - aka you can go to them and they save your location, but otherwise you only get a save for achieving something in the game. AKA you can stroll around for ages, not actually go to a hard save location and not achieve anything, and guess what? None of what you did saved! And then there's the fact the saves only 'save scene'. So, for example, if you partially complete one bit, want a break...well...you can't. Because until you finish that scene your progress in that scene does not save, and if you move on without saving and DO save at a hard save location? Everything you did in that earlier scene is erased and you have to start again. In short, the save system is a mess.
There's also that inescapable feeling that you're just walking around looking at things - nice looking things, yes, but the game's non-linear nature means you can do what you like in what order you want, and it makes it feel disjointed.
There ARE great sequences here, and I won't spoil any of them. One of them actually intimidated me and made me say 'what the h*ll...' which I liked. I like something unexpected and different, and a few scenes achieved this.
But overall I paid £15 for a first-person adventure and feel like I got a very nice looking 5 hour walking simulator more akin to Dear Esther than anything else.
I recommend this if you like that kind of game, but please, know it's what you're getting and not a more energetic, high-octane thriller like I was hoping for. Due to the misleading synopsis I have to regrettably not recommend it, but if they change the synopsis to a more accurate and honest content appraisal, I will reverse that.
Pity it doesn't reverse my £15.

XCom Enemy Unknown consits of two major areas: The turn based combat, and the strategical or tactical screen. The strategic screen takes an amazingly high percentage of your playtime. Things are kept simple all over the game, but there are many different things, making it over all a complex game. Crafting, Upgrading, Building your own 'city', Airfight, Soldier Skills, Skins, Levels, Upgrade, Abilities, Classes - it has it all. The tutorial gives you a decent understanding of how things may work, the story keeps you by the line and tells you what to do. The sympatic Research and Engineering chiefs tell you kindly if you miss something. However, the fine details are often hidden. In advance, you don't know what research unlocks what item. So if you are eager to get that sniper rifle upgrade, you may just use Wiki to find out what research is needed for it. Yeah, I guess it needs one playthrough to get the hang on all things.
Mechanics are overall great. Just as an example: You may build your own Plasma Rifle for high expenses, or you just take more risk in fight and go close to the enemy, stunning him and loot the rifle (It gets destroyed when you kill the enemy normally).
The turn based mechanics are fine. You basically get two actions a turn. May it be run, shoot, or just put your head down. Some actions take both 'actions' at once, others have a penalty when you do it as second (e.g. move then sniper shot). Sometimes it's a bit weird. Like reloading taking your whole turn. But you can run, and then reload.
As soon as you spot an enemy group, they will go into cover. They get this free move in the middle of your turn. I guess it would be unfair otherwise ;)
Fight mechanics are ok. It's basically about getting your folks into cover and flanking the enemy. Or you just aim so precicsely that flanking becomes neglectable. The game gives you a great amount of option with 4 different classes and about 20 or so skills per class. However, you choose between two skills. So you may get two guys of the same class with totally different abilities. The assault class can even have normal guns or shotguns. So you can make a "Run and Gun" All In Assaulter, or a defensive one staying in the back. Your team will have a lot of synergies that you can use. The supporter throwing the smoke grenade, so you don't get hit. The Heavy class blowing up the target's cover, marking the enemy with holographics to get easier hits, and your sniper takes him out. For example. And if the shot misses, just suppress him to reduce his aim, so your guy doesn't get hit.
Your progression in the game is made absolutely teriffic. You have quite a lot of resource materials that you have to handle. Money just being of it. You can build tons of stuff, not only three levels of weapons (normal, laser, plasma), but up to crazy stuff like JetPackArmor, Invisibility Armor, a Robot you can take in fight that acts as mobile cover or a hovercraft flying around. Great stuff! So many things synergize in some way, e.g. your flying armor with a sniper soldier that has a skill that he aims better when he is elevated. Love it! However, while the basic things are quite cheap by time, the OP stuff is accordingly expensive. You may give your whole team just the level 2 armor and one or two chosen ones may get a level 3 armor for quite some time. You have to think well about how to handle your resources.
The game is sometimes very punishing. When your very last action in your turn spots an enemy, you may just load your game. The enemy gets the free move to cover, then gets the turn and will basically rip you off.  To avoid that, you may only use your first action, so you can always react, but then the game will alwys mark the wrong soldier by default and things like that. Aww. Well, often you just feel treated unfair. 95% Chacne to hit and it goes out of nowhere, while this noob enemy scores a crit on your full cover while in smoke. Ugly! And when you do a mistake, you get punished hard. Your lovely max level soldier? Just gone. Rip. Have fun with a level one noob, totally out of the depth, fighting against terminators. No fun! So what will happen. Save load save load save load save load. ;)
I like the story a lot. The cutscenes are sometimes repetetitive, but ok. I think the voice acting is quite good!
Graphics are good enough. Don't know how old the game is actually.
Afterall, even if it's frustrating sometimtes, it's fun to play and comes with great replayability! Definitely worth a try!

Amazing title that dropped like a depth charge out of nowhere!
The balance between hardcore sim and "Hunt for Red October-Simulator" is PERFECT.
A few days ago I had cleared out 6 warships, banged up from depth charges and 3 flooded compartents I was limping to the edge of the map to extract, no contacts, crusing ahead standard at 800 feet. Something didn't quite feel right and I decided to "clear my baffles" (submariner term to check behind you since there's essentially a 60 degree blindspot behind you because your motor/propeller makes too much noise).
I swing around to find a November class Soviet attack sub 2,000 yards behind me who's been stalking me at low speed to get the perfect shot. Knowing he's spotted he fires a torpedo right at me as my sonar starts pinging loudly at a quickening pace (the faster the ping the closer the torpedo.)
Actual sweat forms on my forehead as I quickly devise a firing solution and let a weapon of my own loose in the water.
I drop a noisemaker with Shift+D and immediately blow emergency ballast followed by full rise on the planes. I watch as the enemy torpedo misses my rudder by literal inches as I quickly ascend upward. Halfway up at around 400 feet I watch the now rattled November class take my torpedo to his port side and blow up instantly from the pressure changes at his depth.
I literally performed a movie-worthy Crazy Ivan manuever, all of it transpired in less than 20 seconds and the adrenaline was oh so real. All of it was completely dynamic because the AI is outright vicious in this game. On harder difficulties you WILL channel your inner Gene Hackman or you will die in the murky depths below along with your entire crew.
(Soviet anti-submarine warfare Helos and Bear bombers will hunt you to extinction)
This truly is a worthy spiritual successor to MicroProse' Red Storm Rising back in the ancient days of 1988, with a fully dynamic, long campaign that reacts and morphs with your performance, culminating with either defeat or victory in the bigger picture conflict that you're just a small part of, just like in the real Cold (hot in this case) War. The fact that you see land battalions and surveillance aircraft fight it out over a Northern European map that responds to what you've done makes it feel very real. They even have generated news headlines that take into account your success/failure/partial success the day before. Everything matters and the stakes are high as WW3 without nukes is in full swing.
The small development team deserves support and are quick to respond to bugs, tweaks and suggestions.
Multiplayer  is coming at some point and I for one cannot wait to sit in silence sonar pinging freshbloods storming through shallow waters at 25 knots, just waiting to be picked off.
Couple this with upcoming Soviet campaigns and NATO forces modelled in-game and you've got a bright future for this title.
At first I thought the price was steep but after playing it for 12 hours I can see the effort and detail that went into this game, the sound modelling alone is next level, and with great graphics immersing you as you skirt below an iceberg off the coast of Greenland to hunt nuclear subs, the whole package proves itself to be worth every cent.
Finally, let's not forget the excellent soundtrack, which, while only containing a few songs, perfectly understands what type of music should accompany modern submarine warfare. It's straight out of Crimson Tide, but with its own style.
If you have even a passing interest in naval, submarine or simulated warfare of any kind you owe it to yourself to pick up this gem.

First off, let me just say I'm loving this game. I'd also say the devs have been great since release. Bugs get fixed pretty quickly, and there's been many quality of life improvements to the interface. With that in mind, this game is in kind of a weird place. If you look at the tone of various other reviews, you'll kind of get what I mean here. It kind of straddles a line between more casual military themed games, and more complex military simulations.
On one hand, there is quite a bit more to think about here than just where to steer and where to shoot. You'll need to develop an understanding of how active and passive sonars work and how they are affected by a multitude of different parameters. You'll have to learn to balance caution and aggression very carefully. If you're new to sub sims, you're going to die a lot in the first few hours. It isn't because the game is broken, its because you're doing something wrong. Its okay, mistakes are how you learn. You will learn, and you will get better.
On the other hand, this game still pales in comparison to the complexity of some of the classic modern subsims. I was a huge fan of the old Jane's/Sonalysts sims like
and
and
. Those games were far more complex, especially around operating your various sensors. Whether you can hear a given contact or not is modeled pretty realistically, and is affected by environmental conditions, depth, speed, relative orietnation, etc. But once you can actually hear a contact, the only work from there is analyzing the signal to classify the contact, which is mostly just a simple "match the lines" game. Determining bearing, range, depth, speed of the contact is all handled for you automatically. This isn't instant, it will take time for the computer to do the TMA for you, and the clearer the signal you have, the quicker a solution will be developed. Towed arrays are just automatically "on" when you're moving at 1/3 ahead.   You won't have quite as much control over weapons as you're used to, but the most important capabilities of the Mk 48 are modeled. You don't need to do any work to figure out if there's a layer and how deep it is, it just tells you.  Despite these simplifications, the way you conduct any given engagement will still feel the same. The thought processes, the tactics, the many variables you need to consider, that's all still there.
One area where the game is actually a little more complex than those old sims is in steering the boat. You don't get to just order a certain depth or heading. You will manually controll rudder, planes, and ballast. Getting up to periscope depth quickly but without breaching will take a little practice. Getting down the muscle memory to go fullly up or down on both planes and ballast, which is going to be important to dodging torpedoes, will take a bit of practice.
Overall, I think Killerfish has done an excellent job of finding this middle ground. The game is far more accessible to a broader audience than the classic subsims were. But that's really only becausee some of the most mundane tedium has been stripped away. I know, I know, the mundane tedium was part of the charm for a lot of you. But really, the meat of a sub sim is still there, and it is tasty tasty meat.

This is a revised review, after many patches.
The good:
- Many diverse game modes. And I do mean very diverse.
- Decent modding support and capabilities.
- One of the few games that does give you that old "hard-SF" space vibe. Its a nerdy game abotu space, which feels very refreshign after 100s of "flashy" fiction games on the topiuc of space exploration.
- A decent survival game with resource extracting and base building etc, somewhat minecraft-style, but more rigid and more serious.
The bad:
- The game's physics engine is rough around the edges. When it works its great (does  aphenomenal job of simulating very low gravity on the moon for example). But at times you find yourself tripping over a cable in earth or mars gravity and the physics engine glitches and sends you flying 10 meters into the sky. These sort of physics glitches are annoying.
- Its a "take it slow" game, not everyone's cup of tea. This might appeal more to pleople who play simulator games than to those who prefer action games. Both the manned and unmanned parts of the game
- Shady and inconsistent OS support, something I really need to complain about. When I purchased the game, the Bohemia Interactive site listed "Windows XP / Windows 7 / Vista" in the Reccomended settings.  Now on steam its just Windows 7 and Vista. XP support seems to have been silently dropped and I feel somewhat cheated, as I was not able to play the game for a long time until I upgraded my PC and got a new Windows.
- Some of the textures look a bit dated, though it has to be said that nice lighting and post-processing does a great job at covering this up.

I have a lot of praise for FTL, but I'll try to sum it up in a short review.
First of all: FTL is just one of those games that can have you either chuckling with glee as you blow a ship to smithereens, or yelling with frustration as your ship is blown to smithereens.
Secondly: the system of the game. You have a reactor which generates energy, which can be upgraded to supply more energy. Energy supplies systems. Systems keep you alive. If your shields go down, you send in crew to repair them. If the enemy has heavy weapons, send some Mantis crew into their ship via a teleporter.
But the real praise goes to the visuals and the soundtrack. The track is so calm that I often forget the fact that my ship is in the middle of a pack of giant spiders, and instead think to myself, God, this game is great. As for the visuals: well, the background is so detailed! Just look at it!
Cons: after a while, you do get used to being blown apart. The first time it happened to me, I swore revenge on the Lanius for blowing up my ship.
Overall, this game lives up to its name. FTL: ♥♥♥♥ the Lanius.

Though perhaps not the greatest of the Half-Life series (I would rather the very first HL above this episode in terms of playability and narrative), this quick and fast installment is nonetheless one of the better games that Valve has released. Be sure to play HL2 first, or there'll be a great deal of confusion, but otherwise, a decent episode to say the least.

Half-Life 2: Episode One takes place right after Half-Life 2, and was a begining of an experiment of getting out the Half Life 2 continuations faster... which ended up falling on it's♥♥♥♥♥when Valve realised that after Portal and TF2, no one cared about Half Life anymore, the final nail on the coffin being when valve discovered they could make more money off of selling virtual items for F2P games and promoting e-sports crap than Half Life could ever hope of doing.
Anyways, Episode One is a huge graphical leap from Half Life 2, adding in pretty HDR effects (even though you're going to see a lot of warm colors in this game) and exploring more of the physics based gameplay. One complaint is that it feels pretty short and does feel like you're essentially doing more of the same you did in the last parts of Half Life 2, only in reverse.  You also get commentary, which always a great thing to listen to.
Overall, get this game if you played/own Half Life 2 and haven't played Episode one yet

Half-Life 2: Episode 1 sees our hero Warren doing his best to pick up the pieces left by Gordon Freeman, who for once isn't on the box art. Warren spends most of this game saving the thousands of citizens who Freeman imperiled when he destroyed the Citadel, citizens who are growing increasingly irate after having seen Freeman save, like, 15 people and then leave on a train with the hot chick on the box art. Warren must use his stealth skills to sneak into and disable Combine facilities that are keeping the citizens from escaping, and in a thrilling climax the player climbs atop a Strider and hacks into its neural interface, using it to fend off waves of opposing Striders, dropships, gunboats, soldiers, and APCs. This is the strongest installment in this series yet!

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was one of those ideas that was beautiful in theory but not so much in practice. The story was wonderful and captivating from start to finish and honestly, a story is what is should have been. Yes, the cinematics and absolutely gorgeous landscapes were top-notch; but they only added so much. The fact of the matter is that The Vanishing of Ethan Carter would be a one of those must read novels(if done right). However it just leaves you feeling rather unsatisfied at the end, like, you just ate a great meal; but the meal only included an appetizer and dessert, there was no main dish to it.
I find it rather strange to criticize this game, because for once I see devs out there doing what I love most, and that is making an engrossing storyline that captivates its players from start to finish as they try to solve this paranormal who dun'it. However, at the same time, it lacks the aspects of a game that leave a player feeling totally satisfied.
I'm sure I could go on and on about this as I try desperately to explain how I feel about this strangely wonderful yet vaguely unsatisfying game; but I just don't think it deserves that.
The end all be all is that It was a game that was true to its very first message, that it was a visual narration that would not hold your hand.
I would like to put this out there though. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter should, no, MUST be a novel.

I bought this game on a whim since it was on steam sale, figured it would be just another generic shooter. Boy was I wrong.
This game fits into a very small category of FPS games that manage to do alot of things extremly well: it looks good, it plays good, its got good narative and is legitimtly scary. It also finds that sweet spot where it is extremely difficult but not to the point of frustration. This is honestly one of the most polished shooters I've played in ages.
The gameplay plays out like a normal FPS: go from one big setpiece to another, with some hubs in between to restock your ammo and upgrade your guns. A bit cookie cutter, but the game does it so well that its easy to forgive its linear nature. The action and the narrative will keep you going.
The actual gameplay is quite interesting, having to recharge batteries, swap out gas mask filters, and pump up air rifles in the middle of combat is something new and really adds to the tension. Its also quite interesting that the currency of the game is ammo. You can spend those beauties on a whole mess of upgrades, or toss them into a gun for a couple of shots of powerful incindeary bliss.
The Scrounging for resources and upgrading weapons has a distinct Fallout feel to it, and its quite fun to customize your loadout to fit your play style.
If I had to pick a gripe about this game, it would be the SSAA. With it even on 2x my framerate ate it under a constant 60, even with a 980 gtx. I believe the game must already have another form of AA however, as turning off SSAA the game dosn't appear jaggy at all. Aside from that and a few crashes here and there, the game has run solid.
I'm not usually super big on "normal FPS", with RPG orintated ones like Fallout and Fary Cry being the noticible exception to this rule, and I'm happy to say I'm adding the Metro series to this. If last light redux is also this good, I'm sure I'll enjoy it just as much.

Metro 2033 is a great game that should definitely be played, but I'm not sure if this is the best way to do it. Metro 2033 Redux is an updated version of the original game to run on the engine of Last Light, and while some things have been improved, like lighting improvements and certain characters looking and sounding better (Artyom and the kid who leads you to Bourbon have new voice actors, to name a few), it's far from perfect. Some of the character changes are Half Life 2 Cinematic Mod levels of hideousness, like the new version of Nikki, the stripper who you can pay near the beginning of the game. Certain effects have also been removed, most notably the falling snow in the Tower area, leaving certain outdoor areas looking empty and flat compared to the original.
The game lets you choose between Survival and Spartan modes, meant to be similar to the original game and Last Light respectively, but no matter which one you choose it still uses the Last Light stealth system, in which the old 3-phase darkness system has been turned into a 2-phase "you're either invisible or a walking target" system, where as long as your big blue light isn't on you can literally walk right in front of an enemy unspotted. Some people might think of this as an improvement over 2033's admittedly strict stealth system, but I thought the original's system was fitting in a game that was generally designed to be tough with a tense atmosphere, compared to Last Light's more shooter-ish approach. One thing I was worried about going in was the ranger hardcore functions, since in Last Light the lack of a journal meant that certain things like choosing your side weapon boiled down to fumbling around with the controls listening to the weapon change sound effects to be able to tell if you were choosing grenades or knives, and that has been fixed, but they didn't fix the fact that whenever you get into a QTE it won't tell you what button you're supposed to press, meaning if you're new to the game and aren't aware of where the QTEs are you can expect to die a lot due to not even being aware that you're supposed to be doing something in certain spots if you choose the more atmospheric difficulties.
Overall, I just find it hard to justify recommending this particular version of the game to anyone. It feels like this was primarily made for the console gamers who never got a pretty looking version of 2033 the first time, but for those of us who can just go buy Metro 2033 on steam right now for less than the cost of this and still get a beautiful experience with what I consider an overall better design, it's fairly hard to convince myself that the visual differences are really worth it.

If you want to play it for the story, buy it while it's on sale, or better yet find a copy of the books irl.

A beautifully crafted game. From its start to the very end "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" manages to keep you engaged in every possible way: exploration, puzzle solving and constant thinking.
While you will be sinking into your characters words and while you will be constantly drawing maps in your head trying to figure out Ethan Carter's world and mystery, this game just spins you around. I give you an honest promise - this is one of the most rewarding, emotionally thrilling and beautiful conclusions to a game I ever so. Usually we do not notice some things or see them differently then we should, and "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" just points us into the right direction and tells a story which most of the times are left untold.
And it is not about horror, about survival or something specific - this game pulls everything out of you and out of the game genres it covers: think of it as "Gone home" + "Dear Esther" times two and then add a proper mechanic from "Murdered: Soul Suspect". This will be this exact game. But the story of "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" just takes this game a whole extra mile, believe me. I personally never was to USA, but with this single game I felt this country more and more deeply then with anything else I ever witnessed from or about actual country.
So do yourself a favor - or better yet - many favors and just play this game. You'll see.

Really enjoying Cold Waters now I’m over the initial learning curve and know what things do and what a thermal layer is, why it matters etc.
It really is a very tense game of cat and mouse which rewards players with patience. I can understand why it wouldn’t be for everyone, it’s a not a hard-core sim, but more accessible than that and the hard-core sim guys might not like that. And it is not a shoot’em up instant gratification game either. But really a well-paced game with both tactical and strategic layers and a dynamic campaign map which is going on around you, affected by your actions but not completely reliant on you.
Graphically its nice, and represents what matters well, but it is not outstanding. Sound design is simply brilliant and further adds to the tension of hunting and being hunted.
And the weapons on the subs are truly terrifying, if they are in anyway accurately modelled in terms of intelligence (not being a military hardware buff I’m not sure they are) then a single subs capability is devastating.
I’d recommend this game to anyone interested in an accessible cold war game.

Brilliant game let down a bit by the AI.
I love this game. I really do. I used to play a lot of Silent Hunter III and Dangerous Waters and this game though not as deep a sim as those, is brilliant. You do feel the tension (watching your fire solution improve little by little as a contact is approaching and you just want to press the active SONAR button just to make sure you get the first shot out) or the satisfaction of successfully evading a torpedo or depth charges by fast manoeuvering and careful use of counter measures.
The way they handle the campaign also mean that you are usually not sujected to the boredom bits and you get straight into the action. Which is good for a fast game  but I do feel a bit let down. Submarine warfare tends to be a whole lot of nothing with moments of unrelenting action that makes you wish you were back doing nothing. Here, you miss the boring bits and you are left with action and high intensity action.
If you are interested in modern submarine warfare and want a nice and relaxed simulation, this is the game for you.
A couple of things to bear in mind:
If you come from a background where you are used to playing Silent Hunter or Dangerous Waters, read the bits in the manual you need and you are fine.
If however, you are not used to this type of game read the manual twice! And watch some youtube videos on torpedo evasion for when things go south (and they can go south pretty quickly). I recommend Jive Turkey's Channel as he is quite fun to watch and used to actually work on an LA class SSN. Just watch his videos. I highly recommend them.
That being said, the manual is a bit lackluster on some areas and it does not explain what certain things are and how to change them. For instance, it isn't mentioned anywhere on the manual that if you keep your ship paralel to the target your towed array will have the best chances of acquiring a target solution. It also does not explain what the noise levels on the signal page mean and I suggest you read up on their meaning as it will make your life easier.
Finally, the biggest let down is the AI. The AI simply does not work well. They seem to have trouble tracking you and once they do they send one torpedo at a time after you. AI subs do not know how to evade and well, in the 1984 campaign you have access to the Mk 48 torpedo so that is another cheat right there ^^
All in all, amazing game and I highly recommend it at full price!
EDIT: changed the difficulty settings to realist and increased the spacial scale and the game plays much better. AI still has problems evading. Submarine AI is too easy to kill. They do not manoeuver in the vertical plane making their torpedo evasion lackluster. Devs are aware of this and further updates should fix it.

The best LEGO game out there

I'm enjoying it. Seriously, I am. This is perhaps one of the best LEGO games created in many years. It has a sense of progression without taking things away, it flows nicely, and at many points you can break off and just do your own thing. Driving to a mission and you see a collectable? Stop and get it. Looking for collectables and have a mini-challenge (e.g. ring 3 bells)?  Do it. The characters are fun, the voice acting is pretty good, there's a wide variety of vehicles and areas to explore and play around in, and it just feels a lot more competently put together than the more 'traditional' LEGO titles such as Star Wars or Lord of the Rings.
I'm not going to say it's perfect, though, because it's not. The driving is a little annoying at times (especially during missions where your vehicle's health is important) and the checkpointing is too lax, meaning more often than not you will need to replay the entire mission segment you're on rather than just continue from what would generally be a more convenient point. As an example, I was having trouble with a crash-causing bug during the first mission. When loading the game back up I had to replay the first parts of the mission again despite fairly considerable progress, whereas there should be more thorough checkpointing in place to minimise such issues.
It has had a slightly rough launch, and some people are having issues, certainly. I have had issues myself, some of which stopped me playing. But luckily for me, the game is currently playable and plays very well, and I'm happy with my purchase and I'm enjoying it.

The other fixes of going into pcconfigs did nothing for me. I couldn't even launch the game... until now! If you're getting the 0xc0000007b error, this is what you do.
Go to: C: Local Disk/Windows/System32
Find "d3dx11_43.dll". Delete it.
Go into Lego City Undercover's install location, then _CommonRedist/DirectX/Jun2010
Click DXSETUP.exe. It should install and place a new d3dx11_43.dll into that System32 folder.
Launch the game.

This version of Quake 3 is quite an improvement over the original, at least in the modern age. Not only that, the fact that it now costs 10 dollars instead of being 'free to play' is an improvement. You have every Q3 map, the ability to mod, server browsing and hosting, and support for modern systems with 16:9 resolution options which aren't readily available on the original Quake 3.
But why Quake?
Quake Live is a fast, fun fps where the only advantage a veteran player will have over a newbie is their skill and their skill alone. Everyone has access to all items and weapons in the form of pickups as opposed to using loadouts as seen in modern fps. Everything from health, armor, ammunition, and weapons can only be accessed through using pickups in certain modes, while other modes might give you a set amount of health and armor with all weapons, similar to Counter-Strike.
Unfortunately, the skill level of most other players are fairly high, even among 'noobs', with knowledge of techniques like strafe jumping and rocket jumping are required if you want to stand a chance. If you've played plenty of Team Fortress 2, Counter-Strike, or similar games, then you'll do fine. At a 10 dollar price point and with how much content this game has, and even considering the smaller community, this is definitely worth a purchase. Although I somehow got this game for free, I bought a copy for a friend because I like this game so much.

You must not only survive but upgrade your craft along the way in a myriad of interesting ways in order to arrive on time and then fight in the final battle against the rebellion. I find myself coming back to re-write this review. Neotokyo is very similar to Counter Strike. In fact, it's pretty much "Counter-Strike: Ghost in the Shell mod". It's a pretty old game, and it definitely shows, thanks to somewhat delayed actions, and occasionally clunky-feeling gameplay. There aren't many servers up for the game, and you only see maybe one or two servers kind of filled at a time. However, if more people started playing the game, this can turn around pretty easily. If you decide to get this game, it's best to join the "Active Neotokyo Players" group, as they organize events on the regular to draw in a more concentrated group of players at specific times to help with the mostly empty servers.
Despite it's dated graphics and gameplay, it can be a pretty tense game at times, especially when you first find out that gibbing is in the game after your buddy's head gets taken off by a sniper. There are three classes with their own special abilties, loadouts, and armor to speed ratio. As you progress through a match and rank up, you get access to new weapons that reset after each match, rewarding you based on your contribution to the team. The soundtrack for this game is phenomenal, but unfortunately only plays in the main menu. Like most games of this nature, there are two main factions: The Jinrai and the NSF. The NSF are very similar to Section 9 from Ghost in the Shell, whereas the Jinrai are a rouge branch that seeks to make Japan great again. (Or something, it's been a while.) The backstory itself is pretty interesting, and it makes me wish that the game was remade and given it's own singleplayer story. There isn't a whole lot of Cyberpunk games like this out there, and it makes me sad to see that this game is on the fringes of the Steam community.
Pros
-Ads to the narrow list of games in the Cyberpunk genre.
-Pretty tense moments at times.
-Pretty nice community.
-Fantastic soundtrack and lore.
Cons
-Dated graphics and gameplay.
-Not many players.
-Pretty much forgotten about by the devs due to it's age.
Would I suggest this game? If your steam library is small, your wallet is tight, and you like Cyberpunk games, and a fantastic soundtrack, yes. There isn't much to lose except time by getting this game. But it has so much untapped potential and it really needs to be remade and expanded upon. If anything, I suggest you download this game just for the soundtrack.
