A Game I really looked Forward to given that I really like this Genre and Series.
But what they Delivered is Laughable at best.
The Game Bugs out much too often. And the GUI and HUD are Horrible considering that this Game requires such amounts of Micromanagement to actually work.
The Campaign is fine in itself. But gets Repetetive very Fast. And lacks the finesse many of the 40k Campaigns usually got.
The biggest Strike Point however is the Multiplayer. Which was likely the attempt to give the Game some Replayability to and serve as the Longtime Feature.
Unfortunately they messed it up entirely.
The Balancing is pretty much non Existent. Having Enormus Gaps between Factions which are not Balanced out.
And certain Skills are just so Mandatory that you cannot really Play without em if you want to have any Chance in a Battle. Which results in pretty much everyone having the exact same Skillset while other Skills are pretty much never used by anyone but New Players that dont know better.
The Gamemodes are for most Part more annoying than enticing. And most People are glad to have a Simple Clash rather than any Special Gamemode where the Victor is Decided by which Position you get to Play.
And Finally. (Which might also be an Result of hardly anyone Playing the Games Multiplayer Anymore) the Matchmaking is a complete loss. Even as lvl 2 you are often Matched against Max Level Players. Which then means you get some meager Bonus Points you cant really use meaningful anyways due to your lack of Ships to spend them on.
And then get thrown into a Fight against Battleships having nothing but Light Cruisers. Which on top have less Upgrades and Skills but cost the same to Spawn. Which ultimately more than Negates your Bonus Points and gives the Higher lvl Player an Tremendous Advantage.
Overall Verdict is that this Game was a Fail Buy.
If I werent over the 2 hour Time Limit I would return it.
And I can seriously not Recommend anyone to Buy the Game at anything beyond 10 Euro maybe.

I've been yearning to play Battlefleet Gothic, ever since the discontinuation of the tabletop a few years ago. Sadly, Tindalos Interactive failed at creating anything worthwhile with this game. Although the setting, narrative, and sound design are very high quality and are accurate to the 40k universe, everything involving the gameplay design is pathetically mediocre at best. To be brief:
•	The game modes are unvaried.
•	Faction balance is almost non-existent.
•	Certain ship choices and strategies are objectively better than others in the same cost ranges.
•	Only allows for 1v1 and 2v2 sized battles.
•	Poor optimized with long loading times and texture popping.
•	Grinding for XP and in game currency is an unnecessary slog.
•	Lifeless game to game persistence in multiplayer.
•	Leveling system which leaves higher levels players at an unfair advantage, even when considering the pitiful points            bonus lower level players are given at the start of the match.
•	Annoying GUI quirks.
I could continue all day with ever more minor design issues. Individually these grievances are small but added together, prevent this game from truly keeping BFG alive. Also it seems the community of this game is already dying at the time of me purchasing the game.
I would only recommend this game to those who absolutely love the Warhammer franchise and are only looking for a short single player experience instead of lasting multiplayer. I wish this game could support longevity and proper multiplayer competition but it provides neither.  I give this game a 5.5/10.

It is difficult to follow up on one of my favorite game ever, Saint Rows 3. So, is SR4 able to reach the heights of its great brother ? Not really, but it's definitely a good game. It's just not great like SR3 was.
SR4 was first thought as an expansion to SR3, which later was expanded to become a fully fledged sequel. That all concept explains basically what you will find in SR4. You're playing in the same city as SR3, except a virtualized one, where your main character gets super powers similar to thoses you got during one of SR3's optional quests.
Which mean you will get the same sense of craziness as in SR3. You're free to focus on missions, or wreck havok in the city, or just chill out with your crew. However, it also mean there is a huge sense of deja-vu in the game. Some of the activities are focused on your newly acquired super powers, but many are basically the same as what you already had in SR3.
Similarly, the city itself hasn't changed much, you will recognize most places, and it's permanently nighttime, so it's a lot less interesting to cruise around in the city, which is a bit of a shame in a sandbox game. This is amplified by your super powers, as they rapidly make all vehicles totally worthless, so you will basically never use vehicles to cruise around. Instead you will just go from checkpoint to checkpoint with your super powers.
Another thing that is a downgrade compared to SR3 is that it feels more like the power fantasy of one character rather than the story of a crew. In SR3, you would often hangs out with other Saints, be they named characters, or random AI. It really felt like you were the boss of a crew. This time, since your boss is super powered, there are a lot less incentive to hang with a crew, you're already a one man/woman army by yourself.
However, I do admit the super powers are super cool to use. They are very efficient in combat, with different options to suit your own personal style, but they are also just plain fun to use. I spent countless hours just jumping from roof to roof, spriting on highways, or flying around looking for collectibles, but mostly enjoying my super powers. Similarly, many of the new weapons are a blast. The Dubstep gun, especially it's "Pink acidulated pop" version is probably one of my favorite gun in any game ever. It's silly, it's powerful, and you get to kill in style :)
The main quest is another good point. Many of the highly spirited characters of the Saint Row franchises are coming back with witty dialogs, silly situations and a lot of stuff to blow up. I had several moments where i laughed out loud at the fun dialogs or crazy missions. It has lost some of the novelty compared to SR3, but it's still better than many AAA games with botched main quests.
A thing that may divide people is how the game, especially the main plot, rely heavily on knowledge of the previous games in the serie. Violition is bringing back a lot of characters, and is making a lot of references to past events. People who are unfamiliar with them might find theses sections boring/uninteresting.
In many ways that feel like the game is some sort of conclusion to the Saint Row serie, and that everyone is getting an encore before the curtains close. That might also explain why the game is so over-the-top (in a good way) Maybe Violition thinks the current Saints have gone far and it's time for a final big show where everything is possible, but after that it will be time for a new serie, or at least a new crew.
Regardless of it's that the case or not, i did enjoy my time in SR4, but i can't shake the feeling that SR3 is still the better game. Both are worth playing, but if i had to choose only one, there is no doubt that i would go with SR3.

I've got a good 70 hours into civ 5 and I no longer wish to play it on single player. I have played civ since the very first installment. A lot of the policies and bonuses in the game are downright useless. I have no idea why the developers included them. The game comes down to chance. Getting a good start will ensure that you do well. Start isolated and in a bountiful area, and you can compete. It really makes you want to cheat and restart. Most of the time, on a large map, multiple other civs spawn within 10 tiles of your city. Resources will be great for your capital, but can be barren for your surroundings. You simply cannot settle cities without resources to maintain happiness in the early stages of the game. If you cannot settle cities, you cannot beat the cheating AI. They will outscience and outproduce you. Barbarians on King level, which is a relatively weak level, act like a second civ always at war with you. They coordinate surrounding your troops and go right for your cities. This delays settling because your settlers cannot get out of your city with barbarian camps spawing just outside your territory. The barbs spawn CONSTANTLY. The unique luxuries are extremely unbalanced due to the random spawning of them. If you push to settle a nice city, which will undoubtedly be near the AI, they will attack it with an impossible number of units given their production. Win, and they will come at you with even more units that they produce at double speed. Get through the mid game and then the delegates start annoying you. They will ban every luxury in your city, killing your happiness and ruining expansion. This is quite simply the most annoying, unabalanced, unfair, unenjoyable and frustating civ version I have ever played. On multiplayer, it looks more enjoyable. But, they need to fix these unfair random starts and make the game truly balanced. It should be a game of skill not chance as to where you start.

The core concept of Nova Blitz--real-time CCG battles--is more intimidating at first glance than it is in action. The learning curve is no steeper than it is for MTG or any other game of its ilk, and the first few games should quickly orient you to the most important elements of real-time play.
Nova Blitz builds on basic CCG mechanics and adds plenty of smart digital features like persistent damage, cards that change other cards, etc. At the same time, the designers have made a careful effort to avoid memory overload on the part of the player--once you know what your cards do, you don't have to reread rules text every time you play them.
Battles are very fast and often quite competitive, though if a game is one-sided, at least it'll be over quickly.
Deck-building is fairly clear and intuitive, and there are plenty of resources and guides online to help you make your first non-stock decks.
Overall, Nova Blitz is a great addition to the CCG canon. I'm curious whether the real-time feature will be adopted by future games. Time will tell.

This is one of those times that I wish Steam had a numeric rating system. 1-5...5 being the best I would give it a 3.5*. Tossed on an asterisk, since I think this game could be much better, and evolve into more of a sim with time.
I've been gaming since I had a vic 20 w/ a tape drive. So it's safe to say, I played Red Storm Rising a lot back in the day. It set me up for every sub game after. RSR got a ton of gameplay between my friends and I.
It's been awhile since we have had a sub sim reach the community. I'm talking Sim, not game...and Cold Waters falls in between. When the game slows down, and I'm tracking a convoy, or sneaking a SEAL team in, I really feel that sim experience. Then I remember that it's time to press a key to change direction in 5 degree increments. At least maybe it's time to turn?? The lack of plotting tools, charting tools, way points, and the ability to truly track an enemy shines through. Normally you would place a mark on a chart for first contact, and so on. Not on this, instead you try to match up signals so you can attain a better solution...or wait for 95% and your crew will identify it. BUT only at 95% will it start to track said targets on the map. Sound confusing...well you just see a contact on a map UNTIL you hit that number, and lines start forming on the map.
For me the inability to plot courses into the campaign map, as well as the tactical part is really a step back. As well as the tools to decipher enemy speeds, bearing, course etc.
At times the AI is spot on, and other times its just down right nasty. This is where I feel some of the sim coming back. The ASW helo's, MAD planes buzzing about, sonobuoys, sonar behaving differently with different conditions. At times it is absolutley maddening, and others just a blast. Nothing like hiding on the bottom, waiting for a ship to pass and moving underneath with it to escape an asw patrol, infilitrate, and release frogmen. Good times.
As far as successor to RSR? Not sure yet, but it does bring back memories. I am enjoying it, and I do believe it is worth the money. The mod's have already started to hit, and I have a feeling Killerfish is going to keep adding to it. (Seawolf?? cough cough).
I'd say 3.5* out of 5. Don't expect full sim experience, yet above game. Hopefully over time this game will improve, and I can come back and change my review. For Killerfish's first time into something like this, I'd say they did a good job, and I will continue to support them through their products.

Steam's "thumbs system" isn't very fair to Cold Waters. There's a lot to like about this game, the tension and suspense
of hunting ... and being hunted is great, and is guaranteed to keep you playing for a good while. However, a lot of that

touches on the finer details. A text manual is provided, but it seems so half-hearted and poorly written that I don't see how it can be a replacement for a proper, tutorial.

To be a bit harsh, I find it inexcusable that the campaign lacks a proper save function, and furthermore, forces you to click "continue" to a series of boring and uninspired text.

than most, but in the end fall to the same trap. After a while it becomes frustrating to fight the seemingly all-seeing Soviets and never understanding
what you’re doing wrong.
All said, I’m sure sub sim fans will love it. But for a casual, amateur captain it eventually sinks.

The core of the game itself is good. However, as an online card game, the playerbase and active community is vital to its success. Number of concurrent players of about 30-50 on the day after release is not healthy state of a game. The developers have completely failed to market their game. There is absolutely no information or community for this game. On the 3rd page of a Google search is a subreddit whose last actual post was made almost a year ago! On top of that people a year ago were saying this game was dead.
Card acquisition mechanics are completely thoughtless. They've borrowed everything from Hearthstone, but somehow think they can be even greedier than a AAA multi-billion dollar company. Disenchant to craft ratios for Legendaries are 20:1, that means if you craft a Legendary and no longer want to use it, you will only receive 5% of its value in currency. On top of that, decks that use full playsets of legendaries require 3. A legendary requires 4000 of the 'dust' currency to craft. Which translates to about $20 of real money for a single legendary. Keep in mind decks are 40 cards and you'll be running 3 legendaries in many cases.
As for the unique game mechanics, simultaneous turns is a very interesting concept. However the very short turn timers and lack of time control are unnecessarily harsh. I understand that this game is meant to be a "blitz", however the design of this game is such that the fastest player is already rewarded with initiative. Being able to execute your turn in 10 seconds does not necessarily demonstrate skill. Even blitz chess gives players a 5 minute pool to think about their situation. You will arrive at complex board states in this game where there are 10 minions, many with unique or active abilities, along with any number of playable cards in your hand. For a player to create a decent play within 15 seconds may take a certain kind of skill, however I can promise you that any player will feel thoroughly disatissfied by their inability to think about their possible plays, even if they were able to scramble one together.
I have played every digital card game on Steam, among many others, and I've seen very good card games with 1000+ active players spiral towards death and unplayable queues within months. Unless the game makes a drastic turnaround on its community, I cannot recommend spending ANY money on this game. It makes me very sad to say this, but the game developers must learn that it is their duty not only to make a good game, but it is also their duty to market their product to a playerbase, which they have completely failed to do. The excessively high pricing schemes for a totally unknown card game is only driving players away, and seems to reinforce this notion that they have no clue what they are doing.

BFG has an enjoyable single player experience, for the most part, but there's no longevity to this title.
The game is primarily focused on multiplayer, which has been plagued with issues since day one that will never likely be fixed. If you don't want to play multiplayer, then you have two options: you can play one-off matches with random fleets (hardly enjoyable, since you'll never be given access to endgame skills or faction bonuses) or you can recreate the grind of the single player campaign and play the same cruiser clash scenario a few hundred times until you finally get the fleet you actually wanted to play with 20 hours ago. If you still have any desire to play the game at that point, you're a more dedicated player than I.
Fundamental design flaws fill this title and are likely never going to go away. This is a game that was great on paper, but suffered from abysmal execution.

As a player that only occasionally poked at the original series, I wasn't carrying a lot of expectation for XCOM.  I initially got this before the Enemy Within expansion.  Was interested in a tactical game, and Firaxis tended to be a good studio, so thought I would try it.
I found a lot of enjoyment in the base game, with a difficulty that could be a bit unforgiving at times, but other than what felt like a disproportionate amount of misses during fights, most faults tended to be my own.  There was a lot of repetition in the maps, and mission types were not particularly varied, but the game was enjoyable.
I picked up the Enemy Within expansion at the same time as the Slingshot DLC.  At this point, the game feels truly complete with both in place.  There are now more varied missions and objectvies, and the maps rarely repeated as often.
After a series of fits and starts, I finally sat down and really worked my way through the game.  Found that at normal level, some of the additions were almost too powerful, but at the same time, the scaling of the enemies fit the progression.  Though there was still some frustration at times with the game (like feeling like my people got even worse aim) overall I found the game to be a good experience.
I can recommend the game to anyone that likes the idea of the game, and would enjoy the challenge of it.

This is an awesome game. It really is. You can be male or female which is HUGE (only a handful of developers give us a bigger role than "male hero protagonist's healer and love interest") and there were only a few places where the story breaks your headcanon\the dialogue played doesn't match your gender. I felt there's a lot of misinformation floating around about this game so I wanted to put in my two cents.
First Off:
- If you're on the fence about buying this game, I'd recommend you pick it up on sale. For $20, there's plenty to do for anyone who enjoys the open world/survival genre.
- Don't write this game off just because it has mixed reviews - the dev team has done a great job of squashing the game-breaking bugs that earned this game so many negative reviews early on. All core mechanics are in place and the game is very playable now.
- I have NO problems with desync/rubber banding/lag/disappearing corpses or lost items. You might see these mentioned in earlier reviews but they have since been fixed.
- Gameplay is much smoother now and they've added a lot of optimization.
Pros:
- Totally open world survival game, go anywhere on the map and do what you want.
- Tame any creature in the game as your animal companion (panthers, dragons, boars, goblins, elementals, treants, imps, etc). It's very satisfying when the ground shakes as you and your buddies bring down a huge creature with rope arrows. This mechanic is very similar to ARK.
- The world is gorgeous - seriously one of this game's best features. The map is hand crafted and every biome feels different.
- Build a custom base anywhere. I particularly like that you can even get access to the building materials used to create the beautiful capitol cities you see in the screenshots.
- Crafting system is diverse - weapons, farming, building, cooking, spell crafting.
- Magic - Elemental magic is very satisfying, I'm especially fond of the huge explosion you get from casting fireballs. Shapeshifting is also very cool. You can transform into a wyveryn and take to the sky, or maul things as a panther.
- Devs are very active and have listened to feedback from the community.
Mixed
- Resource gathering is balanced for teamwork on official servers. It's meant for a group of players to pool their efforts for taming powerful creatures, building high-tier structures, etc. This is a pro for some who want a real house/guild/tribe experience. However, resource gathering can feel grindy for solo players. Good solution: play on a private server with gathering/taming multipliers if you are a lone-wolf player.
- There is a decay time on structures so that after several days without logging in structures will disappear (it scales with the durability of your structure...straw, wood, iron, etc.). This is designed to prevent structures of inactive players from blocking resources and choice build locations. If your house has at least 1 active player it's not a big deal, but it can be frustrating for solo players. Again, playing on a private server without this function may be a good a good solution.
Cons:
- long loading times to get in-game is still a common complaint (About 10 minutes for me, but I'm also playing on a 4 year old laptop. This hasn't been a big deal for me but it is for some. I just load up when I get home or while doing stuff around the house.)
- inital learning curve for new players can be steep
- PvP, creature aggression, and structure HP still needs balancing
- Sometimes get weird physics around the bigger creatures
- NPC and town mechanics are pretty sparse right now (although vendors/trading is in place)
- Currently no story driven content or quests besides tutorial
- Early access. Annoying bugs do crop up. The balance of items, resource costs, and creatures has also shifted around a lot. (Obviously you can't hand wave away everything by dropping the letters EA, but there's nothing game-breaking right now and I do feel the devs have worked hard to address issues as they arise).
Conclusion:
I definitely got my money's worth for the price tag ($30 full price, $20 on sale) even being EA. Game-breaking bugs have been squashed and game is very playable, although still needs some balancing. Anyone who enjoys survival games will have plenty to keep them occupied with the current content, and more content is coming. If you're looking for a game with lots of quests and lore I would wait. If you like building/crafting/taming creatures there's more than enough to do right now.

Hello Gentlemen,
Just got Take On Mars by Bohemia Interactive, the early access is available for download on steam. Downloaded it, installed it and double clicked on play. Straight to the options menu and run in windowed mode and then changed my mind and put it back to full screen mode. The first screen that greets you is the Take On Mars menu with the usual game options and a spinning depiction of planet Mars. You can hold down the LMB and spin the planet around and see cool sounding names like - Syrtis Major and Elysium Planitia. A few clicks and the initial tutorial loads up.  Clicked on Real World Time and eventually I make my way to the Lab and Construction Building. Found myself pressing the 'Test Vehicle' panel & see the lander. I see different views and instruments, You see (not manipulate) the outside world. My first test ship wobbled like crazy and the wide angle and telephoto view quality, looked like they had purchased the same cameras used in the Blair Witch project. Maybe it's an early alpha thing? I think Bohemia are simulating the quality of video/pictures sent from Mars back to Earth -- lossy and crap. Like any man on the planet who has never read an instruction manual since making 1/32 Airfix models, I end up pressing every single key to see what screens pop up. Oooh... aaarghhh... what does that do... oohhh.... Esc key goes to Main Menu.  Yawn and fast forwarded to the Launch vehicle 13mins 39secs. Look around the crater for about six or seven minutes and then stumble on the list of tasks required to be completed in this particular mission.
After pressing every key again, q,w,e,r,t,y,,,,,. I find myself at the Capture Gas stage. oooh... aarghhhh.... Click on Capture Gas. Yay! DO NOT MOVE INSTRUMENT in flashing red text. First you capture the gas, then you analyse gas. (Insert Fart Joke) This is one of the Major Tasks completed at the initial first assignment Victoria Crater. Your initial foray in the Victoria Crater teaches you Mars atmospheric pressure differences compared to Earth and also the composition percentages of CO2, N & Ar (I knew learning the first twenty elements of the periodic table would be useful in my lifetime.. thanks to my grade 10 science teacher Mr Clewett). Once you complete a mission, you also get access to New Tech Levels and various vehicle and instruments at tech level 2 become available.  And I got a steam achievement unlocked "It's All About the Science" I then read the rest of the Mission task and see there is another minor task, a photo opportunity requirement.
The light bulb dims and I figure out that mission tasks are comprised of Major task and Minor tasks. Each successful completion of Major & Minor tasks during a mission will allow you access to higher level tech and more cash to spend on stuff. In the Early Access version, I can see some instruments have power levels and charge / drain rates and I guess that there would be that certain tasks that require balancing energy usage from your chemical batteries before they are depleted in the later missions. Don't know yet if there are ways to recharge. It's interesting but not for everyone. Interesting enough I had the game freeze on me twice and waited and waited and waited.... before the three finger salute Ctrl+Alt+Del restarted the game.
My initial thoughts coming from a Flight Sim enthusiast...... Well just like there are people that are vegetarians and there are people who like a medium rare wagyu rump with a side of hand cut fries, mushrooms swimming in a red wine jus. Take On Mars just doesn't have enough meat to satisfy me. Do your own due diligence and make an informed decision. Read the reviews, watch other videos and then make a purchase or not decision. I 'm not satisfied. If I want a space sim, Kerbal Space Program has that creativity streak that Take On Mars doesn't. Would I play Take On Mars often? Only if my Warthog HOTAS was stolen, and every other computer game I owned was destroyed and it was raining outside and it was a Saturday in June. Aside from that, sure I will play it.
Another thing, what is early access, an alpha, beta or in-between? Call it what it is - an Alpha....
Thanks go to my grade 10 Science teacher Mr Clewett -- You were right, I would use the knowledge of the first twenty elements in the periodic table in my life time. :)

Spaceship Looter is a science-fiction top-down twin-stick shooter with rogue-like elements from new indie developers, Luxorix Games.
As the title of the game suggests, you take the role of a spaceship looter, working independently out of the Spaceship Looter Bar to claim salvage from derelict space ships. There's not actually much loot to find; instead you'll come across lots of boxes with nothing in them, a few different types of traps or other defences, and hordes of baddies mostly in the form of strange aliens or robots.
The game features 'retro' pixel graphics with a good feel to them. Human characters look nice and have some personality, and the boss enemies are unique and pretty good, too. Normal enemies are a bit lacklustre for the most part, with each ship featuring only a relatively small number of enemies, which usually include a few reskins amongst their ranks.
Weapon effects are quite nice and the game moves smoothly with half the screen filled with 'bullets' of various shapes and sizes. Animations let the side down a little, though, as do the weapons. I'm not sure who thought a machine gun should look like that (or shoot like that, for that matter).
The camera is fixed in position and angle, as you'd expect in a pixel-graphic twin-stick shooter, and very occasionally you'll have enemies or traps hidden behind room objects, but that doesn't detract from the game at all.
The interface is very simple, but requires minimal interaction to achieve your goals. I particularly like the simplicity of the main menu. The map is good and includes all of the markers you need to remember where you've left unopened chests and the like, though a little legend in one corner would have been a nice addition.
There are no graphics options beyond full screen / windowed mode selection; you can't even set resolution or vsync.
There's a nice title theme that feels appropriately 'spacey and actiony'. The in-game music, too, is quite good and fits well, but it does get a little bit repetitive, as it seems to play continuously until you reach a boss level.
The sound effects are pretty good, too, with nice blasts and shots of weapons and explosions, and little groans when you're hit. There's nothing outstanding, but they do the job.
There are no voices.
As far as the rogue-like science-fiction twin-stick shooter genre is concerned, Spaceship Looter offers very few gameplay surprises or deviations from the norm. Using controller or keyboard and mouse, run about with your left hand to dodge bullets and aim and shoot with your right hand to kill enemies, across levels made up of connected procedurally generated rooms, while collecting two different types of currencies: one which expires when you die, and the other which remains with you across play throughs until you spend it. Each room you enter locks its exits until you kill all of the enemies within, and if you're lucky you'll find some keys and boxes to unlock with them, and those boxes will contain something useful.
Spaceship Looter has multiple difficulty levels -- only Very Easy and Easy are unlocked before you've beaten the game at least once -- and multiple player characters -- only one of whom is unlocked until you've beaten one or more of the bosses. It has a 'lobby' (in this case, a pub) shop where you can buy items using the permanent currency, and it has in-game shops (in this case, arcade machines) where you can buy character improvements for that play through only, using the temporary currency. It has multiple weapons, stat powerups, active and passive items, and skills. And it has the standard level layout, with a few 'normal' procedurally generated levels separating each pre-determined boss battle level, until you reach the end.
All of this is pretty typical for the genre, and this game does most of it similarly to its peers. It's unfortunate, then, that where it differs, it detracts from the overall experience rather than improving it. Items purchased from the lobby shop with permanent currency are temporary, lasting for that play through only, leaving no way to permanently improve your character, and thus no long-term progression. The skills available are very limited -- only one per character -- and they all essentially function as a secondary weapon. And the in-game shops only sell very expensive, and not very good, minor improvements to your secondary weapons. Unlockables are definitely too few and far between for a game like this. Oh, and I don't know who thought it would be a good design choice to have enemies that explode on death, but they really should consider a new line of work.
All of this adds up to a feeling of lost opportunity. Spaceship Looter could have done great things, but with these choices, it becomes yet another game in the ever-growing twin-stick-shooter pool.
Not all is lost, though. Characterisation is good -- though very poorly worded; the game could definitely do with some proofreading -- and the premise is interesting. It has a map, which is sorely missing from some of its peers in the genre, and you can save ammo by throwing a couple of object types around if you want. And there's a welcome small amount of story progression available through rescuing NPCs so that you can deal with them in the lobby on your next game.
I also haven't come across any bugs, which is a good thing. And it's actually quite fun to play. Everything moves about well, the random-number generator doesn't have enough sway to be too evil too often, and there's a feeling of accomplishment when you see half the screen filled with bullets and you manage to weave your way through them and take out the bad guys without getting hit.
The controls aren't configurable, though, for either controller or keyboard and mouse, which is a big no-no in any game, but at least the defaults work well enough. I'd recommend keyboard and mouse, given the need to press a trigger button to fire on the controller, but that's not uncommon for the genre.
If there were more actual 'loot' to be had then I could see more reason for the characters to continue looting. As it is, I imagine after the first ship they'd be looking to throw it all in and wash dishes for a living. After playing Spaceship Looter for a few hours in one go, I feel a bit the same: a lot of effort for too little reward. I guess I'll come back to it again later.
Pros:
+ A good premise, with some good characterisation
+ Procedural level generation works well
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- No permanent improvements or character progression
- The premise is basically just an excuse; it's not developed at all
- Skills are underpowered, even when upgraded
- Enemies exploding on death is not a good way to increase the challenge
- Not enough variation in levels or enemies
Spaceship Looter is a fun retro-style science-fiction twin-stick shooter, but it lacks in longevity compared to some of its peers. It's a long way short of the best in the genre, and the dearth of permanent character improvements and unlockable weapons, items, and skills make it more repetitive than it could be. It's a good game, just not as good as it might have been.

Great game, if you ever wanted to send rovers and probes to Mars (and Deimos), do scientific experiments and exploration there.
Graphics are immersive, physics realistic and parts of your rovers/probes may get damaged ... not only if you mishandle them, but also due to the sometimes violent martian weather.
Likewise, the experiments featured are all experiments that also are part of the real Mars rovers (like Curiosity).
They just took some deviations from reality with regards to the voyage to Mars (which is immediately ... no long space travel required) and with regards to research times 8which is measured in hours instead of years).
Also, you are able to steer the rover in real time ... with no delay between sender and receiver (as it would be in reality) ... the latter one is taken care of however, as they are currently developing a game mode, where you have to give your rover a batch of commands (like, turn around 30 degs, move forward, use RAD-Sensor and so on) which the rover / probe then executes ... even if it may result in its damaging or destruction.
Definitely a game I would recommend ... it is good now and it is getting even better

Most 4x space games are basically Mario Party except all the mini games are thinly veiled spread sheets.  This is not one of those games.  SotS generates stories that stick with you for years.  What did you even do in your last game of Civ, can you remember?  I remember 6yrs ago when I was grossly out teched by the AI who was wielding flashy cruisers with energy weapons when I was still fielding cruisers with basic pea shooters.  I was losing territory slowly but I just researched the dreadnaut hull.  Granted it was just a hull but while I gathered the remains of my old tattered fleet, I had time to research one weapon tech so my new ships wouldn't be armed with only the basics.  I chose siege drivers.  I didn't know what they did, but they sure as heck sounded better than the pea shooters I had.  I built two of the big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and sent them on into the darkness with all of the hopes and dreams of my empire.
I had no defenses.  All the men an women capable of fighting were on their way.  My outer systems flickered dark as the turns slipped by but I hardly noticed.  My fleet of leftovers, of decomissioned defense ships, trudged on to their doom.  When they arrived they were greeted by an entire fleet of dreadnaut class ships with fancy energy weapons.  How many volleys could my dreadnauts take?  Two?  Maybe three?  I could only field one dreadnaut at a time while my enemy could field three.  The ominous red radar blips floated towards me, they were out of visual range when I opened fire.
The siege gun is one huge cannon built directly into the ship's frame and it spits out slow massive projectiles, basically mini astroids, designed for inflicting massive damage onto a planet.  They aren't designed for ship to ship combat, I wasn't  aware of this when I built them.  But, they definitely aren't pea shooters.  The dreadnauts in front of me, bristling with sinister weaponry, could not avoid the shots even from range.  On the radar I saw their ships thrown back by the impacts from the siege weapon.  Spinning wildly out of control they could not correct their course and they plummeted into the planet below them.  The few supporting cruisers in their fleet chewed through my outdated models, but all the while the siege driver spat death on the planet below.
When I first saw their capital it was a beautiful world of green, blue, and fascinating lights.  When I left it was a volcanic hellscape.  The fleet moved on to their new capital.  The cruisers bought time as they were ripped to shreds while the siege cannon spoke of the end times.  Then to their next capital.  And the next.  And the next.
Every single ship and all of their crew that I had in serivice went on that mission and none of them returned.  They did not defeat my nemesis, but they did inflict the mortal wounds.  Many turns later my new fleets returned to that sector to find my nemesis still reeling.  He was defeated.  The terrible sacrifice of the previous generations was not in vain.
Do you remember a single game you've played of civ?  I don't.  That's why I don't play civ.

For me personally Ethan Carter is a pretty disappointing, though still good, game.
I've really come to love narrative driven games that focus on gameplay like exploration and roleplaying, Gone Home and Kentucky Route Zero being two of my favorite examples. Ethan Carter was supposed to be like them so I was really looking forward to it, but it ended up falling real short compared to them. Most of my disappointment stems from the fact that the devs, The Astronauts, have been in the industry for a while (They're ex-People Can Fly, including the founder) so I expected more than what we got narrative-wise.
First of all the game really is gorgeous, the soundtrack is quality stuff, and the atmosphere really is great but this becomes a problem as you get deeper into the game, it’s clear The Astronauts put way too much focus on said environments instead of making an engaging game and narrative. Red Creek Valley is beautiful, but it’s empty. The whole game world is just too big for its own good so you'll tend to find yourself running through deserted forests with nothing to do. The gameplay also starts off promising with the investigation of murder scenes but this eventually becomes extremely watered down and the gameplay just kind of devolves into the exploration version of pixel hunting. And that's another problem of this game too, it’s just too obtuse at times. The Astronauts laud themselves for not holding your hand but it goes too far in the other direction and it can be tricky to find what you need to do to progress. Also not being able to manually save is just dumb and it just seems grognardy. Finally the obtuseness is more of a problem than it could have been because you have to find every puzzle in the game to beat it and if you missed some, which there is a good chance that you might, then it can just kind of kill the pacing right at the very end.
The narrative is also really barebones, which for what is supposed to be a narrative-driven game is a detriment. The characters are mostly all flat *ssholes so you really don’t care about them, which kind of alienates you from the plot. Plus the ending is just unfulfilling and just feels like a twist for the sake of one. In the end it didn’t leave an impression on me at all unlike some of the supernatural story-driven games I love like Silent Hill 2, Rule of Rose, and Deadly Premonition.
The Astronauts should have taken more cues from Gone Home. Gone Home may not have looked nearly as pretty and its world was much, much smaller but it was just so dense, filled with tons of stuff to find that built on the narrative that Ethan Carter really lacks. It also was tightly paced with no padding unlike Ethan Carter's wandering and backtracking.
This review sounds pretty negative, but it’s more out of knowing that this game could have been a lot better and out of disappointment over how hollow it feels due to the focus on style instead of substance. It’s still overall a good game  worth your time.  I’m just happy that so many people seem to enjoy this game. Video games don’t need combat to be games and video games can really tell engaging stories if the effort and skill are put into them. I want games like Ethan Carter, Walking Dead, Gone Home, and KRZ to succeed so  more can be made so despite my misgivings I’m glad Ethan Carter exists and is doing well and I hope The Astronauts can improve for a second game.

Hello,  I picked up this game for £2. on Humble store yesterday.  You will see from other comments that the CD Key is
invalid.  However after alot of searching around online I have finally got the game working.
Here is how I did it -
Firstly install the game and right click local files.
Locate the file 42890_install and open it with notepad.
It reads - "CD Key" - "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX" Change that to "BAD0-C0DE-BAD1-6A2E"
Then run regedit
Go to - registry value HKEY_CURRENT_USER/Software/Valve/TestApp42890
Modify the value of the invalid key to "BAD0-C0DE-BAD1-6A2E"
Use find to search for SOTS and change all key values to "BAD0-C0DE-BAD1-6A2E"
As far as I know Muliplayer wont work with this fix but at least you can play the game.
It worked for me!
Hope this helps.

A solid fairytale-like horror game with unique mechanics (i.e. the save function and placing candles on the ground to light dark areas) ans well as some gorgeous pixel art and bleep-bloop versions of classical music. Every choice you make has a big impact on how the game later plays out. It's filled with puzzles that manage to be challenging without once seeming impossible or frustratingly unintuitive. The story is not extremely complicated, like a fairytale, but it still manages to be interesting and have a surprising amount of depth to it. There's a lot to explore and many mysteries to piece together, which I enjoyed. There also aren't really any jumpscares, which is nice because the game manages to create a creepy and intense atmosphere without them. The game overall is pretty short, about eight hours or so, which I think was pretty good considering its price. It seemed like just the right amount of time for this sort of game.
The only downsides I can think of to this game is that the protagonist walks at only one speed, which is rather slow and could annoy players (although I think he's intentionally slow for the stealth aspect of the game...plus it makes the game more challenging) and that the save function, which relies on throwing a limited amount of gold coins into a well, can occasionally be stressful and frustrating -- though once again, it made the player's choices matter a lot more and made the game more challenging, so I wasn't too bothered by it.
Since the game was pretty hard, every puzzle I managed to complete felt very rewarding -- by the end of the game, I felt like even though this game kicked my♥♥♥♥♥ I managed to kick its♥♥♥♥♥back. It was great.
I highly recommend getting this game if you're even remotely interested.

This port of the famous specialist tabletop game by Games Workshop is great despite the minor flaws in the execution.
If you didn't know it already, in this game you control a fleet from a faction in the Warhammer 40k universe. If you pick the Imperial Navy you can ram gigantic spaceworhty cathedrals into all sorts of alien ships, you can do the same but with scrapyards with the orks, or you can be a bit more subtle with the Chaos, the Eldars or the Space marines.
The game-play is directly inspired by the old navy themed wargames Battlefleet Gothic was based on with a traditional RTS twist. Everything takes place on a 2D plan despite the setting being in space. Plan your actions, move your ships around and micro manage every single aspect of the combat from firing torpedoes to initiating boarding actions as your initial master plan goes horribly wrong. You can then outfit your ships with different upgrades and faction favors to gift them with special abilities.
The grimdark future of the 41st millenium never looked or sounded so good. The sound design, musics and overall ambiance are all great. The dialogs and cinematics of the campaign are true to the spirit of the universe and are good set-pieces in and off themselves. The ships all look magnificent, the only thing missing is a way to pick our own color scheme like you can on a the tabletop.
Now of the things that aren't so great: the multiplayer implementation is puzzling. Doing quick matches against people on your friend-list shouldn't be rocket science but this game manages to make it more complicated that it needs to be. The overal campaign "overworld" in which you decide which missions you want to take part in isn't exactly great either, you'll be faced with an overwhelming number of possible engagements and you'll have to make choices as you can't fight every battle that's available to you.
Overall the game is great but needs some more polish. From what I can see, it's still being worked on by its developers so that's that, and some more DLC's are on their way.
It's probably the first Game Workshop video game that made me want to try the tabletop version; a shame that they don't publish it anymore. At least I have this game!

Spaceship Looter:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

There are many things to discover in deep space and you never really know what you’ll see. That is if you are a space explorer, of course.  But you fearless mercenaries who are looking for drifting, crewless spaceships throughout the galaxy, you know what treasures they may hold. True, most of the spaceships are becoming homes for Aliens, but what the heck, its time for Spaceship Looter!
Spaceship Looter is an action roguelike game where you take control of one of five selectable characters (with one available at the start and four to unlock /rescue) whose mission is to loot spaceships infested by aliens and survive as long as possible.
Each of your mercenaries will have a number of health and accuracy points, and a specific skill.
Before you enter a ship, you must have a look at the tutorial, which is very short and will give you a good overview of what to expect and familiarise you with the controls. Then you are ready to enter the cantine of the mercenary ship. There are three other rooms which will be closed at this point. However, they will be accessible as soon as you rescue the right room occupant within the levels. When you are ready to jump into the infested spaceship, just move your mercenary onto the big green square to start the level.
There are three levels per ship. In the first two, you will need to clear each room of aliens, pick up ammunition, keys, health packs, credits and blue crystals. Each time you eliminate an enemy, it will drop credits and occasionally a blue crystal. Accumulate as many credits as possible and use them on the arcade machine to upgrade your skill.   You can use the crystal to respawn after you die (you need a specific number of crystals per level), or to purchase attributes at the store room (you must first rescue the room occupant). Keys open crates where you might get new weapons, health packs or components, such as mines, health regeneration and others.  The third level is fighting the boss of the ship; beat him and plenty of rewards will come your way. On top of that you will rescue another mercenary which you will be able to use on your next game play.

The gameplay is great! Not only does each spaceship randomly regenerate, but you don’t know how many enemies will spawn within each room and what fire sequences they might have. This game can be very challenging from the first room you enter, which is fabulous. Oh, I almost forgot . . . you can interact with some objects within each room. Some can be thrown to your enemies and explode on impact and others will bounce back and forth inflecting damage each time they touch an enemy.
The graphics are good and the controls are very responsive, whether you use a gamepad or your mouse and keyboard.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	Randomly regenerated levels
-	Hectic gameplay – fun and addictive
-	5 characters to choose from (four to unlock)
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Difficult to throw interactive objects in the right direction
This game is great fun - definitely one to own and start looting!
8/10

I don't write many reviews for games (at least at the time of writing this I hadn't), but I feel that Spaceship Looter is deserving of one.
Now, if you are like me you'd have seen Spaceship Looter come up in either the 'Upcoming' or the 'New Releases' tab and thought 'Here we have another roguelike shooter'.  For me that is a good thing as I love collecting roguelikes of every shape and size but I understand that many will think 'Another one?!?!'.  Well let me tell you now, if you have even a passing interest in this genre, you are in for a treat.
Spaceship Looter does pretty much everything right straight off the bat.  There is a basic tutorial available that lets you familiarise yourself with the controls then you are teleported straight onto your first ship to search for the aforementioned loot.  Many roguelikes at this stage would ease you in gently; have a few easier levels to slowly guide you into the game.  Spaceship Looter does not.  Spaceship Looter hits you square in the face with its first punch and lets you know you're in for a fight!  The rooms on the spaceships are small and often have a fair number of enemies in them, but by the same token the game never seems unfair, it just doesn't hold your hand.  If this is your first roguelike shooter then you might struggle a bit at first but persevere because slowly but surely you'll get better.  This is a game that rewards picking yourself up and trying again after every death, of which there will be many.
In a game like this where the enemies are coming thick and fast you can't afford to be fighting the controls as well and Spaceship Looter does not disappoint.  The controls are extremely fluid and respond in exactly the manner that they should.  I will mention here that I prefer using a controller to play the game but had a bit of difficulty with the first set of bindings that were on offer.  The dev really stepped up to the plate though and contacted me directly to discuss the problem and what could be done to solve it.  I'm glad to say that in my humble opinion the settings for using a controller are now familiar, and very easy to use.  Massive thanks to an extremely responsive dev though, a big plus in this increasingly crowded market.
The graphics of Spaceship Looter are clean, crisp and not once are you left wondering what hit you, or if your shot connected with the enemy.  You can see everything that is going on despite the gameplay being quite hectic.  The sound effects are functional and clear, while the game also has an excellent soundtrack that gets the blood pumping for the fight ahead.
Like every game in the roguelike genre you can sometimes get a raw deal from RNGesus but I can't recall a single death that I've had that wasn't my fault or couldn't have been avoided by playing better.  I'm probably a decent casual player at best, by no means hardcore, but if you are a hardcore player then I feel you will take a lot away from this game as it is squarely pitched at your level.  My playtime isn't the highest either but I feel I have seen enough to recommend the game to you dear reader, and I will certainly return to the game to keep improving and delving further into the various spaceships on offer.
Spaceship Looter is in early access but already has more content and polish than a huge number of games in this genre.  Not only do we have a responsive dev working on the game, we also have a very active dev working on the game.  At the time of writing this review (10 days after early access release), we have already had 5 updates that have all improved the game in their own way.  I have no doubt we'll see many more.  I'd recommend the game to even those who do not like early access games because if this game was released 'as is', it would still be great, but by virtue of being in early access it will only keep getting better.

Ham and Pineapple Pizza or "The Hawiian" did not exist prior to the 1960s according to Sam Panopoulos who claims to be its inventor and recently passed away. Now this is really odd for me because you would think that it occoured to someone a long time ago but supposedly it didn't. So when I sat down with XCom:EU, having never been familiar with the series (but aware of its existance), I had to ask myself - why on earth aren't there more games like this? I suppose it is because XCom:EU is the gaming eqvililent of Ham and Pineapple pizza since it puts together things which you wouldn't think work well together but actually do. And since publishers don't generally like risks, you won't see many games like this around.
So to start with, the game has some solid team building mechanics much like an RPG. The combat systems are clearly 4X in nature with their use of turns and ranges within the zones being little more than grids with scenary. But then you have cover-based mechanics similar to Mass Effect along with character classes and unique abilities to give you a butt-ton of tactical choices and options to consider as you play. And even further again you have economic management like a city or theme park simulator. Add to that details that are lifted from rogue-likes such as perma-death, unforgiving difficulty and random scenario generation and you really can't put Xcom:EU into any specific genre. It is what it is - and what it is is brilliant!
I really cannot recommend this game enough. It has solid visual presentation given its age, the voice acting for cut scenes and audio clips is fantastic and everything just feels so nicely tuned. The one exception I take though is that occasionally (very occasionally) it can be difficult to accurately order your troops around if there is too much mid-scene decoration or multilayer buildings. This only really becomes an issue on some ship interiors or large buildings however. The difficulty may put some people off at first but once you've sat down and learned from your mistakes you will eventually hit that point where every mission is tense but you never feel like things are completely beyond your control. The game just gives you a narrow margin for error and you need to wriggle into it and stay there.
I've seen critisism directed towards the game by fans of the original from back in '94. Although I've seen gameplay videos of XCom I've never played it. But even then I have to say that the negative comments directed at XCom:EU really are unjustified on the basis that this game is great in its own right. If you were to take the XCom name away from this it would still be a great title so using it to introduce new generations to a much-beloved franchise should be seen as a good thing. Also, from what I have seen, the old XCom was much slower paced and involved far more micromanagement than I think the modern games market would tolerate. As it stands XCom:EU strikes the perfect balance between giving plenty of sim and RPG-esque features so you have plenty to think about while keeping the pacing of the game fast enough to maintain interest.
I wanted to end with a little bit of commentary addressing the PEGI or ESRB ratings which talk of the game being gory with bad language. Frankly I think anyone who finds gore or swearing unappealing will actually be fine here with the exception one one scene near the start of the game. (it happens when they find a corpse inside a bus-stop during the tutorial) The language is actually very mild, at least by UK standards. Troops occasionally say a$$ or h3ll but that is really it. The gore may refer to the yellow goo that splatters from aliens but somehow this never really hits home with me as much as red blood going everywhere. But millage may very. Frankly I think the developers could have done away with it all entirely as it doesn't add anything to the game at all - but oh well.

A solid action game mixing the mechanics of Enter the Gungeon and Nuclear Throne.
Spaceship Looter is an action-roguelite. The premise is simple: your character visits abandoned spaceships to pick the abandoned goods there. The game is a mix between “Enter the Gungeon” and “Nuclear Throne”: lots of shooting, using the environment to dodge / kill monsters, some unlocks and money for upgrade purchases.
•	Great style, the game’s colorful pixel-art is pleasant to look at
•	Dynamic gameplay: small movement space and interactions with environmental destructibles make sure that you keep moving all the time
•	Challenging Difficulty: the game is not easy; good for hardcore players, but probably better avoided by casual players
•	Responsive movement / shooting controls
•	Performance is linked directly to your screen refresh rate: on my G-Sync 120hz monitor the game ran at double speed, making it essentially unplayable
•	The interactive obstacles sometimes fail to respond in time when you press E button (you just really need to be close to them, but it’s easy to miss this interval)
•	As with lots of these games, you can get screwed by random: some rooms get too much enemies and not enough obstacles or are too small; that makes it impossible to leave them undamaged
The game solves the problem that Enter The Gungeon had: Spaceship Looter has small rooms and that ensures that you get more action-packed fights and less movement; Right now, the game focuses on core game loop: the plot is close to nonexistent, just run, gun and use your surroundings wisely. There’s really not much else behind the gameplay process, but it’s well polished and addictive. If you don’t mind the lack of plot and consider yourself a seasoned gamer looking for an extra challenge – go for it, you won’t be disappointed.

Easily the best Warhammer 40k game since Dawn of War II and my current favorite Real Time Tactical game of all time.  This is not a genre that I've been able to enjoy much in the past, but the mechanics and lore of the tabletop game and the universe are very well translated in this real-time adaptation by a smaller team that really overperformed on the project.  Combat takes place on a 2d plane (it only looks like space) with players having extreme control of their ships' targeting systems, maneuvering, crew, boarding actions, and special equipment.  It has an engaging campaign as well as a very cool two player coop mode.  They have a fair ranked mode (which does not have a large player base) and they have listened and communicated relatively well on their forums despite not being native english speakers.  I doubt this game will see a lot of future development, but I do expect a sequel.  This is a real Warhammer 40k gem and I recommend it to anyone that enjoys this universe and the mechanics of naval warfare (Battlefleet Gothic was always about naval ships pretending to be space ships).

Take on Mars: The Real Mars Simulator...
Yes the first thing that comes to mind when I play Take on Mars is Gran Turismo. The game is very realistic and beautifully presented. However just like Gran Turismo it does get a little repetitive after a while.
The game is very well made. It is highly informative and gives you a good sense of experience in controlling a unmanned mission to Mars.
When I played it for the first time I found it difficult to understand. But after couple of hours of clicking to find the right screens I began to understand the idea of the game. This does make the main game difficult to play. There is a tutorial which you will need to read. Also researching technology in the game is not clear and difficult to understand. I hope in time that they will fix this. In the mean time you will need to explore the game itself as well as the planet Mars to understand how it works. If you do lose patients with the main game there are many single missions which will keep you occupied. They are all great fun and very informative. If you enjoy exploring then this is the game for you. You will visit actual locations on Mars, using actual scientific equipment to unlock the knowledge and mysteries of the big red planet.
Depending on your graphics card the detail is amazing. When exploring Mars you do feel very alone on this vast world. The highly detailed graphics and sound effects create a atmosphere which leaves you very isolated in the game.
The controls are awkward but I believe that was on purpose to add to the realism of controlling a remote control vehicle across space.
I do recommend this game but you will need to be a little patient at times on how to play it. The game is still in it early stages and the potential for this game is vast. I am personally hoping they add sci-fi missions like a manned mission to Mars or first contact with martians. At time of this review being submitted the developers are currently very active in listening to the players and improving the game.

I've got a good 70 hours into civ 5 and I no longer wish to play it on single player. I have played civ since the very first installment. A lot of the policies and bonuses in the game are downright useless. I have no idea why the developers included them. The game comes down to chance. Getting a good start will ensure that you do well. Start isolated and in a bountiful area, and you can compete. It really makes you want to cheat and restart. Most of the time, on a large map, multiple other civs spawn within 10 tiles of your city. Resources will be great for your capital, but can be barren for your surroundings. You simply cannot settle cities without resources to maintain happiness in the early stages of the game. If you cannot settle cities, you cannot beat the cheating AI. They will outscience and outproduce you. Barbarians on King level, which is a relatively weak level, act like a second civ always at war with you. They coordinate surrounding your troops and go right for your cities. This delays settling because your settlers cannot get out of your city with barbarian camps spawing just outside your territory. The barbs spawn CONSTANTLY. The unique luxuries are extremely unbalanced due to the random spawning of them. If you push to settle a nice city, which will undoubtedly be near the AI, they will attack it with an impossible number of units given their production. Win, and they will come at you with even more units that they produce at double speed. Get through the mid game and then the delegates start annoying you. They will ban every luxury in your city, killing your happiness and ruining expansion. This is quite simply the most annoying, unabalanced, unfair, unenjoyable and frustating civ version I have ever played. On multiplayer, it looks more enjoyable. But, they need to fix these unfair random starts and make the game truly balanced. It should be a game of skill not chance as to where you start.

Classic Dungeon Crawl RPG with stylized and very well-done graphics and artwork. Very easy game to get in to, although not everything is as intuitive as one might think. For example, there's no real tutorial, instead just a brief one-time description of what the various interactive items in the tavern do. The game mechanics take an interesting approach to perma-death. Free your comrades with another character when they die. This can become very grindy if you send a weak character into a dungeon and get an unlucky event roll and the character gets imprisoned. I found myself leveling the Warrior up first (running the first dungeon several times), in order to bail the weaker characters out that didn't make the run on the first go. However, items looted can be transferred between characters, so that's a definate plus.
Overall, although very grindy and with a potential to become a bit boring, I like this game a lot and think it doesn't really deserve the negative reviews it's been getting. If the devs can improve on some of the mechanics (balancing perhaps - the Warrior is a bit OP, while the casters seem a little underpowered), I think this could become a great title.
Also, I'd like to see Steam Workshop support. Perhaps an editor to make and share your own dungeons. Mod support would greatly improve replayability.

Braid is a puzzle game masquerading as a platformer. Once you know the solutions to the puzzles, solving them requires no more effort than, say, setting up a combo in Puyo Puyo. But figuring out the solutions can be tough.
The game starts off easy, but forces you to stretch your thinking in order to proceed. I like how each section requires you to think in a totally different way. Some sections require you think of time as a changeable element you can rewind, others define space, and your place in it, as the wild card. Solving these puzzles evokes the good feeling you get when finishing a big jigsaw puzzle, and it's a joy to look at.
It has a major design drawback: the small written descriptions of the plot that flash onto the screen as you pass books on the way to the level doors. I know a lot of people have responded to positively to the story of this game, but in my opinion the overwrought prose really harms the otherwise subtle and sad imagery you encounter in the levels. The images should be all you need. It's a small point, I guess, since you can ignore the words, but they mar an otherwise excellent experience for me.

Sometimes, when watching a film or reading a novel, you feel a burn of emotion deep inside your chest. Something that affects you so profoundly that it moves beyond being just a form of media. It is internalized and remembered forever.
Braid is one of those things. But it isn't just an example of art in gaming, it's a game full of pure genius as well.
The game, at first, comes off as a platformer. There are relatively little instances of hardcore platforming in the game, and they usually only serve as a medium to allow you to interact with the puzzle that you're dealing with. Make no mistake, this is a puzzle game at heart.
The puzzles here are incredibly good, and very well scaled from level to level. The first two levels are relatively easy and will only take you a few minutes, the third is a bit harder, and the last puzzles will make you feel like your brain is deflated. The amount of time that you'll have to put into each puzzle may be debilitating for some, but the sheer joy and pleasure of solving one overcomes any sense of stress that staring at your screen racking your brain may cause. These aren't just run of the mill puzzles, either. There are a number that are, in my mind, some of the best puzzles that I've ever seen in a game.
The art direction is beautiful. The backgrounds are watercolor constructed, they're vibrant and bright, and dark and brooding. The soundtrack is perfectly placed and flooded with beautiful violin work. Each are augmented by an incredibly written preface that comes prior to starting each level. The story is written so broadly and so metaphorically that it can literally be translated to represent whatever the player would like it to. The ending represents one of the epic twists in video game history, and does so in game -- a puzzle in itself.
I literally cannot think of one thing that I dislike about this game. It could be longer, but length can't really be expected from a game that costs so little.
There is so much value stuffed into the 10ish hours that you'll spend playing this game, it's hard to put it into words any other way than just to spout off the cliche of "buy it and experience it yourself". It's an experience to be had, and it's one of the most artistically beautiful exhibits in gaming history that is guaranteed to affect you in a most profound way.

As I write this I have not gone beyond dungeon 10.  Here's my rebuttal to the two objections  I found in negative reviews:
1) The game gets stuck.  True.  But just hit escape and you exit the dungeon.  You might lose whatever you gained from that dungeon, but you can always replay it.  You can also use escape to not play a dungeon that doesn't have the challenge you want.
2) The game is too grindy.  True.  It's simple.  If you binge play with a specific goal of finishing, it's going to be painfully slow.  But if you treat each dungeon run as it's own mini-game, it's rewarding and short.  You also have the added bonus of being able to adjust the difficulty to the amount of challenge you want.  Go for a really tough situation, where monsters can 1-shot kill you, or something more moderate, where you can do the game and think about something else.
Other Notes:
1) The AI is very simple, at least on early levels -- so simple that the creatures do the same thing everytime.  There is no deep strategy.
2) Most heroes need two stats:  endurance for health, and strength/agility/intelligence for damage.
3) A hero of level X can beat a dungeon of level X very easily.  But you are leveling all 7 heroes, so the challenge is deciding how many dungeons you want to skip.  It's good to have a rough idea of how much Damage and Health you need to clear a dungeon quickly, with maybe 2 hits per monster, and then decide how much you want to push this comfort level.
4) You can waste a lot of time sorting inventory.  I just distribute equipment according to Intelligence, Agility and Strength, and keep everyone fully equipped, with a few items of higher levels in reserve.  I very rarely share equipment, unless something is really outstanding, choosing instead to do a dungeon 1 notch lower, rather than push the limits with the best equipment.  If I were concentrating more in an individual session, I might share more equipment, but I usually play when I can be interrupted at anytime, and prefer not to do something where I can lose my train of thought and have to go searching and re-equiping.
For me this games is great when I don't want to think too much, and want something short that I can interrupt at anytime without forgetting what I was doing.

Apologies in advance for choosing the cliché comparison, but The Vanishing of Ethan Carter takes the visuals of Dear Esther and the storytelling of Gone Home and cranks them up to 11 while throwing in some actual gameplay.  If that description sounds good to you, then you will probably love this game.
You are Paul Prospero, a detective with the ability to communicate with ghosts to see the past.  The gameplay pretty much boils down to wandering around the many beautiful environments while finding the various parts involved in the murder that happened in that particular area.  I am intentionally being vague, because like Gone Home, knowing too much going into the game will ruin the experience.  All you need to know is the story is engrossing in a Twin Peaks/Lovecraftian way.  Often I found myself getting distracted just staring at the landscape.  Early in the game you cross a bridge.  It took me 10 minutes to get across it because looking across the water at the mountainline gave me a sense of awe and wonder.  What is over there? Will I even be able to get over there? HOW THE HELL DID THEY GET IT TO LOOK SO DAMN NICE?!
All that being said, as much as I enjoyed my time, this is not a perfect game.  There isn't really any buildup to your first case.  It just kinda happens before you even get your bearings in the world.  I'm not really an advocate for padding your game for length, but TVoEC would benefit for another 15-20 minutes of exploration before the first event.  What that time would entail is beyond me, but it felt like it was lacking something in the beginning.  They wouldn't even need to add time to the total playtime.  Often times it felt like the world was too large for how little content there is.  Looking at the beautiful scenery can only keep you entertained for so long.  If the distance between different sets were shortened, they could use that time for world building in the beginning.  The other grievance I had with the game is the ending.  It's not possible to say any more than that without spoiling anything, but just beware you may feel like the ending was a bit of a cop out.
The many positives of the game greatly outweigh the few negatives and would absolutely recommend this to fans of this genre.

The game is good. Most of the negative reviews are due to the numerous bugs that rendered it nearly unplayable at launch. But the devs are constantly releasing patches and eliminating the bugs. The game, as of this review's date, is completely playable. I encountered no bugs during my 7 hours of play time.
However there are some down sides to this game. Death mechanic makes the game a bit grindy and it might be frustrating in later levels. If your character dies, it gets prisoned at that level and you have to rescue them with another character. And if your main char outlevels the other ones by far, then you have to level up another character, which might take some time. On the other hand, this mechanic forces you to be cautious. You can't just storm through dungeons. You have to keep track of your consumables, you have to plan ahead before entering a fight, and sometimes it can be better to just exit the dungeon and try again, rather than push your luck. I'm also leveling 3 chars: 1 str, 1 agi and 1 int char. This way,  you can rescue your char as soon as it dies and you can make use of all the loot you get. Still, this prison thing is a bit harsh and I don't know whether I would start again if I lost all my chars in later parts of the game.
Another downside is the merchant. Equipment purchase is like Diablo's gambling. You can't see the stats, you can't see the level requirement (though you get a hint from its cost). I believe we should be able to see the stats of equipments that we purchase and this "gamble" thing should be an extra option.
Even with these negative aspects, the game is still fun and captivating. The fights are fun and it's not mindless button mashing; there are strategic elements to it, like positioning, pulling the mobs one by one, dealing with different types of mobs etc. I played most of the recent dungeon crawlers/board game type rpgs and Rezrog is way ahead of them.
Tl,dr: The game in its current state is playable and any dungeon crawler/roguelike/rpg fan should definitely give it a try.

Company of Heroes two, abreviated as CoH2 from here on out is a game that is famous for WW2 gameplay.
However,  being famous and well known, doesn't dictate quality, as past fancy graphics the same problems that plagued the first game, have sadly been  brought over to the 2nd.
That is the stupid Ai movement system, this have ALWAYS been an issue, and in a game that features so many details and barriers that your vehicles and personell can get stuck on, it quickly turns into a nightmare.
The other problem is the illogical "balanced" weapons handling, tanks keep firing and often illogically have their rounds bounce off the opponent, but that tiny light tank that puffs off a round at your front scores damage on your heavy tank.
All of this adds up to a lot of problems, this problematic system wouldn't have been so bad, unless the movement Ai was... Utterly crap, you need to have your tank reverse out of the field?
Well they provided a nice "Reverse" function button to tell the tank to back out of there, but you have a 50/50 chance of him ignoring it and turning his weak rear to the enemy and getting owned as a result.
And that is the flaw of this game, a flaw that the developers behind Men Of War series realized isn't fixable, no matter how much time you spend on Ai deployment you can NEVER EVER beat a superior human at navigating a tank through obstacles, so how did they solve it?
In Men Of War, they allow the player to take control of the vehicle in question, something that in my circle of friends is called the "END the stupidity key" since you hit the END key on your keyboard and you are in direct command and control.
A function that you desperatly wish for in this game, but alas isn't there, it is time to realize you cannot fix a core problem and implement this Sega!
The other problem this game suffers from is... Microtransactions, camoflauged as DLC.
Think you get the full game by buying this and all the DLC on the Steam store page? Guess again, you are still missing missions, maps and commanders that you have to BUY in game with REAL MONEY!
Unlike traditional microtransaction games, these are things you pay for once, and then own for "life" but it is still the exact same microtransactions at the core.
In short, if you want a fun time playing WW2 RTS games, buy the Men Of War series, yes their Ai has the same navigational problems, but at least you have the option to intervene and avoid a disaster, unlike CoH 2 where you will have to watch that precious tank or squad get smashed doing stupid things.
If you are set on a CoH experience, you are better off buying CoH 1, it is very similar with Skirmish matches for Coop,  but that game is complete without any nasty microtransaction junk.
If you heard about the coop stuff in this game and thought you got a nice Coop campaign? Forget about it, all there is, is some Skirmish missions where you start off with a different loadout, and some scripted Ai, like the Ai getting an illogical reinforcement that is then thrown at your position, there is no such thing as in Men Of War where you do it mission style to aqquire assets, and where that artillery gun may need to come down before you can move on your objective for an example.
In short, CoH 2 was a disappointment at launch, and hasn't gotten improved with the years since then.
