This is a great introduction to the genre of Strategy Squad-Based Shooters.
Some people might find the gameplay unfair, regardless of difficulty, because they're filthy casuals. Some people might say "This isn't XCOM" because they played the originals, and don't like this. To these people I say NOTHING!
This game is fun, you protect the earth from an alien invasion, you go on missions in multiple countries, killing aliens, defusing alien bombs, saving civilians.
You level up the soldiers in your employ, unlocking new abilities and skills.
You have a research lab to learn about alien artifacts and a workshop to create backwards engineered recipes of alien technology.
Many different types of aliens to kill; Depending on which type of alien you kill or kidnap, you can interrogate or autopsy them to learn more about a specific type of alien technology.
Eventually you'll be able to autopsy a specific alien which allows you to develop the Psionic Lab, which allows you to test your soldiers to see if they are capable of utilizing psychic powers!
Also, you'll be able to make Mec Soldiers (Which means Mech, without the H)
You'll also be able to make Gene Modded Soldiers, which have improved abilities that no normal human does such as Super Jump so you can get up on roofs and trucks much more easily.
Basically, lots of really fun stuff to do. Some people feel some stuff might be too OP, but I think it's good for stuff to be OP sometimes. It feels like a good sense of progress, to really turn the tides on the aliens.
Additional Information: This Review is based on an Easy Playthrough, Vanilla Settings with Enemy Within Expansion and DLC Content,
Easy Difficulty is far from the average player experience, but I find difficulty to be quite arbitrary for the casual player because the only real difference I've found between Difficulties is how much health your Squad has, and how much health The Enemies have.
Classical Difficulty is what I wholeheartedly reccomend it is easily the most fair and equal and offers a fairly challenging Vanilla experience, for a small amount of difficulty increase choose Impossible and/or include Iron Man Mode (Which means you cannot load from a previous save, if something happens you can't Save Scum.)
After completing a Playthrough at those level of difficulty and you are looking for a more challenging experience Long War (Available on the XCOM: Enemy Unknown Nexus along with a load of of other small, interesting mods that are compatible with Long War)

First things first: Bare in mind, this was an older mod originally for Source 2006, made primarily in the developer's free time. It was originally released around 2009 iirc, after many years of development (and a newer version of the Source Engine releasing meanwhile). This game looks pretty great, keeping in mind it's running on such an old version of the Source Engine.
NeoTokyo is a multiplayer only first person shooter set in a cyberpunk setting, heavily inspired by anime such as Ghost in the Shell and (to a lesser extent) Akira. The game is more focused around positioning, tactics and communication with your teammates rather than only clutch skill compared to most typical shooters. Additionally, the game features temporary invisibility, different vision modes (night vision, motion detection & heat vision) and 3 classes with different abilities which you have to take into account tactically. During a game, when you get kills or complete the objective, you increase in rank, which provides you with more weapon options and extra equipment.
The main gamemode, capture the ghost, has the very neat mechanic of providing you with "wallhack" for a limited range when you're holding the ghost (flag) and you have to relay this information to your teammates whilst carrying the ghost to the dropoff point, because holding the ghost takes away your primary weapon.
This game heavily rewards teamwork and feels very satisfying when succesful, though it can be hard to get into. There's very little feedback telling you what you did wrong or where the enemy was that killed you, which can be frustrating and it can take a while to fully grasp the different ways you can apply the mechanics. But when you do start to get it, it becomes very amusing to abuse these against your enemies.
Also the soundtrack, which is barely featured in the game, is straight up awesome.

The general exploration of the castle is centered around stealth which keeps the game's focused squarely on its well-designed puzzles. Very few of the puzzles have repeat solutions, impressive for the pixelized limitations, though some rooms are made too easy through seemingly innocuous methods. Similarly, the difficulty of exploring the castle and avoiding enemies drops dramatically once the game is understood, furthered by a lack of enemy variety and a surprising simplicity of the game's more threatening foes. So while the gameplay feels more like a means to an end, some fine tuning and a few additions could have made this an indie darling.
Its story is charming and dissonant with its heavy influence of folklore and fairy tales. It rides a fine balance between its dark horror aesthetics and childish sense of adventure and wonder with its setting and aesthetics. Unfortunately, the actual details of the story fall short of its design despite a few interesting moments of characterizing side characters. Some characters and lore elements could've been fleshed out more to give more life to its world, particularly its multiple endings had plenty of untapped potential to further the world instead of feeling like shallow epilogues.
If you're wanting this game, its art style and sound design are probably why and for good reason. The beautiful chiptune renditions of Bach's more haunting melodies set a perfect tone for the experience as a whole, the sounds of the monsters make them seem more terrifying than their patterns let on, and its pixel art cutscenes are breathtaking. Most of the items and characters are well designed and distinct despite its pixel art limitations, though the more Atari-esque style can make most of the humanoid characters offputting with an oddly lankey look to them due to their arms and legs being only a single pixel wide. And despite a general strength of the horror elements, some of them can come off as rather on the nose and trying a bit too hard.
This game is ultimately marred more by details rather than a greater image, which I find to be very forgivable in a developer's first game. I'd advise keeping an eye on Baroque Decay's future titles as they show impressive promise in understanding core tenants of horror that many developers frequently get wrong or simply forget. For similar games, I can recommend Claire, Lone Survivor, and Stray Cat Crossing.

The Count Lucanor feels like a fairy tale.  Not one of these children-audience-only and listen-to-your-heart boring ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you see most of the time in television. Instead, it's much closer to these weird, unsettling stories from hundreds of years ago, where blood, violence and fear were common and served creating an uncenny setting for a story with questionable morals. That's what you find here as well.
The gameplay supports the story and the story supports the emotions and mood the game tries to offer you. It's one of these "light horrors" stories where even nightmarish images are covered by gorgeous and funny pixel art that won't try to disgust you or make you feel uncomfortable. I'm not sure if it's a good gift for an 8+ kid, especially since you have to read quite a lot, but I don't think you need to look at this as a game "not smart enough" for adults. Quite contrary.
It starts pretty basic, but after some time you find more and more characters that are fun to interact and puzzles which are not easy enough to make you feel embarassed, but also not difficult enough to annoy you. The pacing of the game allows you to relax and enjoy yourself. The multiple endings are impressive, especially since they are not based on your single decision closed in a textbox as much as they are a result of your actions and wit.
It's a small game, but a one that required a lot of heart and became a great choice for a lonely evening, especially during the Halloween season. I highly recommend it.

In terms of "skirmish" tactical mechanics and fleet persistence, "Armada" is the only worthy successor to the "Homeworld" saga that I've run across. Yes, the ship numbers and overall variety of available craft is lesser. Yes, the game is only actually played in two dimensions. But good gravy! Ship placement and mobility actually mean something, for once. Your standing orders for your captains are useful most of the time. You have to play the long-game with your fleet-ship upgrades, because trying to be all things to all people won't work so well.
The honest-to-goodness, custom-designed encounters are really solid, especially in how the challenge ramps up noticeably. If you don't learn anything over the course of the game, you'll be in real trouble by the end. Also, the environmental effects are put to good use in the main "quest line." There's one mission in particular that involves a LOT of asteroid fields - asteroid fields that you must be able to navigate while fighting maneuvering enemies. You have to put it all together for that one, unless you want to go home with a failed mission and some banged up ships.
The unfortunate thing is that what I consider the "meta game" simply doesn't merit a rave review. Tindalos did a standout job on the aforementioned bits, but then seemed to make an overall campaign that's mostly padding. If I can be forgiven for ripping off Jerry from Penny Arcade, I'll go ahead and say that most of "Armada" is "seeing the Matrix's code."
The vast majority of your time is not spent in the curated garden of designed encounters. Rather, most of the game rides on what amounts to randomly generated, Human VS CPU skirmishes. The random number generator picks an encounter type, and then generates a map for that encounter that draws from a few basic backgrounds and randomly placed "hazards" like dust clouds, asteroid fields, and mine emplacements. It becomes very obvious that you're really just seeing the same three or four things put together in a different way, over and over and over and over and...
And the unskippable intro animations! Geeze. We could have done without that.
There are far too many of the skirmish missions, especially when some of them are maddening excursions into the capriciousness of virtual dice rolls. The planetary assaults especially suffer from this, where you have a limited number of attempts to accomplish bombardments. Bombardments can be pretty much anywhere on the map, and more than once I had the misfortune of the "you must get here in time" target points being just about as far apart as was possible.
The game balance also doesn't end up feeling very satisfying in the overall sense. On the one hand, you don't want the biggest ships to be game-breakers. On the other hand, their "Renown" and fleet-point costs don't justify them at all. The big, bad, battle-cruisers are large targets, don't actually hit that hard, and are not really useful when compared with a swarm of light cruisers and escorts. You might think that Nova Cannons at long range are a great weapon, but getting a hoard of ships in your enemies' faces and hammering them with sustained fire is much more effective.
"Armada" is really decent - definitely worth buying - but it's also much more disappointing than it really ought to be. Tindalos did the material justice on numerous fronts. I just wish they had done it the same amount of justice in all areas.

Disclaimer: This game is definitely not for anyone and I am reviewing it as someone who has never played the original board game. In my opinion this doesn't matter, because I don't care if the game is faithful to the board game or not, I'm here to review it as a video game and how well it is executed and how much fun it is in this context.
You will probably like it if you:
- are a die-hard WH40K fan
- are a Battlefleet Gothic board game fan (most likely)
- like tactical, rather slow paced real time battles
- like to maneuver your ships manually into the perfect firing position
- are interested in playing the "same battles" over and over either in SP or MP
You will not like the game if you send your ships to auto attack the enemy and expect them to win you the battle. Even on the easy difficulty you will rarely win a fight without at least putting in some planning and tactical thinking.
What is great about the game:
- So far 5 different factions (more announced) with 4 different ship classes with several sub classes each as well as some support ships (Imperium, Chaos, Orks, Eldar, Space Marines), which play adequately different for the most part
- Fun core game play loop
- Relatively clean and well thought out interface
- An actual campaign!
- Satisfying audiovisual battles that actually feel impactful and are fun to watch
- Battles usually last a few minutes and ships don'get blown up instantly...well, unless you play Eldar...
- Great graphics and assets
- Everyone just loves WH40K ships, come one
- Skirmish and MP mode
- Ramming, Red Button :D
- Relatively cheap for what it offers
What's not so great:
- The tutorial is a bit lacking
- Torpedoes and such weapons are extremely hard to hit and rarely have a real impact on the battle I feel
- Somewhat difficult to find out the exact details of mechanics and skills. Yes, assault boats are nice, but it would also be nice to have a more detailed tutorial about that particular aspect of the game...and other
- Customization of skills are lacking, since every faction seems to have the same upgrade paths available to them. The Crew upgrades are exactly the same for each one, most skills and ship upgrades are also overlapping. The only real difference comes in the form of "favour", which means installing faction specific special abilities and weapons on ships. At least you have 4 different ones to chose from for each faction, but I would have expected a few more differences here and there, especially concerning the crew. I also have not unlocked all upgrades yet, but still...
- Unskippable cutscenes...seriously I don't need to watch my fleet coming into a system for every fight
- Fights feel too samey. There are a few different "modes" (defeat all enemies, steal intelligence, defend or attack transports, defend or attack space stations, etc.), but they all boil down to more or less the same tactic and I can see how this could get really repetitive, especially in the Skirmish or MP mode. That being said, the game is about short space battles, so, maybe it's not so important.
- Campaign has some nice story and cutscenes, but ultimately it's just a big skirmish mode with story progression. You could also just fight skirmish or MP to level up ships, but it's "ok".
- Imperium, Space Marines and Chaos play "relatively" the same way, Chaos has some faster ships and more accuracy at range, Imperium take a bit more punishment, Space Marines have access to very strong bombers early on, but are also bad at range, etc. Only the Orks (slow ships, no quick turns, no "after burner", very bad aim and weapon damage, rely on ramming at full speed, weird magic and (boarding) torpedoes) and the Eldar (no shields, very fragile ships, mainly prow weapons, potentially long range, require constant movement to avoid damage and line up attack runs, very hard to play) offer really different game play, at least early on.
- Uncertain future of the game
- No workshop support as of yet
So, there you have my opinion. I can't understand those who "hate" the game and demanded their money back. Checking out at least 1 review or YT video of it you should know what to expect. It's not Homeworld! That might also be interesting in this universe, but this is just not it. This is (mostly) slow and ponderous space ballet with a handful of ships on each side hammering each other into oblivion.
What this game needs is more DLC, more patching and potentially balancing, more game modes, maybe more campaigns, some deeper customization (I can't even change the colour of my ships). The Tau fleet is currently in Beta and I hope they continue to add DLC factions, because they are comparatively cheap and worth the investment. I would love to see more customization (maybe Dark Angels, Ulthwe, etc. just some reskins or remodels for the different sub factions) as well as more actual factions like the Necrons and Tyranids (could really be unique and take a step away from light cruiser, cruiser, battlecruiser, heavy battlecruiser)...and Dark Eldar. If that means making stuff up, I don't care. I care about the design and different play styles, but I think Games Workshop would have a problem with that. Maybe they can make it work somehow. At least we get Tau. Maybe other factions could be introduced as neutral factions (raiders) or bosses (Tomb ship, Hive ship). Whatever the case, I will continue to support the game. Workshop support is also something that definitely needs to be implemented, because this framework is the perfect playground for new models/skins, fan balance patches, additions and total conversions if I've ever seen one, just say Star Wars, Star Trek or any other space franchise. Make it happen!
You can tell that a lot of thought was put into this game. If you're looking to play a nice, casual spooky game, this is a winner.

This is not a hardcore simulation, but like Killerfish's previous, brilliant Atlantic Fleet, it nails the sweet spot in terms of balancing realism with plain, old-fashioned good times.
For any sub game fan, this should be an insta-buy. Hardware: i5 3570, nVidia GTX 1070, Windows 10.
Bought it because: loved the art style, like procedural RPGs. Inexpensive and wanted to check it out.
- Fantastic art style. The avatar in particular, a Dwarf whose entire body is basically his head, is adorable.
- A nice dungeon feel with good music.
Gameplay right now is super basic; you use WASD to run through the dungeon, which is a single, procedurally generated level. Monsters appear; left click attacks, and right click blocks. There's a blocking animation, but no sense of contact or weight when you do block. Hitting the monsters does produce a sense of contact. They all die easily and you automatically pick up gold. When you get to the end of the level, you're healed to full, transported back to your home room, and get credit for the gold. There's a crafting station there where you can spend gold to upgrade your weapon damage, but nothing else. Then it's back into the dungeon for another short, random level.
Performance is fairly poor. I was not able to get the game playing full-screen, and I recommend you not change the default resolution, as you can get into a situation where the game won't start at all. There were noticeable framerate drops and video lag issues even with my fairly good hardware, though I didn't toy with the detail settings to try to improve this.
The basic game could be made into a nice story-based roguelike with some extra work; right now it's not much more than an excellent tech demo. If you buy it knowing its limitations, you might enjoy running around for a while. Young kids would probably enjoy this as it is.
To the developer: This is cute, and has a lot of potential as a basic engine to become an enjoyable rogue-like, but doesn't have enough content yet. I'd like to see you continue working on it. Just one idea off the top of my head: add another Dwarf at the crafting table, change it to an anvil, and make him do a smithing animation. Allow the player to trade things found in the dungeon, and have him "craft" the upgrades. Change the fictional wrapper to two Dwarf brothers going into the dungeon together to loot / recover gold, a minor fictional wrapper but more satisfying.
Barrels to smash for goodies, direct item drops, buffs (potions, scrolls, weapon enchants, whatever), traps, etc. All the standard things ith this great look you've created would be amazing.

Overall I'm enjoying the game.  A few of the main reasons:
(1) The games are very fast.  This is a nice change of pace for card games.  Due to the nature of the game having you play your turns at the same it greatly increases the speed.  While long drawn out games in other card games can be fun, it is nice to have a game that guarantees quick action where you aren't going to be waiting for three minutes for your opponent to decide what she/he wants to do.  I still enjoy other card games that allow more time for planning, but this is definitely a good change of pace.  Seems like the type of game I will play as a side game while having a main card game that I play when I have more time.  Definitely looking forward to if they get a mobile release out.
(2) Simultaneous attacking/blocking.  Having to decide what to attack with block with before knowing what the opponent is going to do makes for interesting mind games.  It might be obvious I should block something, but if my opponent then just doesn't attack with it my blocking creature wasted its turn.
(3) Initative is a neat idea. It works to give you a reason to want to play quickly instead of just trying to wait to play after your opponent.
(4) Overall fun card design.  I've only played for a few hours but so far the cards have been understandable but still allow for a variety of play styles.  It is possible that after more time the number of possible viable combinations will appear much more narrow to me but so far I definitely see multiple options for ways to try and build a deck that is competitive.

After playing Cold Waters for only 8 hours, I thought I'd offer a few quick comments.  The graphics are awesome.  The game works beautifully.  That being said, I have to shake my head at a few things.
First, I was in the Navy during the 80's.  I know about Sonar & Oceanographic conditions.  Unless you're very close, a submarine is almost impossible to detect by a surface ship (passively OR actively)  if it's under a strong or moderate layer.  Not in this game though.  Even in the 80's the Los Angeles Class Attack Subs were quiet as tombs.  If they didn't want you to know they were there, you didn't know.
Also, while I've always had respect for my Soviet "Adversaries," I can assure you that they were never as good in real life as they are in this game.  Even at the easy level, the Soviets are routinely kicking my butt.  And there seems to be no logical reason why I've been detected.  It feels like the game just decides to attack you whenever it feels like it.  I like simulation games but I like realism, too.  And a lot about the game just "feels" unrealistic.
Not sure if I'd recommend, but here's some advice.  Get good at evading torpedos.  You'll need to be.  And don't forget, Evade in three dimensions.  Turn and change depth at the same time.  Torpedos have a wide left/right field of view, but it's much narrower up and down.
Good luck.

Cold waters is a casual sub sim that's very easy to pick up. It does, however, have a number of flaws.
Depth controls make no sense, they put you in charge of a sub in which you can't access any stations(TMA, view frequencies etc) but you still have to control ballast, rudder angle and dive angle? You should be setting a depth, not a route.
Enemy air is very OP at the moment with no way to shoot down enemy air units(which is fair enough given the date).
Very few playable subs, only US too and no reason to pick anything besides the LA as far as I can tell(thought the skipjack is fun).
The amount you can increase time by a so small it's a joke, you just have to go browse or do something else to pass the time; there needs to be more options, faster ones.
It's not that hard, dodging torps is very easy especially because you can see extremely far.
Land attack missions are an absolute joke. They're the worst thing in this game by far. The only effective way to do them is to spend ages sailing out to the edge of the map to fire missiles, why the game doesn't drop you off at the edge I don't know, it wants you to be inside a Russian fleet well under the range your missiles are capable of. For what you get, I can't say it's worth £30, wait until it goes on offer. Something like Dangerous Waters is much more worth your time.
However, I have enjoyed the game despite its glaring flaws. I'm happy I bought it, but unless you're a hard core fan of sub games that doesn't want a great simulation, this is not worth the full price.

This could be a decent game if there were things to do. You start off in an open hall, and it doesn't matter which door you take, they all lead to the same type of procedurally generated dungeon, with the same 4-5 types of monsters.
You swing your sword by left-clicking, that's all there is in the way of attack variety. You have a player level, which as far as I can tell has no bearing on anything. There's no player stats, no skill tree. The gold you collect is used to craft other weapons at the table in the starting area (each weapon has differing levels of attack power and 'gold find'), but there is no inventory, so for example, if you replace your Axe with a Templar Sword, the Axe is gone, and you have to buy it again if you want to use it.
Challenge is pretty much non-existent, seeing as how there are boxes aplenty lying around that give you gold, or refill your health to 100. You just walk through each dungeon to its end, collect gold, and repeat. I assume that once you've grinded enough to afford the most powerful sword, you've done what little there is to do.
One last detractor, it appears as though the achievements are half-broken. I know I've stored 10000 gold in my vault, but I don't have that achievement, among others I know I've qualified for.
FINAL VERDICT: If the developer adds some variety to the dungeons, fleshes out the character levelling, puts a few spells or special attacks in, adds some challenge, fixes the broken weapon purchasing system.. etc.. etc... well, that's a lot of work now, isn't it?

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a fun game if you want something that is rather relaxed, but mysterious. However, if you're looking for something more engaging, you probably won't find that here.
Overall, the game's visuals are beautiful and stunning. The environments look spectacular and the building architecture even more so. From a distance, everything in the world looks beautiful, but once you start getting closer to structures you begin to see that the once spectacular buildings have been reclaimed by nature.
The story is nice, but nothing special. However, the voice acting for the most part is top notch. In terms of gameplay, you can walk or run; there is no jumping. Solving puzzles in the game is trivial, and even though it's opened world, there are invisible walls in abundance.
In conclusion, if you're looking for a game that will keep you going for hours on end, this is not that game. The whole story can be completed in less than 3 hours, and to my knowledge, I only skipped one murder investigation. However, if you're looking for that atmospheric and visually stunning game, this might just be the game you've been looking for.

This is a great introduction to the genre of Strategy Squad-Based Shooters.
Some people might find the gameplay unfair, regardless of difficulty, because they're filthy casuals. Some people might say "This isn't XCOM" because they played the originals, and don't like this. To these people I say NOTHING!
This game is fun, you protect the earth from an alien invasion, you go on missions in multiple countries, killing aliens, defusing alien bombs, saving civilians.
You level up the soldiers in your employ, unlocking new abilities and skills.
You have a research lab to learn about alien artifacts and a workshop to create backwards engineered recipes of alien technology.
Many different types of aliens to kill; Depending on which type of alien you kill or kidnap, you can interrogate or autopsy them to learn more about a specific type of alien technology.
Eventually you'll be able to autopsy a specific alien which allows you to develop the Psionic Lab, which allows you to test your soldiers to see if they are capable of utilizing psychic powers!
Also, you'll be able to make Mec Soldiers (Which means Mech, without the H)
You'll also be able to make Gene Modded Soldiers, which have improved abilities that no normal human does such as Super Jump so you can get up on roofs and trucks much more easily.
Basically, lots of really fun stuff to do. Some people feel some stuff might be too OP, but I think it's good for stuff to be OP sometimes. It feels like a good sense of progress, to really turn the tides on the aliens.
Additional Information: This Review is based on an Easy Playthrough, Vanilla Settings with Enemy Within Expansion and DLC Content,
Easy Difficulty is far from the average player experience, but I find difficulty to be quite arbitrary for the casual player because the only real difference I've found between Difficulties is how much health your Squad has, and how much health The Enemies have.
Classical Difficulty is what I wholeheartedly reccomend it is easily the most fair and equal and offers a fairly challenging Vanilla experience, for a small amount of difficulty increase choose Impossible and/or include Iron Man Mode (Which means you cannot load from a previous save, if something happens you can't Save Scum.)
After completing a Playthrough at those level of difficulty and you are looking for a more challenging experience Long War (Available on the XCOM: Enemy Unknown Nexus along with a load of of other small, interesting mods that are compatible with Long War)

One of my favorite games of all time: turn based empire-building with total-war esqe real time tactical battles.
The game has a randomized tech tree keeps things interesting, though the chance of a faction getting a particular tech is based on the race they are playing as
The battle AI is reasonable for the time and is still comparable to today's strategy games and the Empire AI is good; able to keep up with the player at the various difficulty settings and is responsive to the composition of your fleets (players are able to gather data on the tech on enemy ships over time and the AI can do this too) and your overall power relative to them: if they are stronger than you they will try to destroy fleets then your colonies, if they are weaker by a large margin they will avoid your fleets and attack unprotected colonies and comparable enemies will do whichever the AI's race would be more incline to do.
Diplomacy options are rather limited, but it is a 4X game with a focus on gunboat diplomacy, so I can't really fault it on that.
Edit: It should be noted that my steam hours are far short of my actual time spent playing this game.

After a rough start during It's first year, COH2 has now become my second favorite game, I have played many RTS games and none of them have stacked up to COH2, I find myself really enjoying just the Ai by myself or with friends, I'm not one that ventures off Into MP games much anymore but when I do I find them enjoyable also, The developers behind the game listen to their community, and the bugs from what I have experienced have all been addressed, the game has a great community backing It and plenty of new maps to always download from the steam workshop so your never tired of the same maps, I have all the DLC'S and while I'm not too big on paying for dlc myself like most people, I do enjoy there DLC, If you like the game as It Is I also recommend some of the faction based dlc as they are great additions, each faction Is different from the other, not just unit or country wise, but gameplaywise, each has many different ways of building forces and progressing.
Moving on to some gameplay reviews.
I like what they have done with It, as I have stated before I mostly play against the Ai but from what I have experienced the ai In this game Is no push over, the ai seems to know just when to use their assets and abbilities, they utilize the commanders and whatever units they may have at their disposal well, The ai knows how to flank, how to use artillery and to get under your skin In everyway possible, They have totally re-done the ai from when they first started, friendly ai will park a half track or truck next your Injured units and expect you to use their vehicle to replenish your own units, they will also repair your vehicles or defensive postions on their own If In the area.
Gameplay Is really what you would expect from an RTS, build up your forces and destroy the enemy from your top-down camera, command a variety of units and take over the map, most units have special abbilities that make them stronger and better In combat, this can vary from weapon upgrades (new rifles) moral upgrades or others such as anti-tank capabilities or an mg to help with enemy Infantry, It has conquest and total destruction game modes, In conquest there Is 3 flags that If captured will cause enemy tickets to lower, however all over the map are little flags that provide supply points, funds, fuel and munitions, all required to build your forces up and use abbilities, taking these points also provide friendly borders so you can setup some defensive positions such as mg nests and other crucial structures such as medical and reinforcement positions, some maps are heavy on urban combat, while some are In the open and make for great tank battles, however the game Is a bit more fast paced than Men of War assault squad, while there Is a lot of multi-tasking, It's not on the same level as MOW where you actually have to load the correct ammo type for a unit, so really you could say COH Is a arcade styled RTS In a certain way but personally I enjoy COH2 a bit more.
Total destruction sounds just like It Is, wipe out the entire enemy force to win.
A couple mods I recommend are all units unlocked (so you can use all units such as other commander-based units In a single game, you still have to buy them through the recruitment buildings of course) and If you want an epic huge battle, I recommend population cap setting mods, that would allow you to use more units In a single game and not be limited.
All of which can be downloaded via steam workshop.
Regardless though, the game Itself Is a solid one and I can't recommend It enough.

I love this game, but I can't in good conscience recommend it.
The game is riddled with awful bugs, so save early and often.
I loved it on console, but hated only being able to pan the camera around from one of four fixed directions. I assumed the desktop would have freepanning zoomable view, but unfortunately it's still locked to the same lousy fixed angles.
The grappling hook is amazing for navigating everything from grounded alien barges to buildings in urban combat, but a strange bug in this version will frequently have it instead send your soldier the appropriate distance, but in the opposite direction from where you directed them - meaning that, if you wanted them to be fourteen squares ahead and on a roof with vantage, they're now fourteen squares behind and inexplicably underground, potentially ruining the entire mission if you didn't save first or if you're playing on Ironman mode.
There are graphical bugs where a soldier will aim in the wrong direction as bullets fly sideways out the barrel of their gun, which, while not detrimental to gameplay, do interefere with tone and immersion. (To be fair, the console version shares this issue.)
The changes in Enemy Within add some interesting options, but new enemies force you to build strategies specifically around countering them, resulting in less diverse tactical options for engaging other enemies until they're dead, at which point you're more than likely stuck in cover and unable to move to engage other foes as you'd prefer. The expansion does have the benefit of giving you more items to craft with alien remains, but also make other changes that limit versatility - for instance, all Tier 3 armors gain immunities that originally only Titan Armor had, leaving it a far less attractive option for operatives to wear, as other suits have additional features in addition to the immunities.
It's a fun game, but unless you're willing to look for mods to fix the bugs, give this one a pass or just play the console version, because this feels like it was built for console and ported to PC. Personally I don't have the patience to dig up mods that patch a game's shortcomings; when I pay for a product I expect it to work. If you're willing to work around the issues, though, this is a fantastic tactical and strategic title well worth your time.

Neotokyo is a free to play multiplayer FPS game that offers a high emphasis on teamwork and tactical combat. The game has similarities to Blacklight: Retribution, and Counter-Strike.
~
~
The game features three classes. Recon, Assault, and Support. These three classes are pretty well balanced. Recon offers endless sprint, longer cloaking, various SMGs and Assault Rifles with silenced variants, two sniper rifles, a knife, and light armor, with the addition of a cloak, and night vision. Assault provides you with assault rifles, SMGs, shotguns, and one sniper rifle, as well as a frag grenade, knife, and medium armor, with limited sprint, night vision, and cloak. Support provides you with Assault Rifles, Shotguns, an LMG, smoke grenades, and heavy armor, but you cannot sprint, and night vision/cloak are traded out for a thermal visor.
But then we get to the weapons. The game offers a fair number of weapons, but the problem is that very few of them feel like they're actually worth using. None of the three SMGs feel particularly useful, the M41 (semi-auto combat rifle) is actually fairly bad, shotguns aren't really worth using either, making the majority of your battles be done with Assault Rifles. The problem, is that the default assault rifle is essentially the best weapon in the entire game, unless you get the Support's LMG, or the bolt-action sniper rifle, both of which are exceptionally more powerful if used correctly.
The combat, on the other hand, ranges from interesting and thrilling, to boring and dull. In some matches, you'll find yourself with a fun, and cooperative team that really makes you feel like you're working with allies. Then there's other matches where some child squealing into his mic rushes behind you the moment you spawn and teamkills you with his knife, leaving you to sit there, and watch the entire match, wishing you could actually do something, since, like Counter-Strike, there are no respawns.
There's also only one mode, which is CTF. So keep in mind that every match you play will be CTF. However, this game does put a twist on it!
Instead of going back and forth between bases, the "flag" is a robot, or "ghost" that is placed in a random location on the map. The idea is to go to the Ghost (the position of which, is made obvious by pulsing circles that are seen through walls), grab it, and bring it to one of your drop off points, which are in the enemy's spawn area. However, when you pick up the flag, you cannot sprint, and can only use your pistol, enemies will also be alerted to the fact that you have the Ghost, and will know where you are. This demands for a good team to defend you, or, if an enemy has the Ghost, you'll need good teamwork to retrieve it.
Cloaking is a major part of this game. The effectiveness of cloaking, is based entirely on how good you are at using it. When you cloak, you release a bright flash of light, so cloaking right in the open is generally not a good idea. If you're wounded, your wounds will be visible while you're cloaked, meaning you'll be killed anyway, by people who pay attention. On top of that, you have an outline, which becomes increasingly visible if you fire an unsilenced weapon, or move quickly. It's also made extra visible if you're not near something that you can blend in with. However, a skilled person with a cloak can easily dominate you. Keep this in mind when playing.
The game also, sadly, does not feature a single-player mode against bots, meaning that all of your practice will need to be against real players.
~
~
The game has a very small playerbase, which seems to be divided between hardcore players that have been around for awhile, and complete newbies who have no idea how this game works whatsoever, with seemingly no "in-between", you either do terrible, or you do excellent.
This doesn't really matter, however, as it doesn't affect anything if you lose. Victory or defeat, the game will end just the same. The whole point of the game is to have fun, which is something that seems to be lost on the tryhard players.
Despite the fact that there is no reward for winning, and not even so much as saved player stats, there are still players that get verbally hostile over their team losing, or a teammate not doing what they were "supposed to do".
Then we have the new players, which will panic on a moment's notice and spray you down, even if they knew you were behind them the entire time. There's also the occasional "troller" which will teamkill you as soon as you spawn. This wouldn't be as problematic, if it weren't for the fact that if you die, you're dead for the entire round.
Also, surprisingly, the game doesn't seem to have many hackers. I see lots of servers that offer the ability to vote-ban if you see a hacker, but I've never once seen one. This is very good for a free to play on Steam.
~
~
I'd say the game is fun, and definitely worth a try. But bear in mind that you will be facing a very small community, and will need to practice a lot against that small community in order to be able to compete. Also, if you're only interested in games where you are rewarded with items, achievements, and/or in-game currency, then this game is not for you, as it is much like Counter-Strike, in the sense that every battle is solely for the fun of it.
When a newbie teammate doesn't just run right up and teamkill you, the game is very fun, and very well thought out, aside from a few weapons not being very well balanced.
That said, I give this game a 7/10, if it had a couple of more modes, a bigger community, and a balance fix, it would easily earn a 9/10. Sadly, these improvements are unlikely to ever come, as the game was released as a mod for Half-Life 2 back in 2009, and now most of the original devs are no longer part of the team. On top of that, it's unlikely the community's size will grow anytime soon.

The Count Lucanor is a game inspired by earlier Zelda and Silent Hill games. With an interesting story and great pixel art it is safe to call it one of the best pixelated horror/adventure games in recent years.
The game features an impressive cast of interesting characters, and is a nice blend of adventure and horror packed into one short little game with 5 different endings, which gives the game some replay value to it.
While it is a challenge to make a pixelated horror game with an over-head point of view truly scary, Baroque Decay has done a great job making the game wicked and disturbing by having great enemy designs, a nice use of lighting as well as simple yet effective animations and sound design.
An overall simple but great indie title I advise you to pick up, can't wait to see what Baroque Decay comes up with next!

First off, I'd like to praise this game for it's art and music.

Now, what I dislike about this game is the save system.
It sounds like such a small thing, but it was enough for me to make me check 'no' in the 'Do you reccomend this game?' section. The saving system makes you sacrifice a coin in order to save your game, which sounds like such a big deal because coins are very valuable in the first parts of the game. I don't want to spoil a lot here, but the coins don't even matter in the long run unless you have a set amount to spare. Metro 2033 Redux is a remastered version of the original Metro 2033 game,both developed by 4A Games and published by Deep Silver. The original game came out in 2010 but the redux was released in 2014. The redux features a high-res graphical update,some minor level changes,and a complete overhaul of the gameplay to bring it up to par with Last Light. Metro 2033 takes place in a post-apocalyptic Moscow after nuclear war has brought the world to ruin. The Russian people took refuge in the metro under their once-great country and from there they began the daunting task of rebuilding the life they once knew. The game features a single-player story with a total of 7 chapters, each divided up into sub-sections that can take anywhere from 10-30 minutes,and a total game length of about 10 hours.The world of Metro is one of the games' biggest strengths and it's very unique in how the Russians handle the apocalypse. There is obviously no shortage of nuclear apocalypse games out there but the focus of Metro is less on the apocalypse itself but instead what happens afterwards.
Metro 2033 is a phenomenal game,due in large part to the unparalleled atmosphere. The atmosphere and immersion that you will find in 2033 is breathtaking. You actually feel like you're in the metro and that everything hinges on getting to Polis Station. The gunplay does much to enhance this immersive feeling and every gun feels satisfying and,more importantly,the guns feel real. These weapons are like you may think,these are the weapons of a desperate people fighting with what they can find against a boundless enemy. The weapons aren't mint-condition AK-47's but instead are things like a shotgun made out of a bicycle or a pressure weapon that launches metal stakes.Every weapon has a multitude of attachments that you can purchase at a shop. These attachments range from a suppressor on your AK to turning your double barreled shotgun into a quad barreled shotgun. The weapons fire either dirty bullets,bullets made in the metro after the war,or Military grade bullets,pre-war bullets that are more rare. Metro has one of the most interesting currency systems I have ever seen as you use these military grade bullets as currency,as well as ammo if you're desperate. The military grade rounds are much harder to find but if you decide to use them in your guns they deal massively more damage and they seem to set enemies on fire as well.The gameplay of metro takes one of two forms,stealth or loud combat. Almost every time you fight human enemies you can choose which of these methods you would like to use. Against monsters however there's only one option:go loud and hope for the best. There are multiple types of monsters and each is very unique in different ways.Each level is incredibly well though-out and each one feels like it's made for either option. Every map has different approaches and ways you can go about taking out,or even in some cases sneaking around, your enemies. These also aren't exactly easy levels either as stealth in 2033 is challenging and requires ample amounts of patience and even more skill.
The story of Metro 2033 is that you play as Artyom,a ranger who wakes up in his home station of Exhibition. You are awoken to find that your old friend,Hunter,who is also a ranger, has returned and you go to the airlock to greet him only to find that your home is yet again under attack. You,Hunter,and your stepfather Alexei,defend the airlock from Nosalises which are the basic mutant enemy.Hunter leaves Exhibition but before he does he gives you his dogtags and says that if he isn't back within 24 hours that you need to head to Polis Station and tell them what has happened. So begins your journey and along the way you will meet several important characters,each wildly different in both looks and behavior. The first character you meet is Bourbon,a gambling drunk who offers to give you his AK as long as you help him through the tunnels. The second character you encounter is Khan,who you go with after you cannot follow Bourbon any farther,and he is more of a spiritual pacifist character who prefers reason and negotiation over fire and sword.After that the next,and final, main character you meet is Miller and he takes over for most of the rest of the game and is a very orderly and patriotic soldier.
Metro Redux is nothing but an improvement in every department. Better shooting,improved UI and graphics,etc. This is one post-apocalyptic game you don't want to miss.

I have played "Red Storm Rising" since you started it with a dos prompt. I still have it... and by 'it' I mean the actual 3.5" disk. It wasn't a 'submarine simulation' like we got later on, a myriad of micromanagement options confounded by a million keybinds. It was a CAPTAIN SIMULATOR that put you in the control room barking commands, not at every individual station trying to crew the whole boat at once. It was more about managing information and making solid tactical choices rather than telling crew members when and in which bunk to sleep (looking at you SH3). It also captured Pact naval tactics very well at a time when the wrong person could get a "9mm brain hemorrhage" for talking too much about them.
Cold Waters captures that perfectly from what I've seen so far. You are not expected to run from station to station, trying to crew the entire ship yourself. Your navigator keeps you updated on course and speed. You XO's fire control team works out your TMAs. Your sonarman will identify contacts. You are the 'Old Man'; your job is 'fight the boat' in such a way that you get it and a hundred-odd souls back to Holy Loch... while costing the US taxpayers a fortune in expended ordinance and as little as possible in repairs.
It isn't nearly as easy as that statement makes it sound. The AI is good, and their equipment is better the later you take them on. You've got a decent advantage early on as far as sensors go; the Sovs are using equipment a generation behind you, and it shows. Especially for surface ships, their first warning is - like as not - when your weapons hit. They are, however, ruthless in prosecution and you might pay dearly for that kill. Later, you get a larger variety of weapons and decoys; on the other hand, the Sovs start getting better technology into their fleet and they are much harder to spoof. Soviet subs are also a boogaboo, especially some of the easy-to-underestimate late-game SS's. Nukes make noise (especially the Alfa, it's as quiet as a Mardi Gras parade). They have pumps, turbines, etc. A Tango milling about at steerageway is the antithesis of noise, and a Kilo doing the same is literally 'a hole in the water.' It would be a shame to die to a cheap commie diesel boat - so get ready, because you WILL be ashamed of yourself... probably several times.
This game is worth it at full price - especially if they make it highly moddable. Workshop content in this game has the potential to make it into a virtual masterpiece of naval wargaming, simulating every post-WWII submarine class on earth.
Also, the Devs have mentioned the possibility of a Sov campaign... so here's to sneaking up on NATO convoys in a Tango, or trying to creap up on the US coast in a Juliett to park a nuke on top some imperiallsts!

In the thick of a match, I found myself having to quickly assess my priorities and forcibly cut my thinking short so I could play faster. It felt more like a Boxing match than a Chess game, as the cards my opponent played would force me to adapt on the fly.
Playing a card before your opponent gives you ‘initiative’ and lets your units attack first, but playing a card second lets you watch what your opponent does and react accordingly.
If your opponent plays a unit that is buffed by having initiative, it may change the pace you want to play at—otherwise you’ll risk taking extra damage.
Similar to Hearthstone, damage done to units is persistent. However the combat is closer to Magic: The Gathering where you choose whether you want to attack the opponent or block your opponent's attack, except that this happens simultaneous and in secret. After both players have declared attackers and blockers, combat plays out and the player with initiative attacks first.
You can hand craft your own deck using up to two aspects (colors) with exactly 40 cards in a deck, with up to three copies of each card in the deck.
Drafting follows the same rules for decks, but you pick each card from one of three options until your deck is filled. You draft the deck ahead of time and then choose when you want to queue up for a draft match.
All in all, I am having a blast playing Nova Blitz.

Rezrog is a decent time sink, and priced accordingly. I picked this up at release and I’ve certainly had fun with it so far, bar a few moments and a couple of things that I would change. This will be long, TL;DR will be at the bottom.
Story: Nope. Other than a short opening cut scene after the logos, there isn’t anything to add. This isn’t a problem for me, but if you’re looking for something with a deep narrative then this isn’t that.
Visually, it’s good. I enjoy the aesthetic of the settings, the little character avatars and the like. It’s a pretty standard thing, but I like that your character’s look changes when you switch gear. . While it can be extremely helpful being able to rotate the camera angle 360 degrees, I personally feel that once you do rotate, the game looks very…weird. I can’t think of a good way to describe it, but it looks ‘wrong’ for want of a better expression. Lastly, on visuals, I would say there isn’t enough variety. There are 100 or so dungeons, split into areas of the map, 10 dungeons per area, and realistically the only visual change between areas is the colour of the walls/floor. The dungeons are procedurally generated, which is something I appreciate.
Audio is a bit of a mixed bag, in my opinion. A lot of the time it seems I’m listening to the same 5 notes on repeat, and my brain just filters it out as noise. At first though, I thought it was somewhat soothing, and charming but, like I say, after a while it just becomes either background noise, or a mild irritation when you do notice it. As for the combat/item etc sound effects, I would say they’re passable. They don’t stand out as ‘well done’ or very ‘annoying’, they simply get the job done.
Gameplay is the most important part of the game in Rezrog. First off, the ‘Tutorial’ is absolutely not helpful. There is virtually nothing offered, except your starting weapon(s). This is not helped by the mechanics of the game also not being explained. Now, a lot of it is relatively simple to any gamer (click to move/attack) and the UI is something I think we’ve all seen before. However, attacking an enemy from the side/back does more damage. Yet the game does not indicate this in any way. There is no ‘backstab’ icon that appears, there is no text, the cursor doesn’t change shape…nothing. Gems are not explained at all, that I can remember, and even though I am several hours in, I still have no idea where to gain more skills.
The general idea with the game is simple. You play through a dungeon, kill enemies, get loot, level up. So it does become somewhat of a grind. This is made more so by the fact that only one character can enter a dungeon at a time, and only they receive XP from doing so. Therefore each character (there are 7 in total) must go through and level up individually. Now, some people may want to just have a single “main” to cut out some of the grind, and that is technically feasible. However, the game encourages you to have multiple characters of similar level with the ‘Captured’ mechanic. When you’re defeated in a dungeon your character is held prisoner there, and you must send in another hero to rescue them. So if you’re playing one “main” and that happens you’re going to have to go through the whole game up to that point again, to level up another character so that you can rescue your main. Like I say, this can be a bit much for some, if you hate ‘grindy’ games. Now, the game is described as a Roguelike, but personally I see it more of a Roguelike-light. I say this because you can save your characters if they’re captured, albeit with some grind, and the game is only ‘over’ if ALL 7 of your heroes are ‘captured’. I am not a particular fan of the ‘quests’ in a dungeon. For me, they simply offer no variety in real terms. Pull all levers, destroy all crystals, rescue someone, collect the key parts, collect sword parts, kill everything. I think that’s all of them, and since you don’t know what you will get until you enter the dungeon, it’s not like you can prepare yourself in advance with healing items etc, so for me it always descends into; Go to every room, loot everything and kill everything then run to exit”. I honestly don’t even look at the quests anymore.
Combat was described by some people I watched on YouTube as being ‘very tactical’. I don’t see it myself. Beyond “Which of these 2-3 skills should I use first?” and “Okay, I’ll try and get to the side/rear to do more damage’ there isn’t really much more than that. It is functional, certainly, but I don’t see anything here that makes me think of a real ‘strategic combat’ game. Although they’re not the same, I would suggest that Darkest Dungeon has a deeper combat system. On the subject of combat I found Mages to be terrible early in the game. It’s worth noting that, while I never played paper D&D, I am somewhat of a veteran when it comes to D&D style games. I’m aware that Mages start of terrible and get super strong late game etc, but for me they just don’t seem to do enough with their spells. The next bit is about Mages, but also the Archer class. Kiting an enemy is possible, and advisable, for ranged characters, and this works well, even though you cannot attack diagonally (same for all characters). However the issue I have is that the *vast* majority of rooms that I have seen have been too small for viable kiting, or contain multiple enemies, which would draw more aggro, so it never feels like something that seems worth while.
The loot system is nice, although anyone who hates RNG will not appreciate it. On a side note, I wasn’t a huge fan of constantly getting swords and the like with no Strength stat, but almost always “Intelligence”. Regardless it works well and you’re always on the lookout for that shiny new piece of armour, and it is satisfying when you get it. It helps that getting new gear happens just often enough to be meaningful, but not too often as to be ‘just another door’. The single, most negative thing, about this game that I can say is inventory, and stash management. Currently the Shared Stash of your characters is bugged (I assume it will be fixed soon). I’ve had page one ‘lose’ my gear twice so far. The biggest annoyance is passing gear from one character to another. It’s not well implemented, and is very tedious.
If you’ve made it this far, well done. In summary? Well it’s a bit of a tricky one, with only thumbs up or thumbs down, since your opinion of this game will be (like most things) subjective. If you like the dungeon crawler, loot fest, with some grinding, then this may be for you. If you hold those things (or turn based combat) in a negative stead, then this will most likely not be for you.
While it may seem that I have complained about many features, I would actually recommend this game. Simply put, I’ve had fun, and that’s what a game should be. The price point is perfect for what you get, in my opinion. I don’t see this being a game where you sink 300 hours in, and it’s probably not a game that you play as a ‘main’ game, but it’s something to pick up and enjoy. There are certain aspects that I would like to change, but overall I’m still playing and still enjoying.
TL;DR: Top down dungeon crawler, very simple turn based combat, nice art style, lots of loot. Has a decent selection of characters, with 2 styles of either ‘ranged’ or ‘melee’. No puzzles or story/narrative. Has some quality of life issues such as inventory management, but overall offers a decent amount of entertainment for the price point.

Being a fan of a few different kinds of simulator games and being particularly excited to see a modern sub game. I was happy to see someone having a crack at the genre since we don't have a lot of modern options.
First up, the game is not the next Sub Command. There is nowhere near the level of detail or complexity and that works as both a plus and a minus. The obvious minus being that the game plays slightly more simplified than a proper saltwater-in-your-beard sub sim.
It falls a little below Silent Hunter in complexity. What makes this work however is it streamlines the gameplay and lets you focus on 5 or 6 tasks. You feel this stripping back was a definite gameplay decision. You are usually managing contacts, trying to fix a firing solution, manuvering between thermal layers, avoiding their sensors and planning your course. Love it or hate it, the devs put it in there or cut it out for a reason. And you have to respect their commitment to what they are going for if nothing else.
I have no doubt that salty dogs who played 668 Hunter Killer could play this in their sleep while grumbling about the simplification of the genre. But the games ramped up speed and tighter focus means that the moment to moment gameplay is actually neat and hectic. As a person who enjoys ponderous and slow building in sims and other games. I can understand people writing this game off. But it does a really neat job of having entertaining gameplay (so far)
At first I was slightly disappointed when I saw the UI. It is deceptively basic. And I will hold that against the game to a certain extent.
However, within a half hour I had grasped all of the concepts and was ready to implement them all. This game is sim lite. It's hard to compare it without being reductive. But when it's cooking it's cooking with heat.
However, a problem this game faces is that the kind of people who like sub sims are already well served with some very detailed older games that would daunt a newcomer who was not intimately familiar with thermal layers, knuckles, (No not him) towed arrays and cavitation in submarines (as opposed to pistol shrimp that could probably solve the energy crisis in we could harness the energy in their Fist Of The North Star punches with the heat of a sun that cavitate so hard it scrambles a fish's nervous system, (ahem, excuse me))
To be fair, Cold Water is a game that anyone can get to grips with after the tutorial and master after a few encounters.
It also does not hurt that the specs are pretty low and the game looks nice if a little sparse and simplified. This is not like Silent Hunter 5 where you can see the despair rendered in your W.O.'s eyes or the tide gently lapping the boat. It's low budget, sparse and tightly focused in presentation.
The game certainly has flaws. It's tutorials, while decent for someone who has played a lot of sub games, could do with being fleshed out and assuming the player knows nothing about modern sub warfare. I would be happy to see a link to a bunch of youtube videos. It's a fascinating subject and I think you could draw in a lot of people if you could explain the appeal. There are bugs, to be sure. Some graphical and gameplay, I got some horrible graphics problems installing it on my laptop. I also really wish the camera was tethered to your ship. It's too easy to pull your camera around and see the position of an enemy target. A great part in Silent Hunter was listening to your Sonar operator calling out bearings and you trying to draw a picture of the scene. The periscope feels utterly pointless except for the firing solution points it gives you. It should be fun and cool to use. While I praised the overall design earlier, this is the stuff that really bugs me. The game has zero athmospere. Whereas Silent Hunter felt like an adaptation of Das Boot. That's a game where when you set off on patrol you end up at your computer eating lemons and discussing the pros and cons of Nazism with the guy who got his arms ripped off in Judge Dredd. (Unless you do that anyway.)
I also have to wonder about the long term play. While I am the last person to moan about including multi player. It is something that really could have added some longevity. Also, having explored and getting handy with all the gameplay features, it's only a matter of time before it becomes stale. Other sims tend to have huge expansive worlds where something as simple as a patrol mission can be wracked with tension and excitement at the prospect of oiled dudes ramming torpedos into launch tubes. (Seriously watch Das Boot, it's such a good movie.)
In Silent Hunter. You know if you try and go to certain areas, you are crossing patrol and shipping lanes. And while they try something similar here, it feels like small potatos. (or lemons)
I normally hate to harp on about game costs. But €36 for the game and charging €10 for the alright soundtrack seems a bit much and I am certain will put some people off. I certainly considered a refund after seeing the simplicity of the game, but I gave it a chance and while I am sure it will drop to €25 in the next sale, I am enjoying it, so I guess I am happy enough with the money spent. Your experience might vary
I will come back and edit this review as I get deeper into the game. I just wanted to try people like me who are happy to skate by that arcadey line in their sims. If sims or subs are not a subject you find fascinating then this game is not for you. It's a neat lite-sim that captures the mood and feel of commanding a nuclear sub.
I will say if you like Silent Hunter, there is a good chance you might enjoy this. If you live for the old school low res sub sims, then I guess you will have an unhappy(ier) life.

If you know the general gist of Nova Blitz and want the good stuff, just scroll down to the Pros/Cons section. <3
Nova Blitz is one of the few Online CCGs that manages to carve out a unique niche for itself in the post Hearthstone era. As someone who has played NB since early, early Alpha I've had the pleasure of watching this game go through it's many, many transformations. From the days when Energy used to be in card form ala MtG to when creatures sported ungodly statistical numbers even at early levels. So I can say with complete confidence that the game you see here is a long running work in progress, and very much the best version of the game ever presented.
Curious? Well, allow me to be concise then so we don't waste your time.
Gameplay Summary:
Like Hearthstone, NB uses a One-Energy-Gain Per Turn. .
Like Magic the Gathering, it utilizies a faction/color system.
After that, the similarities end.
You're allowed only two of the five facions per deck and (as of now) there are no 'neutral' factions. Unlike any other card game at present, both players take their phases in unison. This allows for a chaotic yet very tactical style of gameplay where you have to consider what your opponent might do, what they might have, and how your hand matches up with or without initiative.
Games are fairly quick. Lasting anywhere from 3 to 5 minutes on average. (There are slower deck that can boost this average, but even a control heavy game likely will not go beyond Turn 12 maximum.)
Pros & Cons:
P's
-Big, big, BIIIIIG plus here for any Hearthstone player reading this. The Devs actually NERF and BUFF cards, in a timely manner no less!
-And while I'm addressing that playerbase. That RNG-factor most post-Hearthstone CCGs are know for? Not gonna find it here. There are very few 'random' effects and none of them are game-deciding. The ones that do exist you can mostly play around as well. (Play out your units early to counter Goblin Fireworks, hold your units until your opponent plays their Blastbarrel Ogre, ect.)
-The Development Team is one of THE most accessable for any CCG on the market. They respond to their forums, Steam forums, Discord chat, ect., ect. in a very timely manner. Not even Blizzard responds as quickly as they do to bug errors, feedback, ect.
-The Development Team actually does consider player suggestions. Reasonably, they're not going to act on each and every one. But if you have a really, really good idea it might wind up in the game. The effect  'Double Block' is one such proof of this.
-You can earn quite a few cards for free. If you're having troubles playing against humans play against the AI for a while. Quite literally I've played over 100 AI matches and it took quite a long time for the game to stop handing out freebies. Not just Commons or Rares either. Once you have what the game considers a 'base set' even the AI games will super rarely toss out an Epic. No to even mention the free Smart Packs you'll get from Achievements while doing so.
-You can, and WILL win with the cards you recieve to start and earn against VS AI games. Most of the learning curve comes from figuring out when to attack or block, how to synergize your deck, ect. The card pool is deep enough to allow diversity but shallow enough to prevent you from being swallowed whole by it. Take it from an old veteran who hasn't earned enough cards to make anything other than 'random' decks yet. The playing field is pretty fair. (Minus a rare exception or two, which I cover in Cons).
-And hey, most important yet objective Pro in the batch. Nova Blitz is FUN. Like...legitimately play and smile fun. Can't say that about many multiplayer games anymore.
C's
-As of writing this, there are no Daily Quests or anything to help spike your income should you only be able to play for a small amount a day. Granted, your first win seems to always give you 50 gold. But after that the rewards are kinda small for play-and-dash players.
-If you weren't part of the Kickstarter Campaign, you might wanna shell out a little money in the shop just to fluff up your collection. Even though I list this as a con; the price points for their /month options are pretty fair. If you buy all three bundles ($30 total) you get the following (assuming a 30 day month).
*35 Smart Packs
*7000 Bits (The crafting currency)
*3500 Gold (10 Drafts or 28 Packs)
-Certain Decktypes, and their counters, are very Legendary Rarity heavy. Want a Construct deck? At the time of writing this; that'll set you back at 'least' 6+ Legendaries. A whopping 24000 Bits, not even counting Epics. Want to counter a Construct deck? Most of the good answers are also Legendary (such as Nature's Brawl card). So a 12000 minimum investment.
Thankfully, such decks are very rare right now and might possibly be adjusted in the future or their counters might be made more readily avaliable to the common player.
-At the time of writing this, certain small Quality of Life features are missing. Such as a 'Disenchant All' button for your spare copies. At present you have to manually go in and deconstruct each card on a case by case basis. You cannot search for 'Power/Spell' cards without having the units that effect them pop up as well; and there's enough of them to turn that into a visually scrambled mess depending on which faction you're rooting through.
_____________________

After all these years this remains the go to 4x space combat game. The combat is a joy and the variation in research routes - especially with the return of the idea that not all research is open every game - makes for interesting and replayable campaigns. The strategy overview is on the light side, especially on planetary development, but actually this works in the game's favour, as combat is what it is all about. At times there can be too much of it, but the joy of seeing your new weapons come into the fray is hard to beat, and it is one of the few games where zooming in to watch the action is well worth it. Probably it is most comparable to the Total War series but in space, but with a bit less meaningless combat (though it does still become heavy at times). Seriously recommend you add one of the more popular mods for even more weapon and ship options.
What's it worth? £25 / $30

Well, after some 20 hours, I feel I finally understand how to play the game. It's actually pretty good and well worth the effort, but unless you're willing to put in that kind of time, it's going to be confusing. The documentation gives a good overview, and there are tutorials, but neither really prepares you to play the game. They talk about Command and Control ships, for example, but don't tell you how vital they are; they talk about formations but don't make it clear how to set them up. Nor will you likely be able to play the real-time combat without reading the documentation very carefully and making sure that you have the keyboard shortcuts clear in your mind. There are also odd design decisions, and the ship are definitely low polygon models, but all told, the gameplay far outweighs these negatives.
Sword of the Stars is a 4X space exploration, colonization and conquest game released in 2009, and what sets it apart is the ship customization and that the real-time combat is very detailed and depicts the nature of the weapons during combat, graphically but also in terms of their power, range, rate of fire and accuracy. You can also target individual components on enemy ships to blast out the most important weapons, or perhaps to disable the ship to take it over with a boarding crew. In addition, there are various defenses for different sort of weapons and you can see these in operation as well.
The tech tree is sensible, interesting and mostly useful, and has significant depth. Each of the six races shares this tech tree with the exception of their FTL drives, and surprisingly, this detail alone makes the races significantly different to play. The Hiver ships, for example, are horribly slow but they can create a gate for instant teleportation to any other gated system, making their defense second to none. The Morrigi, on the other hand, can fly up to 10x faster than the Hivers, and so can raid almost anybody before they can bring in reinforcements. Their speed increases with the number of ships in the fleet, though, meaning that their defense is often quite weak.
In addition to combat, you have to manage your economy and you can engage in diplomacy and a limited form of spying as well, but in my estimation, the combat is the defining feature of the game, as your objective is always to take over the place. And that will take you hours, even in modest systems with 50 or so stars. With hundreds of stars, games will take you days.
Lastly, the internet multiplayer aspect has long since been disabled, and so you either play solo against multiple AI opponents, or on a Lan against friends. Fortunately, the AI is decent enough to keep you challenged for a fair while.

Nova Blitz is a fun and fast-paced card game with similarities to both Hearthstone and Magic: the Gathering. Unlike those games, however, in Nova Blitz both players take their turns simultaneously.  This can lead to a quick series of actions as players act and react.
As well, the combat system is bluff based, making for fun strategic decisions. When combat starts, each player decides what they want each of their units to do in the combat. They can attempt to attack the opponent directly, attempt to block an enemy unit you think will be attacking, or just not participate at all. So to make the proper decisions you will need to get in your opponent's head and try to determine the choices they will make. Of course, they'll be doing the same thing, getting in your head, which may change their decisions from what you think they'll do! Choices are not revealed until they are all made, and then combat resolves. The player with Initiative has their attackers resolve first, in the order that they were declared as attackers (this can be important! some units have effects that could change other units in combat!). Then the other player's attackers resolve.
You gain Initiative by NOT being the last person to play a card in that turn. This leads to interesting decisions in the main phase of the turn, too. Do you play cards quickly before your opponent so that they'll give Initiative back to you? Or do you wait to see what they play so that you can react to it but lose Initiative?
The cards themselves are very fun. There are lots of neat and varied effects, including some which affect cards still in your deck, which is possible due to it being a digital CCG. Card art is beautiful, as well.
Effect graphics are alright, but there's not a lot of variety at the moment. Sound effects are nothing exciting yet either.
Gameplay itself is great, though!
The games last less than five minutes, so you can still get a game or two in when you are in a rush.
If you prefer to think a lot about strategy every turn, then this game may be too fast for you.
