Honestly, this is probably one of the best 4x games I've played.  And, thinking about it, I'd have to say the biggest strength as to why it's good is its straight forward design that offers a lot of depth, which makes the game pretty easy to pick up and learn but quite difficult to master.  For example, rather than having dozens of resources and currencies to manage, such as production, science, faith, diplomatic capital, food, trade goods, and so on, you only have one resource:  credits.  All of your colonies produce credits once they're going and everything cost credits.  It's very easy to get a handle on, but managing that budget between your research, ship production, fleet maintenance, colonization, and everything else optimally definitely takes a lot of knowledge and practice.  Everything else in the game is more or less like this.  Everyone is at war by default and not being at war takes some active effort on your part, such as talking to your opponents in chat during multiplayer rather than setting up pre-defined treaties for pre-defined durations.  Star systems have only one planet and colonies have no buildings to build, just some terraforming and infrastructure to automatically build.  And so forth.
...there are some exceptions that are a little obtuse.  I've never really figured out how to use spies effectively and, while I'm sure I could eek out some edge in managing civillian populations, default settings work just fine.
But what you can do within all that is staggering.  Although there's only three classes of ships, they can be customized to a crazy degree.  So you want a long-range attacker?  You don't research the technology to build an "Imperial Missile Cruiser" unit, instead you put the design together yourself, tweaking it based on your own needs and what you've researched.   Want to execute a specific strategy to assault?  Arrange the ships in your fleet and adjust your reinforcements and then have them do that rather than relying on numbers to hopefully do it for you.  Need to crush an opponenty but can't hold the territory?  Engaged in a sorched earth campaign and have mining ships strip resources from the colonies you defeat so the planets become worthless and you don't need to worry about holding the point.
Some other tidbits is there's tons of customization options to set-up your game, making for a unique experience every time on its own.  On top of that, each of the races play vastly differently by virtue of different modes of travel.  This isn't like... Civ V where a race has two units and a perk to slightly distinguish it.  No, playing the Zuul might as well be a different game entirely from the Hivers, who both are entirely different from playing Morrigi.  And on top of that, the tech tree is somewhat randomized, meaning you have to adapt based on what's available.  Each species has areas they're more likely to get techs in than others, like the Liir get lots of energy weapons usually but struggle on ballistics, but it's not a 100% given.  If you find yourself without a tech you want, you'll have to adapt your strategy and perhaps wage war with someone who has it in hopes you can steal it.  Or maybe trade for it instead if you're friendly.  ...this, admittedly, isn't for everyone, but it really makes each experience more unique.
Oh, and also, combat is real time.  This might be a little off-putting for some, but it's pretty easy to control.  You can aim at any point on a ship so, if you wanna blow out its engines, you can.  Heck, aim can even be precise enough that you can strip individual guns off of ships to get an edge against them!  There's been times where I've taken advantage of this features to cripple fleets I stood no chance against, leaving them stranded in uninhabited systems with no repair, forcing the owner to keep paying for useless ships or scrap them for little to no return all the while I flee to the safety of my colonies.
Also, one feature I wonder why other games still don't include:  end of turn count down.  Instead of ending instantly, you get three seconds to change your mind.  I can't tell you how many times this has saved me from forgetting to do something on a crucial turn.  Why does this not exist in other games?
The game does have its downsides, however.  Multiplayer is kind of shot since the servers were knocked out a few years ago by the third party host being utter♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to the devs of this game and others.  However, using direct connect or VPN, it's still certainly possible, just makes it hard for you to find games with randoms.  Meanwhile, the A.I. gets a bit... predictable.  Difficulty only buffs or nerfs their income, they behave the same otherwise.  Expect them to lob massive fleets of outdated crap at you frequently rather than scrapping it to make something that'll stand a chance, always charge  into close range, ignore certain weapons, be very flaky at keeping their peace treaties (unless it's the Morrigi... sometimes), and rush certain techs even before its feasible to do so.  ...on the bright side, they're not entirely stupid as they will research techs and design ships that attempt to counter whatever you're spamming to keep you playing honest.  And, really, they're actually quite good at doing that, enough they can nullify your entire fleet if you're relying on just one type of weapon.
...all in all though, why are you still reading?  If you like 4X, get this game and get it now.  Kerberos has hypothetically discussed a possible HD remake, but they've openly stated that, if it even does happen, they've not started working on such a thing.  So, if you want to wait for something like that... don't because it'll be a looooong time.

Unexpectedly good. The graphics are a bit dated but good enough for me and it runs like a dream with max hard A.I. players. The races have interesting lore and the randomized tech tree stuff is pretty cool. The strategic play is turn based like any 4x game. Nothing too special there (though my largest pet peeve about the game is how annoying it is to move around. You can only do so by selecting something and zooming towards it. No arrow keys or mouse movements over the map. After a while you get used to it though). It has some fairly straightforward mechanics for a complex game which is always a plus. It took me about six hours without any tutorials to get used to it.
The game is great because of the ship customization and tactical combat. With three ship classes with a few dozen different modifications for the three ship sections you can create hundreds of different unique ships. The tactical play is RTS and is generally quite fun. The only annoying part is how the ships A.I. sometimes don't account for one another and you get friendly fire. However the need for fuel makes moving fleets a tricky business and I genuinely feel like I'm running a large scale military campaign when I play this game.
I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who might like a space strategy game with RTS elements or turn based strategy. As long as you don't mind some rather odd controls and dated graphics then it's an excellent and easy to run game. Just do not ever get the second one.

If you are willing to invest the time, you will find a lot to love in Sword of the Stars.

After a decent amount of hours in this game, I thought I'd give it a review!
I wanted to purchase this game for a while, but having to purchase individual charaters kind of steered me away from it. But I bought this game when it went on sale for $19.99 that included all the fighters except for Mai and Naotara Li. Graphics wise, I think the game looks pretty amazing. At first, I thought the gameplay was simple but after going into the tutorials that included a ton of advanced techniques - I realized this game has some pretty deep mechanics.
Just like a lot of other fighters, there are the standard game modes - Story, Arcade, Time Attack, Survival, etc... and you can either do solo matches or tag matches. Clearing a mode on a character unlocks costumes for them, so that's a plus. The CPU's can get pretty tough after "Normal" difficulty for beginners - so I recommend going through most of the tutorial first otherwise it'll get frustrating. There are a TON of tutorials that teach you beginning to advanced mechanics and I feel this game does a great job of teaching it.
As far as multiplayer, you can either search for online ranked battles or enable this feature called "Throwdown" where you can spar against CPU's and while you're playing, the game will search for an opponent for you to fight. There is slight lag at times, but overall my online experience has been pretty smooth. Some of the players online are veteran players so don't get discouraged too easily, as practicing is the way to improve :)

What this game is:
Turn-based tactical combat where you command humanity's efforts against an alien invasion while managing panic throughout the world and keeping the nation funders happy.  As you progress, you learn to reverse engineer some of their stuff and adapt it to give you a better fighting chance against your enemy.  There's also a base-building feature similar to an ant farm and aircraft against the enemy UFOs.
I find there to only be one con to this game:  the panic system.  As the aliens attack different nations, panic will increase in those countries up to 5.  Successful missions in those countries will lower the panic.  If a nation is at 5 panic, they will probably look to leave XCOM.  This permanently removes its funding from the game and the bonus for having a satellite up in all countries on one continent.  This wouln't be bad if the aliens occasionally conduct 3 missions at once in 3 separate countries, meaning panic will rise in 2 of those countries.  You're effectively put on a timer for the game, something I dislike as a long campaign is quite fun.
Then there's the question of DLC.  The big one being Enemy Within.  This adds in the MELD, a "glue" between flesh and metal.  This allows you to either turn your soldiers into supemen/women with various bonuses, like the ability to jump up buildings without having to climb up a drain pipe.  You can also mechanically augment a soldier by giving him a robot suit called a MEC.  In the long run, I believe the MECs are much stronger than the gene modded soldiers.  There's also EXALT, a group of humans that work in opposition to XCOM to secure power for themselves.  You'll have to be managing a fight against them as your campaign goes on.  Lastly, there's  2 new enemies to fight, Mechtoid and Seeker, a few special missions, and some more research and items to build.
Then there's the Operation DLCs.  These add in new side campaigns that you can encounter.  One has you take down an alien battleship that the aliens are trying to fly.  These add nothing overall to the game, and there's not much wrong with skipping them.
Finally, there is the unofficial DLC, Long War.  Its almost a new version of XCOM:  Enemy Within designed to be much harder, much longer, and have a lot more than the base game.  I suck at it, but its still fun to play with.
Overall, this game is really fun, even though at times it seems like it hates your guts with your soldiers missing 99% shots (actually happened to me), aliens taking lucky crit shots and killing off soldiers, Chryssalids, which you will hate along with everyone else who's played XCOM, and encountering new enemies that can mess up your day.
My final advice to anyone playing is "Don't be afraid to save scum".  This is where you go back to previous saves, like the one before you ran a soldier into a pod of 3 Chryssalids and got them killed.  Its a perfectly legitimate strategy in my eyes.

When I first booted this game I thought to myself "oh god what have I done" a still image with a narrator explains the dire situation and a minute in I realised it's time to skip. So I get into the game and I'm in some snowy place with zombie kind of creature slowly walking towards me. The idea is to kill them all to get to the next round, beat that round then kill a boss NPC, next level, rinse repeat.
Giving this game a chance was a great idea though. I found 5 minutes into playing I could actually adjust the time of day and weather, that was cool. Also a big pile of guns is presented to you each level which I thought was awesome too. The graphics aren't pretty, but they aren't down-right horrible.
Simple crafting is a great addition to the gameplay, creating a little hut with stairs and stuff is possible and the added "multiplayer" mode would compliment that style of gameplay more as one person could focus on killing whilst the other person builds. However there isnt a huge incentive to do this as once the levels are over, they're over.
Considering the full retail price is $6 NZD and I got it for $0.63 I've gotta say this game is fantastic. Sure if they were asking a higher price I would be very suspicious, but for that price you get a game that's actually enjoyable, has steam leaderboards and trading cards and yes MANY ridiculous achievments but I'm sure that makes some people happy.
I've looked at the other games from this developer that have been accused of "asset flips" and I've gotta say even if it's true you shouldn't allow that idea to get in the way of a good game because I guess this one got a little more love.
Overall at full price I'd give it a 8/10 and at $0.63 I give it a 8.5/10

Warlock's Tower is a unique puzzle game with a good sense of humor- I was very surprised at how long it took me to get to 68% complete in the game, somewhere around 6 hours.  And this was with a Twitch audience watching and helping me along too!  I welcome the challenge it presents- and the music is well done!
The game developers really did a good job in teaching the game mechanics to players in a fair way before dropping them off the deep end to the challenging stages.  You may find yourself 10 minutes into the game wondering when it will become challenging. Trust me, it will get quite difficult soon enough my friend!
The twitch chat integration works really well- so long as your audience is up for the challenge.  It works by allowing viewers to provide suggestions which are actual inputs of movement to each square so wwaa = up up left left.  It gets much more complicated later on, but surprisingly some of my viewers were still able to provide complex solutions to puzzles. Pretty interesting to collaborate with an audience in a puzzle game- definitely one of the reasons why I consider Warlocks Tower to be unique.
If you enjoy challenging puzzles, pixel art style, chiptune music, and have a good sense of humor then you will certainly enjoy Warlock's Tower!

This isn't a run and gun like Bulletstorm (from the same team) was. This is a simple story, one where nothing is as it seems. Gameplay is simple -walk around, interact with objects, and then solve the resultant puzzles. You play as Detective Paul Prospero, a supernatural investigator of the occult with some unusual powers. I won't spoil the story, but it's layered. You want to solve as many puzzles as possible while encountering them, and take the time to enjoy the show.
There's not a lot of replayability - once you're done the game, unless you want to go back and see more and look for missed clues (like I did - and I found some), this is a non-linear one time playthrough. That being said, this game is absolutely worth the price. There's an emotional range from fear to sadness to elation at solving several of the puzzles, and the scenery is absolutely stunning.
The majority of the game isn't scary, just tense. There is one heart-pounding section with some truly creepy/scary content, but nothing to disuade you from playing more if you're averse to scares.
The game is a $20 movie, basically, and it's worth every penny. I don't think I've ever played a game that looked so 'alive.' It looks and feels like a valley in the middle of the Appalachian valley of the eastern United States, and the setting and gameplay ties together well.
Buy it, play it, and enjoy it.

Early fighting is atrocious. It takes several weapons to fight back a small group, so you can’t really fight at all. It is a game of running away, which is fine, except it is pretty easy to simply run away. There is no actual challenge in scaling buildings that zombies cannot climb. The challenge is supposed to be in combat, and when you start you can’t kill anything with the abysmal weapon damage and durability. To say nothing of the cost of stamina to actually fight.
If you want to fight, you kick everything because it takes zero stamina. Meanwhile, you can only swing a melee weapon a few times before getting tired. L4D2 learned this lesson a decade ago. You cannot have endless shoves. It ruins the game play. As you get skills dealing with the zombies is even easier. You can stealth kill, stun and kill, and counter kill. Or, you can just kick them all to the ground and stomp on their heads to finish them. All of which leads to not using melee weapons; something you would think a player would be highly inclined to experiment with and enjoy using.
A handful of hours into the game you get your hands on the firearms, which makes melee even more irrelevant and descends the difficulty down to a dreary efficiency. Now, instead of running away using your parkour skills, you climb to high ground and mow down the horde. Again, there’s no challenge. Even the toughest zombie in the game can be whittled down from the safety of high ground. And those few zombies that can climb? You just kick them off the building. Satisfying, very satisfying, but simple.
To make matters even worse, the in game economy is an absolute joke. It costs thousands to tens of thousands for melee weapons, and a trifle $250 for ammunition. What are you going to spend your money on? There is no scarcity for ammo, so there is no disincentive to not use your guns at every opportunity. You end up with excessive money throughout the game since quests throw it at you, so being fully stocked is never an issue.
Ultimately, the combat in this game isn’t what it should be. The most fun to be had is in navigating the open game world. Alas, you will quickly find yourself dying when you shouldn’t. Like because a grab doesn’t catch, the grapple breaks mid fire, or the roof you thought you could grapple to you actually cannot. This wouldn’t be a big deal if the punishment for death was not so high. Every time you die you lose progress to your next survivor level, and as you level up you lose even more on each death. It is a cumulative punishment, and when you die because of game mechanics and not your own mistakes, it is increasingly frustrating.
Sadly, the story is anemic and boring, and the antagonist is a shallow nihilist. It doesn’t excite you to pursue resolution of the main quests so much as push you to finish quests through urgency and dire necessity. The result of which is poor pacing. You don’t have room to breathe or explore the way the story is laid out. It is a nonstop fire drill. The voice acting is good and the characters are decently developed, but it is uninteresting. The need to help the bitten that suddenly stops being a priority is a disappointing outcome. There could have been a lot of fun in elements around trading, finding medicine, and keeping your allies healthy. It is disappointing that there is so much unfulfilled potential with this game.
For a game with such positive reviews, I expected a great experience. I did not get that. I got an average one. If you really want to play a zombie game because you like the genre, this mediocre game will be fun to play through. There is enough to like about the gameplay that you won’t regret buying it. However, if you’re looking for a great game to play with your limited free time, this isn’t it.

Dark and Light has the potential to be great, but it's not quite there yet. I have put about 30+ hours into the game, and while I have enjoyed most of the time I have played, as the game is now I do not recommend it. Below are the biggest negatives I have found while playing.
For starters, the lag. It's horrendous at times. You'll be walking one minute and the next you'll be slingshotted back to where you started. When I first started playing, the lag was absolutely terrible to where gathering materials was a pain, and you couldn't hit a target to save your life. It has since improved, however it definitely needs addressed some more.
Same goes for the snapping points for building. I cannot convey the amount of annoyance I feel when I have this idea for a house in my head and I cannot build it because the wall keeps snapping onto a random part that I'm not even looking towards.
Then there's the official servers.  I can't find a server where I feel safe enough to log off for a day. The other players on my server are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and destroy the house and kill the tames I've been working so hard on. It is terribly frustrating to log on to "so and so killed you". Like, cool. Glad I wasted hours of my life gathering materials to build a home, tame mounts, and craft all of these items only for some♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to log on and wreck my life. Great. Just logged on today to find that my entire house, all of my items, and my mounts are gone. Not sure if it was a server wipe after the latest patch, or someone was bored and decided to ruin my day.
Pretty much every enemy is OP. I made the unfortunate mistake of building my house a little too close to where reapers and skeletons spawn. They can literally kill you in 1-3 hits, no matter their level. Imagine being a low level and running into one of those, because on my server they spawn right outside of the elven city.  It's not fun. In fact, pretty much every enemy that you can agro is OP. A month ago, I was killing level 100s, no problem. Now, a level 80 panther can kill me in 1 hit. Power levels need to be changed back to how they were before.
Like I said, for the most part, I have enjoyed this game. However, there are still many things that I would like to see change/improve before I would recommend this game to others. I don't discourage anyone from playing by any means, that was not the intention of my review. The above are mearly the negatives that I have found in the game to hinder my experience in the Dark and Light world.

There's a lot of GOOD in this game, and a fair bit of BAD as well.  And let's not forget the UGLY...

The GOOD:  Spooky atmosphere, effective jump-scares, logical puzzles, genuinely interesting storyline (complete with clever red herrings), nice in-game graphics, and well-designed sound.  Oh, and it's mercifully short, at least thus far (though I believe there are more episodes to come).

The BAD:  A slight lack of check- and save-points (especially at the very beginning and very end), cheap/amateurish cut scenes (with, granted, their heart in the right place), and a fair dose of "what the hell am I supposed to do next?" confusion throughout.

The UGLY:  Frustratingly frequent and mechanically awkward "chase" sequences in which obstructively-placed foliage has as much chance of killing you as you have of successfully making it to one of the clearly-designated hiding spots (the convenience of which is dependent upon which direction you happen to run in).  The first such sequence, barely ten minutes into the game, nearly made me throw in the towel right there and then...but you get used to it.  Kind of.

Overall I'd say that the good emerges triumphant, but we'll have to see how future episodes pan out. And here's hoping said episodes will be free or dirt cheap to those who have already bought the game (five bucks a pop being a bit of a stretch, in all honesty).

Verdict: 7.5/10.

Company of Heroes 2 is the successor to the RTS Company of Hereos, and whilst I have played very little of that game and cannot judge which is better, I can still see the glaring differences. Company of Heroes 2 is not an RTS in the general sense; It has little base building, no worker management and a reliance on strategic points to gain resources. This system has turned many a person away from CoH 2 and Dawn of War II, Relic's other less RTS-like RTS, but are these things so bad? I'll discuss the pros and cons of CoH 2 and how well it draws it's mechanics from it's predecessors (CoH 1, DoW II and  DoW I).
I write this review targetting those who have already taken an interest in the game and are yet to decide whether to buy it, consider this piece as a more in depth description from an aspiring, competant 1v1 player.
This is the least important feature of the game, it could look much worse and still be playable, but it's these graphics that immerse the player and let them believe they are in WW2.
Ever been annoyed when your Predator tank turns around when trying to escape on 100hp and gets shot in rear armour? Well luckily Relic improved this from DoW II and added a reverse function to vehicles, allowing them to reverse over long distances instead of short, frantically mircroed distances. Another example is climable cover, meaning cover can be long and winding, with units able to move across it without taking ridiculous paths. Showing enemy setup arcs, very small but very good for planning an assault with.
Every faction has access to many units bought from base, ranging from mortar teams to riflemen squads to assault rifle armed Panzergrenadiers. This makes for the possibility of a wide variety of units employable right from base. But this is further augmented through the commander system, allowing for otherwise unavailable units to be deployed: Light AT Guards Rifle Infantry, Airdropping Paratroopers and fearsome Tiger tanks. The unit variety is excellent and makes for fun and fresh plays after many games.
Evolved from DoW II's hero selection system and CoH 1's doctrinal tech trees, CoH 2 changes this dynamic to make it more flexible on the battlefield. Able to pick from three commanders during a game allows for situations to unfold before deciding the best tactical move. Do you want one that swarms them with infantry? One that buffs your infantry and provides artillery support? Are you churning out vehicles and looking for commanders who can repair/send out the big tanks? Although it doesn't have the two path trees of COH 1, it offers more variety between games with extra doctrines that can be mixed and matched.
The game allows users to reconnect to games if disconnected for whatever reason. This problem has plagued DoW II due to random drops and Steam disconnects which makes it a very useful feature.
This is not SC II and it's 300 actions per minute, you can sit back and evaluate your strategy, which makes it more tactical with less emphasis on micro and more in-depth combat.
The term "Relic lag" has not evolved within the playerbase for no reason. The game occasionally lags for varying lengths of time for no apparent reason, it happens in base, it happens when your oppenent launches an assault, it happens just at the critical point when you might lose a vehicle but haven't moved it yet. Relic lag gets everyone, no matter how many supercomputers are running this game Relic lag will always persist.
I mentioned unit variety, well yes, unit variety exists, but functional unit variety does not. The same unit will be spammed all game because the meta and balance decree it so. Low level to medium level Soviet players will spam Maxims and Zis guns and simply camp the victory points, waiting for games to end whilst they sit and watch. They may also spam T34 tanks because they're cheap. Ober Kommando West players will 99% of the time use the dreaded "Schreck blob" technique, building four or five Volksgrenadier squads and outfitting them with Panzerschrecks. They level up so quickly and become so powerful nothing is safe from their attack move blobbing. Spam has been looked at in recent patches and tactics for facing it have become more viable, e.g. suppressing Light Infantry Howitzers and better overall Heavy Machine Gun AOE suppression.
This is not the fault of Relic, and at least they put profanity filters in game to make insults seem farcical, but many players are silent tryhards or raging players who blame you for their lack of skill. The times when you meet talkative players are ones to be relished.
There are a fair few commanders for Ostheer (Wehrmacht in game) and Soviets, and whilst variety is nice to playa round with, there are definite strong and weak ones. Mechanised Assault/Elite Troops/Close Air Support for Ostheer, Fortifications for OKW, Rifle Company/Airborne for USF and Shock Rifle/Guard Motor for Soviets. These doctrines get abused for their huge early game pressure and late game dominance that doesn't offer any opponent room for manouver. Not to mention you can buy these commanders instead of having to wait to get them dropped. As of recent updates these commanders have been changed so they rely less on call in units that are more powerful than stock, meaning base units are more desirable and gameplay has been directed to make sure players get rewarded for teching to higher tiers without waiting for call in armour.
The Panzer fires it's last shot at the escaping T34, hoping to clear it up and win the day. But no, the shot bounces off front armour and your Panzer gets immobilised on a mine, and then at the critical moment when it dies, the crew decide to hop out and leave it abandoned for the enemy to take. The RNG is a massive feature, stray shells, tank accuracy, model kills. It makes for punishing plays that you don't deserve but the RNG gods like to inflict upon you. This is not skill, this is stupidity.
Certain units can spawn from any building on the map, vehicles can crush infantry and Soviet tanks can cap. Nuff said.
There is so much DLC, commanders, skins, missions, campaigns etc. This allows for Pay to win scenarios in multiplayer as well as huge money sinks like Ardennes Assault.
Company of Heroes is fun but occasionally frustrating RTS/RTT with well fleshed out mechanics and interesting design descisions, just with poor execution. The game was in a fairly unbalanced state whilst Relic pushed more and more DLC out to the masses, allowing for pay to win and money grabbing methods, but gearing up to the Britsh Forces expansion the balance has been getting much better and Relic listen to the community when it comes to progressively balancing the multiplater experience. The game is fun, but the enjoyment can be spoiled by some poor map design (Bystraya Voda/Stalingrad), iffy (but much improved as of late) balance and cheap tactics with pay to win stratergies (Elite troops/Close Air Support). I am lucky that I can overlook most of this and enjoy the game.
I like the game, and whilst much work is going on to improve it, with the British expansion coming out there is much uncertainty as to how they might affect things. But one thing for sure is that such a large update will keep the game fresh for a while longer.
Things are vastly improved, and the review has been editted above. Relic are listening to feedback, they are making intelligent choices and the game is getting a much needed revamp. Shame it didn't come two years ago.

It all starts on a nice summer night where four best of friends are sitting around telling ghost stories. One of the group decides to tell the story of something that happened right there at the camp they are staying at. Now of course you know they have to see if the story is true, and what ends up happening will have all 4 separated from each other, and lost. You will play the part of one of those characters, the one that actually told the story. It is up to you to try to figure out what is going on and where everybody went.
Graphically I have to say that I was pretty impressed with this game. The cut scenes that were done in a mature comic style looked amazing. There was also a lot to the models used in the game for the main character as well as the camp setting. One of the things that I have to say was a nice change of pace was the fact that even the mundane items that you will not have to interact with looked just as good as the items that you are going to interact with. Also, as much as I hated to see them, the death screens were also very well done and some were quite creepy.
Now this being a game that has gone through some crowdfunding I can kind of understand that there is no voice acting in this game. They didn't meet that stretch goal, but I really really wish they had some voice acting in this game. It would have added an element that would have caused a deeper immersion into the game.
The controls are a bit odd if you are going to be using a keyboard, the preferred method of play was with a controller. You are going to be using 'E' to interact with your environment. You are going to be using WASD to move around, although you will notice that because of the way the camera is situated you are going to experience some drifting from side to side as you move. Finally you are going to be using the Enter key to pause and pull up your inventory.
Alright so you are at this camp that you and your friends have spent many summers at. There's definitely a sense of misfits banding together. Now this being the first installation of the game you are not going to solve every mystery that this game holds, but man would I have like a little bit more to play. I think it was really at about the 40 minute mark of the game where I caught my stride and wanted to see where the game could really take me. There of course is the scary♥♥♥♥♥bloody woman that will chase you down in a heartbeat that always kept me on edge. There was also a lot of items that I picked up that I guess will have relevance down the road, or maybe not. The biggest problem is that this game is barely over an hour long. I do understand that there's more to come, but I really wish that there was at least a little bit more to grasp on to.

I wanted to like The Count Lucanor. The trailer showed its beautiful visual appeal, and I'm a sucker for well developed characters and story. I got a huge kick out of Undertale, which while a little simplistic and saccarine at times (at least on the mercy playthrough), had solid pacing and never grew overambitious. I say this because, when I bought The Count Lucanor, I was really hoping for was another Undertale -- solid gameplay (point and click puzzles instead of bullet hell shooting) with strong narrative to keep me invested.
I just don't feel The Count Lucanor met me half way.
Count Lucanor wants to explore the duality of European fairytale: Something that opens with childhood whimsy but seems to turn morbid the moment the storyteller decides their impetuous little charge is starting to lose interest. It wants to be a "Heinrich Hoffman, eat your heart out" kind of story.  Good concept, I was behind it 100% of the way. Depth and dichotomy are the cornerstones of good characters and plot. So where were they, Baroque Decay?
I played this game the way I play most creepy games. I get some friends together with some snacks, and we sit around a computer, alternating who plays and who sits around eating snacks, berating the current player's decisions, and making snarky comment on the dialogue. Pounding horror games in single sittings where psychological fatigue would otherwise slow us down. Good old family fun. But by the end of our most recent session, it was kindly recommended that I return the game and get my $10 back. We made it in about 1.75 hours, so I'm going to do just that.
Let's start with the character, Hans. Hans is your stereotypical fairytale child. He's fussy, entitled (somehow, in spite of being a peasant), and wouldn't be bothered to learn any moral lessons if fate didn't occasionally provide some horrifying shoggoth to sprinkling chopped nuts on his head while he considers his life choices. There wasn't inherently anything wrong with this choice, but it doesn't mean the writers had to forgo making him the slightest bit relatable.
Hans is a little prick. Maybe they're setting up his character development for later, but an important part of intriguing characters is that they have redeeming qualities, because otherwise I'm practically thrilled when bad things happen to them. But he's the protagonist, so I'm supposed to be invested in him accomplishing his goals, because otherwise Hans and I have a severe conflict of interest.
In the time I played, no other characters stood out either. Each one was wholly one-dimensional. I'm sure the excuse could be made that this was in keeping with the European Fairytale theme, where complexity is an afterthought at best, but the use of inspiration is that it's a jumping off point, not a pig sty to wallow in. Characters are simple in fairytales because they're geared towards children.
The morally choices early on are also blandly inspired by European fairytale, where nuance flies out the window. 3 people will ask you for handouts on the way to your medieval feverdream. Cast out of your mind any questions of, "will this come back to haunt me later?", the answer is no. The items you're given in the game are either readily replaceable, or just plain unnecessary anyway, so the moral dilemma is "do you want these characters to resent you later or not?"
And because all those characters are bland and uninteresting anyway, the correct answer is yes.
The puzzles are ripped directly from The Legend of Zelda, so maybe that'll be a strong point for you. I'm a heretic who never played the series, so Zelda and his green tunic don't hold any nostalgic value to me, and neither do dated block-pushing puzzles. Indie games have the privilege of getting so beautifully experimental with their puzzles because they're not expected to maintain broad accessibility, why you'd settle for the white noise of the puzzle world is a troubling curiosity.
Maybe the experience starts to pick up past the second hour? Sorry Baroque Decay, you knew you were releasing on steam, I don't think asking you to get me hooked within 120 minutes is an absurd request. Theatres earn their $10 on ~120 minutes of content alone, and I can't even tug it during the boring parts.

Long Night is a wonderful new game that recaptures the style of  the Playstation era horror games. Along with that style, it has many of the quirks and gameplay flaws that are expected. Overall it is a very enjoyable experience, it is erie, the story is interesting, and the characters are likeable. There are however some huge flaws in the game, and I hope that the developers listen to the fans before releasing Episode 2.
Major Flaw #1: The speed of enemies. I am just fine with having fixed camera angles that sometime interfere with the controls, it's the style of the game, and frankly I enjoy it. The only problem is that enemies move as such a ridiculous speed, that when a camera angle change occurs it can completely screw you up. It no longer becomes a frightening pursuit, and instead becomes a series of trial and error.
Major Flaw #2: Without spoiling too much, there is some bad puzzle design at the end of the game, specifically one that requires no brains, and merely trial and error (it involves a stain glass floor). Really that whole last scene was just trial and error, I hope we don't see more of that in Episode 2.
Final verdict: It's a great retro-style game, and if you enjoyed PS era horror you shouldn't miss Long Night, in spite of its flaws.

A review of Diehard Dungeon in less than 350 words.
Diehard dungeon is a Rogue-Lite game. It is a fun game but it can be pretty hard and the bosses are tough in my opinion.
In Diehard Dungeon you control a character that has a sword and a gun that shoots out bombs. The gameplay and controls feel very similar to an older Legend of Zelda game. There is even the spin attack. Each time you enter the dungeon you fight against random rooms of enemies. Eventually after clearing so many rooms you fight a boss. You do this about three times and then you fight the final boss. I think the gameplay is fun but it can get repetitive. Maybe I just suck but I rarely can beat this game. That being said I am trying to get to Diehard rank. This is like playing the game on very hard. The game has multiple challenge modes if the main game mode gets boring.
If you like the look and feel of an older Legend of Zelda game, for example A Link to the Past and you like Rogue-Lite games then this game will be fun and I recommend it. That being said if somewhat repetitive dungeons and irritating enemies and bosses is a turn off then maybe you will not like this game. Like most indie games I would recommend watching some gameplay on Twitch/YouTube.

I'd probably call this game a cult classic, but I don't even think the following it has would extend that far. Which is a shame, considering how epic this game is. Honestly I can say if you want a 4X space strategy game, get this, and ignore the sequel.
Why? You might ask, surely the sequel is better! Wrong, it had a terrible, terrible launch, released in a bad unfinished state, to the point where even clicking the new game button would crash it. Which isn't the developers fault, i'd like to add, they suffered the same problem that plague's most games today, the publisher forced them to push it out the door.
But back to the original topic. SotS is addictive and more importantly, fun. Six races to choose from, each with their own quirks and style of play. You can set up a galaxy with a number of options, ranging from amount of stars, to the galaxy shape, the size of the stars themselves, the distance between them... basicaly you can create any game you like and choose who you want to play and play against.
It has a randomised research tree, every game. So don't get comfortable with those awesome beam weapons, come the next game, you might be unlucky and not get that tech. There are some essential techs that every race gets, every game, like the very basic laser or mass driver tree. But each race has different probabilities of getting access to the much more advanced technologies that are in the various trees.
The empire management is... basic, you colonise planets and they develop on their own, terraforming till they are suitable for your race, and building infrastructure. Some planets are so hostile that you can't even colonise them, although there are technologies that you might get access to that can improve the hazard they impose.
Ship design is another interesting and fun part of the experience, as you pick different sections and weapons to put on your ships. Maybe you'd like a ship fully loaded with missles? Sure, go ahead, just be mindful that if the AI has a lot of point defense, that ship will be nearly pointless. So a lot of designing can revolve around what gets thrown against you, or what you come up against.
Then, theres the random encounters... which is an option you can fiddle with in the game settings when you make the galaxy. Basically, it is what it says on the tin, a random encounter can range from a asteroid shower, which can wipe out a new colony, to getting attacked by slavers. But there are special types of encounters, which often turn out to be dangerous and can take massive fleets to stop. I'll give you an example of a grand menace I encountered in a game I played, The Peacekeeper. This dude comes into the map and travels to the center of the galaxy and makes a speech, telling you to stop all hostilities with each other and stop prodcution of war ships. Break these rules while he's on the map, and he attacks you. Sounds reasonable, right? Wrong, this guy is... holy mother of god frightening, he will literally tear your fleets to shreds, no matter what tech you have. Luckily, he doesn't discriminate and will love wailing on the AI as much as you if they step out of line.
All in all, Sword of the Stars is an impressive, and addictive game, that is starting to show it's age graphically, but the fun factor and replayability keeps me coming back to it. I deffinitely reccommend this title to any 4X fans, and especially to space strategy fans. It's an easy to pick up game, thats difficult to master.

The game design.
I have no complaints regarding the art, music, and story. A few of the puzzles are a little wonky to me, but overall they are very well made and really make you think.

While I'm all for letting the player discover the limits of what they can do, giving zero indication of what can be done is where I draw the line. For example in world 6, you gain a new ring power. A ring is referneced in the intro to the world, but indication is given that it is an ability, much less what button it is on. Once you figure out the rules it is ok.
This absolute lack of direction in a game with surprisingly complex mechanics simply left me feeling lost and frustrated. I almost ragequit a couple times, but I got through. It would just be so much better with a simple 1-2 line tutorial. Or even just introduce the next set of rules in the previous level in an obvious, easy to understand way. For f***'s sake, even Dark Souls has a tutorial.
It is a good puzzle/platformer. But just know what you are getting into.

Also, what level of hazard do you colonize, and when? (With what level of technology) This is also a process of trial and error, since there is no way to calculate exactly when a colony will become profitable based on X number of colonizers times Y technology divided by Z hazard. The balance between races is also pretty off, and you will most likely want to stick to only 3 races out of the 6 or so available.  This game would probably be alot more fun on multiplayer and in any case, is definitely not for the casual gamer.

As a longtime fluff-enthusiast, whilst dabbling in the 40k tabletop for a bit in my youth (there never was enough money to force-feed it to GW to keep up an army), I am very happy to finally get a shot at the Battlefleet Gothic experience, since I am too young to ever have gotten into the specialist tabletop games.
And it is just great. The campaign manages to capture the setting's flair and style with astonishing accuracy.
You will want to pledge your life eternally to the Emperor's service (Blessed be his holyness and feared be his wrath) about 5hours into the Gothic War and ever after.
There are balance issues, yes. But as far as I can see, the devs are actually doing something about them bit by bit.
Otherwise the game is just the all-out, balls to the wall slugfest you (rightfully) expect from the 40k setting. Giant ships clashing with each other, annihilating little support vessels as an afterthought and generally wreaking havoc on each other. All this with a surprisingly intuitive control scheme, if you ever played a rather fast paced RTS before in your life.
If you start online, be aware that you WILL lose the first few games in a rather humiliating manner, as the matchmaking can and will toss you together with players of much higher experience and/or skill.
As of writing this review I actually start winning my first multiplayer games. And I do this, because those more experienced players have tips for you in abundance on how to actually beat them, instead of taunting the n00b.
So thumbs up to the player base. They are usually great, too!

So you may be thinking if 4 of your squad member have a 20% chance of hitting then you have a pretty good chance one of them will hit, but actualy they have cluck all chance so may as well not waste the turns.
The aliens also cheat constantly and thier weapons can destroy your cover when they miss leaving you in the open for the next alien to kill even though you were totally hidden from thier sight when the turn started.

This game has enchanted me. I adore this game. Even if this doesn't really look like something you'd be in to at first, please give it a try. It's cheap, and it's gorgeous.
Meadow is a quiet little game about being a forest creature wandering through the world, and potentially meeting other players who are also little forest creatures. They run the gamut of the badger cub (you start out as them), rabbits, frogs, foxes, bear cubs, lynxes, pheasants, goats, and more. There is no way to hurt other players in Meadow. It is a purely co-operative experience.
The catch to this game is that you cannot use any form of words to communicate with other players. Only symbols and gestures may be used. Even so, communicating is not so hard. As a result, there is basically only nothing but kindness radiating from this game. No hate, no bullying. Suddenly boundaries like language, race, gender ... all of it is lifted, and you are communicating with your fellow animals as entities. Despite being different species, you are all the same, and not different. You feel as if you belong somewhere. It comforts you.
I've made a few short friendships in this game, my most cherished one (so far!) being with a pheasant, a yellow one. I met them in the early hours of the morning, at about 1 am when it was still dark out in the game. By 6:30 am, we were still adventuring. Many animals had joined our group and left as we adventured, but we never split up. We were inseperable, and they were very patient and interested in just exploring. I wish I knew who they were, I feel as if I bonded with them.
You CAN see other player's usernames by pressing alt right, but this pheasant had their username hidden, which I can respect. Still, I hope they're doing okay. I liked them a lot.
Again, please just try this game. It's a beautiful experience and it's won my heart over.

I am legitimately SHOCKED at the positive reviews this game is receiving. I played 105 minutes or so, mostly because of the infuriating and deliberately clunky "running puzzles" that compose the last HALF of this title. I sincerely wish I could have my $4.99 back, because I wouldn't spend more than $1 on this game or any subsequent chapters. The only thing I can think of is that people who backed the game feel overly fond of it, or the friends of the developers are being very outspoken here.
To elaborate...
THE PROS:
*Great cut-scene graphics, very Gone Home meets Telltale games. A pity they flash so fast that you can't read the text, though.
*Retro-style nostalgia in abundance, even the year it takes place in.
*A fairly interesting storyline.
*A "creepy, scary" villian type that is pretty unnerving.
*Decent cliffhanger ending. I feel sincerely intrigued by what happens in the rest of the story, but...
THE CONS:
*Horrible controls. I understand the Retro static camera, but the poor controls paired with the "running puzzles" and the fact the main character has asthma simply make the game 100x more frustrating than fun.
*Short -- If the clunky running mechanics hadn't have doubled my time, I'd have finished this in 35-45mins. Tops. Totally not worth $4.99 in my book!
*No audio controls -- not to disable the music, nor slider-bar it down. The music isn't -bad- it's just loud compared to the other sounds, and it somehow makes my head want to explode when getting frustrated with the running puzzles.
*Poor Storytelling "plot devices." I'm all for foreshadowing, or having a plot arch that spans the entire series of episodes. However, when you present a LOT of story elements that the player can't unravel and decipher until they purchase the later episodes, it just feels weak.
...and that's just what I can think of, off the top of my head. If the other episodes were included FREE with this $4.99 purchase, I -might- be able to recommend it. Maybe. But probably not, because this game just left me insanely frustrated and completely confused as to why the reviews are so overwhelmingly positive thus far.

This game is a mess.
The bulk of the game is spent running around a huge, empty campground stuffed full of cabins you can't enter -- outside of this main map, there are only four locations in the whole chapter, and as near as I can tell one of those is optional. But don't worry, you'll find a whopping two puzzles in the whole game to help pass the time!
The whole time you're outside, you're constantly being assaulted by some sort of ghost thing who runs after you, and since the whole place is linear corridors, the only way to escape is backwards. The only way to get rid of her is to either outrun her until she gets bored or you reach one of a handful of hiding spots which get rid of her 100% of the time (a heavily oversimplified take on the system from Clock Tower). You can get this down to a science after a couple of attempts and every time she shows up -- about once every 45 seconds by the end -- it's just an annoying detour.
The story makes absolutely no sense, and the giant walls of text that make up the notes do little to give a sense that any more thought was put into what happens than Weird Things Are Afoot. The closest it ever comes to a coherent narrative is in that one area that I'm pretty sure you can skip entirely.
The final area is kind of cool visually, but it's an absolute dog to play and starts and ends abruptly with no real attempt at coherency. Near as I could tell it had NOTHING to do with ANY of the other ~spooky stuff~ in the rest of the game. Finally, after about fifty deaths or so, I reached the end, it played a cryptic cutscene that wrapped up nothing and dumped me unceremoniously back to the main menu.
Graphically it's sort of OK and the controls are decent when you're not wrestling with the camera (camera-relative controls and dramatic camera angles clash once again) but outside of that there's really nothing that gets me itching to play episode 2.

My first impression:
Long night indeed looks and feels like the old horror adventures I used to love during the Playstation era. I am not very far in the game (I hope), but I am already certain, that I will finish it.
A few (unsorted) notes:
- The controls are as good or as bad as most action adventures of the era Long Night tries to connect to.
- There is no combat. Think Clocktower, not Resident Evil.
- There is little explanation of the health system. Sometimes I die, sometimes I don't.
- You can turn off checkpoints (there are save points, make sure to memorize the locations) and interaction popups (tapping A/X while bumbing along the wall is back, yay). This replaces a difficulty system and greatly improves immersion.
- The game is not dubbed.
- Story is represented by short visual novel style films.
- Make sure you are a quick reader! The text in the videos is so fast, reading the text, looking at the picture and understanding what's going on can be a pain.
- There is a lot of text to read. Books, notes, journals, diaries. You can also click on most items and read a description. This is a feature most modern games are missing. Yes, I want to read more about that picture on the wall, that plate on the table and that empty bed with smelly sheets. Well done!
- Most of the text was obviously not written by an English native speaker. This might be bad for some, but it brings back the charme of the genre ca. 2000, when all games like this came from Japan, with weird translations. This one however, rather sounds like good French English... and I was right, it's a French developer!
- You can freely roam the camp, as free as you can roam any place in a horror game at least.
- As the main cast is a bunch of teens, be ready for a lot of teen tropes.
- There is an actual inventory.
- I spent 88 minutes in the game without finding a map. The camp is not that big, but...
- ...the camera angles do not really help in finding my way and knowing where I am. I actually have no idea of the geometry of that camp, thanks to that camera. Like I said, the game reproduces a late 90's charme, including those fun details we actually never missed. EDIT: According to the comments, there is a map. Thanks to Choux.
The first five minutes were full of "Ugh, the visuals!" and "Err, controls...", but then it was like "Aaaah, I missed it!"
Best five bucks I have spent in a while!

"Welcome to the good ol' Steam Powered Store! What do you here?... Oh, you're looking for a retro Zelda-like game?... With good pixelated graphics?... What more? Infinite randomly generated dungeons, an always changing difficulty... and a diversity of challenges scattered around?
HAHA! You're joking, right? There's no way something like that can actually exi-..... w-wait..... I think I just have what you're looking for..."

Note: This game was reviewed with a key provided by the developer
The Count Lucanor is an adventure horror game inspired by Legend Of Zelda and Silent Hill and it's not messing around.
In The Count Lucanor we play as Hans, Hans is  a young boy who wants to become an adventurer. On his birthday he get's angry at his mom and runs away from home to look for treasure. Meeting a few people a long the way, Hans passes out and wakes up in a nightmarish world where he is led to a castle where he has to complete the trials of Count Lucanor to win all of his treasures.
When the developers said that this game is based on those two titles, they are not joking about it. The looks maybe childish, but trust me this game is not suitable for children. The game is incredibly violent and not to mention it's pretty scary at moments.
While the horror elements are borrowed from Silent Hill, the adventure aspect is borrowed from Legend of Zelda. Now while you can't fight against the monsters you can hide giving the game some stealth segments. But what they borrow the most is the adventuring and puzzle solving. The puzzles are perfect and figuring them out is a great feeling. All of the puzzles are not cryptic what so ever, so everyone can solve them no problem.
The art style is fantastic and is one of my favorite looking indie games. The cutscenes are awesome and the game graphics are awesome as well. Everything looks crisp and is pleasing to the eye.
The game might prove difficult to some because you need coins to save the game and every save costs 1 coin, the game tries to help and makes the coins the most common items in chest, but you will also need food to keep your health up, so you don't die.
The soundtrack is pretty decent, nothing too special, I wished it was more memorable, but it's still pretty good and helps out in the more tense moments in the game.
The game ran perfectly and I encountered zero bugs while playing.  I think if you have a good PC you shouldn't have any problems running this title.
The game lasted me 3 hours, but the game has tons of replay value, cause there's 5 total endings to see and all of them require different choices to be made in the game.
Overall, I can safely say The Count Lucanor is a fantastic title and I highly suggest all of you to play through it as well. It's well worth the full price purchase.
Final Rating:
8.5/10 - Worth Purchasing at Full Price

This is the first review that I felt compelled to write. I never heard of this game until I saw that the soundtrack was recently released. The story concept and art style was really appealing and I read some good things about this developer, so I decided to pick the game up. I was pleasantly surprised. This game is a really fun throwback to retro arcade games from the 80's. You play as a 'good' robot that must avenge the human race and kill all the 'bad' robots in increasingly difficult levels, with a few boss battles in between. The gameplay is easy to get into, but difficult to master like any good retro-style game. The graphics look great, and successfully blend in some nice modern visuals into its retro style. The powerups are really cool and make you feel powerful. Good play will reward more currency and you can buy upgrades. The user interface is easy to navigate and looks really nice. It's very simple to upgrade your robot, and not confusing at all. The audio fits the game's story very well -- the sound effects and robot voices are perfect and the music is really awesome too. The music ramps up in intensity as you progress through each level, and it really fills you up with a sense of impending doom as you blast wave after wave of evil robots. I bought the soundtrack too. Seriously, thumbs up on the audio design. It really lives up to the art style. This game is all killer, no filler. There is zero fat on this game. It's one of those gems that you are glad to find and have in your collection. I got Titan Attacks too, which looks great and I can't wait to get into!

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers here from Universal Gaming Reviews to share a small summary of our review for The Count Lucanor by Baroque Decay. If you'd like to read our full review you can find it here:
The Count Lucanor is a pixel art horror adventure game that follows the story of Hans, a 10 year old boy who has grown tired of being poor and on his 10th birthday he sets out on an adventure to find riches. Eventually he finds himself in Tenbre Castle where he must guess the name of a goblin to become the heir of Tenebre Castle.
The game is widely puzzle based and features a wide range of unique ones to solve. Many puzzles are similar in style to the classic Zelda games and are quite fun to solve. Puzzles become increasingly more challenging as you progress through the castle but never become so difficult that they're impossible to figure out.
The game takes around 5-6 hours total to complete if you're taking your time so it's a short and entertaining romp.
I'll also say that the animation in certain points of the game is also fantastic as is the soundtrack, characters and pixel art. Very well done game overall and highly entertaining. I highly recommend giving it a shot.

"FTL" is nothing short of amazing. It is deceptively simple in look and interface, quick to play and intuitive to learn. Yet behind this classic look and simple feel is a game of incredible depth and replay value. I've put 60 hours into playing it (so far) and have been deeply absorbed every minute--which is an immense amount of stimulating entertainment per dollar of the game's unbelievably low price. Every time you beat the game and think it's time to put it away for good, you unlock a new ship with new features that keep you playing. And playing, and playing. When you're not playing, you're thinking about play or wishing you could play. Visions of different battle tactics will haunt your dreams. The minimalist but alluring soundtrack will sit in your subconscious. For fans of classic sci-fi and excellent game design, "FTL" is utterly addictive.

If you're a 4X space fan, and like gigantic space battles then this is the game for you.
With a very easy to get into interface, and fairly intuitive interface this game is good for a quick start and lengthy games. The customization options on your ships, in terms of weapons and missions, are excellent. The fact that you can take one mission module and outfit it for different roles makes it very easy to set up your fleets however you want with whatever you have available to you.
Gameplay is fairly quick, and you can set different options up for how long real time combat can take at max as well as your strategic turns time limit if you're playing a live game. Customization options are excellent when it comes to setting up games and maps. You can set up how many stars are in the game, how many players, what shape your map will take, etc. While star names will repeat from game to game, you won't ever really run into the exact same map twice.
The different races are all unique, with differing rates for certain techs, and different strengths and weaknesses between their ships and trade/money generation.
Finally, combat is by and large the best part of the game. Although you're somewhat limited by how your ships move during tactical battles (no intentional vertical movement, although ships will move up and down to avoid obstacles and other ships), the physics simulation is excellent, with a ship moving forward requiring time to stop proportionate to it's speed, and even having your ships knocked around and sometimes into planets by heavy hitting weapons. Plus, it's awesome to see a bunch of ships blast each other with volleys of missiles and plasma weapons.
Overall, this game is the♥♥♥♥♥♥ and  should be played by everyone at least once.

How do you describe a game that you love, yet you wouldn’t spend more than a few hours on? It’s like telling someone you love that you’d rather spend time apart and lust for them longingly – while cherishing the good memories you have with them – than continue being with them just to watch as the emotion fades away before you. That’s kind of how I feel about Meadow. You’ll embark on a journey and likely find others who will be your compatriots for the short and long term. Some will run off, wishing to have nothing do to with you, and others will stay for a while. But if you play long enough, say, an hour or so, you may find yourself accompanied by someone you could only call a friend. That one animal that chose to follow you through thick and thin: through the damp and muddy waters of a mundane swamp and the long swims of boring lakes; and through the bewildering cave systems and ravines with waterfalls that seem to have no end. You’ll share an experience with that animal and well, is that not what friendship is, in a sense? But again, this is no lifelong journey and it must come to an end, so, lacking any form of complex communication, you let out a few squeaks of comradery from your badger cub embodiment, and exit the game. Once you leave the meadow there is no way to find someone you have journeyed with before, so when you decide it’s over, it’s over. But you can always start again, and forge new experiences with new people that don unique animal apparels.
Overall, I think Meadow is worth a try. It’s a unique experience that I feel everyone should be exposed to.

My review for Meadow is long overdue. So I've finally decided I should probably write one.
Meadow is a social, online animal world where you communicate only through emoticons and actions. The aim is to work alongside the other animals in the Meadow to find a variety of collectibles:
Gold, blue and red shards, flowers, mushrooms and food. Shards are the main collectibles as they grant you animals, skins and new emotes.
On the subject of animals, there are currently 12 animals unlockable in the meadow. For some reason, I have seen many (recent) reviews complaining about having to buy other games to get other animals. Only 5 animals in the game currently require other games: The badger, lynx, lynx cub, bear cub and eagle. The other 7 (and any other animals added to the game in the future) are unlocked through collecting gold shards: The badger cub, frog, rabbit, goat, fox, pheasant and hedgehog are unlockable in the base game. The animals unlocked through other games are no better or worse than the ones unlocked for free, excluding the eagle, which trades its ability to collect collectibles for flight.
Ok, so obviously I have to put a few warnings forward, as much as I love the game:
. If you are around over 8 players, the lag kicks in and is pretty bad, although I've never had a game crash because of this.
. There's no tutorial whatsoever, you'll have to figure things out yourself or check the controls in settings (embarrassing secret time- I didn't know there was a pause menu until I had around 50 hours...).
. Exiting the game causes a game crash unless you go back to the den first and you can lose essence from this.
Those are really the only complaints I have about this game, Meadow is fun, social and actually quite amazing, it's like a whole language has been set up and people use different emote patterns for different meanings and create their own traditions.
Meadow does not have a chat or survival elements and the developers have stated that those will not be added, so keep in mind Meadow is not that kind of game.
The gameplay differs depending on your playstyle and that of the players around you. Meadow can be peaceful if you want to stroll around with a few buddies, or stressful if you are in a pack full of screaming goats trying to lead you in all different directions. Or maybe you could find it the other way around. Want to roleplay? There's a grove dedicated to roleplay where animals goof around or pretend to hunt one another. Basically, you and the players around you create the whole experience.
You should definately consider trying out Meadow, hopefully you will enjoy it! :D

TL;DR - The Prologue/Tutorial is worth the $24 price tag by itself! Spoilers have STRIKETHROUGH TEXT to make it harder to accidentily read.
I love Zombie games, especially when they're multiplayer compatible. After browsing the Steam Summer Sale today for a few hours, I was trying to decide between this and another game that was like $45.
I joined the subreddit, then joined the Discord for DyingLight and was greeted very warmingly. People were friendly, and answered all of my many questions about the game. This ended up in me doing a giveaway on /r/DyingLight as well and gave a copy of the game away for free.
I bought the game, and the few cosmetic DLC's that were not included in the enhanced edition, as well as convinced a friend to buy the game. I finished the prologue about 10 minutes ago and had to post this first impression review to help influence anyone's decision if they're debating on buying or not.
Visuals/Graphics
The game looks stunning. I have an i7 6700k, SLI 980TI, and an Acer XB270HU 144hz 1440p monitor. I can run this game at max settings, highest resolution, at 144FPS consistently. The feeling when running and doing parkour around the map is pretty fun. I've only experienced the first few minutes of the game so far, so I can't wait to see the other parts of the world!
Performance
Not much to say here. I have a computer more than capable of running this game, and have played very little of the game so far.
Personal Experiences
Played through the prologue and had some fun. Lost track of time and ended up ignoring some friends messages by accident. As a new player, I'm unsure how hard it is to kill the zombies with a wrench, but it took quite a few hits while on top of a car hitting the head of a zombie. Enough to scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me when I fell off of a car near a group of zombies. "The floor is lava" takes on a whole new meaning for me so far.
My first impression of night time was all I had hoped it would be. When I opened the door, it was dark and I didn't expect it. It didn't hit me that I was outside and NOT in some kind of service tunnel when I saw a barrel with a fire inside of it a few steps to my left around the corner. Then I realized I was indeed outside, and knew absolutely nothing about my surroundings. I ran about half way to my destination over the course of 3-5 minutes before I figured out I had a flashlight, which I turned on by accident. Talk about a huge sigh of relief; However, I can't quite pinpoint why it was a little scarier with the flashlight on then it was before I knew I had it.
Needless to say, The first night was easy, but that's the tutorial - It's supposed to be easy. Can't wait to see what the future holds! Hopefully my buddy will finish the prologue tomorrow morning and him and I can both play together. We plan on running the story mode together (hopefully that's possible! Pretty sure it is.)

A beautiful, poignant, yet somber game wrapped up in a short but bitterly sweet story.
The first thing that will jump out at you for this game is the visuals. Thanks to photogrammtery (photographing real world objects and then using tools to translate them into 3d objects) the game has some of the most beautiful and detailed textures in any game to date.
The game at heart is about exploration, puzzle solving, and a short but memorable storyline. You are free to explore the world however you wish from the start. The goal of finding stories or solving murders as you come across them. How and in what order you do this is entirely up to you as you roam around the landscape. There is absolutely no hand holding in this game and that makes it all the better as you figure it out on your own accord.
The few minor drawbacks for me were:
1. Invisible walls and lack of a jump button. The world, although "open" is a bit limited in scope and with the lack of a jump button you feel glued to the landscape and can't jump over short objects which you might be used to doing in many exploration games.
2. Voice acting was a mixed bag. Some characters sounded great and fit their part, others seemed out of place and a bit hammy with the line delivery/emotions.
However neither of those took away from what to me was a very enjoyable game.  The storyline was short but sweet, the graphics are some of the best in a game to date, and the overall game, although short, was well worth the price tag.
If you like adventure games with puzzles and story focused games that don't hold your hand then this game is for you.

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #46 - Diehard Dungeon
Playing Diehard Dungeon feels like reading a love letter to the original Zelda game.  And I don't mean this to accuse this game of being Zelda ripoff, but you can clearly see the inspiration.  The gameplay is very Zelda-like in how you move through dungeons and unlock new rooms while fighting various enemies.  There are also various destructible crates and other items that you can break open for loot.  Rooms often have traps, triggered by floor plates, that you have to keep an eye open for.
The art is also retro styled.  It's a bit on the dreary side, but I get that it's supposed to represent a dungeon.  Sometimes it's nice to see some color though, and not just on the loot that drops. Mostly my only complaint about the art is sometimes the background and items have a way of blending together to make it hard to tell which items are 'destructible' from already broken containers littering the floor.  This can also cover up items that you haven't picked up yet, which can be a pain because often the rooms require a key to get out, and you don't realize a key has been dropped.
I liked the music okay, and felt like it blended well with the environment and gameplay, but I can also see where it's going to start feeling repetitive.  Hopefully it changes up some after more gameplay.
Combat is pretty straightforward.  You have a melee attack with a sword, and a hand cannon.  Melee attacks work just like you'd expect.  The hand cannon takes a little more getting used to.  It shoots a cannonball and hits anything in it's path, much like firing an arrow would.  But the cannonball will bounce off of walls if there are any in it's path, meaning you might find your shot coming right back to you.   After a few seconds the cannonball explodes.
As a roguelike, the permadeath may be a bit of a turnoff.  Some roguelike games have something of a progression so that as you play you unlock things that make subsequent playthroughs easier (and thus enable even harder areas).  But this seems more like the classic roguelike where the game starts the same way each time.
My hour of play wasn't enough to get a good sense of how progression works in the game.  It was enough time to get several playthroughs, but most of them ended in the same way.  That would be making it to a boss fight with 1 or 2 hearts of health left, and then failing to kill the boss.
It seems like you are really at the mercy of the random number generator when it comes to getting life back.  I've seen some rooms that will drop 3 hearts (which at the time I didn't need), and other rooms not drop a single one (when I'm down to a single heart).  I won't go so far as to say this is Dark Souls difficult, but I definitely had a hard time making it to the boss unscathed.
I really hestiate to call this an RPG, even though it's tagged as one.  For one, there really isn't any story to speak of here.  There's no experience points or levels or classes or skills.  Also there isn't really any character customization to speak of, other than customizing your look from the main menu.  So it seems a stretch to call this an RPG.
The most unexpected part of this game was the minigames.  There are 3 minigames total, but to start with you only have access to 1, and it's called Mayhem, which is a good description.  In Mayhem you have 3 minutes to get the highest score possible, but instead of exploring a dungeon, it turns the game into a dual stick shooter.  I have to admit, I ended up having more fun with this minigame than I did the main game itself.
I still have some reservations about the long term enjoyment of this game, but I'm going to give it a lukewarm recommendation nonetheless.  For $4.99, I do think there is enough fun to be had in this game to justify the price, even if it doesn't end up keeping your attention for the long term.

I'm going to give this game a recommendation, but with a warning that it may not be for everyone.  It only takes about 5 hours to complete, maybe an hour more if you want to unlock all of the achievements, and you will see about 95% of what the game has to offer in only one playthrough.  The room puzzles are fairly simplistic - they consist of block/lever puzzles, avoiding tiles with traps, and timing your movements over grates that periodically spew fire.  There are also a few objects you need to find and bring to another location, but they are all very obvious solutions.  The controls are adequate for completing the tasks, but movement is slow, and overall a little clunky.
Thankfully, the game compensates for these shortcomings with a nice little story (think Wizard of Oz but more demented), and a cast of characters that manage to be both horrifying and charming at the same time.  The pixel art cut-scenes are lovely, and the baroque music is very evocative, although it would be nice if there was more of it.  I strongly suggest
watching the videos or looking at the screenshots, as they give away many of the most pleasant surprises.
This game is being over-shadowed at the moment by lengthier indie games with more content, but I do hope it finds its audience eventually.  It was compelling enough that I did play through to the end, which is becoming something of a rarity as my Steam library has grown to a ridiculous size.
