The Count Lucanor is a pixel survival horror game. The story focuses on a young boy named Hans who has grown tired of being poor and blames his mother for their poverty and for his father's disappearance.
So on his tenth birthday he decides to abandon his loving home in search of riches. In the woods he encounters a blue kobold that tells him he can inherit great wealth if he can overcome the trials of Count Lucanor and prove his worth. Each trial reveals a letter of the kobold's name which Hans has to piece together to reveal the kobold's name and win!
The gameplay consists of solving puzzles, avoiding traps, stealth (Hans can't kill the monsters) and using candles to illuminate the dark rooms in the castle.
Candles never run out and you have to strategically place them so you can have a clear view of your surroundings. Monsters do a lot of damage if they get you and healing items are limited so walking around blind will only lead to death. Also, to save the game you have to spend your money so you can not save every few seconds which in my opinion is a big plus in horror games.
The characters you will meet are either charming or creepy and I love their design and backstories/agency. The cutscenes are beautiful and it is hard to believe someone can create something so gorgeous using pixel art.
Your first playthrough should take you about 6 to 7 hours to complete but there are multiple endings and secrets to keep you coming back for more.
All in all, I highly recommend the game to fans of pixel horror games.

Sword of the Stars has two types of gameplay. You will spend most of your time on the galactic map, which is played as a turn-based strategy game. When your fleets engage in combat, you have the option to either auto-resolve or switch to a battle-mode which you command in real time.
The different civilizations in the game genuinely feel unique to one another, and a lot of this owes to them each having a different method of traveling through space. Humans have their hyperspace lanes, tarkas have their warp drives, and so on. This can make maintaining a border challenging, as you may be faster than your opponent(s) in some areas and completely incapable of responding in others.
This is barely scratching the surface. Sword of the Stars is a pretty complicated game, and there's only so much I can cram into a review.

This is my first SERIOUS review.
A serious review for a quite serious game.
To specify exactly where the pros and cons appear,I will divide the review into reviewing various factors in the game,in this one review.
~Gameplay~ 8/10
Once the player enters a server,using the good old Source server search,the player will be seeing a choice of 3 classes each with disadvantages and advantages.For example,the support class is very slow but with large amount of health compared to the two other classes.
The goal is simple each gamemode,obliterate the enemy(TDM),capture the flag(Capture the Ghost) etc.
The shooting is similiar to Counter Strike,only without the hip fire always on screen.This is understandable since iron sights will make the gameplay less fluid,less realistic and immersive,something this game did very well.
Two classes have the ability to turn invisible(silhouette is visible) something which will increase their chances of survival and evasion.
This game is unbalanced.My best technique of getting a lot of kills is going support and throw smoke grenades,which cannot be seen through and use the support's heat vision,which allows me to see through the smoke cloud and decimate everything that is beyond the smoke cloud.This has made me very strong and I used that technique every round to see the other team die in moments.Maybe it just me being smart,and the others not using their sight good enough,or just being all around stupid.
A thing I like very much is the way you earn XP to gain more weapons in a server,but resets if you go to another server.Every action that helps your team win(kills,assists and team capture) will earn you xp.
The lack of game modes is bearable,and I guess enough for a mod.
tl;dr-gut gempley,shooting mechanics are nicely done,very fluid.Not enough gamemodes.
~Graphics~7.5/10
Graphics look good for a game that has been around since 2004(?)(Source version came out 2009)
Your surroundings look very real and urban,making this game live up to its name.
Graphics don't matter,right?
tl;dr-grephics beyond most mods of today,very gut.
~Sound~10/10
Beautiful soundtrack which I recommend to listen to at Youtube. <3
Great sound quality,weapons sound realistic and immersive.
tl;dr-gut muzic en gut relod sound.
I think this mod has been developed for a long time(Since 2004!) and deserves more popularity,up to a game of its own,with cool gadgets,larger maps and prehaps a better engine so vehicles(which were planned) could be implemented.

This gon' be a lengthy one. If you're too lazy to read, buy the game instead and go play it. At the end of this waits an unconditional wholehearted recommendation.
XCOM is a tactical turn-based strategy game. Those used to exist in plenty supply, in the prehistoric ancient times of video gaming, also known as the 90s. It seems to me that by the year 2012 they had died a quiet and slow death, however. And then this thing comes and turns out to be the pinnacle of human achievement!
XCOM is the name of the Defense Initiative you're being put in charge of, cobbled together to combat an alien invasion of Earth. In the beginning you're dangerously underfunded and you are only given the nation's last-picks-of-the-schoolyard in terms of personnel. It's the fate of the planet after all, so why bother?
Once deployed to a mission, you and the aliens take turns in moving your soldiers around and, once visible, start massacring each other in a gripping spectacle that traditional chess has always been severly lacking. As you combat the odds of the aim percentage system, as much as the actual enemy, you lose. Soldiers, Airplanes, supporting nations, funds, faith, your will to live, the rest of your privat life ... you lose it all. This game, in its first in-game months, is nothing short of frustrating. You'll be ranting about the promissing chances the game dangled in front you, only to make you miss anyway and not follow up on 'em. If nothing else, XCOM teaches you empathy for the cat you've been tormenting with the laser pointer!
But overall, the game always stays fair. Every mishap seems to be rooted in your decisions. A soldier's (permanent) death is a result of your failed planning. And that's where they get you. As you start wondering about the 'what-if's?' and the 'why's?', you don't realise that at this moment, the drug has kicked in. From this moment on, you send your squad into the next mission, always with an additional goal in mind: Save Earth and be as efficient as possible about it. How do you mop the floor with these 1950 B-movie aliens AND don't lose a man or woman in the process this time around?
The game has flaws for sure: After the first third of the game, for instance, your soldiers will have gained enough experience and fairly rad abilities, tailored to their respective classes, to floor every level with alien corpses by the truckload. In addition, your progression through the tech research will put any military industrial complex to shame. Thus, the game loses much of its edge as time passes, ultimately disappointing at the final boss fight. Also, the levels are predesigned so if you play long enough, you'll work from memory more than strategy. Lastly, soldier customization doesn't go as far as one would wish for a game this willing to set up moments of utter heroism (or soul crushing incompetence).
All these issues were fixed in Firaxis' follow up, XCOM 2. However, out of the two titles, I'd recommend this one as the more balanced, and therefore more enjoyable, version of Awesome-Anti-Alien-Chess-5000! Pick it up. Even at full price, it's worth its salt. And if you got even more money to dole out, pick up the expansions 'enemy within' and 'slingshot' for some really weird, but profoundly enjoyable additions to the formula described above.

Great if you like RTS-style war-at-sea style combat between ships with a lot of actions per minute and lots of activatable special moves and skills.
Great if you're a huge fan of the 40K universe and don't mind a few, or many, things that just don't really fit.
Not so great if you do mind a bunch of fairly silly little things added to make the game more 'skillful' or more 'fun' with more cooldown-based abilities and random activatable skills thrown in. Personally I'm more of an immersion-first type of gamer who likes to imagine what it would really be like to command a huge starship or a few troopers or whatever, and this is just ...kinda sad sometimes.
TAUNT? Really? Since what the f when does a skill like that belong in the 40K universe? I will just arbitrarily force an enemy to come closer or focus their attacks on me? For an arbitrary time of ...wait for it - 15 SECONDS! Yaaaaay, just because.
It's a good game that most RTS fans and most 40K fans and most broadside-warship-fans will enjoy. I have some problems with it but oh well, most people won't. I base my recommendation on the general population of gamers, for those people who don't really care about small minute immersion-related issues. Because the vast majority of gamers aren't like me, and it'd be insane to design for people like me, you'd just lose money.
That said, I'm still sad at some of the more silly skills and abilities and artificial game-y constructs in the design. Other than that it's a pretty cool game and any 40K diehard will enjoy.
On second thought it seems the original games were a case of "hey, we've got this awesome cool imaginary world battles that we'd like to simulate and make a game out of". This iteration is more of "hey how can we make a game with progression and upgradeable abilties and other standard computer RTS stuff, and then kind of make it fit on top of this old 40K universe thing?" Not that they didn't make a great game, I think they did. I just don't want to play it because I don't want to game a game system. I don't want to fight an artificial-as-f UI and progression system. I want to pretend that I'm a BFG 40K commander issuing orders and fighting battles, not putting one more point into this or that in order to reduce a ...cooldown skill, wtf? It just doesn't make sense if you come from a 40K reading background.
But obviously most people playing computer games disagree with me and that's okay. The devs have to make money, so go for it. I hope it's successful and eventually I get more 40K games, some of which I'll like more than this.

I first received Shelter 2 as a gift and adored the style and gameplay. Then I was lucky enough to find this gem on sale! The beautiful combination of M&D's unique artwork and altruistic/nonviolent/ team-based collect-a-thon gameplay is the most calming thing I have ever played. Very easy to pick up, at least for me.
WARNING!!: I would recommend this game to nearly EVERYONE, regardlesss of typical interest, unless they get nauseous easily via visual stimulation. Tried to get a friend to play it and he got a small headache due to the busy art style, then slightly dizzy after an hour.
GAMEPLAY:
There are 10 (I think) animals to unlock, starting with baby badger, and working to unlock frog, rabbit, pheasant, goat, and hedgehog, and owning other M&D games to get mama badger, mama and baby lynx, and bear cub. The eagle can only be played whilst you occupy a top 100 position in the game (spots determined by essence).
You run around collecting sparkly flowers and shrooms to gain essence, which is really only for rank. Find some friends and break relics together to gain shards of essence: Yellow for unlocking animals, Pink for unlocking emotes, Blue for unlocking skins. All can be found around the map randomly. Yellow appear most commonly from relics, pink are plentifully scattered throughout the map, and blue are in relics but appear less frequently than other types.
There are several skins and voices for each character that can help distinguish who is who in-game and make it more fun to play as what you like--though I would love if there were new animals in future updates HINT HINT.
In order to break open ruins (big dark tall rocks with little diamonds and symbols on the front) you need at least 1 other person, but larger groups get larger relics and bigger payout. You always have the option of tracking down herds with the map and joining them. However, even when there are over a dozen people in a server (I usually play East U.S.), it can be difficult to form a group simply because people aren't good at staying together, are new/confused, or don't know how to communicate. So it often takes a while just to find/form a decent herd unless you have a STEAM friends group.
Now I deeply appreciate the method of communication in Meadow using symbols and emotes, but there are plenty of gaps. It is fantastic because it is literally impossible for anyone to be rude, crude, or a troll. It is also great for younger (and all)  players because it forces you to think outside-the box and "decode" the symbols and combinations of symbols in order to understand and convey what you need to to play most efficiently. It is active communication. However, there is no way to help people figure out controls when they start (unless they did their research). Even when you use the little "group" symbol to ask if someone will travel with you, I have come across many players who do not know that it means and end up running off randomly. [Some of these people were even rabbits, so it made me wonder how on earth they made it that far without decent communication.]
GRIND:
After unlocking all the animals it becomes a pretty tedious grind to gain skins in between bouts of having a decent herd.
_________    ________
I have only had the game for a couple weeks, but unlocked all the in-game unlockable species by my third play, which probably took less than 8 hours, but ya never know since there are always times where groups are scarce. I also have the mama badger and lynx from the Shelter games. But since unlocking everything I care to, I have been working towards collecting all the skins for the animals. It is a bit *underwhelming* to work for hours searching with a herd for relics and getting mostly yellow pieces that don't really benefit me or many other players anymore. I have found that yellow essence is most common, probably because devs figured people would be too antsy about getting all the species, but that collection completed too quickly in my opinion. I'm not sure if others share my experience, but I think making all the types equally available, or at least blues equal to yellows, would be nice. I will get waaay more hours in this game regardless of how many _____s I have unlocked, but this grind is a bit much for what it is. Since blue shards are so rare, either more relic spawns or more balanced type occurence would be a fix.
It would also be amazing if another map was released later on. Perhaps even an easy way to find Meadow herd members out-of-game, like having their STEAM name appear when you toggle over their character.

Meadow is a calm, visually appealing cooperative mmo.
I was expecting a chill, walk-around short of mmo (which it can be) but it actually has gameplay. (I wouldn't call it "a forum in game's clothing" though)
Pros:
-Gameplay is cooperative, not competitive. No fighting whatsoever.
-Communication is done solely through actions, animal cries, emotes and signals. You don't have to worry about nazis trying to convert you or people caps-locking swear words at you here.
-Keeps the same visual style of the other shelter games - well-constructed naturalistic environments, soft colors, and Might And Delight's trademark pattern textures.
-Large map(s), lots of exploring to do even if you're alone
-Rewards you for owning the other games (which you should definitely try), but most of the species and their respective variations come with the base game.
-Being part of a pack/herd just makes me feel happy. It's like a little, temporary family.
-Animals. Cute animals
-Very cheap
Cons:
-Poorly optimized - 10+ animals at once creates huge lag on high settings (in comparison, I can play Fallout 4 on high and The Witcher 3 on medium). When you exit the game or select "go back to den" the game freezes for a time. I always have to force-exit the game.
-Camera bothers me, but I don't know why, so maybe that's just me.
-Jumps are pretty finicky, if you don't time it right you have to kind of rub against the wall as you jump until you reach the top.
-Can't progress without at least one other player. Thankfully they're easy to find and people are very helpful and kind, usually waiting for the whole pack before moving on. (Also you can just walk around alone if you don't care about unlocking species and fur patterns)
-I jumped off the edge of the world and fell through the void for a full minute

Braid is a brilliant and innovative 2D puzzle platformer.
The main character has the power to rewind time and this is used in novel ways in almost all the puzzles. Additionally, each world has a unique mechanic that alters the gameplay in one way or another.
The puzzles themselves are typically quite clever and well-designed. The first few worlds are reasonably easy, but the difficulty ramps up pretty quickly and by the end of the game you are facing puzzles that feel nearly impossible until you figure them out.
The hand-drawn art is gorgeous and the beautiful soundtrack is a great fit for the game too. The only thing I didn't particularly like was the rather pretentious story.
Overall Braid is one of the best puzzle games ever made and easy to recommend to any fans of the genre. However, the game does have some rather difficult puzzles, so if you are not very good at puzzle solving Braid can get rather tedious and frustrating.
I did get stuck on a couple of puzzles for a while, but in general the difficulty level was pretty much spot on for me.
The good:
- Innovative time manipulation mechanics
- Clever and well-designed puzzles
- Gorgeous hand-drawn art
- Nice soundtrack
- Good level of challenge
The bad:
- Pretentious story and writing

I'm certain that there are quite a few people who will call The Vanishing of Ethan Carter a boring and pointless walking simulator. Well, they are partially correct.
The Vanishing is not exactly what I would call a game. It's more like... an experience. If I had to name a similar “game”, it would be Dear Esther.
Don't expect to run around and kill things here. What you will do is walk around and investigate the disappearance of a boy called Ethan Carter. You will solve some puzzles, find some "hidden" objects etc. Now... I'm not sure, but it may be possible to “finish” the game without solving anything, so far I have looked into every corner of the Valley I laid my eyes upon, found a few “secrets”, solved every puzzle and I'm not done yet, though I guess I'm not far now from the end.
The game has absolutely phenomenal atmosphere. There is a sense of calmness but also you have a feeling that something is not right, and it might not be a good idea to stick around. That atmosphere is built by impossibly pretty visuals. Graphics are... let's just say: I made quite a few wallpapers for myself during very first minutes of the game.
Apart from visuals the sound is also 1st class. Ambient sounds of the forest are very realistic, other places have their own specific ambiance. Also music fits the game perfectly: it is there, you are aware of it, but it's not too intrusive. Also it changes depending on your location.
And there is the voice acting. The main character is perfectly calm, a bit bored detective who just wants to finish the job and go home. Other characters are voiced maybe not as well, but still I can't complain.
Overall visuals and sounds are great.
As for not so grand things:
Save system is not good. Auto saves are rare and far between, there is no manual save, if you exit the game you loose everything since last save, and sometimes it's not easy to know if you will loose 2 minutes or half an hour. That being said, Game now downloads a patch that is going to improve that, so this point may not be very valid.
And... well, that's it really.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is not a long game that should be treated as an experience rather than an adventure. Fans of Dear Esther will love it. Fans of Call of Duty... won't. I'm the former.

Just finished The Vanishing of Ethan Carter
This game is a game in the mystery genre, some say it's a horror game, but there is really only one part of the
game that scared me, quite a lot actually. That certain place made me wanna quit the game, and when I actually had to return to it after finished all the other puzzles I had to be brave!
Anyway, the game has two different mechanics, one is to solve these murder cases, you get to find the murder object, how the murder happened, and so on. You also get to point out the chronology of the murder, one example: Did he lose his legs before or after he was hit in the head?
That mechanic alone is quite unique in gaming, at least if you compare it to similar games I've played.
The other mechanic is more puzzle solving, some harder than others, one was particulary easy, too easy.
But the cool thing with these puzzles is that they reward us with more details of the story and also visually stunning places, also here some more than others. That particular easy puzzle rewarded us with one of the coolest settings in the game. The story of the game is very mysterious and you are throughout the game thinking "Where is this taking me? Who am I? How am I related to all this?"
And that is good, and do the story answer these questions? Yeah, sure.
Am I happy with it? Yeah, sure... I mean, it could have been a lot better, but it was still good.
And now to the visuals, wow.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is one of the most beautiful games I've played, it's the most beautiful game I've
played that runs on the Unreal Engine 3.
Overall this is a game like Dear Esther, but with game mechanics.
Some unique ones, some not so unique. I was happy with my purchase of this game even though I think
it could have been a bit longer than four hours.
My verdict is 7.5/10

An absolutely beautiful game, but not for everyone.
It took me around 4 hours to complete the game, finishing the side stories and finding everything the game required me to find.
The puzzles are fairly simple, often requiring trial and error to find the correct order for something, or simply having to follow the obvious clues and find all the required items.
However, the beauty comes in piecing together the story and exploring the surroundings.
Keep in mind that this is a narative driven adventure title, so the major focus is on soaking in the atmosphere and enjoying the story that you are experiencing.
If you are a fan of games like Dear Esther, then you will enjoy this (it is both visually and naratively similar to Dear Esther), if you like games like Amnesia then you may get some mild enjoyment out of playing this (it has a similar atmosphere, but does not focus too much on scaring the player, there is maybe only 1 section of the game that could make you jump and it is very mild).
If you're expecting a lengthy game with difficult puzzles and difficult gameplay, you will come away dissappointed.
Ultimately, as with Dear Esther, there is little need to replay the game upon completion unless you just want to enjoy the experience again.

Dying Light is a great game but with flaws that nearly ruined the game for me.
Keep in mind that I play on Hard mode so maybe this is me being bad, maybe not.
Pros:
-I love the free running aspect. The entire platforming is fun and there are nearly limitless options on how to run and get wherever.
-The level up system is fairly decent as for the power/agility trees. I'll get to the survival tree in a minute on why I have my personal struggles.
-The side quests of the game are pretty interesting and I tend to enjoy them.
-The environments are actually well designed, and I feel like the developers actually ENJOYED putting together every building, every zombie, just about everything.
-Playing with friends is intensely fun. Not gonna die it for a second.
-Night time feels like it should. Intense, frightening, all about where to run and where to hide. It truly is an enjoyable but horrific time. Good on you game.
-Zombies feel like zombies. Granted in a one-on-one scenario I should kill them easier, butttttttttttt I'll skip that for now cause I am on hard mode.
Cons:
-Combat is so clunky sometimes it hurts. I can't tell you how many times I meant to dropkick a zombie but jumped off them in a pathetic attempt and had to reset my entire setup.
-I thought Dark Souls punished players, but I was wrong. This game takes away survivor points every time you die, and there are a fair amount of cheap deaths. Mainly bombers in close areas when turning a corner. you lose the resources you used as well, but thankfully, the zombies retain the damage. But holy ♥♥♥♥ I have died so many times that survivor points became a delicacy as it became increasingly hard to earn them. They take away so many points each death that it feels like a stab to the stomach instead of a slap on the wrist.
-The humans dare I say are absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. They have the health of Panzer tanks and have the damage output of one as well. Where it takes me 7-8-9 shots to kill one of them, it takes them maybe 3-4 shots. And yes I know headshots are a 1 shot, I have hit quite a few in my day. But that doesn't excuse any of the deaths to human enemies I have had.
-The story is sub-par at best SO FAR. Upon beating the game, I will possibly change this portion of the review.
-Multiplayer WOULD be good if the matchmaking wasn't very...bizarre toppled with I'm assuming what is hacker as he gave me 3 stacks of 99x healthpacks. I wish I was joking. The Hunter multiplayer if solo fighting the Night Hunter (or whatever the hell the thing is called) feels dragged out and sometimes just too unfair. With 2 players though, it finally becomes a possibility. Not saying you can't win solo, I have, but damn is it hard.
-This is probably going to be my biggest gripe ever but here it goes. No bars, nothing to hold me back. The boss battles are ♥♥♥♥ing awful. They are legit the worst ♥♥♥♥ing things I have experienced in a game since Deus Ex: Human Revolution, only difference is DE:HR knew to keep some things correct. I'll say it here, taking away all my equipment and forcing me to fight a boss with a single weapon makes it feel almost like all those hours I spent gathering and looking for items was wasted for the large upcoming battle. Now again I haven't finished the story so FOR ALL I KNOW THIS MAY CHANGE. But in the first two battles I had my items stripped from me. First time was fine, it was made to fit the story. Second time, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Nothing would make me just magically *blip zoop beep boop* and lose my items. Lemme use my ♥♥♥♥ing gear, Dying Light.
-Sometimes controls feel clunky in the sense of they don't work like they should, but this game is so massive that I will give this one some slight relief on this complaint.
TL;DR version:
Dying Light is a game worth it when on sale, but for 60 bucks I have a little struggle recommending it. Still, I will admit it is one of the best zombie games I have played in quite a while.
Hope you enjoy the review and have a nice day.

I do not like this game.  I've tried, but something is wrong when the tutorial level has enemies with WAY too much health.  A tutorial level should help the player get adjusted to the game, and, in a sense, I suppose ANR's (A New Reckoning) tutorial level is no different.  You start by phasing through a bus door, the bus is surrounded by police cars, (which are not to appropriate scale to the character), and are greeted by floating text blocks which give you a run down how to select the 'teleport' spell and use it.  As of this writing, the UI is little more than text (I hope they get a rudimentary iconic UI up soon, as the text is dull and quite ugly, maybe a spell selection wheel with spells that are not available grey'd out.)
After learning to teleport, you are invited into a building that opens the way to the rest of the map.  It is largely a walking simulator at this point, where you can marvel at indoor street lamps (the kind you see on the streets, generally not indoors), snow on the floor (though it has no way to get there), and some bushes curiously growing out of the snow.  After teleporting to the other side of a fence, I am attacked by a demon-thingy.  Simple affair, bullets, death, move on.
After destroying the demon dog thingy, I am then accosted by a flaming spider of significant size.  As I fight it, it poops out smaller, not flaming spiders every time it teleports near me.  If you ignore the smaller spiders, they become a life syphon, and eat all your health.  I found myself unloading an entire clip just to get rid of one of the spiders.  Circle strafing and typical FPS skills don't count here, as the baby spiders stick to you like glue.  I died.  Quick.
Trying again, I teleported up to the rafters in the building, so while the baby spiders couldn't reach me, I couldn't get any health pickups, and quickly ran out of ammo and spell juice.  I lobbed a couple fireballs at them, taking down two or three at a time, only to have flaming titan spider pop back next to me and poop out more.  I dropped back to the ground, and picked up the health pickups, and ammo, and was swarmed.  I died.  Again.  On a tutorial level.  No matter HOW GOOd or BAD a player is, they should NEVER fail on a tutorial level.  And if they do fail, they should be allowed to try whatever they are trying to do again, without having to be dropped back to the intro screen, or text, or whatever.
Right now, the game plays like a bare bones Unreal game, without, well, the fun.  If you are thinking about getting this game, I would suggest not, but if you do, at least wait until:
1.)  It's closer to completion
2.)  It's on sale for really, really, really cheap
or
3.)  Know what you are getting yourself into.
It's not good, even for early access, not at this point, anyway.  And believe me, I am a huge Early Access supporter.  I have many Early Access titles.  The congative dissonance I've witnessed from the developer in the forums (like those who do not like the game being called "trolls") is another turn off for me, and reminds me of a great quote I once read:
"If one person has a problem with you, it's likely their fault.  If two people have a problem with you, I can still give you the benefit of the doubt.  But if three or more people have a problem with you, the problem probably lies with you."
A vast majority of the reviews, even for an early access game, seem pretty negative for this title.  Many games that are early access, if their supporters see potential in the game, regardless of the bugs or lack of polish (Look at The Forest, or Dead State, or Dungeon of the Endless, or 7 Days to Die, etc etc) they will still net largely positive reviews.  That says something, doesn't it?

This game is all about fun skirmish battles. I enjoy it quite a bit. It has just enough customizablity to give me a sense of being able to fight the way I want to, while maintaining distinct strengths and weaknesses among factions.
It is a decent real time adaptation of the tabletop wargame it was based on.
The Devs do patches and bug fixes every two weeks, and while they aren't at the top of the "responsiveness" charts, they are active on the forums. The official forums even includes a stickied thread in which one of the Devs will come on and answer any posted questions about understanding the game's mechancics (and to tell really bad jokes).
One of the best things, in my opinion, is that the game is not sticking everyone into a set, boring, tacticless, mindless brawl. There are numerous ways to fight with any given fleet, and very often cunning can win the day over brute strength. It very much allows a player to outsmart an enemy, and win matches in some very unorthodox ways.
The game is very young though, and it's issues are still being worked out.
While some factions are fairly solidly put together, others like the Orks, seem to be stuck on Nerf/Buff pendulum that can't quite find the right spot and always takes things too far in either direction. You know, nothing we all haven't seen in so many other multiplayer games before.
The Other major problem is matchmaking. Like most games, this one's matchmaking program starts a narrow search for a partner matching your own rankings. If it can't fidn one, it expands the search. Due to the game's current low population, this results in some unfair matchups. Many solutions have been proposed, but this is one that we don't hear much back from the developer's about.
Despite those problems, the game is fun. It also has one ofther upside: It uses Unreal 4 engine, which means that those whith the knowhow can mod it. Some of the mods I have seen look fantasic and enhance the game a great deal. I highly reccomend checking out mods until th e game is just right for you (kinda like we all do with skyrim and fallout 4).

I'm a big fan of UFO: Enemy Unknown (the original). I spent countless of hours playing this game. We used to go to my house or to a friends house and play till our parents would lose it, lol. The original UFO is an incredible game with a lot of depth. When comparing old and new, people are often blaming critics of the new version that they are overwhelmed by melancholia and are thus idealizing the original. While this might be true to some extent, I'm convinced the old game, given the standards back then and now, is superior in terms of mechanics, story and athmosphere.
The biggest gripe that I have against the remake is the lack of action points. The way action points were implemented in the old game was simple but effective. It gave you the opportunity to combine many actions in one turn, provided that you had the action points. Apart from the action points, where were many other score points that determined accuracy, resistance to mind control, resistance to panic attacks, ability to carry heavy loads, ability to interrupt the enemy turn etc. In the remake, this has been replaced by perks that you can chose from. The idea is very good but why remove the action points alltogether? Why not implement these abilities on top of the action point system? The combination of both would've been a huge improvement over the old system and would've given the remake a lot of addition depth that it lacks compared to the original.
Another thing that I didn't like in the remake was the athmosphere and the art direction. The old game was built around the whole alien grey conspiracy urban myth. The guys that wrote the story took the most interesting aspects of the conspiracy theory and implemented it in the game. Element 115 is used as fuel for the alien ships (Bob Lazar), alien abductions, mind control, alien underground bases etc. The story was interesting. In the remake we have alien greys that seemingly know karate. They seem agile as *beep*. Cartoony guys in suits jump around like I'm in some sort of kung-fu movie, later they turn out to be aliens but that doesn't make it any better. The night missions are a joke. The night missions in the original were terrifying. You had to throw chem-lights to illuminate hard to see areas. That tactical element is gone in the remake.
Overall, the new XCOM: Eenemy Unknown isn't a bad game, it's actually quite fun to play. But I feel that it lacks depth compared to the original game. There's a strategic element in chosing the right perks and positioning your soldiers properly but there's a certain degree of freedom that is missing because they've removed the action points system.

This is more than just a game. It's an experience!
I was kinda sceptical at first because it seemed so simple, but exactly that makes this game so unique.
Here a "quick" summary of my experience with the game so far:
I was set as a young badger cub into the world. The first 10 minutes I wandered around aimlessly, not knowing what exactly I should do now. Then I encountered another fellow badger. We quickly became friends. We only squeaked at each other and used simple "caveman-like" signs to communicate and yet it felt like each of us knew exactly what we were trying to tell each other.
After about 20 minutes of collecting plants and exploring the woods we met another friendly creature. A white bear cub. It seemed to be more experienced than us, since it showed us how to gather more herbs and treasures that I would later use to reskin myself, get new emotes and even unlock new creatures.
We kept exploring for a long while and I felt a connection building up to my new two friends. I noticed that especially after our badger friend lost track of us and we split apart. Soon though we would meet a large group of hawks, bunnies and two lynx cubs we decided to join. It was almost painful to shut down the game later, because you knew exactly that you would never meet these nice fellows again.
To make it short: Meadow is a lovely game with an unique art style and the same flair as its sister games "Shelter" and "Shelter 2". A wonderful way to communicate with others and explore the extents of your social skills in a unique way.
The only con there is, is that it runs very laggy, even on low settings. This takes away a lot of the games atmosphere.
I don't have the fastest computer, but I would definetely expect it to run a game like Meadow. Especially since my PC meets the minimum requirements.
9/10

Meadow is probably the most special, most interesting mmo(rpg?) I have played for quite some time.
Often when the game mmo is mentioned you think of grind, progression systems and interactivity between players over a longer extension of time.
Meadow is a bit different. You can progress through the game to unlock a few different animals play as but yeah, you play as actual animals! (?)
So what do you do? You pick flowers for once, eat fruit, explore the world and crack open relics with the help of other animals in the world.
It is an extremely family/kid friendly game.
But here is the stinger, when you meet other animals they all are other players.
Like another game that was released on the Playstation 3/4 called Journey you lack the ability to properly chat with other players (wether it being text or voice).
Although, here in Meadow you have way of communication: emotes, symbols and cries.
This surely makes this game unique, since you cannot properly tell other players where to go- even if you know where stuff spawns.
Some times you can see a flock of animals roaming the lands, join them and see where they take you or if you manage to- take lead of the pack yourself.
This kind of communication in the game removes all language barriers, which is something when you think about it- is awesome!
I remember when there was this flood of chinese players coming into the game since someone over there had been speaking of the game in social media.
They all had cool symbols for names I could not read, but with the symbols and emotes in the game I could properly play the game with someone while lacking the understanding of their own language.
It also an extremely relaxing game to play after a stressful day, pick some flowers, meet up with other players and explore the world!
In my opinion this is a game worth more than it's asking price, but it surely a special game.
A special game, which will hold it's place in my heart.

It's strange because in theory this is exactly my type of game, but I just wasn't feeling it. I found it far too difficult, to the point where it was so difficult it just wasn't fun at all. Most of the puzzle solutions felt like exploits rather than solutions. Which I think I'd be OK with if the game wasn't real-time with penalty for failure. All of the different time-based gameplay mechanics were interesting and playing around with their implementations was pretty cool, and the puzzles were extremely well-designed - this game is a classic example of introducing some reasonably simple mechanic and then wringing every last gameplay idea out of it just like Nintendo is pretty good at. Only problem is that it just wasn't actually fun.
I thought the graphics were... bad (I've never seen something that looked like it was drawn in MS Paint AND looked horribly blurry before), and the music was annoying (not the fault of the music per se but just the fact that it's bound to be annoying when you're constantly rewinding it, pausing it, speeding it up, slowing it down...). The "story" was unintelligible garbage like Hotline Miami - there's metaphorical and then there's just noise.
I suppose if you come at this game with the idea that the only thing you want is a sequence of increasingly difficult real-time puzzles, and you're happy that the game will give you absolutely nothing except those puzzles, and you don't already have a headache, you could enjoy it just fine. But silly me, I tried to pay attention to the story, I expected low-stress areas between high-stress areas, I expected the game to explain its mechanics to me (don't need to explain everything, but the arbitrary/esoteric corner cases of the less obvious abilities, that are necessary for progression? yes), and I already had a headache when I started.

It's indie. The most indie. It's respectable, sure. But was it really worth my time? Eh.
Standard puzzle game with platforming elements. Braid is charming in its aesthetic; that's for sure. Classical music plays as you traverse levels filled watercolored backdrops. It has the presentation down, yeah, but its a shame that the rest of the game really doesn't hold up to my standards.
A puzzle game lives or dies on its difficulty curve. If puzzles are set up logically, with difficulty that builds over time, then that's standard. However, Braid introduces new mechanics, and then immediately expects you apply these mechanics in extraordinary ways. The game will typically give you one dead simple level, and then dumps you into a level where you need to apply something uncommonly or use a trick to get through. No thanks. And while I'm ragging on level design, something feels off about this. Levels are usually longer affairs, with several different separate puzzle compartments. This feeling is exacerbated the longer the game goes on. Really, the idea of having levels as a sort of divider seems more natural and cohesive to me. If puzzles have nothing to do with eachother except that the same mechanics are being used, then why shove them on the same map? I'm not entirely sure what the intent was.
I'll be more blunt, Braid is a time waster. Every puzzle in Braid could probably be solved by anyone if they were given enough time to mess around with it. The amount of time you need to waste to get through would vary though. I simply don't have the patience to just waste time until I somehow solve the puzzle. Trying things until you have the solution is not logical. There is no process, the way I see it. There are just some things the game expects you to know. In a game like Dark Souls, that might be passable, but this has no excuses. If a puzzle game doesn't lay itself out in a logical way, there isn't any way to complete it without a walkthrough, or an excess of time to burn. That's a no-no.
I guess I'm more lukewarm on this because I've played more interesting puzzle games that feel like less of a waste. The aesthetic is nice, but can we really justify the puzzles when flash games have been around for so much longer? I guess that's my biggest complaint. This entire thing feels like a flash game I had to pay money for. It's older, sure. But like I said, that doesn't hold water when older games did the genre more justice. The Prince of Persia time mechanics are cool and all, but they don't exactly hold the game up on their own. Later mechanics feel even worse when they begin piling on top of eachother. Unless you got the time to burn, you'll probably end up looking up a walkthrough.
Speaking of wasting time, I'll mention the books in the clouds. There's several in every room before the start of each world. I felt robbed, because functionally, these books are worthless. Sure, they provide some color to the game, but anyone who's beaten the game will agree that they're really pointless fluff; akin to books found in the Elder Scrolls games. I'd recommend just ignoring them entirely or just being savvy of intentional misdirection by the game developer. Thanks.
What else is there to say. Fairly standard puzzling, with a neat little aesthetic. It's ok for what it's worth, sure. I wouldn't exactly call it time well spent. That ending really sealed the deal for me. Instead of making the twist too obvious, Braid decides to lead you on, and then completely switches on you last level. And all this to one of the most played out twists in the book. There are better puzzle games.

I play a lot of rogue-like games, and some I fall in love with, while others either don't hold my interest, or worse, annoy me and get deleted. Diehard Dungeon is one of the few that I really love.
I'm not a fan of 8-bit style anymore, but it works well for this game. Sometimes the screen does get cluttered and you accidently step on a pressure plate, triggering a trap, but you learn how to watch out for things like that.
You have a loot chest (like a mimic) who follows you around and collects the treasure, leveling up when it gains enough. At higher levels, the chest will gain ranged attacks and join you in fights. But there are also little imps who only attack the chest, and prevents the chest from collecting any loot while it's being chased around the room.
The games difficulty adjusts with your success or failure, so you always get a suitable challenge. It took me 6 attempts before I first escaped the dungeon, and it unlocked optional champions who wander the edge of the dungeon on top of the walls and jump down to attack you... all while you are dealing with the regular room stuff like traps, monsters, etc.
The game has a large variety of perks you can gain through a single dungeon delve and the ones you find are randomized. In one game, I gained the ability to hide in my loot chest, so monsters wouldn't be able to find me. Great if you need a breather and accidently bite off too many monsters at once. Other times I'm gained throwing knives, or flame resistance. All of them offer different ways to play the game, so it always keeps it fresh and interesting.
Overall, I think this is the first rogue-like game in a long while with enough variety to keep me coming back time after time. Highly recommended.

Randomly generated Zelda dungeons, but all combat and no puzzles or exploration (you can't go back to a previous dungeon room, it's just one long gauntlet). If you really love classic topdown Zelda combat, you could get something out of it. Still, you're probably better off with Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, since this game is just a less fun version of that.
Other things that suck about this game:
-The powerups you get are all really minor and inexplicably rare.
-Really awful graphics. Blocky 16-bit sprites can look great, but this is muddy and ugly.
-The ranged weapon they give you highly discourages actually fighting enemies, since you can plink at them forever and not risk taking damage. This is boring.
To its credit, the game does the following well:
-Good difficulty curve. Tough but almost always fair, you can generally learn from your mistakes.
-"Champion" mechanic where your character can screw with other people's games after you beat it once. AI controlled, so this is more just a "oh, that's cute" thing than really interesting or annoying - it basically just puts your name over an ingame monster.
-The combat itself is fairly solid, if you don't just hang back and shoot at enemies 1 damage at a time.
This one is up to you. Personally, I won't be playing any more of it, but like I said, if you're super into Zelda combat, go for it. Either way, though, play Binding of Isaac: Rebirth.

Diehard Dungeon is a homage to the dungeon crawlers of old, mixed with some new, combined into a retro styled game that is not only aptly named but also a lot of fun to play.
Diehard Dungeon has you making your way though a series of dungeons, collecting gold keys and fighting various monsters and other enemies in an ultimate search for loot and glory.  It has a surprisingly large amount of depth for a game with no story, and oddly enough, has a mini-game included that is almost worth the purchase price alone.
The game starts you off alone, in a dungeon with nothing.  You quickly find your sword and a few stages later the Companion Chest. The Companion Chest stores your treasure (you never actually access it though) and will even help you fight your way through the dungeon.  Upon your first boss battle you will also pick up a hand-cannon, which is literally, a handgun that shoots cannon balls.  These make up your primary combat abilities in the game, with your sword being the focus ultimately. At the core, Diehard Dungeon is a hack and slash, but positioning yourself properly against certain foes is still important, as is proper use of the hand-cannon.  As one might expect, with such a simple combat system the controls are also pretty simple.
Speaking of abilities, rather than leveling up and using experience points or any system like that; Diehard Dungeon simply has you find or win extra abilities. You can find them in chests that operate like slot machines, a mini “trap-door” game or just laying on the ground. These range from becoming fireproof, adding shrapnel to your hand-cannon or as suggested before, an ability that allows you to kill everything on screen in exchange for one heart of life by pressing B.  These abilities are random and make all the difference in your ability to make it through the dungeon in one piece.  This makes finding and collecting the abilities incredibly important, but also leads to one of the main downsides to the game.
While Diehard Dungeon is a blast to play, the name is very appropriate. The game uses a simple “heart” system of health, where each hit takes one away and you can add more (if you find some) along the way.  That said, when you die, there is no check point; you don’t go back to the beginning of that dungeon room with all that you had when you got there; no, you go back, all the way back. To the beginning. With nothing. While this certainly makes death a big deal, it is frustrating when you seem to have a fairly decent start but then a really tough middle-range area in the game.  Basically, if you get overwhelmed in a single room (which happened to me on a couple of occasions) you drop all of your progress from the last half hour and start over again; something made even more possible by the fact health can sometimes be quite rare.  Does it add more weight to your death? Absolutely. Does it make you fight that much harder to not die? Of course. Does it make you absolutely want to stop playing the game for a few minutes after? You bet your♥♥♥♥♥it does.
Luckily the game does offer another mode of play to distract you for a bit while you let the anger inside you dissipate.  The mini-game “Mayhem” is not only fun, it comes close to overshadowing the main game. Who would have guess that built within a dungeon crawler would be one of the better twin-stick shooters on the XBLIG service?  Mayhem has you playing as the Companion Chest in a room that quickly fills with enemies.  The goal is ultimately to get as high of a score as possible in only three minutes, but the “gimmick” is that your score multiplier only goes up if you don’t get hit.  It is, simply put; a blast and you will strive to reach higher and higher on the leaderboard (I managed to take first place for an evening).  The one downside to this mode is that quite often it seemed I was “being hit’ when there was no conceivable way that I actually was (unless the game punishes you for standing still).  I was clearly not near any enemies (or crates) yet felt my controller vibrate like I was hit and saw that my multiplier had gone down as well.  I’m assuming there was a reason for it that I just didn’t realize, but for the life of me I don’t know what it was.
Back to the main game, there is one other… issue that soured Diehard Dungeon’s experience.  Despite playing through the game well (well? I kicked♥♥♥♥♥ and killing everything in sight and breaking every crate open, I still made it to what I presume is the end of the game without enough golden keys to open the giant chest at the end; so I died and lost anyway.  Looking at the developer’s website, “gold key rarity” is something that is planned to be patched in an updating coming any day now, so this is hopefully a non-issue going forward but it was incredibly frustrating to have gotten to the end and still lost because the game simply didn’t generate enough of a crucial item.
Death resetting everything is rough, but it is part of the game and what makes it work (even if you kind of hate it in the moment).  A lack of a crucial item that makes an otherwise successful run a waste of time though is very, very close to being a deal breaker. Luckily for Diehard Dungeon, it was fun getting to that point and the mini-game Mayhem compensates for this oversight.  Hopefully the patch will fix it, along with a lot of other changes coming soon as the patch is approved, but it is enough to take a great game and knock it down from where it should be; for now anyway.

Having never played the original Metro 2033--although interestingly enough its in my library, I figured I would give this a try. I have always been a fan of survival horror and this one looked good, and the price was right, so I figured why not.
Now first off, I have seen a lot of negative reviews associated with crashing. I'm not sure if this was an issue with a previous patched version or not, but I played this game straight through without any crashing whatsoever. So its entirely possible that these issues no longer exist.
First the game starts out pretty quickly trying to get you familiar with all the differnt buttons this game uses, and its a lot. I wonder whatever happened to the games that only required two or three buttons maximum. Spending my youth in the 80's I played a lot of NES and and later Genesis, and it seems crazy how far we come and how many buttons are required now in a fighting/FPS style game.
The story seems to revolve around your character trying to get from point A to point B in a world that exists post-world war three. Most of the story takes place underground in Russia's metro stations which have now become a refuge for the survivors of the war. Here they have adapted to living underground and only visit the surface if a need arises, as its contaminated with radioactivity and poisonous air.
But the world isn't all it seems, there are monsters all around, what might be life that has adapted in this new cruel world. It doesn't really say, and I know this is based on a book, although I've never read that either.
Now the story is well, pretty damn awesome, and the game really does make you feel like you are in the drivers seat, literally sometimes as you mount rail cars and other contraptions that allow you to freely move within the metro tunnels. From station to station you run into different characters who either help you or well, don't and what sets this apart from other FPS games is the ability to not engage in combat if you choose to. You have a limited supply of weapons, ammo, gas mask filters and other things you need just to survive, and so it makes sense that choosing to hide in the shadows and conserve your ammo as you stealth through a level can not only be helpful but sometimes necessary.
What I really loved about this game is that stealth element. I found myself sneaking about trying not to get caught and sometimes crouching behind someone to stab them in the back. Why this work really comes down to the nature of the environment you are in. You are sneaking about deep underground tunnels sometimes with barely any lighting, you can play as careful as you want. I did find myself trying to hide often but after a while, I sometimes just went balls deep and started unloading on people. This was especially true against the nazis who at times felt like they were multiplying on me like gremlins or something.
Now there are a few things I didn't like. I kept getting lost, this happened to me a lot. Sometimes I don't mind so much, especially in games with a map, but this one doesn't have that and at times its just a big open space with lots of little tunnels and things you need to navigate. They do give you a compass which sort of points you in the right direction.
I also didn't like the first moment during the tutorial when you enter the room with the grates on the walls and you have no weapon to start. I found myself running around like a chicken with his head cut off as the monsters chased me about. I finally found a revolver that was sitting there, but in the heat of the moment a nice arrow or something to tell me where it was would have been nice. After all this was the tutorial part of the game.
Sometimes someone wants you to do something, but they only say it one time, and then there isnt any kind of log to help you remember what they wanted. So sometimes I just found myself ignoring them and pushing ahead.
Overall this game was pretty awesome.

Overall opinion: a must-have for anyone who is a fan of 40K or looking for a strategic naval warfare expereince...IN SPACE!
Disclaimer: I've only played against the AI so far (which on Normal offers a significant but satisfying challenge to beginners)
Regarding the races: I have played Imperial Navy, Orks, and Space Marines so far. The Navy is great for starting out; tough ships, lots of firepower, pretty forgiving if you make a mistake (lol, unlike the Imperium itself!).
Orks are always fun; they focus heavily on getting close enough for their guns to reliably connect and ramming. You can outfit your Line Ships (the medium-sized vessels that form the backbone of your fleet) to be one of four major Ork Clans (Evil Sunz, Goffs, Blood Axes, and Bad Moonz. Sorry, Death Skullz...), each giving different benefits and ablities. You can mix-and-match to create an all-inclusive WAAAGH! or one huge singular fleet and set out to prove that your Clan is the Meanest.
Don't let negative views on the Space Marines deter you. They may need some tweaking, sure, but their ships are pretty tough for their points cost and punch plenty hard. Their primary focus is boarding actions, which between Thunderhawks and standard Assaults, you can luanch multiple of at the same time to hit different targets or focus on one.

A refreshing, multiplayer break from the all too common toxicity of the internet. Communication takes place solely in little animal vocalizations and pictograms you can display to others (sad animal face, happy animal face, frustrated animal face, arrows and symbols to help give directions, etc.), guiding players to positive, productive communication.
I spawned into the blocky, impressionist world as a badger, and was quickly coaxed into following a rabbit, a fox, and eventually a lynx and another badger on a grand tour of the world, finding collectibles used to unlock new emotes, animals to use as your avatar, and fur patterns to make those avatars a little more unique. No lootbox slot machines here, no entitled players whining and directing abusive comments at the developers or berating others for lack of knowledge or skill, no enemies (NPC or PC) to kill or avoid, just gentle exploration and cooperation at a price that you might be able to recoup by searching between your couch cushions.
Be advised, however, that it may not be for everyone. The only true gameplay element seems to be the collectible hunt (some of which require multiple players to unlock). Everything else is sightseeing, achievement hunting, and figuring out how to work together towards a goal without words, similar to using gesticulation in real life to get around a language barrier. This is actually kind of fun in itself, to be honest. The only real downside I see is that this world will feel incredibly lonely (at least to me) once the population dwindles, but all it takes is a handful to have a good time.

This is probably what people will call a "walking simulator", not that that's a bad thing. While there are puzzles and a plot to piece together, a lot of the experience is in the atmosphere - and what an atmosphere it is!
Good:
+ The game looks and sounds absolutely beautiful, even on my 5-year-old PC. Fantastic effort from a small team.
+ Puzzles that require some thought - a good challenge without being frustrating.
+ An absolutely huge and detailed map with no loading screens (except the very start). Very open.
Bad:
- Some (few!) game-stopping bugs - for me, one progress-critical valve was unusable until I reloaded the game.
- I can see people struggling with the size of the map - if you explore everything (like I did), you won't have to backtrack. But if you have to backtrack, it might take a while to get from point A to B.
- The game uses only checkpoint-saves, and only seems to have one slot.
Other:
~ The game is short. I finished in about 5 hours' time, and I can see people sprinting through faster. Not a bad thing, necessarily, but if you really care about the length-for-money thing, keep that in mind.
~ Very slow-paced. It's not about a run-and-gun private eye, but a guy trying to piece together a string of crimes. No explosions, gunfights, or interrogations. Again, not bad, but if you're looking for that, this isn't it.
~ The plot takes some thinking to piece together - each crime is a part of the whole story, and you probably won't run into them in order. Then the ending complicates things further.
tl;dr: Slow, atmospheric, interesting and confusing story. I enjoyed it, but others might not.

This was my most anticipated game in quite some time.  I was even following the developers on Twitter, reading their blogs, etc.
Having just finished it, ultimately the game left a bittersweet taste in my mouth.  The graphics are incredible, but even with a 3GB of VRAM and 16 GB of RAM, I was experiencing frame rate hiccups on high settings.  Lowering them to medium and turning V-Sync off helped some, but didn't eliminate the problem.  The atmosphere is great though and it really feels like the countryside.  Very immersive.
There also seems to be some kind of a weird bug in customizing your controls.  I like to use arrow keys instead of WASD to move around, but the left and right arrow keys would only turn the camera, not strafe.  After I tinkered with the .ini file I got it straightened out, but this should have been addressed before release.
Also, there is no ability to save, the game autosaves but it's pretty infrequent.  My computer crashed and I had to replay a solid 20 minutes worth of the game to get back to where I was.  The ability to quicksave or more frequent auto saves would be a nice patch idea.
Music is outstanding, the soundtrack alone is almost worth the price of admission (if you pre-ordered).

Of course, this is an adventure/mystery game.  The gameplay mechanics are unique, and there's no tutorial or hand holding (it even warns you of this at the first).  So basically what you do is stumble upon a body, scour the area in search of clues/evidence, once you have found all of the evidence you can "touch" the body and it will reveal certain "freeze frames" in the sequence of the murder.  You then have to place the events in correct chronological order and once you do so the scene of the murder plays out like a movie.
You do this a few times throughout the game, none of it was overly difficult, and although there is no tutorial or explicit instructions, it's pretty intuitive if you've played video games before.
The story was certainly interesting, I won't put any spoilers in here, but the game takes 4 hours max to complete.  I was very disappointed in the length.  Felt like the game was just starting to blossom into it's full potential when the credits rolled.
All in all a good little mystery game, but the short length robbed it of it's full story-telling potential.

Let me start off by saying that this is an Early Access title, in case that was missed on the main screen. So far, I have put about 35 hours into the game, but put in over 2000 hours into ARK survival (which is made by the same company). Yes I know that is a ridiculous amount of time placed into one game but it is still tame compared to my Fiance's total towards WoW, but I digress.
The Positives:
-Despite the early access, this game has a lot to offer. You can wield magic, a sword, a hammer, or a bow with the click of a button and change your mind anytime.
-There are many different building options with amazing textures and a handful of decor options
-If you enjoy splunking or exploring, this game can scratch that itch (they just added a new cave with new monsters and a large boss)
-One of the biggest blessings is having a starting town. In Ark, you can end up on a beach and die within a minute of loading in. D&L loads you into a town of your faction (Elf, Dwarf or Human) so that you can get your bearings.
-This town gives you an option to rent rooms and purchase items from vendors. The pricing is still a little  steep with some things but it isnt all that difficult to gain currency.
-You can edit what you look like which doesnt sound like a big deal, but it's the little things. The character creation process is still a little rough around the edges, but still gives you that personal touch to help with the immersion...or allow you to make one strange looking character. To each their own.
-The taming is very similar to Ark. You feed them, make sure they dont escape and protect them from rogue beasts or pain in the a.. players. The biggest difference is that you use something called a hook arrow which is placed into the ground after hitting your target. As the beast fights against their bindings, they grow fatigued and will eventually drop. (I found it to be an interesting aspect compared to other games Ive played)
The Cons:
-The loading screen takes quite a bit of time. I was lucky enough to have an SSD (solid state drive) to put the game on but my friends would have to wait sometimes twenty minutes to play.
-Taming higher level beasts take quite a bit of time on official servers (6+ hours sometimes depending on the feed available for your tame). Since my play time is limited, I will have to run an unofficial server for higher level tames.
-There are bugs...duh. This game has been out for a month and as far as early access games go, I really have to hand it to the developers. They have updated sometimes once a week, worked on performance and try to add content all at the same time. There are a lot of compaints about the roll backs on patches but please, think objectively about this. One early access game I had would do up to 3 hour rollbacks with no warning whatsoever. These developers warn you ahead of time. I have had 35 hours worth of enjoyment thus far with the bugs and problems, I knew that going in.
There are some who are currently unable to log in, I am now one of them. What am I going to do? Post it to their bug forum, try it again tomorrow and play other games in the meantime while I occasionally check back. This is steam...I have a lot of choices and It isn't a permanent problem. If it turns out to be (which is usually my luck), Ill cross that bridge when I get there.
Do I recommend this game?
-Do you enjoy building glorious structures?
-Does the thought of you dressed in a long robe, your face hidden by your hood while you charge up that sick fireball get you all excited?
-Does exploring a massive map filled with danger and hidden nooks n crannies rev your engines?
-Does riding on the back of a damn dragon, direwolf, griffin, wyvern, etc. sound pretty epic compared to your mundane life?
Then yes...I recommend this game, but there's a catch. You need to look at the words early access and realize that this isnt a finished product. Youre purchasing this game so that you dont have to wait to do all those glorious things I just mentioned above. Youre buying this game knowing that it can crash any time and erase what youve done over the past month. That is the risk, and they told you that ahead of time. Youre not buying a finished product, this isn't EA games where you get a half polished game, micropayments and no support for the money you give.
Youre speeding up the release date and helping these developers fix bugs, improve gameplay, and optimize all while playing a pretty solid game despite its infancy.

I feel I've played enough to give a fair opinion on how the game handles up to this point.
I guess I'll go ahead and start with some of my complaints. The loading times... yes, the initial loading screen takes forever. I'm talking, I'd start the game and walk away for about 8 mins knowing I wouldn't miss anything. That's just a tad ridiculous even considering the map size. Some of the animals (looking at you panthers and lava tigers) are a nightmare to fight. Aside from being very overpowered, it's a lag-fest trying to attack them. If they could work on some combat features, that would be wonderful. Last but not least: land claiming. I honestly don't mind too much when people place posts around claiming land for themselves, but it does make taming very challenging when trying to place troughs. Maybe troughs could be unaffected by land-claims or some other system could be put in place to help while trying to tame creatures.
As far as pros for Dark and Light, I can't say enough! The game is gorgeous, even on medium settings with only textures running on high; the enviroment is such a beautiful setting. The crafting/building feels very well balanced and easy to use even for those who don't enojy building a large base for hours. The combat, though a little wonky at times, has been polished very well and where you spend your skill points after leveling, actually matters. Attention is required to how you want to play because building a tank who is going to weild magic is not going to work out very well for you, so there's a complication that seems to be missing from other titles. As someone who plays on PvE and PvP servers, I like how the clans are set up. Not only can you recruit for your own clan but you can join an alliance with a fellow clan. If war is declared between two tribes, the game could potentially have large scale battles of epic proportions. I would love to see this occur in the future, the framework is there. And of course, the updates. I complained about loading times but I've already seen a drastic decrease in the time it takes to get in the game now. It would appear the devs are active, quick to fix issues and actually listen to the community; and that's something that I love to see!
All in all this IS an early access game and that needs to be considered before purchasing. I think Dark and Light is well worth diving into but there are also risks involved. After the latest update, I watched 130 hours of work... disappear. Was I salty? Yes. But that's part of the trials of EA and it's bugs and patches. So if you don't have the patience to allow the devs to continue working on their game, you might want to stay away for now. With that said I love the idea of having a true survival-rpg and I cannot wait to see more questing elements added, new biomes to explore and the various creatures they will unleash on us!
As it stands on 9/3/2017 I would have to give Dark and Light a 9/10 and say it is by-far my favorite game in my libraray right now. All we need are more gamers to fill up these servers and spice things up!

Dark and Light is a pretty awesome game, has some interesting features and takes a lot of the good ideas from ARK. Currently though, I don't think its worth playing, unless you are a hardcore tester, because it is at that stage where you will encounter many, many...many bugs. And the game is punishing, when you die, and when you die constantly because of bugs, the game is even more punishing, which is why it is not recommended for most but the hardiest of players.
Pros:
Melee is fun, once it is fixed it will be quite an interesting fight vs PVE mobs, still needs much work for it to ever work for PVP.
Magic in this game is awesome, something you cannot get from ARK, but again like melee needs more polish.
Tames are not overly strong, which is a good thing, but the balancing act during alpha does raise a lot of questions on where this will finally sit. But overall the tames, types, skills and harvesting are all pretty cool, and they do keep adding more.
Building is unrestrictive and you can be as creative as you like, and a lot of working will probably go into this before release so expect much more interesting textures and formats. I enjoyed this part of the game most.
Difficulty range is from easy to hard, generally normal mobs/animals are pretty easy to kill, but once you first encounter a wraith the diffulty shoots up incredibly (you meet them everywhere).
Cons
Questionable community manager updates, they kind of forget that you actually put time into this game, and sometimes it feels like they are trolling you. (not a good feeling)
Bugs are at the crazy levels for this game currently, mainly because of the direct effect to your gameplay, not only can you lose all the equipment on you when you crash (I can crash 7 times a day..), you can lose your tames, if you leave your door open and crash, all your belongings, and if you are in a middle of a fight, all your tames. If you have a short temper, and/or care about your tames and equipment more than you should, then this game will give you white hair.
Server rollbacks and updates, the team does this often (kinda expected) but gives you about 30 minutes warning in doing so, actually scrap that, at worst gives you NO warning in doing so. So coupled with additional and lengthened timers for tames, more restrictions to buildings and how long before they despawn, makes for an extremely frsutrating experience.

So overall, I would NOT rate for a normal run of the mill player to try this game YET, it has way too many punishing problems. Dying Light is a great game but with flaws that nearly ruined the game for me.
Keep in mind that I play on Hard mode so maybe this is me being bad, maybe not.
Pros:
-I love the free running aspect. The entire platforming is fun and there are nearly limitless options on how to run and get wherever.
-The level up system is fairly decent as for the power/agility trees. I'll get to the survival tree in a minute on why I have my personal struggles.
-The side quests of the game are pretty interesting and I tend to enjoy them.
-The environments are actually well designed, and I feel like the developers actually ENJOYED putting together every building, every zombie, just about everything.
-Playing with friends is intensely fun. Not gonna die it for a second.
-Night time feels like it should. Intense, frightening, all about where to run and where to hide. It truly is an enjoyable but horrific time. Good on you game.
-Zombies feel like zombies. Granted in a one-on-one scenario I should kill them easier, butttttttttttt I'll skip that for now cause I am on hard mode.
Cons:
-Combat is so clunky sometimes it hurts. I can't tell you how many times I meant to dropkick a zombie but jumped off them in a pathetic attempt and had to reset my entire setup.
-I thought Dark Souls punished players, but I was wrong. This game takes away survivor points every time you die, and there are a fair amount of cheap deaths. Mainly bombers in close areas when turning a corner. you lose the resources you used as well, but thankfully, the zombies retain the damage. But holy ♥♥♥♥ I have died so many times that survivor points became a delicacy as it became increasingly hard to earn them. They take away so many points each death that it feels like a stab to the stomach instead of a slap on the wrist.
-The humans dare I say are absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. They have the health of Panzer tanks and have the damage output of one as well. Where it takes me 7-8-9 shots to kill one of them, it takes them maybe 3-4 shots. And yes I know headshots are a 1 shot, I have hit quite a few in my day. But that doesn't excuse any of the deaths to human enemies I have had.
-The story is sub-par at best SO FAR. Upon beating the game, I will possibly change this portion of the review.
-Multiplayer WOULD be good if the matchmaking wasn't very...bizarre toppled with I'm assuming what is hacker as he gave me 3 stacks of 99x healthpacks. I wish I was joking. The Hunter multiplayer if solo fighting the Night Hunter (or whatever the hell the thing is called) feels dragged out and sometimes just too unfair. With 2 players though, it finally becomes a possibility. Not saying you can't win solo, I have, but damn is it hard.
-This is probably going to be my biggest gripe ever but here it goes. No bars, nothing to hold me back. The boss battles are ♥♥♥♥ing awful. They are legit the worst ♥♥♥♥ing things I have experienced in a game since Deus Ex: Human Revolution, only difference is DE:HR knew to keep some things correct. I'll say it here, taking away all my equipment and forcing me to fight a boss with a single weapon makes it feel almost like all those hours I spent gathering and looking for items was wasted for the large upcoming battle. Now again I haven't finished the story so FOR ALL I KNOW THIS MAY CHANGE. But in the first two battles I had my items stripped from me. First time was fine, it was made to fit the story. Second time, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Nothing would make me just magically *blip zoop beep boop* and lose my items. Lemme use my ♥♥♥♥ing gear, Dying Light.
-Sometimes controls feel clunky in the sense of they don't work like they should, but this game is so massive that I will give this one some slight relief on this complaint.
TL;DR version:
Dying Light is a game worth it when on sale, but for 60 bucks I have a little struggle recommending it. Still, I will admit it is one of the best zombie games I have played in quite a while.
Hope you enjoy the review and have a nice day.

This game isn't even in HD, somehow.  The only graphic options are 640x480 and 960x540, with a bad fullscreen mode that doesn't work well with my TV.  You can maximize the window, at least.  And don't count on a patch to fix it either, this game hasn't been updated in ages.
Technical problems aside, the track list is based on Lumines 2, but without the licenses.  That game is widely regarded as the black sheep of the Lumines series, so it's very odd that they went with it as the base for Lumines PC, as opposed to the original.
And a side note, if you're still wanting to buy this, the game is very reliant on the player having a good D-pad, so this is absolutely not a game you'd want to play with a Steam controller.
Or, you know, just don't buy it.  You'd absolutely get a better Lumines experience out of just running the original PSP game in an emulator.

---Let me describe my experiences with each boot. Keep in mind I am completely aware that this is an early alpha, and I'm loving every moment of this adventure.
