Sadly, the most accurate words I can find to describe Diehard Dungeon are 'tedious' and 'clunky', which is a shame because this could have been a very fun game.
The second descriptor, clunky, is the easier to tackle so I'll go with that first. The controls in Diehard Dungeon are not particularly responsive and the combat mechanics make things awkward. Using a controller does help with some of the problems but even so, moving and turning in combat is generally bad.
As to the 'tedious' part; well, many of the game's mechanics seem to be based around wasting as much of the player's time as possible. Here are some examples of what I am trying to convey:
The majority of rooms can only be exited once a key has been placed in a lock. The key will be hidden somewhere in the room; perhaps in one of the many random objects in the room (every one of which takes multiple strikes to break open), perhaps on one of the hit-sponge enemies. There's no indication as to where the key will be and you will often spend fruitless minutes hacking away at boxes to find the key.
Little pixie type creatures will often appear (most of the time from one of the previously mentioned boxes you are hacking open in search of the key) and steal your companion chest. Well, not properly steal the chest, like take it away to be found later on; they just grab it and run to the other side of the room. You can't collect any treasure without the chest so you can't just leave it behind. What you must do instead is chase the pixies around the room, slashing at them with your sword until you've killed them all and can get your chest back. The problem here is that the pixies are fast and will continually move away from the player character, whilst the character cannot move while swinging his sword. And so a merry game of trying to manouvre the pixies into a corner ensues. And this will happen every few rooms. It's not that difficult to get the chest back, it's just tedious and annoying.
There are other exmples that I won't go into an extended explanation of as they all tend to end with the same reaction of 'Why am I doing this? What's the point?' and a feeling that your time has been wasted.

The final negatives about Diehard Dungeon are the bland graphics, uninspired dungeon design and the completely 'meh' soundtrack. Overall this is not a game I would recommend unless you have a whole load of time to waste on pointless tedium and absolutely nothing else to play.

Your primary weapon (as in Zelda) is a sword that is somewhat satisfying to use but is otherwise unremarkable. Your secondary weapon is a very strangely ineffective canon that fires weak, timed mortars that never go where you want them to. Well, this is an all new record for me.  I've played less than thirty minutes of this game and already love it.  As you know me (if you have read past reviews of mine) I am a frugal gamer.  Perhaps that should be my thing?  Anyway, this game went on sale recently for $2.24 and couldn't resist.  "Zelda" was in the description, so I threw my money at Steam.
So, like I said I love it.  It'll probably get stale with time, but this is a great pickup-and-play-rogue-like adventure.  The way it plays reminds me a lot of "Binding of Isaac".  You go through various rooms picking up keys, hearts and power-ups.  Every so often you enter a room with a big-ol' boss baddy you have to defeat.  And just like "Binding of Isaac", the level layout is always changing so each time you die, the whole structure gets rearranged (thus my "rogue-like" description) and you lose your power-ups and have to start over again.  This makes each time you play a bit unique and different.  Any subtle hint of change always gives a game a bit more life to it so it doesn't become stale so easily.
Now, I'm going to say this and I'm sure many people will disagree, but I like this much better than "Binding of Isaac" (Sorry to keep comparing it to that, but it's the only relation I know as far as style and I know MANY people have played "BoI").  The main, and probably sole reason, I like this more than "BoI" is that it is much more forgiving.  I'm not a great gamer, but I'm also no newbie. With that said, "BoI" is TOUGH for me.  Bosses are tough to get through, and when I make it I'm shocked and awed.  This does make it all the more rewarding, but like I mentioned before, when you die in "BoI", you lose everything and have to restart.  Needless to say, I die a lot in that game, become discouraged after ten minutes of play, and don't touch it for four months. With "Diehard Dungeon" I feel like I can make it pretty far without dying.  There's still a challenge, but I'm not getting slaughtered after only a handful of rooms.  I also feel like they're a little more generous with the power-ups, which makes this a little more rewarding and fun.
Now, enough comparison.  Overall this game is addictive and makes me want to go deeper and deeper into this dungeon.  The style is very much in the vain of "Link to the Past" which is a lazy description I know, but it's the first thing that comes to mind.  It's got that heavy pixelated look which has become ever so popular.  As far as game play goes, yes it is like "BoI" (I swear that's the last time) BUT there are mini-games, too, with a global scoreboard, which definitely adds some replay value.  If you have just a bit of hardcore gamer in you, but also just want a casual game to play, this will be a perfect game to fulfill that need. A great edition to any gamers' Steam library.

Dying Light is a fantastic zombie parkour game, which reinforces you to keep looking over your shoulder when you're not on the move.
Coming from only playing the vanilla game, no DLC content, I found the game to be full of content and challenges. The game scales really well with content and player's abilities, so there is a constant challenge to what ever you do. And you'll never be over powered.
Got friends who equally have a love hate relationship with zombies? Then I highly recommend this title. Don't get me wrong, this game is fantastic on your own. Hell, that's what I did for my first play through, and I am currently doing a second one with two other friends. The game as a nifty competitive system where you can open up a challenge to the other players to try and kill the most zombies, college the most valuables and run the a destination the fastest. This opens up a lot banter with you and your friends, just hope they're not a sore loser!
The Parkour side of the games is just fantastic on its own, and opens the game immensely. It enables the player to fight their enemies based on the terrain, be it densely populated housing to open rocky areas outside suburb areas, making encounters ever more interesting. Once you unlock the grappling hook, oh boy, does the game become more fun :D
The main and side quests are interesting. It opens up the player to the world around him, showing the power struggle between innocent people trying to survive, vs the power hungry enemies who want everything for them selves. It also shows what a world like this can do to a person who is separated from communities and try and survive on their own, driving them to insanity.
If you get bored of doing the quests in the game, there are plenty challenges around which mix the game up a bit. These challenges range from parkour speed runs, to raiding heavily infected & enclosed areas to gain beneficial resources for survivors. They're very rewarding as well, and are well worth doing between quests and running around the city areas.
The skill system reflects the time / work you put into your game session. Over time as your running, fighting and helping others you gain experience in different areas where you can improve upon yourself and make the game easier / more interesting for yourself as you battle the undead hordes. The skills basically parkour more fun, fighting easier without getting winded after 4 swings and allowing you to craft more interesting items to use.
This balances the game out quite nicely, so you'll level up along with the game as you play.
The game provides a lot of content, what you'd expect from a triple A title. The extra game content, not the cosmetic DLC, will nicely add at least 10+ hours of game play for you. With that estimate, I am taking the year of free DLC into account, assuming it is not just cosmetic lark.

I'm so conflicted on whether or not I want to recommend this game. On one hand, it has great visuals, awesome parkouring, and believable (albeit short-lived) atmosphere; but on the other hand, it has quite a lot of flaws. I'll focus on said flaws for my review.
Chunks of poor level design
Dying Light is a game that emphasizes running and pathfinding during certain sequences, scripted or otherwise. Often times I find myself perfectly able to navigate the landscape... but some instances, like the mission where you arm C4 inside a half-built skyscraper, have downright confusing level design. I've died plenty of times and lost uncountable numbers of survivor points due to simply getting lost. And not only that, but randomly placed explosives that enemies (somehow) set off has killed me more than what's acceptable. Having a "wtf killed me?" moment is not enjoyable. There are also several instances where an exploding undead appears out of nowhere (scripted or otherwise) and insta-kills you because you did what the game taught you to do: attack the zombie. Gimmicks like this don't help the game.
Goons are unfair and poorly designed
The idea to kill Goons (the undead with rebars) is to use ranged options. But if that doesn't work, then what? Guns attract more undead, so you can't use that. You'll simply have to get in close to finish them off. But there's a big problem; a Goon's range is far longer than your dodge skill. This makes for an intensely frustrating encounter where using the dodge function is effectively useless. You just have to take the hit (since you can't dodge far enough), get knocked flat, wait to get up, rinse and repeat. You also have to use power attacks, or you'll be repeating this process for a long, long time. Overall the game limiting you to one effective method of killing Goons is a discredit.
Demolishers are unfair and poorly designed
Much like Goons, Demolishers have a ridiculously unfair attack range, though they don't have the AoE ground pound like Goons do, so using dodge is somewhat viable. Instead, they can swing and charge on a dime, and each attack will knock you flat and take a lot of HP. You'll also be forced to use guns - or power attacks only - to finish them off. Their ranged attack is also ridiculously hard to dodge up close (since it locks on to you), so you'll be S.O.L. when trying to melee.
Main villain sucks
Rais is uninspired and spews the same tired tropes of bad guys in modern media. The whole "I am chaos" spiel has gotten pretty old by now. Nothing new or surprising about him, and killing him at the end of the game wasn't impressive at all.
Cliche, predictable plot
You figure with zombie genres being so interesting and mainstream that people would come up with something fresh. The only twist that surprised me was Jade dying. The rest was mostly ho-hum. Not much to write home about.
Mini map sucks
Goes hand in hand with the bad level design. I've found several points in the game where HUD markers don't correctly account for what floor they're on, or even show the proper way to an objective. The mini map also doesn't help me when I'm desperately trying to figure out a way into a particular house because all the windows and doors are locked up, which usually means I have to figure out some obscure, gimmicky parkour-based way to get inside (this has happened far too much).
Moves like Grapple suck
I never got the hang of grapple, because a lot of key combos the game requires don't translate well on a keyboard. There are also skills I never bothered using, like the ones for 2-handed weapons, since they don't seem all that feasible in a fast-paced game like Dying Light (2-handers are simply just too slow and cumbersome).
Zombie drops don't scale and are essentially useless mid-to-late-game
It doesn't seem that the items zombies give are useful at all after a certain point. The amount of money or items you get from them simply don't scale with the player. After a while its just not feasible to loot corpses anymore.
"Swarm" events happen randomly for no reason
Specifically when you cause an explosion or fire a gun too much - you'll hear infected screams in the distance, and a few runners will spawn and attack you. In Old Town, these events would happen again and again and again, even when I wasn't doing anything. I've also seen swarm events happen after simply getting an elemental effect on a regular undead, who will scream and writhe and then cause a swarm. Makes little sense to me, and adds a ton of frustration to the game since I was already being quiet.
Artificial difficulty
Slowly but surely, Dying Light lumps more and more zombies onto the player, especially in Old Town. This combined with the bad Demolisher and Goon designs, infected and humans that can magically dodge your swings, and the random swarms makes for gameplay that's far more artificially difficult than it should be.
No fast travel
The parkour is fun and the levels aren't so big that its entirely a chore to navigate, but fast traveling from safe house to safe house would have been a good addition, especially since some safe houses are extremely inconvenient to get back to (i.e. the bridge safe house, the tower safe house in Old Town, etc).
Ruins its own immersion
Dying Light started out with a fantastic atmosphere. The sound design, before getting used to all the ques, was fantastic. It eventually wore off due to a combination of factors like limited sound effects for zombies (especially the Toad, which makes the same damn sound every time), a few whacky, immersion-breaking characters, and overuse of gore and dead body piles. I mean seriously... there are points in the game with Dante's Inferno levels of gore in the form of mountains of corpses, and it made me think several times "how did these bodies even get here? Are there even that many people in Harran?". The devs abused this aspect of horror and it broke the immersion for me.
Uninspired special infected designs
Runners. Undead that explodes. Undead that charges and throws rocks. Undead that spits acid. Undead that screams. I basically just described the special infected cast of Left 4 Dead 2. None of the undead besides the Volatiles were unique or interesting. The only special infected that have alternate appearances are Volatiles, runners, and Goons. The rest have the exact same appearance throughout the entire game. Additionally, the Volatiles are barely the stars of the show, despite being the most interesting and intimidating. They only appear twice in scripted main quest events (to my knowledge) and in the unscripted main map at night.
Terrible final boss "fight"
I've almost come to expect triple-A FPS titles to have poor, uninspired final bosses. Dying Light, unfortunately, was not an exception. Leading up to the final encounter was a frantic chase, where you run from undead and then eventually Volatiles; but at the top of the tower, all that waited was a quicktime button pressing event, which was not satisfying in the slightest. Was very disappointed with how dull it was.
Overall I'm on the fence (pun not intended) about Dying Light. Its definitely not worth a full $60 purchase, so I'm glad I got it on sale. My review is neutral overall, but just for the frustrations the game put me through, I have to set it as not recommended.

This game well and truly earns the label "Early Access". In fact, that's the abbreviated version. The full label is "Much Too Early Access". If you ever played ARK: Survival Evolved, then Dark and Light will be very familiar to you. VERY familiar. Like, 'someone bought a really old and buggy version of ARK, swapped out a few character and NPC models, and tried to present it as a new game' familiar.
According to the main menu, this game is precisely 30.02% complete.....and oh man does it show. The lag is real. Everything from little framerate stutters to 45+ second freezes in which the world goes on without you. Harvesting materials and melee combat are hit or miss, no pun intended. There are long periods of time where desynchronization causes hits to simply not register. These things are especially problematic in a game like this, where you can literally lose your weapon, your armor, your mount, everything you've worked for, for good.
The game world is beautiful. It looks fantastic. It's also deadly. Not because of monsters or hostile players, but because of holes in said world, where you can fall through invisible cracks in the ground. If you don't have friends and/or a flying mount, good luck getting yourself out of that little pickle.
The client is unstable. HIGHLY unstable. That was the final nail in the coffin for me. I crashed to desktop something like 9 times over the course of an evening. I called it a night, and tried again the next morning. The crashes began immediately. The second one cost me a griffon, which is a pretty decent flying mount. Dead. Not coming back. The third one left a second flying mount, a wyvern, stuck at about 3,000 feet in the air and me without any way to retrieve it. No new software or hardware on my PC. Drivers updated. Purely a server side issue.
Finally, the developers of Dark and Light seem content to make posts, public statements, in-game notations, etc with a command of English that seems rudimentary at best. What does that say about the depth of your commitment to developing a game, if you won't even spend the money to have someone proofread your material?
Good luck, Snail Games. At this rate, you're going to need it.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a slow and foreboding game that has you exploring a section of scenic countryside whilst trying to find a young boy who has gone missing (the titular Ethan Carter). You play a paranormal detective who is able to pick up clues from murder scenes to piece together what has happened. As you find a scene and investigate, you must figure out the sequence of events that led up to the murder, which will unlock a final extra scene giving further context to the killing.
The scenery is beautiful, rivalling (and topping) the natural beauty found in games like Dear Esther. It could be described as a 'walking simulator' (apparantly a derogatory term for slower games where you wander the environment without killing anything), you don't use weapons or directly fight anything here, this game is rooted in exploration, investigation and a building sense of uneasiness. The story isn't exactly subtle with its fantasy, horror and sci-fi genre tropes, some of which really clash against the beautifully natural feeling of the world, forcing your suspension of disbelief early on. However, if you accept that the game goes to wacky crazy places, you can have some fun here.
The story is both subtle and heavy handed at times, I recommend taking it slowly and reading every item and looking at environmental clues to get the full story.

Bloo Kid 2 is a platformer game where you control a blue haired character to save your kid. There are 5 stages in total which have 9+3 special levels in each stages. 1 of the levels will be a boss fight and in later levels, 2 of the levels will be a unique custom level.
The music sounds great and you won't get bored listening to it for several times. It's all sounds relaxing and fun.
The game is using 2D pixelated graphics; It reminds me of those retro styled games i played back in the day. The game graphics look great in each levels.
There is a story in the game, although it's mostly serve as a seasoning for the game.
As i said before, there are 9+3 special levels in each stage. You'll unlock the next stage once you finish all 9 levels in the previous stage. The 9 levels will usually consists of 5 normal levels, 2 unique levels (in later stages), and 1 boss level. The unique levels varies for each stage; for example, the last stage will require you to move fast because of the moving screen, the second to the last stage will require you to pay attention to your jumping skill because you'll ride a moving cart in high speed, and so on. Although the cart level seems to be annoying at the start, it becomes a "freebie" level on higher difficulties.
Speaking of difficulties, there are 4 difficulties in this game, with the hardest one being unlocked after you finish the game once. The difficulty will affect the number of health you'll carry, the number of health you'll obtain from chest, and the time that's needed for the "time attack" star (will be explained later). This game has one checkpoint in each level (except if you play in the hardest difficulty) and your heart will be restored in easier difficulty.
Sometimes, you'll get a star(or stars) after completing a stage. These stars can be obtained by obtaining balloon (which will spawn near the end of the level), finishing the level with full heart, obtaining 3 blue stars (rare stars which are tricky to get), obtaining all yellow stars (common stars which varies in each level), killing all monsters, and finishing the level before a certain time limit. Although the level itself can be completed in less than 10 minutes, it'll take longer if you want to collect all of them. Luckily, you don't have to do all of them in one run.
Completing enough stars will unlock special stage, although you don't need to collect all of the stars to unlock all of the special stage (it's still required for the achievement though). The special stages are usually harder than normal stages. There is even one level which looks like
(a difficult platformer game), where you have to jump between fireballs in one session. I might find it challenging, but other people might find it frustating (especially if they suck with timing)
Each stage has their own set of monsters. While there are some easy ones (like those mushroom guy in mario games), there are also some annoying ones which can kill you if you aren't careful. Some monsters also need to be killed in a specific way (not just by jumping on it) and you'll need to be careful in doing so.
There is also a red potion in the game which can deflect all incoming attacks and kill all enemies (including the unbeatable "obstacle" ones) in one touch for a short time. This red potion is usually put in tricky places and will wear off in water, however.
There are 5 bosses in total, each has their own attack pattern and killing strategies. All of them can be killed in 3 hits and they'll drop a heart after each hit.
After completing a game on any difficulty, you'll be granted a time attack, which is basically the same as redoing each of the previous stages at faster time, and boss rush mode where you have to kill all 5 bosses in a row. I honestly really like the boss rush mode.
While i love the game, i kinda feel weird that you have to change the screen resolution in order to get a balloon in one of the level.
Pros:
- 5 stages with 9+3 levels in each stage
- Unique stages
- Unique and interesting bosses
- Boss rush mode
Cons:
- Time attack mode can be boring
- There is one level that needs you to change screen resolution to 100% the game.
This is a solid platformer game. If you like mario games, you'll love it.
If you like platformer games, this is a must. There is also an easy mode (which is super easy) if you suck at it.

Neotokyo was a Source mod when it was first released, but since then it has become a standalone product that I must say, is possibly one of the best multiplayer FPS's I have ever played. I am overjoyed that the release of the Steam version has revived the playerbase, and I hope to see this many servers active for a long time.
Neotokyo is a beautifully designed, clever, cyberpunk FPS that takes a lot of inspiration from the series Ghost in the Shell, and makes use of Counterstrike-esque gameplay improved in several distinct ways. The first is the addition of 3 different classes, Recon, Assualt, and Support. Recon is a quick moving glass cannon, whereas support is a slow moving tank who boasts utility such as smoke grenades and infared vision, and Assualt is a mixture of the two. The second is how these classes play. Both Assualt and Recon can go nearly invisible to rush across pathways, and Recon can "Super Hop" to either quickly gain hieght to meanuver around the splendidly designed maps, or to quickly gain forward momentum for an escape or rush down. These simple changes to how one moves combined with the map design makes for a game that demands robust tactics from its players. A silent team of lone gunmen will surely be destroyed by a team that works together to flank and flush out their opponents. Make no mistake, this is a thinking man's FPS. Bullet penetration also exists and is frequently a tactic made us of in many maps.
To end this review, I have to say that it's impressive the sheer amount of unique assets, textures, models, animations, and sound clips that were put into this game considering it's something a small team did in their spare time for free. I also have to give a shoutout to Ed Herrison's Neotokyo Original Sound Track, which is also amazing, though not much of it is present in the game.

Bloo Kid 2 is a standard and casual platformer. Gameplay is as simple as it gets - double jump and bonk on enemies to kill them.
So why do I recommend this game? Two things were executed well here:
1. Separating optional goals from main progress in a way that increases the difficulty way more than just beating every stage casually. (Not extremely hard, but it's harder)
2. Cleverly using the game's basic design to make you figure out how to obtain secrets or perform certain tasks, which was my favorite part of the entire game.
I would recommend this game only to completionists who will truly be able to enjoy it, since by ignoring all the optional stuff will make the game very dull, unexciting and too quick to beat.
There are plenty of other platformers do better what Bloo Kid 2 offers in terms of gameplay.

I really wanted to like this game, and with 12 hours under my belt I can testify that it's not without merits, but I still just can't recommend it.
In many ways it's similar to a bunch of SRPG games, such as Tactics Ogre and Final Fantasy Tactics (which I love). You have your grid-based movement, elevation and cover, and a number of characters to level up and give gear. All of this is great.
The combat system itself is not.
Everything is so RNG-based that strategy is almost pointless. It doesn't help that everything can die in one hit. You can be very careful, and meticulously arrange your units in perfect flanking positions behind full cover, and still get one-shot from accross the map after you miss a 94% accurate shot. Being one-shot like that also often means that some of your other units "panic" and shoot each other.
Let me break that down for you: A perfect ambush from an elevated position, with a scoped sniper (with bonus height perk) can miss a completely open 90%+ shot at a small enemy, which then ends up getting a free attack opportunity and wiping out 2-3 of your guys in one hit.
Rocket launchers and grenades are the best weapons in the game - Not because of good damage output, splash range or destructive powers, but because they are the only reliable weapons in the game. You NEED rockets and grenades to be able to attack something with confidence.
Now, old Xcom fans tell me "that's how it's supposed to be", because the risk makes everything a thrill, and you have to adapt to the situation no matter what happens.
I don't buy it, to be honest - It just seems like bad game design, and it makes every battle unsatisfying. Even if you do well, you feel like you have to chalk it down to luck more than skill.
Other problems include bugs, save corruption, and cluttered visuals. It's also hard to tell where the lines of sight go, and your units are given classes at random.
There is so much potential here, though. I just wish it was more about strategy, and less about sacrificing virgins to the RNG gods and savescumming every step along the way.

FTL is a journey. A real unforgiving journey where everything bad happens. But you keep going on this journey because you're reeled in with promises of treasures and fun. You go in wanting to be Picard, but come out as a redshirt ensign. That's been killed a million times over and over. FTL is what you show a starry-eyed ten-year-old with dreams of being a spacefarer to destroy all of their hope -- forget footage of the Challenger explosion.
You will be stressed, you will be angry, you will be unsatisfied. And there's no Snickers bar satisfaction at the end of this game. If there is, it has eluded me for nearly 60 hours of gameplay. You can't "git gud" at a game that knows your every move before you make it.
But it is one of the funnest games I've ever played. Great music. Good minimalism that fosters a vivid imagination. Soul-stompingly relentless difficulty. Amazing customization options for your ships (provided you can unlock a lot of them). Name your crew after your friends and family and let the blood and tears flow.
9/10

I really wanted to like this game because of other people praising it. I thought this game would be fun with the time manipulation concepts but I am finding all of it confusing and tedious, making it really hard to enjoy the game. I feel like the mechanics are just throwing themselves all at once at me and the developer is just expecting the player to know what to do instinctively. When I do get something working, often I feel it was just through dumb luck more so than analyzing the situation and executing to see if my strategy would work. This could have been avoided if the concepts were introduced better and how to take advantage of each one.
I also feel that the game is cheating me, like I obtain a key and then I lose it if I backtrack (not rewind). I do realize that a green "aura" object or enemy is immune to time manipution, but other things, such as moving right makes enemies "play forward" while moving left makes enemies "play backwards", isn't clearly marked. I think that particular key is that kind of object but I just gave up after not understanding why I was losing the key.
For some reason, the game likes to shift between 30 and 60FPS. This isn't frame skipping. This is kind of annoying because the game started out slow and then suddenly became faster and then become slow again. I don't understand why.
I do applaud the developers for trying to do something ambitious but I don't think it was designed well in execution. It might be an indie game and not a AAA game, but that doesn't automatically mean good. The art style and music playback of rewinding, fast-forwarding, and slow-motion distortion are interesting to see and hear come from a game, but that's all I can really say is good about it. The rest is just meh to me. I don't think this game was meant for me. I'm glad I gave it a try though. At least I know it's not for me.

If you get Long War you will lose people on missions and feel that you genuinely couldn't have done any better. That the loss wasn't BS or RNGJesus condemning you.
For example: I got Longwar and I hadn't had a devastating mission until I downed an alien carrier. I landed with my squad of 8 troopers and ended the mission with 4. I lost 3 and had to leave one downed man behind as the enemy overwhelmed me from the start and seriously messed my team up. I lost 4 good men and I couldn't have done the mission any better than that with my current loadouts and abilities. You can't win 'em all. That's what I like about Longwar.
In Vanilla unless you're playing on insane difficulty you aren't going to get epic moments like that. You're either going to completely steamroll the enemy or get screwed over by RNGjesus. If you get this game play vanilla first then get Longwar so you know how much it improves this wonderful game.

And when you finally beat it with the Kestrel and watch that infuriating, overpowered, battered Rebel Flagship explode, you'll cheer. On easy. Then it'll tell you you've unlocked another ship. Yes, that's right, there are multiple ships to choose from other than the Kestrel. 2-3 different layouts per ship, 3 difficulty levels, AE or non-AE content. They all play a little differently, and what works for one will absolutely get you slaughtered with another.
I poured 50 goddamn hours into this game before I beat it on easy mode. It will probably be 30 more before I manage normal. Then I tried the Nesasio, a shield-less, cloaking ship, and died in the second sector. This is a game that manages to make you feel perpetually like a noob, but it's so much fun that you don't care. Getting a cool, rare weapon that you've never seen before, threading the needle and timing your weapon shots perfectly to keep your enemy's shields and weapons suppressed, developing a strategy to kill the end boss (you WILL need cloaking the first time you do it, and whatever you do, don't kill all of the enemy crew members.)
Upon first glance, it feels like there's a huge randomness factor. In some ways, that's true. But it's less of an all-or-nothing coin flip, and more of a spectrum. You will never get so RNG-screwed that it's simply not possible to win from the beginning of a run. My only tip is this: Abuse pause as much as possible, no one's keeping track of how much you spam it.
Buy. This. Game. Unbelievable amount of content for $10.

I remember playing the first Battlefront all the time in Middle School. I'd have friends over and we'd literally play it day and night. It was easily one of the best, if not THE best Star Wars game ever. We believed it couldn't get any better.
Until 2005.
When the trailer for Battlefront 2 came out, everyone who eas anyone would watch it on repeat. We picked apart every detail of the trailers and the excitement grew with every time we watched. We could finally go to Space! We could finally play as Heroes! The wait was enough to drive us insane. We were almost as excited for it as we were to see Revenge of the Sith. When it was released, it completly blew us away. Seemingly everything about the game was perfect. It's a game that will not onlly live on in our hearts for nostalgia, but will continue to be one of the greatest games ever made.
However, it has it's flaws. Despite being one of my favorite games of all time, it takes steps up and down from the previous Battlefront, which I now consider to be an overall better game. Here's why:
PROS
+Space Battles!
+Heroes!
+More Maps!
+More Classes!
+Cool Campaign!
+Cool Galactic Conquest!
CONS
-The Space maps are the only ones to include air vehicles, as opposed to the previous game where you could jump into aerial vehicles and dogfight.
-The Space maps, while fun at first, are essentially empty and unimaginative, and become rediculously stale after the 'I'M IN SPACE JESUS CHRIST WOW" mentality wears off. I remember fondly in Galactic Conquest sighing in boredome evry time there was a space battle. The process remains the same: get in a ship, destroy the frigate, fly onto the enemy ship, destroy their♥♥♥♥♥♥from the inside, and whoop-de-doo, three hours of your life are gone. Maybe they could have added a few more activities or modes in space or even had more rooms on the space ships.
-The Heroes, while amazingly fun to play as, are rediculously overpowered. Most of the jedi heroes are simply reskinned versions of eachother with a slight difference. Their Lightsabers are practically one hit kills, they have an insanely high jump, and can sprint faster than you can have time to see them. The lightsaber moves are usually the same three slash animations over and over, and blocking barely does anything against other lightsabers. It would have been interesting to see a bit more swordplay mechanics come into play, where you have to block the enemy's strikes at the correct time or something. The heroes could have been more interesting if their abilities/controls were a bit more similar to Jedi Outcast, but with destinct abilities that set them apart.
-The maps in Battlefront 2 suffer from being very close quarters and confusing to navigate at times, and are generally smaller and less memorable than the previous intallment's. I remember Battlfront 1 had literal all-out brawls going across the maps, this one mostly consists of running around in hopes of finding an enemy to shoot. Compare a map like Battlefront 1's 'Dune Sea' to Battlefront 2's 'Death Star'. On Dune Sea, you could go to the Sarlaac and shove enemies in, jump in a skiff and drive past the Tusken camp trying not to get killed by Sand People, snipe rebels in the Sandcrawler, and then hop into a tie fighter next to the Homestead and dogfight weaving in and out of the stone pillars. On Death Star, you can look at the Laser go off, walk through some empty hallways to a hangar and shoot 3 rebels, and then fall in a pit by accident. Invigorating!  Not a real big complaint, but should adressed none the less.
-The classes in Battlefront 1 were balanced so they each had roles to complete as a team, which each had a special distinct look, ability, and weapon. In Battlefront 2, they tried to do the same thing, but made it a little confusing. You had to unlock the 'Special' class, which was more often than not just a noobtube class. The PM's for alot of the classes on the Republic team were just shoehorned tie-ins for Episode 3 that ended up getting a few seconds of screentime. (I still can't tell most of the clone classes in Battlefront 2 apart.)
-The Campaign was really fun, I was really interested in the story, especially on Hoth. I felt like I was on a roll, and loved shooting rebel scum. When I finished the mission, I was suprised to know that was it was over almost prematurley, especially with the large selection of maps they had. Not a big complaint, just feel like hey could have added more.
-Fewer max players than the last.
Other than that, it's a must-play. Hope I could help.

I've just finished the game, and while generally I think people should allow some time to decompress before reviewing the game given the dearth of reviews out there from any trustworthy sources I thought it may be of some help to those who are on the fence whether to buy or not. Before I get into it, I also just want to note I'm impressed with how communicative the dev team has been both throughout the day on Twitter and on these forums answering peoples questions and helping them get going on the game, it's far too unusual in this day and age. I will try to keep this relatively succinct.
Graphics: The game is beautiful, right up there with the best of the AAA titles (if not better than them). I have a hard time thinking of a game that has done environments at this level. (5/5)
Sound: The music and sound effects are spot-on, moody and atmospheric without ever bashing you over the head in that regard. (5/5)
Gameplay: The gameplay felt, unfortunately, a little more straightforward than I might have otherwise liked in a game of this nature. To wit, the only time I was really "stuck" was because I couldn't find a fifth environmental item - it had nothing to do with being stumped by a puzzle, rather I just hadn't stepped in the right area to cause something to pop up. That is to say that I would have liked the puzzles to require more ingenuity on behalf of the player and a bit more creativity. Everything was very straightforward. While that avoids frustration, it also limits the sense of achievement when you "solve" the puzzles as it never felt like you were really acting as a detective or solving puzzles in the way that games like Myst did. This is puzzle-lite. Some people will like that, but it definitely felt very casual friendly in that regard despite the warning at the start of the game that it does not hold your hand. (3/5)
Story: That being said, the story was original and lovely. It wasn't momentous in the sense that games like Walking Dead and Last of Us made you care so much about the protagonists that you were brought to tears during the climax, but it was thoughtful and engrossing enough to keep you want to keep going to unravel the mystery surrounding the eponymous character. Intelligently things that seem cliche at one point make sense as you grow an understanding of what it is that's going on. (4/5)
Value: The game is on the shorter side. I just beat it in less than 4 hours - solving every puzzle along the way. It's up to you to decide whether a four hour game warrants the price - for me I equate it to going to see a movie, so in my mind this is money better spent. But for those looking for a game where you are getting dozens of hours of playtime, this isn't it - especially considering there is really no reason for replayability (as it wouldn't change on multiple playthroughs).
Overall
+ Graphics are superlative
+ Sound and music is terrific
+ Story is original and engaging
- Gameplay is simple
- Puzzles are very easy
- Game is quite short

As I stumble through the overgrowth outside of Red Creek Valley I suspect I'm not a welcome visitor. Within five minutes of getting off the train tracks I've stumbled upon a series of gruesome traps, and not the sort you'd leave for any wild game. Flails and springs and pits. No, these traps are for curious outsiders. And intuition tells me it's claimed more than a few of the less observant ones... intuition and the shattered bones that litter the forest floor. This little hamlet has a dark secret, one tied directly to the disappearance of one Ethan Carter. And I intend to uncover the truth.
After a few (seemingly) close calls I stop in a clearing to appreciate the sheer beauty of this pristine place. The trees sway lazily; some have made the transition into their fall colors, and some remain stubbornly verdant. The grass has grown high and unruly, claiming patches of neglected road, working in tandem with a blanket of primeval ferns. Freight cars sit unused, decaying on the tracks. It's at that moment I realize I've encountered no people, no wildlife. And the world around me suddenly grows still, anxiously waiting for me to move, to stop dawdling, to leave. But I can't. I may not be able to see it, but I know something is watching me, this clumsy outsider. Something malevolent, old, and hungry.
“The Vanishing of Ethan Carter” can best be described as a mystery horror exploration narrative. While it isn't overtly frightening, it has an overwhelming atmosphere. The community of Red Creek Valley is a lot like iconic Silent Hill - except with an older, more sinister vibe. The decrepit setting slowly being swallowed by nature, the eerie crime scenes, the soft music, and excellent, grumbly narration all marry together to form a very unsettling, hypnotic surrounding. This is a town where Lovecraft's ancient, twisted gods rule. You are most certainly unwelcome. And you will feel that from beginning to end.
But like any good paranormal detective you'll press onward in spite of traps, murder scenes, and inexplicable, disembodied narration. You're Paul Prospero (Shakespeare's “The Tempest” anyone?), and this is your last case (you're roughly two weeks from retirement!). And this kid Ethan, with his special gift... he's relying on you. To find him. To save him. And to find out what's happened to this place and its colorful denizens.
As you explore you'll find clues and piece together what happened at certain locations. You'll spot abnormalities, anomalies, and the like. Sometimes something will be missing and there's a mechanic in which the item, for instance a crank, will show up as scattered text. If you look in the right direction the text will come together and you'll be able to see where item is located using your occult powers. Finally, if there's a victim in the vicinity and you've gathered enough clues, you'll have the opportunity to piece together what happened by “communicating” with the dead and reliving their final moments. And when you gather evidence and set the chronology of actions in order, man does it feel rewarding. And there's enough variety to keep these paranormal encounters fresh. And while the game is linear you'll have the freedom to explore and solve puzzles in whatever order you like.
This is a slow, methodical, meticulous sort of game. The sort of game you should play by yourself with your favorite comfort drink and no distractions. Really immerse yourself. It's one of the best looking games I've ever played – near photo realistic. The story is riveting, bizarre, and unflinchingly violent. This is an exploration game done right, with gameplay that challenges you to be observant and thoughtful. It's short, sure, but every hour is worthwhile and it doesn't overstay its welcome. “Ethan Carter” is a love letter; to Lovecraft and all things weird, and to classic detective stories. This is easily one of the best indie titles released in 2014.

"The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" is an interesting experiment in narative driven game design, with just enough gameplay to keep even the most sceptical person interested for the duration of the experience. The puzzle and murder solving gameplay is interesting and engaging, although the murder solving part becomes quite easy to figure out after solving the first murder. Also, the story itself is doesn't feel as tight and well written as the developers, keeping much of the game a secret, led me to believe, and the twist is predictable and not very satisfying... but that is simply my opinion.
However, the most damning thing about this game is it length, clocking in at around 2-3 hours with no reason to replay other than to admire the gorgeous world design and graphics.
Overall, "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" is a title I would recommend for fans of adventure games and people interested in an interesting, if a bit lackful, story. Just know, the current price of 19 euros might be a bit much for most people for an three hour experience, which is understandable.

If you are expecting Arma 3 and Crysis engine concepts, you will be let down, but if you take this game as it stands (free) and  grasp the concepts between the classes, you will have fun.

Straight up no eyefinity support. Just gutted. If any game needed support for eyefinity it is this atmospheric game. Just can't fathom why??? It supports changing view angles and uses the Unreal engine.
I think walking simulator is an apt description as you will spend most of your time doing this. The puzzles are reasonably cerebral however so if you liked Myst I think you will really enjoy this game. If you are content to let the world seep into you there is a lot to like, however the on rails nature of the world is too restrictive and I got sick of hitting all the invisible walls. The graphics are wonderful, but there is micro stutter everytime the unreal engine loads new content (ala Remember Me).
There is no journal, no map and no goals or progression. Whilst this is refreshing I can see many wondering "what the hell am I supposed to do?"..which is possibly the point! But this is sure to put many off.
I will update this review as flawless widescreen has hacked in support for eyefinity and nvidia surround resolutions, which makes a massive difference to immersiveness of the game. I have also modified the .ini files for a smoother experience, the game has also had a healthy 1GB patch. So out of the box the experience needs some tweaking but it can be made incredibly beautiful on a high end rig now. As the game progresses it feels a little less restrictive but it is still mostly a linear game. There are a few jump scares so it's not all mood, but not as effective as Outlast (a better designed horror experience and my game of the year so far). Again if you loved Myst you will love this game, but personally I found Myst a mountain of obtuse frustration and ended up following a walkthrough..however somehow Ethan Carter manages to provide enough logic for me to figure out the puzzles without too much difficulty. Still more variation in puzzle design is sorely needed from what I have played so far.
And it's all over. A very short experience despite my attempt to backtrack and check everything. By the time the credits rolled I had experienced and solved all the puzzles. It's really only half a game and that makes me a sad panda. Steam sale contender folks..

This game is borderline unfair. There's challenging gameplay, like with XCOM or Xenonauts, but then there's this. This is unfair.
I set the game to normal setting, since I didn't know what I was getting myself into, and every single battle I could only win by the skin of my teeth. I would always lose my escort ship and the line ships would suffer heavy damage. The battles that I lost, which were many, were one-sided massacres where the enemy had more ships and I got stuck with the same 3 over and over again.  The AI seems to be a model of efficiency, always maneuvering and knowing EXACTLY what to do, and here I am trying to keep a handle on, well, everything. I wasn't having fun.
The graphics were nice, perfectly capturing the look of the Warhammer 40000 universe. But my praise ends there. The tutorial was minimal, only going over the barebones of ship engagements. So when I was left to my own devices against enemy AI who knew their ship's every strength and weakness, I got crushed. XCOM's a punishing game, and it's one of my favorites, but XCOM also had the courtesy to give you a basic battle plan in the tutorial: flanking, use of cover, special equipment, the works.
Battlefleet left me totally lost most of the time. And what's worse is that I couldn't even have the pleasure of playing as the Orks, who were the primary reason I bought the game.
So, yeah. Battlefleet Gothic: Armada. Great concept, but man oh man, it needs some serious rebalancing. This is a game that demands you be good at it as soon as you pick it up.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown and its expansion, Enemy Within is a game about choice.
Will you favor your R&D team, allowing you to use powerful alien weapons, or will you spend your credits on satellites, which will help you monitor countries part of the XCOM project, and potentially getting better funding? Will you only bring your veteran soldiers on this mission, knowing that if you make a mistake, your rookies will have little experience in fighting aliens and will probably get slaughtered in the next mission, or will you 'blood' your rookies in a 'safe' environment by mixing them and your vets?
Will you use your engineers to build a MEC suit -a powerful armor that can interface with a cyborg-, helping with your ground team's survivability, or will you build a Firestorm, an interceptor capable of splashing down the biggest UFOs with ease?
Whether it is on the tactical or strategical level, XCOM has incredible depth, depth that is furthered if you play the Long War mod.
If you have been left unsatisfied by vanilla XCOM, give it a try.
Long War extends the campaign, with more frequent and more numerous missions than the original XCOM.
It allows you to bring more soldiers to battle as well, and lets you choose which kind of soldier you want them to be -Assault, Infantry, Sniper, Scout, Engineer, Medic, etc...-
It modifies perk and abilities trees, adds new technologies to research. It expands psionics gameplay, overhauls the Alien AI.
And if you play it on Ironman mode -no save scumming- and Classic or Impossible difficulty, as you should, then you'll need to micro & macromanage everything to even have a hope of winning.
Long War is XCOM as it should have been from the beginning, and while it is nut-crushingly hard, it is also incredibly rewarding.
If had to rate the game, I'd give a 7/10 for XCOM:EU and XCOM:EW. With Long War, it's easily a 9/10.

Cliff Bleszinski is famously quoted as to have said to have a great game you just need "to nail that 30 seconds of gameplay and be able to repeat it". This applies to certain genres more than others, but it certainly can be used to describe twin stick arcade shooters, where without a story, expansive world, or other conduit typically used to draw you to the experience, it all comes down to getting the core gameplay right.
gets it.
Making no false claims as to what it is,
twin stick shooter drops you into a level and asks you to kill everything that moves. As you destroy enemies they drop credits which you can use to upgrade your bot, replenish your shields, or adopt an array of gadgets to help you stay alive. It's intentionally uncomplicated and that is what makes it so freaking fun!
Gliding around in your little homicidal robot feels like an extension of yourself, and the resistance put up by your endlessly spawning enemies coupled with the ensuing explosion when they bite the dust is absolutely perfect, and never stops being satisfying no matter how many times you repeat it. Enemy patterns are varied just enough to keep the experience fresh, and  over the game's 40 levels various levels are sprinkled challenge events and boss fights that become increasingly challenging the further in you get.
Although I've never been known to suffer from epilepsy, I appreciated that the developers didn't go as crazy as they could have with the visuals. There is a lot of graphical flair going on at any one time, but rarely did it become detrimental to the gameplay by obscuring enemies, and is actually used as a clever way to increase difficulty as later levels are darker lit and require a keener eye to pick out enemies (but never to the point of being unfair).
For pure arcade shooting I've rarely had the pleasure of playing one as fun and well crafted as
. While it may lack content up front, it makes up for it by being replayable just for the sake of revisiting the game (with the added benefit of local co-op, which is a literal blast). As a fan of the genre I found it an absolute joy to play, and am sure to be comparing similar games to it from now on. If you are in the mood for an easy to pick up but hard to put down bit of robot blasting carnage, I think it would be hard to do much better.

I clicked a thumbs up because I think the author tried their best most likely, and I had fun streaming this game on Twitch and hanging out with my friends while I played it. There are also two mustache characters (the dev should add a dating system so I can date George).
So since I enjoyed my time with the game, I decided to pick "Yes." But this is a heavily flawed game. I feel many people could feel like even their $1 was wasted on this game, so please read the review if you might want to use your money on another game.
The concept behind the game is quite clever. Basically, the core of the gameplay revolves around making dialogue choices to uncover things about characters you can use to frame them, as well as choosing two items to use in your deed (generally, an 'evidence' item to plant, and a weapon, though you can choose two evidences or two weapons if you want).
With many conversation paths and all of the various combinations of evidence, rooms to plant evidence, and weapons to use, there are a lot of different ways the game seemingly can unfold. The main entertainment in the game is from playing repeatedly (the game is only 20 minutes long or so the first couple of times, and you can go as fast as 5 minutes on successive runs if you're not bothering to read all the text you already read before)
But this is where the first real problem with the game arises. You don't have to be perfect and make every "right" choice in order to frame someone, which is good, since there are tons of possible combinations of things to say and item usages. But what's very disappointing is that the solutions are so obvious and loose to success that you once you frame one person, you can pretty much follow the same 'formula' to frame anyone just as easily. There's almost no variety in the solutions, and everything is so obvious you'd have to purposely try to fail. I got an "unsolved" case my first game because I was just experimenting with the systems and choosing whatever, but after that I solved everyone on my first try without any effort.
Which items are connected to which character are so obvious you don't even need to talk to the characters to guess who it should be linked to. Your dad's shotgun is obviously linked to your dad. Your mom's diary is obviously about your mom. The descriptions of the items will usually just tell you almost directly who it will help frame.
The conversation paths are pretty much the same. Basically just make sure you talk to the person you're wanting to frame, and they'll just reveal something you can abuse as a motive and you're done. There are like one or two cases where you'll have to be careful about what you pick or actually talk to more than one person. But that's rare. You generally will have the option of being extremely rude to the person which will make them not talk to you, or doing literally anything else which will have them reveal a motive for you.
As for evidence dropping, it seemed to me as long as you dropped the evidence in a certain room, it would always point to the person you're wanting to frame. For every character in the game except one, I dropped the evidence in that room and it worked perfectly.
By the end of the game, I was starting to become convinced you could use any weapon you wanted and still frame whoever you wanted, too. The solutions seemed loose enough for that. I think you could even shoot her in the back with a shotgun and get it ruled a suicide.
But if you somehow don't realize the best solution right away, you could play through a few times and still be curious about how to frame someone. Plus, you have a lot of dialogue options to play with, so you can at least try a few different branches to see what they say.
But that's the biggest problem with the game -- the writing is abysmal. And I don't just mean the fact that it obviously was not proofread. But the author is definitely an amateur. Expect the story quality to be on par with something like the Jeff the Killer creepypasta.
There's a ton of awkwardness that arises from the story not being thought through well or proofread by another person, from the character knocking on the door to the house when he is expected and the butler is already escorting him, to being able to kill someone with a few whacks with a lightweight broomstick, without them causing any kind of struggle or reaction.
Most of the story revolves around getting to know the characters and the aspects of them you use to frame them. And almost none of the murder motives make any sense. And the conversations all feel a bit rushed and unnatural. Everyone's motive seems to boil down to one character trait about them. "He has a temper, so obviuosly he would kill someone." That kind of thing. Sometimes the "character flaw" you're exposing doesn't even make sense as a murder motive. "He sexually harasses women" is not a murder motive. "She's a lesbian" is not a murder motive.
Even the main character who really is the killer -- I don't really understand why he wants to kill his sister. He hates his family and left them to start his own independent life, where he was apparently doing just fine. But now he decides he is going to go through the trouble of killing his own sister and framing someone for it so that he can get an inheritence... of a family name and property and business that he hates and wants to have no part in?
But by far the worst part about the writing is that the story attempts to cover a lot of serious themes -- mental illness, suicide, child abuse, sexual harassment, murder motive, etc. -- but the author clearly doesn't know much about these things and did not research any of these topics and handles them all completely inappropriately and unrealistically. These topics are portrayed with ignorance and shallowness.
The portrayal of a person suffering from mental illness amounts to pretty much how a small child would describe a "crazy person." I realize that in the 1940s, mental health issues were not commonly understood at all, and doctors did indeed just diagnose "insanity." It would make sense for the characters to talk about mental illness in an ignorant way -- but a character who is supposed to actually suffer from a mental illness should, well, actually be written like a person with a real mental health issue, even if it's not understood by the characters themselves. I feel like the author doesn't understand mental illness any more than a 1940s doctor would.
Pretty much every serious topic in the game is handled in the same manner. The game is clearly meant to be taken seriously, and it is story-driven, so the story needs to be well-researched, proofread, and developed, but it sorely fails in this area. If I hadn't been playing while talking to everyone on twitch and being able to talk and laugh about it, I may have been extremely frustrated with the poor writing. Instead, my friends and I have some new in-jokes based on some of the ridiculousness (poison turns you green, cunning pixie, etc.)
If you're wanting an interesting or intriguing story, or gameplay that requires a lot of tough decision making to solve (or rather, commit!) a murder, don't waste your dollar. Stay far away from this game.
If you're wanting to see a clever idea despite its clunky execution and don't mind that the solutions will be too obvious and the writing may as well contain a Sonic the Hedgehog self-insert OC, go ahead and try it. I had fun for 4 hours with it.
Although the game was marred by severe game-wide flaws, I appreciated the idea behind the game and what it was going for, enjoyed the mustaches, had some laughs, and even felt a bit inspired by the concept of the whole thing. Maybe I'll try to make a game with a similar type of concept some day. All of that is worth a dollar. I got this as a gift for my birthday, though, and so I definitely can't complain. It was a good gift.

The Deed is a very short RPG game (completed within about 20-30 minutes if you read everything, 10 if you just click) where you have to murder your sister at a dinner party and not get caught. You have to pick up two items, one evidence item and one weapon. Or, you could plant two evidence items and use your bare hands to kill her.
Was the game worth the $0.60? YES. Would you say it is worth more? Yes, but not much due to its length. However, you can play it over and over again and as you do, you realize that the story behind the game is actually quite detailed. It's amazing how the creators of this game managed to portray every character's personality so well in the short amount of time the game takes to play.
An interesting thing in this game is the fact that you get to see some flashbacks from your past when you look at/interact with certain items, such as the mirror in the hallway and the chair in your parents' room. It's a nice touch and it really helps you get a sense of what the main character went through as a child and why he has his mind set on killing his sister.
And on to the best part: the weapons! Although this game takes place inside a house and runs a very short time, there are a great deal of weapons and things to choose from, such as but not limited to, a pool cue, a broom handle, a broken mirror, a shotgun and even a fencing sword! The variety in this game is phenominal and you can tell just by looking at it how much love and effort went into creating it - the atmosphere, the characters and everything.
Overall, if I was to give this game a rating out of 10, 1 being terrible and 10 being absolutely groundbreaking - I'd give this game a 7/10 for being a good, simple, and creative way to spend 20 minutes and $0.60. If you have a love for murder mysteries and the like, I highly recommend this game. Seriously, it's so cheap and so much fun, you'd be a fool not to buy it.

Oh where to start? I just finished the game which according to Steam took me 7 hours and all I can say is that I had no clue I'd been sitting here that long. No wonder I'm hungry. Right out the gate, now that I've finished it I can see why they are only charging $20 bucks for it.
While the game can be as long as the 7 hours I took and possibly longer if you really have to see every single rock in the game, the game can also be ran through and beaten a lot quicker if you're not too busy stopping to admire the view along the way. In my opinion they made a mistake including the ability to run because while you do have to cover large distances to get from one plot point to the other, the game is so breathtakingly beautiful that it's nice just to walk through it, looking around and taking your time. I must say I'm in love with the tech they used for the graphics. The Next Elder Scrolls game could learn a thing or two from The Astronauts if you ask me.
Graphics - Doesn't need much of a review. The screenshots and videos speak for themselves although Youtube's compression really doesn't do it justice. Ran the game on High settings at 1920x1200 using a GeForce GTX 560 and the only time I really experienced any stuttering was when I was running. (Another reason I chose to walk everywhere) They made a great choice using the Unreal Engine because in my experience Epic's engine is one of the most optimized game engines ever. You get a lot of graphics bang for your buck. Probably why so many games use it.
One thing I did notice about the graphics because I looked very closely at everything is that despite them saying you won't see any tiling textures in the game, you do indeed see some throughout the game. One completely obvious and unfortunately not that well done texture that you can tell is tiled is on the train at the beginning. As you walk up to the front of it, if you go to the left and look at the cab you can see the same texture tiling over and over again horizontally wrapping around the cab of the train all the way to the other side until you get to the door. Also there's an area I think on the way to the cemetery where you can find some dead trees that are reletively in the same area and every single one of the dead trees is the exact same model just rotated a little bit around the Z axis a little from the others. I don't know if I just catch these because I 3D model or they are this obvious to everybody but I was assuming that I wasn't going to be seeing stuff like that. I mean how hard is it to apply a bend modifier to a few branches to make a few variations? Those types of things were the only part about the graphics I had a problem with and only because they made a huge deal on their website about how their game wasn't going to do that kind of stuff.
Voice Acting and Story - They are both top notch. The story is pretty melancholy. The ending made my eyes water up a bit but that could be because I've been sitting in a pitch black room staring at a bright monitor for 7 hours straight. There are two different types of plot points to find. There are story pages and crime scenes. While the crimes scenes helped to piece together the storyline, the story pages are where this game really shined for me. I just wish that the story pages were more drawn out. They had some amazing scenes but unfortunately just like the main valley they were mostly aesthetic.
Gameplay - If you enjoyed Gone Home or Dear Esther then you're probably going to like this game. I'm a bit more action oriented myself and while I love a good mystery and story this didn't really provide much gameplay for me. The game basically consists of looking at pretty stuff and solving around 8 puzzles (random trial and error in some of the puzzles probably increased my playtime.) Also, while the game does appear to be some sort of open world there is an obvious path to take and branching off the beaten path usually just rewards you with a wall of impassable boulders or trees and occasionally a steep cliff. There's no jump in the game so some of the large boulders that aren't used as barriers you can walk right up and over which is weird because some boulders the same size being used as barriers you can’t. Also if you encounter an elevator and the button isn't working you can walk off the edge and fall 3 or 4 stories and nothing happens to you. The problem with doing this is that you'll see all the plot points in reverse. While doing it is immersion breaking it isn’t game breaking to my knowledge. I personally reloaded a checkpoint before I fell down to the bottom so I could be wrong about that though.
[Edit] Apparently a day after it was released, enough people (me included) e-mailed them about the elevator shaft bug and so they have gone and fixed it so that you can no longer fall down it. Glad to see they are listening to the fans. Awesome job Astronauts!
Sound - Sound can be a big part of a game if it's done right and in this game they definitely got it right. Using 7.1 surround sound headphones I found myself turning around in a panic several times because I heard some strange noise behind me. The game definitely has some atmospheric moments where you're wondering what's going to be around the next corner. Oh and the music is pretty great as well. Works with the story. Not my cup of tea music wise but it was what this kind of game needed. I probably wouldn't listen to it outside of the game though so the digital soundtrack I got for preordering is going to be useless to me. So will the digital map for that matter now that the game is over for me.
Controls - You walk, you run, you crouch once or twice, you click, and you press spacebar to perform scene skips and such. It's hard to screw that up and luckily they didn't. I did find myself hitting spacebar a few times only to smack myself in the head after remembering there is no jump for the 10th time.
Replay Value - Extremely Low. Besides jumping back on the game to show it to a friend, screen grab some wallpapers or just to stare at a forest for a while because like me you live in an ugly desert there really is no reason to load it back up. A modding tool or story editor would have added to this games replay value immensely. They should have taken a cue from Amnesia. Heck, they mention Frictional Games in the credits so hopefully at some point they'll create some sort of editor to increase the replay value.
Things I would have liked to have seen but didn't - Varying weather like rain and thunder storms and a day night cycle. Guess without giving our protagonist a flashlight the night cycle would have probably detracted from the beauty of the game by hiding a majority of it in darkness. But the rain, thunder, flashes of lightning, and high winds would have been cool especially in the graveyard area. You kind of see the high wind effect when he's doing his whole psychic thing but not to the extent I would have liked. I'm just a big fan of rain because I live in a desert though.
Should you buy it? -  If you can afford to drop $20 bucks on a game with pretty much no replay value and it looks interesting to you then I'd say go for it. I personally sort of wish I had waited until the price dropped to something closer to 10 bucks (I’m a cheap♥♥♥♥♥ but at the same time this game was so absolutely beautiful that the hard work the developer put into this game is most definitely worth the whole $20 even if the game itself isn't. Retopologizing high poly models is a PITA (I know from experience). Support hard work and innovation. I was hoping this was going to keep me preoccupied until Alien Isolation and The Evil Within came out but it's really a one sitting and done kind of a game. I probably won't go back to it again if they don't add anything new or enable us to mod it.
All that being said I'd give this game an 8 out 10. Would have been a 9 if there was more to do, a 10 if it had replay value.

NEOTOKYO offers some refreshing FPS dynamics between playable classes and objective-centered gameplay, accentuated by a surprisingly large choice in mapped environments. Its community (a rather small one, I admit) consists largely of people willing to engage in teamplay, which does players' experiences a lot of good. I'd say the best thing about the mod is its setting, however. A cybernetics-focused and futuristic look at Tokyo and its surroundings, with a war raging between two groups: extremist nationalists by the name of JINRAI, who's aim is to perform a coup and establish a military dictatorship; and the Interior Ministry's National Security Forces (NSF), who attempt to maintain the political status quo and thus fight off the extremist forces. The mod's art (modeling, maps, sounds, etc) complements its setting extremely well, and succeeds in immersing you within the set universe, even if its story is minimal at best. Even if the game's content does not succeed in convincing you of its ambience, it is hard to deny the large amounts of work that the developers put into the creation of said assets.
NEOTOKYO is by no means revolutionary, however, and one should not enter its universe with high hopes or broad expectations. It's a simple shooter with some fun and fresh mechanics (particularly its recurring objective and the classes players can choose from) with well-done art direction. That said, its potential is great, but is held back by the mod's age and lack of significant updates. Let's hope its steam release proves to be a communitary catalyst for things to get clicking once more. And even if it doesn't, it's still bloody free-- so give it a shot, people.

At its best, Saints Row IV is a love letter to the franchise. At its worst, the game is just a copy and paste of Saints Row The Third with aliens and superpowers.
Superpowers! Blast, Telekinesis, Stomp (each with varying elements like Freeze or Fire), Super Jump, Super Sprint (previewed in SR3 The Trouble With Clones DLC) and several more form the core of the game play, and are the primary attraction. Why take a car when you can run faster than a car? Is that building in your way? Jump over it. Too tall to jump over it? Not to worry: you can wall-run! Need to take out that group of enemies? Sure, you can use guns; but why not drop into the middle of them and stomp your foot once to send them flying? Much easier! The catch is that the superpowers do make the game generally easy (the Superhero Fight Club activities being the frustrating exception).
The story of Saints Row IV is, of course, completely over-the-top. But that's not out of place in a Saints Row game. Rescuing members of your crew requires visiting a simulation of that homie's worst nightmare. There are some fantastic nostalgia trips (you even revisit some of the original Saints Row game) and funny satire (no game or movie is exempt, not even Metal Gear or Mass Effect). Much of it is accompanied by a great selection of songs; shooting up a Genki challenge with a certain character (long thought dead) while “The Boys are Back” was hilarious. While not every character from the franchise appears, all the major ones do.
The downside is that Saints Row IV is, at its heart, a copy-and-paste of Saints Row The Third. Steelport is virtually unchanged; the city map is exactly the same. Activities are exactly the same; Tank Mayhem, for instance, is the same activity with an alien Zin tank instead of an Abrams tank. The planes and aerial vehicles are reskinned SR3 models; they fly and function exactly the same. Hijacking cars is even still a thing; the in-game explanation makes sense, but doesn't hide anything else. With superpowers, cars are a waste anyway. Weapons are unique and fun; but if you've played Red Faction: Armageddon, more than a few will be familiar (Volition developed both games). There's a lot more, but you get the idea.
If you're looking for originality and uniqueness, you won't find it Saints Row IV (outside of the superpower implementation, which is superb). If you're looking for a game that is simply a blast to play – one that will make you laugh far more than it will make you scream in frustration – then absolutely get this game. In a time when all forms of entertainment are getting more serious, the absurdity of Saints Row IV is an absolute breath of fresh air.

This is a very nice game for two dollars. What is the game? It's a silly slice-em-up top-down view game of a pirate dual wielding curved swords whilst floating above the ground, slicing his way through armies and armies space zombies.
The controls are very simple. WASD to move. Left mouse button to attack in a direction. Space to use your super ability. The game is also controller friendly, which is very nice. However I think the keyboard is the better selection for gameplay because with the controller you have to face the direction in which you want to attack and the keyboard you do not have to do that, you can attack in a direction without facing.
You can collect gold coins or small piles of gold coins off of some defeated enemies and after you collect a certain ammount of gold you can start buying upgrades for your character in the upgrade menu. You can access this from the post-death screen or the main menu. You can also check the leaderboards to see your score, your friend's scores, and other player's scores.
The soundtrack adds to the silliness, as when you begin your slaying, the music in the background is What Shall We Do With A Drunken Sailor. It's very funny when you first open the game and you hear that playing as you slice up zombies in space.
I believe this game is definately worth the two dollars and a playthrough.

Dark and Light has HUGE potential as a sandbox mmo with pretty significant rpg elements, if the devs keep on it. It has a stunningly beautiful world, fierce mythical creatures, and mechanics that have been improved, and are improving, over the devs' predeccesor, Ark.
While the current playable map is Ark sized, you'll see in the lobby screen that the game map will be expanded by at least 8x what Ark has provided, and for me, that means a lot. Ark was much too small for all they wanted to put into it, and the amount of players that could be on it.
I'm absolutely loving my experience so far with what the game has to offer.
That being said; it is most definitely an Early Access title. It's buggy, it's glitchy. You will lose things/progress due to these bugs and glitches. If you're interested in this game, but not okay with bugs, put this game on your follow/wishlist and watch it for a while. Don't dive in to an EA game if you're not ready to battered with bugs/glitches. Especially when it could ruin what would have been a great game for you; just be patient.
However, if you're okay with bugs and glitches, and potentially losing progress to them, I definitely recommend giving this game a try. Generally, of the few different servers I have tried, the community seems pretty fair, and quite helpful. I personally have not experienced consistent crashing, as others have claimed to have. I am, however, purchasing a better video card for it. ;)
An ssd is also reccommended, as the game will have quite long load times without one.
