I've been playing Enemy Within.  My opinion: great game, 9/10. Entertaining, nice graphics, plenty of strategy on both tactical and macro levels, a number of possible play styles, research options, buildings and equipment set ups, reasonably interesting story, and an enjoyable if unmemorable soundtrack that does a pretty good job at being foreboding, or getting you pumped--mostly rock, trancey stuff, and some music that sounds like it's from the 80's.
I have to say the characters and acting are pretty wooden--but my number one disappointment is that I find the engine too much rules-based. For example, I'm somewhere in the vicinity of 40-80% the way through the game now, and for a few weeks in-game time I've been waiting to build a second Satellite Nexus, which would quickly have allowed me to pretty much max my income. But, lo and behold, it turned out I couldn't build the thing. Why?
Turns out I need more engineers. I only have 48, but I need 50. WTF? If this were many, many other games out there, I'd be able to begin construction of my Satellite Nexus now. Of course it would take a bit longer with 48 engineers than if had 50 to do the work--but I still should be able to START building the thing now. Silly rules.
This is literally probably the single most disappointing thing I've encountered in XCOM: Enemy Within, and it's really not even that big of an issue; but there are a bunch of smaller annoyances I have with the game, which is why I can only give it 9/10.
Now, to the nitty-gritty. First, a few points about my expectations before I played this game.
I heard about this game ~2013, around when it came out. I'd watched a few online vids of the XCOM from the early 90's and so had an idea of the gameplay. After reading some reviews and watching videos, I was really interested in playing this new game, someday. And just a few weeks ago, I bought Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within for cheap. I have been very pleased.
I was kind of worried. When I saw that it was on sale on Steam a few weeks back I took a look at some reviews, and a couple concerns grew. I saw a number of complaints about bugs, and several people complained about difficulty too. I was concerned I might be throwing my money away, but I'm happy to say I did not. I encountered one bug very early on--after I put a soldier on Overwatch, I became unable to issue further orders or end my turn, and had to exit the game. This was so early on that I got worried it was a portent of things to come; but I think a day or two later I played again, and I don't think I've encountered a single bug in all the dozens of hours I've played since.
So far as difficulty, I haven't had trouble. I don't remember if I'm playing on easy or normal difficulty (whatever they're called). What I did was play for 2 or 3 hours until I had a decent feel for the game, and then started over again, feeling quite a bit more aware of the basics. That's basically what I'd recommend for new players. After all, if a bunch of world governments have given you tons of money and placed you in charge of a secret organization that combats invading aliens . . . they're probably gonna make sure you're pretty competent at your job first, right?
I also admit I've used save and load game a lot. There are just too many things that annoy me about the game engine. So I guess you can try the Ironman mode if you want, which I gather basically turns the game into a roguelike, with only one save available. But I just really don't feel that the game deserves an Ironman mode. There are just too many stupid rules for it to be worthwhile, IMO.
Let's talk about some of those rules. Each turn, each of your soldiers gets two moves. If you take an actual action--fire a weapon, throw a grenade, use a medikit, go on Overwatch--you use up both moves. Or, you can use the first move to move your character a few meters, and then use an item/go on Overwatch, which is what I usually do; or you can use both moves to make your character move twice as far across the map.
Maybe I just am too spoiled from FPS's and stuff like FTL, but this isn't how it should work. FTL: Faster Than Light does it better, if you ask me. There are no turns in FTL. You can pause the game and give your characters orders, but while it's unpaused both your guys and the enemies act all at the same time. XCOM would be better off doing something like that.
Other annoying XCOM rules: the game will show you EXACTLY where your grenades will land and how much they will destroy before you throw them, which feels pretty silly compared to the randomness of firing guns; on the other hand, you characters can only throw a grenade perhaps 10-15 meters, when the maximum should be about twice that (and in fact, the Battle Scanner your snipers get can be thrown at what I consider to be a realistic distance); you can only have one base; only one dropship; only 4 Interceptors per continent; a maximum of 6 people in a squad at a time, and even then you have to pay money to get the limit from 4 to 6; your base really isn't very large, so you can only build ~20 facilities, and only in two dimensions, not 3D, which is a huge lapse considering how the devs harped on the "ant farm" concept; electricity production results in a hard limit on stuff you can build, just like engineers--so you're using 73/77 of your produced energy? You can't build something that takes 5 energy. In reality, you'd just do it and cope with some slight brown-outs/blackouts, or turn off the lights in buildings you're not using right now.
There are some other issues I have with the rules, but it really shouldn't be too surprising, considering XCOM comes from the same guys that made Civ 5 (I had a strong dislike for the happiness and production systems in that game).
But if equipping and moving a badass squad around, shooting and blowing up aliens, scavenging and assimilating their tech, managing global panic and finances, and overseeing base constructions sounds fun to you, XCOM is your game. I've been more absorbed by this game than by anything in quite a while--I think it really is a great game, and 9/10 is well-deserved.

*Edit - I made a few comment updates to this review, the updates are in a single paragraphs wherever you see "*Edit".  There is a tiny bit of new information but nothing has been changed otherwise.*
There is a lot of misinformation about this game, and I'm only really posting a review to correct some of it.
First yes, it *currently* is online only because it was meant to be an online game played with others.  Nowhere in the description does it say "Single Player".  Nowhere.  It says it's an online survival game and single player isn't listed anywhere in the tags.  And yet people buy it and complain there isn't an offline mode because it didn't hit them over the head enough with the warnings that it's an online game?  It gets all the data from the server for the areas and such you're playing in.  It's not as if it is just needing an online connection for no good reason.  The game was made to be multiplayer and doesn't list itself as single player, and yet so many down vote the game because it doesn't come with something it never said it did.  Anyway they're making an offline mode, which I can't say if it's a good idea or not for a game meant to be played online but it's coming down the line.
*Edit - I do admit they could have done a better job explaining this is a hub based "light MMORPG"- and I feel they would have had more sales if they had done that.  You see other random people in game if you're in the same town areas as they are and can group up with them to play together as well as friends you invite.  Still they never said there was a single player mode anywhere so to complain that it's not single player is odd to me.  It would be like complaining Guild Wars 1 didn't have an offline mode.  These hub based light MMORPGs usually don't...*
Next the cut scenes - this game is based on the lore from the TV show Grimm.   Nick and Hank are looking through one of Nick's books of Grimm for information, and you're basically playing what they're reading about.  The cut scenes some people complain about that are just "two guys looking at a book" - that's the whole connection to the TV show and if you've watched Grimm you'll be happy with having that there.
On to the "slowness" of combat.  You start out with a huge piece of tree and then a giant club you're fighting with.  They are slow because they are meant to be more realistic.  You're a Grimm that's stronger than a normal person by far but still these are pretty huge weapons you're swinging.  You also start with a shield that's slower because of it's size.  Later on you can switch to faster weapons and a much faster shield.  Maybe they should have started you out with faster equipment so people would see how the game plays with them from the beginning, but they are an upgrade choice you are supposed to earn as you play.
I've had no issues at all with server lag, but my play time isn't very long yet so I'll keep playing and update a comment here if I do start to have server issues.
*Edit - Still no lag issues for me.  The game is made to learn the patterns monsters use and to avoid or block them early.  Some people play and think the game is being slow when it's performing like it is supposed to, but others may be out of the two server areas so actually would be having lag.  I've not had even the smallest amount personally being a US based player.*
When I connected there was a US server and a server in Europe.  Yes, if you are not in those areas maybe you will have issues playing.  There isn't just one or two servers that go up to 600 people - if a server in a region gets full another will appear, so you always get to play.  You're not locked out if you buy it and there are already 600 people online.
On to character creation - this is a little weird but you do have control over the look of your character it's just you have to let it randomly assign your look and then keep clicking to go through random looks.  If you click the gender button on the character creation screen it will randomize your look.  To get what you want you have to keep clicking the gender button of your choice and wait until it randomly comes up with a look you like.  It's weird and a bit annoying but not unheard of.  The way they do it definitely leans towards the "con" side, but you *do* have the ability to keep rolling random looks until you find what you like.  So you're not just forced to look one certain way.  I'm guessing some people just never pressed the gender buttons up top to see that it randomly changes the look each time you press one or the other.
The game is supposed to feel more like being in the real wilderness, so there are some open stretches without as many things to fight on them as some people are looking for I guess.  Having played other "survival" types of games it really isn't too much different than the way a lot of them are made like that.
If you're a Grimm fan you'll probably be pretty happy.  Being a Grimm fan myself, I am probably influenced towards liking this a bit more than I would have otherwise.  The game is fun to me and I would recommend it.
I can't really say if it should be $15 or $10 though yet because I need to play the game a lot more to decide.
*Edit - Yeah it's worth the $15.  The landscape seems repetitive if you stay in the same areas searching for stuff a long time, but the environment does change around a bit as you continue further into the game.  I do wish there was more variety earlier on, it's so beautiful, but it does change up slowly.  The game also gets much more active as you go along with lots of dangerous creatures all over.  It starts up a bit slow with mostly normal woodland creatures but it won't be long until you're swimming in harder and more interesting stuff.*
If you want the solo offline version you'll need to wait until they update it to say it's here.  If you like playing multiplayer games with friends on Steam and you both get this, it's pretty decent though.  It's also really cool for Grimm fans.  Other people may want to wait for a sale to get it.
Like every game that exists you should go check out longer gameplay videos before buying to see if it appeals to you.  That's pretty much a given but I felt I'd mention it anyway.  The game is quite beautiful but you should see it in action to help you decide if it's what you want or not.

After ~60 hours with the PS4 version of this game, and ~2 hours with this version (Core Fighters), I can safely say that DOA5:LR Steam is almost the same game as its 'next gen' counterpart.
First off, at its core, the gameplay is the same. You get the same fast, fluid, fun fighting action as you would in any version of this game; it's 100% intact (which should be the main priority for any fighting game). A few characters seem a little easier to win with than others (esp. DLC characters) but that's to be expected of any modern fighting game. However if you're playing the Core Fighters version (like me!), Kasumi & Hayabusa are more than good enough to get your feet wet online.
Secondly, having previously played the full version of this game and just now playing the Core Fighters version, I have to say that for a F2P title Core Fighters gives the player a lot to do from the start. Except for Story Mode, you can play every game mode with the 4 free characters given to you: Kasumi, Hayabusa, Ayane &
Hayate. That's Arcade Mode, Time Attack, Survival, Versus, Tutorial, Combo Challenge & Ranked Match. You can still earn costumes and titles for all 4 starting characters by playing these modes, too. To some, this isn't going to seem like a lot of content, but for others, everything you get in the F2P version is what you'd expect from a fighting game in 2016.
I've seen a lot of people complaining about this port, and the main issues seem to be:
1) Lack of online lobbies
2) Arcade port graphics
I'll admit that not having online lobbies to play in with friends is a bit of a let-down, but most of my time with every version of DOA5 has been spent in Ranked Match anyways, so I can't really weigh in on that one. As for the 'downgraded' (although not really because DOA5LR is technically still just a port of X360/PS3 DOA5) graphics...I can honestly say they don't matter all that much. You
increase the resolution and the quality of shadows to make up for this issue, but the games art direction and overall look are almost identical to every other version of this game.
As for other issues, I tried playing with Keyboard, 360 controller & DS4 controller and had no issues with any of them besides having to remap a few buttons. Achievements are fully implemented and working. Netcode is alright, but can take around 1-5 minutes to find a match. DLC is really overpriced, but of course you're not expected to buy all of it (also besides characters it's all just cosmetic fluff anyway).
To finish up, I'd say that if you want all of DOA5:LRs characters & story mode, wait for the 'Full Game' DLC pack to go on sale. Don't judge this port based on launch/early reviews; the game works and is both stable and good looking enough to play. If you just want a few characters to get stuck in with Tutorial, Arcade Mode or Ranked Match, definitely download Core Fighters and give it a chance.

One of the finest FPS games ever made. I have been playing it off and on since its initial release in 2009.
You can choose from three different classes which all have different strenghs and weaknesses.
Rounds play out similar to Counter Strike where when you die, you are dead until the next round begins. There are a variety of guns that can be unlocked during each individual match. The more points you earn from kills or doing objectives you will be able to access the higher tier weapons. There is no xp or leveling and your points do not carry over each map.
Gun play can be comparable to Counter Strike. Firing from the hip you will not have a crosshair and you will be slightly less accurate, but you can right click to bring up your crosshair and increase your accuracy.
Two out of the three classes have an active camo which will make them invisible(more invisible while standing still, and more visible while moving). Two of the three classes have a vision(motionvision and thermalvision) to combat the active camo. All classes start with different grenades/explosives and a different set of weapons unlocked at the beginning.
If you are looking for a highly skill based, tactical shooter, NEOTOKYO will satisfy your every craving.
I can firmly place this game next to CS 1.6 as being a masterpiece in the multiplayer FPS genre. PLAY THIS NOW.

I am not really a fan of fighting games. Only ones I played before this was Soul Calibur IV for PS3 and Killer Instinct for Super Nintendo. Actually loved both those games... But that being said I had a lot of fun with this game too. I read all the reviews before playing this and I knew online play was limited and I also knew the console version is somewhat superior. Softer looking skin and online play don't matter to me. I just want to play the damn game. No nonesense. And I got what I wanted. So if online play doesn't matter to you either, then please try this game!
The basic mechanics of a fighting game are all there. You get solo play, you get survival arenas where you fight enemy after enemy, time trials and team arenas.
The thing I liked is some of the stages are dynamic. You can be fighting in a quiet old looking apartment, blowing through walls and smashing tables and then bust through another wall onto the yard outside. Or throw your opponent off a tower and jump down to the street below. The changing settings is fast paced and doesn't break the flow of the fight at all. I also appreciate the amount of detail the settings have and the amount of it that can be destroyed. Destroying the environment doesn't appear to alter the stages that much, other than asthetically. Fires bursting from the walls or sparks flying, lots of flashy effects and busted pieces of metal and other things. The amount of environment damage gets pretty intense in prolonged fights.
You only get to choose 4 characters which is a disappointment but it is a free game afterall. The amount of content in the F2P version is incredible. Lots of people complaining about lack of content but I found there was a lot of content especially for a free game. You get all game modes except story mode, you get to choose all stages. NeoTokyo is easily one of the best Source mods ever made, and I'm so glad to see it join Steam's roster of high-quality mods. With some of the best gunplay you'll find in any Source engine title, and stellar game design and balance in general, it should be considered a must-play to anyone with even a passing interest in game development.
As a side note: this mod's sound design is simply the best of any mod I've ever played, with each shot and impact being satisfying beyond belief. Also, the soundtrack, produced by the incredibly talented Ed Harrison, has fir cemented him as one of the best mod composers of all time. Which is rather incredible, given how little of it you generally hear while actually playing it.
All in all, the whole package is a thing of genius; and you really do need to try it out for yourself. I guarantee that if this were remade with flashier graphics on a newer version of Source, the potential for its competitive scene would be incredible.

Strategy game that really does it own thing, A.I. sucks after a while, but well its an older game. Would recommend playing this with people after you get to know the game.
A bit more in depth:
In Perimeter the most important things is your main building, to which your first energy nodes have to be connected, and energy. you build an energy network by building energy nodes, which will collect energy(only resource in the game) for you and allows you to build other buildings in an area around that node. Every energy node has to be connected to your main building or another energy node that is connected to your network. If a piece of your base becomes unconnected it loses power and all buildings and nodes in that area become unpowered(neutral) this allows you to steal portions of your eachother's base. Energy management is key to this game, because almost every action will cost somewhere between a bit and alot of energy. Luckily you can also create a rainy day fund by building energy storing buildings.
Terraforming is the next important thing in the game. Sadly you can't build your own worlds. But if you want to build somewhere in Perimeter you need to make that area to "zero layer" (flat) ground. The closer the non-terraformed land is to zero-layer the faster it goes. You also can't extract energy from non-terraformed ground. You get 5 units that can terraform OR build. which gives you the choice for faster terraforming or building. Terraformed land can be destroyed again by any sort of explosive which leaves a crater that will slowly destroy any buildings on the now non-terraformed land, which could cause your building to blow up and leave another crater, which could cause buildings around it to be destroyed (and a chain reaction if you built all your buildings next to eachother).
In Perimeter you don't just build units and attack. The focus lies more in attack with your base, by building your network towards eachother and start firing some howitzer turrets to destroys eachother's base and land. attacking weak spots of the enemy with units or just sending wave after wave on a spot you know is not going to hold forever. You also get some special units, like an unit that can steal energy from the other, one that makes your units (except the unit himself) invisible or a few that can ruin terraformed land in a few ways. Units fill more a support role or raiding role in this game for me,
Turrets are your main way of attacking/defending. and the two factions each get a special turret (bit superweapon-ish but not OP, also costs alot of energy to charge)
Another important thing about units is they can transform into other units. How does this work? you have 3 basic units in the game: The soldier, the officer and the engineer. all other units are composed of a combination of these 3 units, example: 6 soldiers, 3 officers, 0 engineers. This allows your units to transform on the fly if the need arises(altough it leaves your units exposed while the transformation happens). Or change the units later into something else when you have better laboratories set up.
If all hells breaks loose and an area needs just that few extra seconds for your turrets to finish building and your force to arrive, you can throw up your Perimeter shield. The shield is indestructable but it drains your energy. Every energy node has the ability to throw up the Perimeter shield around the area of effect of the node and it will protect all buildings in that area of effect. Connected nodes will connect their shields. You can activate the shield individually per node or press Enter to activate all.
You win the game by destroying or capturing your enemy's main building.
NOTE: it took me a while to know how to capture a base. Some campaign missions ask for it and they don't tell you how to do it ingame. you have to build an energy node right next to the enemy's base and let his main building take off in the air. (destroy the ground under it so it takes damage) It's a bit annoying but you'll find out :P)

For a long time I got an impression Braid was too hard for me, as I'm not very experienced with puzzle games. When I finally played it, I learned that there is not much to be afraid of. As Jonathan Blow mentioned many times, Braid is the kind of game that just sort of came with a set of rules, caused by the specific relation between time and position. It's an idea that he decided to explore using creative, well thought-out puzzles that all show the player different results of the ruleset. There's no repetition as you walk through beautiful, stylish worlds of Braid and carefully observe the laws that rule them. Though the game can be hard at the beggining, it's logical and fair once you learn the rules. This mindset can be observed in The Witness as well, though I prefer Blow's experiments with speculative physics.

It has been a while since a game made me lost track of time. After finishing XCOM, I can safely say that XCOM is one of those games that managed to do just that.
The game has a strategy layer which involves researching and base building and also a tactical layer which was presented by battle against the aliens. The strategy layer is quite decent, though it boils down to simply choosing which upgrades to get first. I just wish the game offers more options in the beginning. For example, later on you can build a robot for your squadmate, but since it was unlocked a bit later, all my troopers are already strong enough without needing to add the robot.
The tactical layer is where the game truly, truly shines. Everytime a battle starts, I have this mixed feeling of joy and dread, excited to kick some alien♥♥♥♥♥while also afraid of losing a soldier. And surprisingly, the battle never lets up, whether it's early game or late game. As my troops got better, the game also introduces stronger enemies to keep up with me. And since a wounded soldier cannot participate in the next battle, every encounter with aliens in the battle is tense and exciting.
In the end, if you're a fan of strategy or tactical game in general, XCOM is a game for you. The game would easily satisfy your itch for a nerve-wraking and head-scratching battle.
Oh, and I also highly recommend getting both the base game and the Enemy WIthin expansion. The expansion adds more game mechanics and less story missions, so unless you don't mind going through the same campaign again, go get the expansion for your first playthrough.

I've been playing Enemy Within.  My opinion: great game, 9/10. Entertaining, nice graphics, plenty of strategy on both tactical and macro levels, a number of possible play styles, research options, buildings and equipment set ups, reasonably interesting story, and an enjoyable if unmemorable soundtrack that does a pretty good job at being foreboding, or getting you pumped--mostly rock, trancey stuff, and some music that sounds like it's from the 80's.
I have to say the characters and acting are pretty wooden--but my number one disappointment is that I find the engine too much rules-based. For example, I'm somewhere in the vicinity of 40-80% the way through the game now, and for a few weeks in-game time I've been waiting to build a second Satellite Nexus, which would quickly have allowed me to pretty much max my income. But, lo and behold, it turned out I couldn't build the thing. Why?
Turns out I need more engineers. I only have 48, but I need 50. WTF? If this were many, many other games out there, I'd be able to begin construction of my Satellite Nexus now. Of course it would take a bit longer with 48 engineers than if had 50 to do the work--but I still should be able to START building the thing now. Silly rules.
This is literally probably the single most disappointing thing I've encountered in XCOM: Enemy Within, and it's really not even that big of an issue; but there are a bunch of smaller annoyances I have with the game, which is why I can only give it 9/10.
Now, to the nitty-gritty. First, a few points about my expectations before I played this game.
I heard about this game ~2013, around when it came out. I'd watched a few online vids of the XCOM from the early 90's and so had an idea of the gameplay. After reading some reviews and watching videos, I was really interested in playing this new game, someday. And just a few weeks ago, I bought Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within for cheap. I have been very pleased.
I was kind of worried. When I saw that it was on sale on Steam a few weeks back I took a look at some reviews, and a couple concerns grew. I saw a number of complaints about bugs, and several people complained about difficulty too. I was concerned I might be throwing my money away, but I'm happy to say I did not. I encountered one bug very early on--after I put a soldier on Overwatch, I became unable to issue further orders or end my turn, and had to exit the game. This was so early on that I got worried it was a portent of things to come; but I think a day or two later I played again, and I don't think I've encountered a single bug in all the dozens of hours I've played since.
So far as difficulty, I haven't had trouble. I don't remember if I'm playing on easy or normal difficulty (whatever they're called). What I did was play for 2 or 3 hours until I had a decent feel for the game, and then started over again, feeling quite a bit more aware of the basics. That's basically what I'd recommend for new players. After all, if a bunch of world governments have given you tons of money and placed you in charge of a secret organization that combats invading aliens . . . they're probably gonna make sure you're pretty competent at your job first, right?
I also admit I've used save and load game a lot. There are just too many things that annoy me about the game engine. So I guess you can try the Ironman mode if you want, which I gather basically turns the game into a roguelike, with only one save available. But I just really don't feel that the game deserves an Ironman mode. There are just too many stupid rules for it to be worthwhile, IMO.
Let's talk about some of those rules. Each turn, each of your soldiers gets two moves. If you take an actual action--fire a weapon, throw a grenade, use a medikit, go on Overwatch--you use up both moves. Or, you can use the first move to move your character a few meters, and then use an item/go on Overwatch, which is what I usually do; or you can use both moves to make your character move twice as far across the map.
Maybe I just am too spoiled from FPS's and stuff like FTL, but this isn't how it should work. FTL: Faster Than Light does it better, if you ask me. There are no turns in FTL. You can pause the game and give your characters orders, but while it's unpaused both your guys and the enemies act all at the same time. XCOM would be better off doing something like that.
Other annoying XCOM rules: the game will show you EXACTLY where your grenades will land and how much they will destroy before you throw them, which feels pretty silly compared to the randomness of firing guns; on the other hand, you characters can only throw a grenade perhaps 10-15 meters, when the maximum should be about twice that (and in fact, the Battle Scanner your snipers get can be thrown at what I consider to be a realistic distance); you can only have one base; only one dropship; only 4 Interceptors per continent; a maximum of 6 people in a squad at a time, and even then you have to pay money to get the limit from 4 to 6; your base really isn't very large, so you can only build ~20 facilities, and only in two dimensions, not 3D, which is a huge lapse considering how the devs harped on the "ant farm" concept; electricity production results in a hard limit on stuff you can build, just like engineers--so you're using 73/77 of your produced energy? You can't build something that takes 5 energy. In reality, you'd just do it and cope with some slight brown-outs/blackouts, or turn off the lights in buildings you're not using right now.
There are some other issues I have with the rules, but it really shouldn't be too surprising, considering XCOM comes from the same guys that made Civ 5 (I had a strong dislike for the happiness and production systems in that game).
But if equipping and moving a badass squad around, shooting and blowing up aliens, scavenging and assimilating their tech, managing global panic and finances, and overseeing base constructions sounds fun to you, XCOM is your game. I've been more absorbed by this game than by anything in quite a while--I think it really is a great game, and 9/10 is well-deserved.

So I'm a "try before you buy" type of guy. You know what I mean.
This is one of those games that I tried, bought, then bought again. And again. And again. Because I looked at my "time played" statistic in game and realized I was getting close to 100 hours without giving the developers a dime. So I gave the devs money for copies for myself and several friends who I knew would like it. Whenever a friend has some money and is looking for a game to play, it's one of the games I recommend.
Now, how's it play? Well, it's a roguelike (or as the devs have called it, a "rogue-lite"). There's a set series of events you can run into (which is large) and a semi-randomly generated layout of sectors (which is itself part of a semi-randomly generated layout of systems). There are a
of different events you can run into. As I said, I had around 85 hours of gameplay in this game before I bought it on steam. At the time of this review, I have 47 on steam. When they added Advanced Edition, I still hadn't run into all of the vanilla events. I still haven't run into a few (namely the crystal sector ones, which if you buy the game, you'll learn to hate the elusiveness of), never mind all of the ones AE added.
A fair splash of the events are neutral. A small selection of them are outright-beneficial (sometimes if you're
lucky, and the gods smile on you, you can even find a random weapon floating around in space, but don't count on it). A lot of them are hostile encounters. What's a wonderful touch are the "blue options" that can show up if you meet certain requirements. Have some powerful weapons and a pirate is trying to extort you? Flash them at him and make him turn tail without a fight. Unsure if an empty station is free loot or a dangerous trap? Use your advanced scanners to scout the way instead of going in blind. Sometimes there will be multiple blue options, some with better results: The station with defective turrets would prefer you EMP'd them to repair them than blast them outright, afterall.
The combat itseslf is a beautiful blend of frustrating, rewarding and deep. On the surface, it's pause-based realtime combat. Your weapons charge up, fire at their targets, pop their shields, then continue on their merry way to their systems. Missiles require ammo and penetrate shields, beams can hit multiple systems but can't get through shields at all, lasers can usually fire multiple rounds, but have to hit each layer of shield before they can go through. But there are dozens of small ways that the system gets complicated: Boarding the ship (or using mind control systems) can have fights breaking out between crew even as the lasers and missiles are flying. If you're confident in your shield-operator's skills, you can drop the shields to let a single laser get through to give them time to recharge and stop the more-devestating beam weapon. Light a fire in their hold and keep them occupied, and you could starve them of oxygen and pick their intact ship clean, netting better loot than if you destroyed it completely. Combined with environmental hazards like asteroid belts and solar flares, you'll eventually come to the point where you're deciding if it's worth sticking around to fight, or if maybe you should jump out and leave the crew that boarded the enemy ship behind.
The combat also relies on a power-to-systems setup that will quickly make you feel like Captain Picard (presumably, I never watched much Star Trek). Systems have a maximum power capacity, but so does your reactor. An oft-overlooked mechanic in the game is that the difficulty is scaled based on your reactor's total power output, rather than your system strength. Which is to say: You're meant to be unable to play the game with full power to all systems (save for towards the very end). Do you push more power into your shields, forcing you to deactivate one of your lasers? Or do you maximize power to your engines, in the hopes of dodging their intimidating missiles? Maybe you're better off battering down their shields and taking out their systems before they can retaliate. In practice, you'll have to use a mixture of all of these if you want to make it to fight the rebel flagship at the end (and good luck once you get there, for the record).
There's a pretty wide variety of ships in the game, too. Advanced Edition changed the unlock system to be slightly more forgiving, by beating the game with one ship you unlock the next one (which isn't necessarily an easy task), you can also unlock them with specific event-based quests (which was previously the only method, and is also not an easy task). The game does a good job of making each ship feel unique. They each start with varied system capacities, weapon/drone layouts and crew, and though they can (and depending on RNG, will) fill the role of nearly any form of ship, they each tailor  themselves to a specific style of play. The mantis ships are all clearly designed for a boarding approach over weapons, whereas the engi ships are meant to focus primarily on drones. The federation cruiser soaks up punishment until it can unleash its artillery beam and annihilate the enemy, and so on. The different races/crew each have specific benefits (even humans, the normally boring-template race, get a bonus in that they learn skills faster), and though you may start up with a sparse selection, you can theoretically attain any crew on any ship (though some are harder to get than others, such as the elusive Lanius).
Because of the random nature of the game, sometimes the game will throw up moments that can make you tear your hair out, an hourlong run ended because of an opponent whose shields you couldn't quite break through who wore you down before you realized you should've jumped away, or a fire breaking out in your engine (or life support) room from a missile battery that refused to let up for just a few seconds. There's a reason that until AE, the game only had "Easy" and "Normal" difficulties.
But similarly, the random nature of the game can make it
when you overcome ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t odds and emerge victorious despite everything that stood in your way. Two sectors without a chance to repair, a dozen fights with automated scouts that dropped next to nothing for loot, slugmen trying to swindle you out of your hard-won scrap and trying to burn your crew alive for saying no? It's all just a day in the life of a Federation pilot on the run from rebel scum.

Whenever I see a game published by "Dagestan Technology", two things come to mind:
1) A clever, low-budget idea, marred by
2) Shoddy execution.
I was actually going to give this game a "mild thumbs up but only for $1 or less" until the moment I lost the game. This is a sort of "Choose Your Own Adventure" set in a 3-man rocket stranded in space, in which the three inhabitants of the craft move around, fiddle with various systems, sleep, eat, and (infrequently) come to you, the ship's computer, for advice regarding a problem, or psychological issue they're having.
This is a "Play once" game that lasts about 30 minutes; although you could play through again, the nature of the major choices makes it unlikely you would do so. The writing is uniformly trite and unintentionally hilarious at times because of the hackneyed translations (hint to developers, always have translations done by a native of the language, who knows YOUR language as a second language). My two favorite lines:
- "Jackie, it is the First Contact!"
- "Please don't throw me out of sluice!" (Sluice = Airlock).
The reason I'm giving the game a negative review is that, towards the end, I was presented with information that would require a major, difficult decision, but was not asked to make the decision immediately. Rather than waiting hours in real time for the ship to get to its destination, I took advantage of the time-forwarding feature. Did I drop to real time at the moment I would need to make this difficult decision? No. Time forwarding shot me right past it, and into a 30-second window in which I could only watch helplessly as I lost the game.
I remember a saying from my Army days, though not the exact quote, which went something like this: Why do 90% of the work and fail because you quit early, when you could do that extra 10% and succeed? That's my impression of this game: development stopped at 90% effort and resulted in an unfulfilling game experience, when finishing the job with that extra 10% effort could have resulted in a cute little casual game.

Space Incident has you playing as a damaged rocket AI who just starts becoming operational again after a huge system failure on your ship that leaves almost everything in critical condition. You successfully locate the two crew members you have on board and one drifter that stowed away in your escape pod when it was back on earth who is interested in discovering extraterrestrial life. Through conversations with the crew, you must get your ship repaired, deal with the alien threat and get the crew back home safely.
Now, I want to say here, this concept sounds really good and would seem pretty interesting for a game. However, there are a few key parts in which the game falls flat with its gameplay.
Firstly, the game plays entirely through conversations that you have with your crew members, which leaves gameplay being restrictive, but that wouldn't really matter if the conversations you were having with your crew were interesting, which they aren't. The game promotes its self as "an interactive story" but the story is really uninteresting, and presents its self as not really knowing what it wants to be. There are stats for your crew where you need to manage food, water, health, and panic, but you're actually out of control of 3/4 of those, because the crew go get food and water of their own volition, they lose health from oxygen loss which you don't' really have much of a say in besides for one critical dialogue set that you have to follow to prevent the loss of oxygen. The only aspect that you have control over which is one of the good things I'll give the game is the control that you have over the panic state of your crew and this is where the dialogue-driven gameplay really shines in the game. Depending on things that you tell the crew it can either lower or increase their panic state, and if you put them into too much panic, this could result in them committing suicide.
One fault, going back to the promotion of it is an "interactive story" is that the player doesn't really have too much interaction and doesn't have too much to do themselves to control how the story plays out. There are multiple dialogue choices within the game, but only two sets have any real critical impact on the endings. The endings of which really depend on which crew members come back to earth with you and if you still have the escape pod attached by the end of it, but again, these two things can be determined through two sets of dialogue which controls both of them, and that's it. Meaning out of a good 20 different dialogue sets in which multiple choice is given to you, only two have a critical impact.
Additionally, the game is short, which again wouldn't matter if the game had a story worth telling, but once again, it doesn't. The game doesn't have you really care much about the crew members, you don't get to know them personally, the only thing that you see them doing is them fixing a spaceship and that's it, no connection is formed between you and the crew.
Also, I want to point out, despite the game being short, there are a number of grammatical errors in the text, with things such as there being no apostrophes in the game and there also being some words misspelled.
The gameplay does have potential and elements of enjoyability with the panic meter monitoring and the multiple choice dialogue which can seem cool at a glance, but a lot of this stuff is not built upon and under delivers to make it uninteresting to go through, and if you're making an interactive story, making your story uninteresting is a huge problem.
Probably what this game does best is the graphics and sound. The mesh of pixel art and a gritty overlayer really serves the game well to make it present it's self visually well. The talking heads that come up in dialogue are presented as if the characters are on the other side of a computer monitor, and it's little touches like that that do make me like the game's style of presentation.
The soundtrack is also pretty good. It's got this warped-esque music playing over the top of the game that is typical of space-themed games. I'm not necessarily saying that in a bad way, I'm saying that the music is fitting of the game and is pleasant to listen to.
As I stated earlier, the game is really short, and can possibly be completed in 30 minutes. However, the game does offer replayability with its endings and tries to get the player to figure out if they can make it back to Earth with their crew and shuttle intact, and also offers additional achievements for players that are willing to try and obtain all of the endings, but there are 11 different endings that you can get.
Space Incident is a game that has a lot of potential going for it, however, a lot of that potential is let down and is underdelivering in a lot of areas. While the game's graphics and sound are great alongside with offering replayability, it doesn't really seem enough to carry the game onwards from how flawed the gameplay is.
Pros
+ Good concept
+ Graphics
+ Sound/Music
+ Replayability
Cons
- Gameplay is heavily flawed
- Dialogue choices don't really matter
- Short (excluding replays)
- Underdeveloped
Final verdict: 4/10

So I don't know why there are so many reviews from people who have played this game for less than an hour and given it a negative review.  Yea, there are some things that are a little clunky here or need fine tuning there, but this game is insanely fun and has a lot of potential (especially considering that it's only about 30% complete).  Since I'm not playing this game on a potato like so many other reviewers, I will attempt to fill in the gaps beyond "I couldn't run it" or "I don't like EA games" which, while valid, don't actually do anything to REVIEW the game.
Graphics:  Good, but need optimization.  I have a pretty beefy computer and had to turn a few settings down to keep it above 30 fps.  Outside of that, these are on par with Ark - if you've ever played it.
Gameplay: A few minor issues here, likely from features that aren't fully developed, but I have yet to run into anything game-breaking.  Some of the creatures get stuck, and occasionally you get jumped by a panther or something which can kill you pretty quick (though I think this is intended and you can snare them with an item craftable pretty early on, effectively neutering them unless they ambush you).
The game system overall is designed very nicely, there are some minor resemblances to Ark (since they use the same engine). The leveling and crafting system is quite intuitive (unlike Ark) and you dont have to spend time trying to plan what skills you're going to not invest points into.  You learn new skills and recipes by doing things related to the task, rather than by leveling and spending accumulated points, though you do still get stat points to raise your health, stamina, mana etc. on level up.
Each starting area has a town with it's own unique look (buildings, flora/fauna, etc.) and has npcs you can buy and sell items to and invest money should you choose to do so.  There are guards which will kill you if you attack a citizen, but they will also kill any monsters that chase you back to the gates.
There also appears to be plans for player housing, a market system, and even the ability to become the freaking KING of the starting town for your race (which seems interesting for MP).  You start the game off with a bunch of quests to help you get oriented, and there are more when the starter quest line is done to help you level up a bit.  There are a plethora of monsters (the bestiary has over 50, and I think there are way more than what you'll see in the bestiary actually in the game), biomes, POIs, and more to explore as well (most of which I've still yet to uncover even after 60+ hours of gameplay at the time of writing this review).
So...tl;dr - this game is a lot of fun and has a lot of potential.  Ignore the reviews from idiots who didn't even get past the loading screen and actually try it yourself or watch some gameplay videos before forming an opinion.

Low and behold, he did not! He turned to me and started barking. Then, he ran off. I continued to muttle around on my own as a little baby badger. After a short time, the fox returned to my location, barked at me again, and ran off. This time I followed. He'd occasionally take breaks to let my little legs catch up to where he was. Eventually, we encountered a large group of other animals. Wave and happy emotes all around! We ventured on with them on a hunt for big rocks to bark, meow, squak, croak, etc. at until they broke. Some stones only resonated to the sound of certain animals. When there were no such animals in the group, cry emotes were abound. Some of the animals would have to go hibernate. Emote goodbye, emote cry, you feel like you lost someone dear. But you continue venturing with the group that's left because you know there are still stones out there to bark at!

This game is fantastic. If you're a fan of retro games, this one nails it. The challenge level is perfect for a casual playthrough, but going for the achievements really amps it up. I've had the game for about 24 hours now, and I've beaten it five times going back to finish all of the achievements. My arm is numb from mashing the fire button at the last boss over and over again with different handicaps, and it was fun the entire way through.
For it's length, the game has a good amount of items and power-ups that keep you excited about exploring. There's a decent variety of enemies that are consistently satisfying to kill because of those crunchy retro sound effects. I haven't even checked out the level editor or custom maps yet, but the ability to create and play as custom characters is such a fun touch. Even though I never found beating the game multiple times tedious, it was that much more interesting going through each time with a different character that I already like from other games. My last run was for the no deaths, healing or saving achievement, and I did it with Donkey Kong, because coconut gun hurt. It was great.
I can only think of three minor things to complain about. One, the enemies that move horizontally and shoot up and down. Sometimes they were pretty much impossible to get through without taking at least one hit. Not a big deal though. Two, enemies stuck in walls at bad spots for you, and not having a consistent way to kill them. Again, not a big deal, and reloading the room could sometimes fix both of those issues. Three, the speed upgrade should have just been the default. I mean, you can get it within 16 seconds of starting the game, but with all the integrated speed running incentives and leaderboards and whatnot, I was restarting runs a lot when I first started, and this was the only thing that I felt was a weird choice. Just makes each restart a bit slower, and you're pretty much required to go get it immediately.
But who even cares, game is great. I was fully sucked in by its charm and I'm honestly disappointed that I'm already finished. I know that this game was a prequel to Ghost 1.0, which I will probably have to check out now, but I'd really love to see more of this style. Cannot recommend it enough. Beyond worth the $2.

It's a Mini-Metroidvania as advertised. While it follows the pattern of wandering around a map collecting power-ups, there's a special emphasis on buying power-ups as well. While I did not buy every one available, I still had to grind a little bit to get the ones I wanted, along with the ones I really needed. The game lets you save on every screen if you've cleared all the enemies, so save scumming is a natural strategy to go along with its clunky retro mechanics.
For this kind of simple display of Metroidvania tropes, I prefer something like K.O.L.M or Dungeon of Zolthan, but this was a fun little diversion nevertheless. I clocked in about 2 hours for completion.
If you've played Ghost, there's a cute little comic strip before and after you beat the game that you might enjoy. But if you were expecting something profound out of this "prequel" you're not going to find it.
If you're into streaming games, this has a few options that are intended to enhance that purpose. You'll also get a lot more out of this game if you enjoy hunting for achievements, or modded content.

I've always loved the concept of space combat: massive laser blasts arcing out across the void, torpedo salvos inextricably advancing onwards their targets, individual fighter pilots twisting and dogfighting across the void... just great stuff.
But forget the huge library of science and hard sci-fi that shows that space combat would be nothing like the ship-to-ship broadsides popularly depicted in the majority of modern sci-fi space battles like Star Wars, and the gameplay of BFG: Armada. Fighting across the real distances of space would be done in a timespace I can't define, because I don't know the word for it, but it's way less than milliseconds, as everything is essentially moving at or near the speed of light.
But forget that.
BFG: Armada largely ports the tabletop version of Games Workshop's side game, Battlefleet Gothic, which involves large sci-fi representations of essentially World War 2 ship to ship battles with the flavor of interstellar combat in the 41st millennium. That means you're are controlling your ships in broadside based combat (or frontal based, if you are Eldar or Orks), seeking to establish the best angles of attack from slow moving, multi-million ton spaceships with massive salvo's of ordinance, torpedo's, lances, and small attack craft to attack the enemy.
Think Battlestar Galactica, with evil and the warp and stupid space elves (♥♥♥♥ the Eldar, 40kplayer here) all vying to keep you (at least in the campaign) from securing the Gothic Sector from Abaddon’s 13th Crusade. If you are familiar with 40k lore, this is big time, as you get to fight the "current" wars of the "current" 40k timeline aka where the rulebooks stopped us in the lore.
To that end, the voice acting is great, and I enjoyed fighting through the campaign. It's a tad slow action, although a million things are happening a minute so you will likely spend most of your time in cognitor mode anyway (aka slow mo from any of the Total War series battles), but at the height of battles you will still find yourself rushing to complete all your intended orders to your ships. Thankfully, there's the ability to automate all of the special abilities your ships take, but besides depending on the AI to maintain pre-set engagement distances, you will and will want to manage the paths your ships take through the interstellar battlefield to allow them to use their pre-approved abilities.
If you like 40k, or enjoy the strategy of "naval" combat from the newer Total War series games, but way more complex, you will enjoy this game.

As it stands, this game is a monstrous disappointment. I'll edit the review in a few months if the devs get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together by then. I'm not going to hold my breath, though.
- the Admiral system is a nice quirk in the campaign, it can even be fun in skirmish/MP fights, BUT it becomes an unnecessary and annoying restriction when that is the only way you can play (there's no way to get around it and play a custom game with whatever ships you want to throw together).
- the addition of 'ship abilities' to personalise and specialise ships was a very nice idea which I gladly approved off when I first learned of it in beta. As it stands, though, it's been so horribly implemented the game feels more like DotA than an actual strategy game in space. Once you're past the low levels with your Admiral, you begin facign bomb & taunt spams in almost every fight. This is about as fun as passing a kidney stone the size of a football, coated in chilli sauce and ground glass. Instead of having a game focused on maneuver, it's devolved into a clickfest. Especially when you consider that the maximum points level is 700, with most games being at 4-600 points (that's 3-4 cruisers per side - SUCH FLEET< WOW).
- for some inexplicable reason the devs refuse input from the community, all the while saying how they love to communicate with us. Escorts are single ships (not squadroned) and without any limit. They gave almost all ships 5k detection range, while almost all the weapons in the game have 6k range, many of them going out to 15k (that's 2 and a half times their sight range). There is one upgrade that increases detection by 2.5k, but taking that you're gimped compared to close-range fighters who just take weapon upgrades to kill you even faster. Critical systems can be critted just like in the bgame (yay!) but for some unknown reason they can't be repaired. At all. Ever. So if you get your engines critted at the start fo the game, that's it, that ship will be a slow-as-molasses brick for the rest of the fight.
- balance is crap. Eldar are the biggest community pet peeve, with their ungodly powerful pulsars in the right hands, but at the same time all their other weapons are garbage. The latest patch, called a 'major update' by the devs, has had no balance changes at all. I suspect the devs are too stubborn to let go of their special snowflake ideas such as pulsars being an activated ability rather than a regular weapon and are thus stuck in how to balance it to be good in the hands of most players rather than broken in the hands of some.
- also regarding balance: all the ship upgrades, favours and skills increase ship points cost by exactly ZERO. So a ship with a whole bunch of upgrades, skills and favours will cost the enemy just as much as your freshly acquired version despite the fact that it will easily mop the floor with you.
On the positive side: the campaign, as much as I've played, seems nice and fun. Most folks I've talked to were happy with that, at least. The music is nice (but nothing extraordinary) and the graphics, as can be seen in the screenshots, are absolutely gorgeous. The UI looks good, though it works kinda clunkily, and the devs do love the universe, which can be seen even in the upgrade names and tooltips.
Frankly, my only sliver of hope is that some time in the next couple of years a good mod team will pick apart this game and do it right, otherwise it will be my biggest purchasing regret since Payday 2.
And unless they increase the size of fleets, this travesty should be called Battlepatrol Gothic: Squadron.

Well, now add a more assertive parkour system that feels even more free-flowing and fluid than one by ID software on the giant boat thing... sure it began with a B or something... and throw in all your classic gmaing Zed tropes and a sun drenched, middle-eastern locale and let your adrenaline start to buzz.
Seriously, the combat is brutal, especially at the beginning when you have all the combat stamina of a plague-riddled asthmatic with nary a gun to be seen (but there's, like a metric bum-tonne of NPCs lolly-gaggin' around and they're all like 'not givin' you nuthin'), but as you begin to survive the days and become more proficient throughout the nights, you begin to really feel your bad♥♥♥♥♥ness peak.  There's a very definite sense of achievement as you move around the city, un-fogging the map and saving the occasional red-shirt from an imminent, horrific and bloody demise, only to have the character NPCs dump you with all their tasks.
What really works here is the Co-op, especially with people that communicate, or better yet, a few like-minded friends - that's when this game really begins to shine through.  I'm not expecting much from the story, but then, this is a zombie horror flick: of course there's very little plot.
Asking for a plot from a zombie survival game is as pointless as asking a politician to revea; their megalomanical plans for world domination - it only turns up at the end when it's all doomed to failure and the locals have just gotten utterly sick all the same.
In short, I heartily recommend this gorgeous romp and plan on slapping more zombies in the face with a wide variety of blunt weapons for a while to come.

Dark and Light is great! If you have played ARK, then you will enjoy this game. It is very much an Alpha - NOT an early access. It is currently in the same stages that ARK was, early on in its development. So there are glitches that will get you killed and cause you to lose progress. That said, I think there are significantly fewer glitches than during ARK's development.
The game itself is great. Magic is fantastic and the taming is very satisfying. Skills are leveled through use and it still tickles me that you can be lower level than someone else, but have access to items that they don't, because of specialization. Everything is useful - you won't really run into a resource that doesn't get used in some way.  The map is stunningly beautiful. Everyone should see the map in epic settings at least once - even if it is only through singleplayer.
TLDR; If you enjoyed ARK, buy this game. Be prepared to report a good few glitches and bugs. If you can get this for $20 or less, you got a good deal. $30 is pushing it for current level of content.

Somewhere between Mars and Earth something has gone wrong and it's up to you to save the crew.

I finished this game for the first time in one hour. I think even less because it is possible I idled it for and half hour...But there is replayability. Let me start with the price: 6.99€ Is way to expensive. Most people will play it only once, maybe twice and it is just to short for such a price. Now for the game. You are in space and need to get to earth. You will control three characters. You control them by talking to them and making certain dialogue choices. Some choices will make characters die, and you can get achievements for getting to earth with certain characters alive and certain dead. You can even get to earth with nobody alive. And get a achievement for that. Do you listen to the characters or do you tell them to shut up and do their work. Do you send someone without knowledge to do a certain job? Will you get to earth with the crew alive and the space shuttle still hooked onto the rocket? Since a play true is only one hour, you can do different runs with different choices and "different" endings. The graphics are pixelated, nothing special and sound is nothing special either. Bottom line is that the asking price is to much for this game in my opinion and if you buy it at full price you probably will not be satisfied. I would not be satisfied since I maybe play it one more time and then I probably will not play it anymore soon.

Grom, leader of Clan Battlebeard; a warrior of unrivaled skill and valor. I set out on my journey from the dwarven homeland killing foul spiders and untrustworthy sheep.
Upon reaching the edge of some dark and undoubtedly UNHOLY wood(s?) I decided to make a hunting lodge for my clan. While doing so I saw a battleboar snorting a patch of swamp land, the sign of a true warrior pig; so I decided he must be mine. It was a fight for the ages, I punched my faithful hog into submission and then saddled him up. It was glorious.
We were only together for a short time, my battlehog and I; it started when the other boars saw my new friend "Grunt" and decided to attack him. Three on one, it was an uneven and dirty fight; those boars never stood a chance.
As I was congratulating Grunt a pair of Treants came near, now let me explain something about battlepigs and Treants; they don't like em. Grunt charged the massive elf-lovers while I ran in after trying to mount him to ride him to safety; but then it happened, I started to believe in Grunt. I watched as he battled the treemen, tearing into them as they knocked over the nearby trees, but finally with a crash one stomped Grunt into the ground as I cried out in anguish... mah pig was gone.

Extremely good fighting game. However please keep in mind that I prefer to play against AI and don't care about multiplayer with cheaters on pc or pianists on consoles. Good stuff in this game for me:
+ Solid mechanics where each fighter feels rather different and not just a variation of robotic movement like it feels for me in MK series
+ Good combo flow. Meaning that you don't need to memorize some weird directional dodging jumping all over the screen in order to do some weird teleportation jump like in other games. What I like in DOA5 - combos kinda grow up in your head as logical continuation of what your character is doing on a screen. I absolutely love this!
+ Very helpful feature of displaying combo list right there on the screen during fights and it changes depending on your input so if you have fast eye - you can hit up combos from there too
+ Very good looking ladies in both normal cloth and swim suits.
+ Rather fast paced combat.
+ Plenty of game modes
+ You do not feel that you control robots in there. Again - fluidity of animation and combos is amazing in my opinion. My other favourite fighting game is King of Fighters 13 and it has similar great rythm there.
+ Rather big story mode
+ It is free2play now from what I understand, so it shouldn't be a problem to pick this game and give it a try
+ Very good looking feature of sweat and dirt! That's very arou... exciting.

Meadow is an absolutely beautiful game where you can play as an animal and run around collecting things with friends, and you can also meet NEW friends on this game! I saw this game on Xbox Live about 7 or so years ago before posting this review. It looked interesting when I played it, and I remember always wanting to do a full playthrough. After a long time, I finally did.
This is a puzzle game, and it's a very unique one. Rather than simply going through a maze a certain way or doing things in a certain order, you reverse time and manipulate objects around you. Certain objects have certain characteristics, like some objects *only* move if you move as well, or some objects are unaffected by time reversal.
It's a pretty cool game with a pretty good storyline that's kind of a spin-off of Mario, with you chasing a princess to other castles/fortresses, etc. Maybe not worth $15 if puzzle games aren't your thing, but still worth a playthrough.
